en: The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara: The Section on Fixed Times (Niyatakālakāṇḍa)
Salutation to him by whom,
through daily rites such as bathing in the waters of the celestial river and through sacrifices— performances that cast away the Kali age— the highest exaltation was attained.
That Dharmma, who has forgotten the pain of separation from his beloved Lakṣmīdhara, composes this third section for the delight of the virtuous, which is to be observed at a fixed time.
The vow consists of cleaning the teeth, morning bathing, the ritual procedure for bathing, recitation (*japa*),
libations (*tarpaṇa*), and thereafter the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) beginning with the *vaiśvadeva*.

The meal is accompanied by *pallavas*; whatever ritual duty follows the meal is likewise with *pallavas*. The nocturnal ritual is with *pallavas*, and immediately thereafter is the ritual for the festival day (*parva*).
The duties pertaining to the lunar days (tithis), the procedure for offering lamps in the wilderness,
service to cows, the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga), and the rules for listening to the Purāṇas.
Thus, by the one named Lakṣmīdhara, possessed of pure intellect,
are described the fourteen sections in this section on the obligatory daily rites.
[3] Now, the skilled person should attend to those duties that are fixed by time.
The ritual action has been declared, but the sequence was not stated, nor indeed the time;
therefore, Dakṣa himself spoke for the benefit of the twice-born.
I shall fully explain everything that must be performed day by day by a twice-born man after rising in the morning, which is for the benefit of the twice-born.
From sunrise until sunset, a Brahmin should not remain idle,
being engaged in obligatory rites, occasional rites, and other blameless optional rites.
If a twice-born man abandons his own duty and performs something else,
whether out of ignorance or greed, he becomes fallen by that which has been forsaken.
The duty pertaining to him is prescribed for the first part of the day,
as well as for the second, third, fourth, and fifth parts.
In the sixth, seventh, and eighth divisions respectively,
I shall now explain in their entirety whatever actions are to be performed in each of these sections.

[4] "Action" (*karman*) has been described by Manu and others, but its sequence and timing have not been stated. For that very reason, Dakṣa, for the benefit of the twice-born (*dvija*), has explained both of these. Here, "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) refers to one who is devoid of activities permitted by the scriptures. "By others that are not censured" means by those that are not prohibited and have visible purposes. "One's own duty" (*svakam karma*) refers to that which is prescribed for one’s own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). "Having abandoned" means having relinquished it for a long time. The word "day" (*divasa*) here refers to the period of time beginning from dawn until the end of evening, through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that does not abandon its primary meaning; for Dakṣa himself, after mentioning "of the day," describes the duties starting from the time of dawn up to the end of evening.
Manu [4.93]: Having risen, performed the necessary duties, and accomplished purification, he should remain concentrated,
standing while reciting the morning twilight prayer for a long time, and likewise at its proper time, the evening one.

[5] "Necessary" refers to the voiding of urine and feces. "Composed" means with a restrained mind. "The latter" refers to the evening twilight (*saṃdhyā*). "For a long time" means even after the rising of the stars. And this applies to one who maintains no sacred fire (*niragni*); for one who maintains the fire (*sāgni*), the twilight rite is completed by the procedure for the oblation (*homa*) before the rising of the stars.
Regarding the cleaning of the teeth, Yājñavalkya [1.98] states:
"Having attended to the needs of the body, the twice-born man who has performed the rules for purification..."
One should perform the morning twilight devotion preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Dakṣa says:
When the time of dawn has arrived, having performed purification according to the rules,
one should then perform a bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.

The "time of dawn" (*uṣaḥkāla*) is the period characterized by a slight manifestation of light in the directions prior to the time indicated by the reddening of the quarters. "According to the rule" (*yathārthavat*) means according to the prescribed number of foot-washings and the count of earth, water, and so forth. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: "When the mouth is stale, a man is perpetually impure."
Therefore, with every effort, one should consume the tooth-cleansing twig.

[7] “Impure” means unclean. The term “should chew” (*bhakṣayet*) is a figurative expression based on its connection with the teeth, intended to convey the ritual requirement of chewing that includes the preliminary and subsequent rinsing of the mouth. Regarding this, Yama says:
Of the *āmra*, *plakṣa*, *bilva*, *apāmārga*, and *śirīṣa*...
Having risen in the morning and remaining silent, one should chew the tooth-stick.
The *paunāla* is the *āmrātaka* tree;

[also] the *hārīta*. At the proper time, one should avoid the *palāśa*, *kovidāra*, *śleṣmātaka*, *tilvaka*, *śāka*, *vṛkṣa*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *śikhaṇḍī* bamboos. Some say that the *plakṣa*, *māṣaka*, *badarī*, *karañja*, *śamī*, and *śāka* trees are always suitable. Others say that the *dadhittha*, *harītakī*, *karṇaśāla*, and *āmalaka* are also suitable. One should chew a tooth-stick made from any one of the *bilva*, *khadira*, *āmra*, *paunāla*, *śirīṣa*, or *apāmārga*—provided it is not fresh, not too dry, not too thick, with its tip crushed, and free of knots at the base—facing north, remaining silent, and sitting down.

[8] “At the proper time” means at dawn. “Kovidāra” is a white-flowered tree resembling *kāñcanāra*. “Śleṣmātaka” is the *bahuvāra* tree. “Tilvaka” is the *cillaka*. “Śākavṛkṣa” is well known in the world as the *śākavaṇa*. “Nirguṇḍī” is the *mayūraśikhā* or *sinduvāra*. “Śikhaṇḍī” is that which is named after the peacock (*śikhaṇḍin*); others say it is a thorny shrub. “Dadhittha” is the *kapittha*. “Śāla” is the *śaṅku* tree. Regarding both “some” and “others,” the word “excluding” (*varjayitvā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Here, “fresh” (*ārdra*) means recently cut; anything other than that is “not fresh. Because of the expression “not too dry” and because washing is prescribed, mere freshness is necessarily required. “With its tip crushed” means with its tip slightly pulverized. “Without a knot near the lip” (*anauṣṭhagranthi*) means that in which there is no knot in the vicinity of the lip.

The tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) should not be made from *pālāśa* wood; nor from *śleṣmāntaka*, *ariṣṭaka*, *vibhītaka*, *dhava*, or *dhanvana*; nor from *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, *pippala*, *iṅguda*, *guggulu*; nor from *bandhūka*, *nirguṇḍī*, *śigru*, *tilvaka*, or *tinduka*; nor from *pāribhadra*, *āmlikā*, *mocaka*, *śālmalī*, or *śaṇa*. It should not be sweet, nor sour, nor dried at the top, nor excessively hollow, nor foul-smelling, nor slimy. One should not face the south or west while eating it; rather, one should eat facing north or east. [The wood should be] from any one of the following: *vaṭa*, *āsana*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *karavīra*, *sarja*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *kakubha*, or *bilva*. It should be astringent, pungent, or bitter.
Having its thickness equal to the tip of the little finger, provided with a brush, and twelve finger-breadths in length,
one should eat the tooth-stick in the morning after having eaten [other food], remaining silent.

“*Ariṣṭaka*” here is the *rīṭhā* tree; “*dhanvana*” is well known as *dhāmiṇa*; “*pīlu*” is the *guḍaphala*, which is well known in the western regions as *pīlu*; “*iṅguda*” is the thorny tree *iṅguvāka*; “*pāribhadra*” is well known as *phalahaṭṭa*; “*amlīkā*” is *tintilī*; “*ūrdhvaśuṣka*” means dried while still on the tree; “*sasuṣira*” means possessing holes; “*asana*” is well known as *āsana*; “*arimeda*” is *viṭkhādira*; “*mālatī*” is *jātī*; “*kāṣāya*” means bitter or pungent. Other [trees] that are neither prescribed nor prohibited should also be understood. “*Sakūrca*” means having a tufted tip. By the phrase “and having eaten in the morning,” it is stated that the brushing of teeth mentioned there is to be performed at two times of day.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* (1.7.138–140) states:
"The tooth-stick prescribed by Nārada and others should be made of wood, eight finger-breadths long, unsplit, with its bark intact; one should clean the teeth with its tip."
Having risen, washed his eyes, become pure, and composed himself,
he should rinse his teeth with the mantra after reciting it over them.
O Lord of the Forest, bestow upon us through this food long life, strength, fame, luster, offspring, cattle, and wealth, as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and retentive memory.

“Nāradādyuktavārkṣeyam” means produced from a tree as prescribed in the *Śikṣās* of Nārada and others. Accordingly, the *Nārada-śikṣā* states: “Having risen in the morning with speech restrained, one should consume a tooth-cleansing twig (*dantadhāvana*) made from mango, *punnāga*, *bilva*, *apāmārga*, or *śirīṣa*.”
"The *khadira*, the *karañja*, the *karavīra*, and the *kadamba*—
all thorny trees are meritorious, as are those that exude milky sap and are renowned.
Regarding the phrase "having recited the mantra," the meaning is that one should consume the tooth-stick after having consecrated it with the mantra.
Yama says: One who desires prosperity and is self-possessed should always avoid using a seat, a bed, a vehicle, sandals, or a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood.
One should not make sandals, a footstool, a seat, a bed, a vehicle, or a tooth-cleansing stick out of *pālāśa* wood. "Vehicle" refers to a cart and the like. [12] Uśanas says:
One should not clean one's teeth with the fingers.
Viṣṇu [61.17]: Having washed and broken it, one should carefully discard it in a clean place;
and on the new moon day, one should by no means consume a tooth-stick.
In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* (58.46–51):
"A man whose mouth is stale remains perpetually impure;
therefore, he should chew a tooth-stick, whether dry or moist."
The Khadira, the Kadamba, the Karañja, and likewise the Vaṭa;
the Tintilī, the Veṇupṛṣṭha, and similarly the two Āmranibhas.
Apāmārga, bilva, arka, and likewise udumbara—
these are declared to be recommended for the practice of cleaning the teeth.
I shall describe, in brief, the excellence of the tooth-stick:
all thorny trees are meritorious, and those with milky sap are glorious.
Its measurement here is said to be eight finger-breadths; or else, one should clean the teeth with a twig of that size, measuring a span.
[13] O virtuous ones, on the first, the new moon, the sixth, and the ninth days as well,
the contact of a tooth-stick with the teeth burns the family unto the seventh generation.
If tooth-sticks are unavailable or if the day is one on which they are prohibited,
purification of the mouth is prescribed by means of twelve mouthfuls of water.

“Veṇupṛṣṭham” refers to the inner bark of the bamboo. By this, it should be understood that Hārīta’s statement, “excluding bamboo,” pertains to other parts of the bamboo. Because of the mention [in Hārīta] that it may be “either dry or moist,” the prohibition of the dry applies; however, because of Viṣṇu’s statement, “not one that is dry at the top,” it should be understood that the prohibition concerns that which is dry at the upper end. In the Mahābhārata: One should always avoid those tooth-sticks that are forbidden.
One should consume those things permitted by the scriptures, and one should also avoid them on the sacred festival days (parvan).

Regarding the phrase "on the festival days" (*parvasu*): the festival days here are as follows—"The fourteenth and the eighth day, as well as the new moon and the full moon; these, O King of kings, are the festival days, as is the transit of the sun."
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.11.118]. Likewise:
"Having thoroughly washed his hands, feet, and face, being well-composed..."
Then, having raised the right arm and placed it between the knees;
One should use for cleaning the teeth a twig that is bitter, astringent, pungent, fragrant, and thorny, or one derived from milky trees or shrubs.

One should avoid leaves that are unknown, those with upward-drying veins, those that are split, those deprived of their bark, those with knotted tips, as well as those of the *pālāśa* and *śāṃśapa* trees.
A man, sitting facing east and maintaining silence, should eat [the tooth-stick] which is straight, a span in length, and undamaged by insects or fire.
Having rinsed it, one should discard the tooth-stick in a clean place;
when it falls properly facing toward oneself, one obtains the desired food.

“Having raised the right arm”—the meaning is, having arranged the sacred thread (*upavīta*) over the left shoulder. “Shrubs” (*gulmāḥ*) refers to jasmine and other such plants that do not grow on trunks. “Śāṃśapa” means produced from the *śiṃśapā* tree. In this context, although the specific rule regarding the particular types of tooth-sticks for the purpose of cleansing the teeth—which brings about purity—has already excluded other woods by its restrictive injunction, the subsequent prohibition is intended to exclude their use even as substitutes when the primary items are unavailable. As for that which is both prescribed and prohibited, because it is slightly inferior to that which is purely prescribed due to its connection with a prohibition, it may be employed when the purely prescribed item is unavailable. Even in the absence of that, one should employ what is neither prescribed nor prohibited. However, that which is strictly prohibited must never be used. In that case, the purification of the mouth must be accomplished by exactly twelve mouthfuls of water.

Hārīta states: One should chew a tooth-stick that is not bitter (*avirakta*) and has been washed with water, discarding it in a secluded place; then, having bathed, being restrained in speech, pure, and wearing unwashed white garments, one should perform the rites for the *agnihotra* and other deities.

[16] “Not bitter” means succulent. “Washed with water” means rinsed. “For the sake of the *agnihotra* and other deities” refers to the *agnihotra* and so forth, as well as the rites for the deities, such as the worship of the gods.
Thus ends the section on the cleaning of the teeth in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, regarding the morning bath (*prātaḥsnāna*), Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [1.7.137]:
Just as during the day, so too every morning, one who is not ill should bathe regularly;
having cleansed his teeth at a river or similar place, or at home, if it be there, he should do so without reciting mantras.
Likewise: "Because the time for the fire-oblation is short and the ritual of bathing is extensive, one should not shorten the morning bath; for the omission of the oblation is censured."

Regarding the phrase “*yathāhani*”: the meaning is that one should perform the midday bath with the same procedure (*yathākṛtyatayā*)—such as the touching of clay (*mṛdālambha*) and so forth—as one does during the day; that is, exactly as one does in the morning. Because of the mention of “*anāturaḥ*” (not ill), one who is ill is exempt from the impurity caused by bathing; having attained purity through cleansing and other means, he should perform the *saṃdhyā*. Brushing the teeth is an additional requirement in the morning. Regarding “*gehe cet*”: if one performs that morning bath at home due to some cause, then one should carry it out devoid of the mantras that are ancillary to the bath; the meaning is that one should perform it in an abbreviated manner. This abbreviation is of the form described by Yogiyājñavalkya: “the preparation of the sacred site (*tīrthaparikalpana*), the consecration of the water (*jalābhimantraṇa*), sipping water (*ācamana*), sprinkling (*mārjana*), and the bath within the water (*antarjalasnāna*) and so forth, performed three times with the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Such is the nature of the abbreviation.
The body is extremely impure, endowed with nine openings; it flows [with impurities] day and night. Morning bathing is the means of purification.
The sense faculties of one who is fast asleep become moist and leak;
the limbs, both superior and inferior, sink into a state of uniformity.

[19] Likewise: A man who has risen from his bed, covered with saliva and sweat, should not perform any ritual action whatsoever, such as recitation (*japa*) or fire-oblation (*homa*), without having first bathed.
They praise the morning bath as auspicious, bringing both visible and invisible benefits;
one who bathes in the morning, being pure in soul, is worthy of performing all [rites] such as recitation (*japa*) and the like.

“They attain equality”: even the superior parts, such as the eyes and so forth, become equal to the inferior parts due to contact with moisture. The reason for the rule “one should not perform [rites] without having bathed” is given as: “covered with saliva and sweat”; the word *yataḥ* (since) is to be understood as the ellipsis. “It effects the seen and the unseen”: the seen is the purification of the body through the removal of impurities; the unseen is the destruction of sin by virtue of its being a daily obligation (*nitya*). Viṣṇu [64.40–42]:
“One who has bathed becomes entitled to perform rites for the gods and for the ancestors.”
[20] Likewise, regarding purificatory rites, the recitation of mantras, and giving as enjoined by the rules;
It is the firm conviction that misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams,
and evil thoughts perish for one who has been consecrated with even a mere drop of this water.
Indeed, one who bathes daily does not behold the suffering of the torments of Yama;
even those people who are doers of evil are purified by daily bathing.

*Kālakarṇī* is the daughter of the *rākṣasa* Duḥsaha. *Durvicintitam* means thought of as inauspicious. *Amātreṇa* means whether it has been drawn up or not drawn up; such is the meaning. *Dhāraṇā* means a firm resolve. *Yāmyam* means pertaining to the world of Yama. Dakṣa says: "The twilight bath [should be performed] with the end of a *ṛc* verse at midday, and then again."
That Brāhmaṇa, especially, who does not worship the two twilights, is indeed a Śūdra while still alive;
after death, he is born as a dog.
[21] Viṣṇu [90.29]: He who desires vast enjoyments comparable to the moon, the sun,
and the planets should always bathe in the morning during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna.
Yama says: One who constantly bathes at dawn during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna,
having duly honored the gods and the ancestors, is liberated from all sins.
Viṣṇu [89.1–4]: The propitiation of the gods and ancestors through libations and other rites;

the month of Kārtika has Agni as its presiding deity, and Agni is the mouth of all the gods. Therefore, one who bathes outside during Kārtika, is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī, and eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) even once, becomes purified from the sins committed throughout the year.
One who bathes daily throughout the entire month of Kārttika, with senses subdued, reciting prayers,
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and remaining tranquil, is liberated from all sins.

“*Japet*”: at a time free from other necessary duties. “*Haviṣyam*” (food fit for an oblation): as indicated by such statements as “among *haviṣya* foods, barley is foremost. [22] According to the *Viṣṇusmṛti*, because this occurs after the section on ritual bathing (*snānaprakaraṇa*), it constitutes a separate topic based on the principle of a distinct context (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇanyāya*). Here, the word “morning” (*prātaḥ*) refers to the time preceding sunrise; for according to the statement of Viṣṇu [64.9], “One who bathes in the morning should bathe after observing the eastern direction seized by the rays of the dawn,” that very time is prescribed for all morning baths. As for the statement in the *Matsyapurāṇa* and other texts that “the morning consists of three *muhūrtas*,” that refers specifically to the context of *śrāddha*. Likewise, the practice of bathing outdoors in the month of Kārtika is also optional (*kāmya*). By this, it follows that women and Śūdras also possess the qualification [to perform this]. Thus, bathing outdoors in Kārtika at a time other than the morning is also another optional form of bathing, by that same reasoning.

Āpastamba [1.30.6–9]: Now, the observances of a *snātaka*. He should practice exiting and entering the village by the eastern side, or by the northern side. During the two twilights, he should sit outside the village and remain silent. In case of a conflict, that which is characterized by the *Śruti* is more authoritative. "He should practice" means he should act in such a way that the habituation to it is accomplished. "In case of a conflict" refers to a contradiction with Vedic rites such as the *homa* sacrifice; in such a case, that which is characterized by the *Śruti*—namely, what is prescribed by the *Śruti* itself—is more authoritative for performance than that which is prescribed by the *Smṛti*.
Dakṣa says:
At the conclusion of the twilight rites, however, the performance of the oblation by oneself is prescribed;
for the fruit that arises from an oblation performed by oneself is not produced by another.
An officiating priest, a son, a teacher, a brother, a sister’s son, and a husband—
whatever is offered by these very persons is indeed as if offered by oneself.
“Guru” refers to the father and others; “viṭpati” refers to the son-in-law. Yājñavalkya [1.99]:
Having offered oblations into the fires, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantras dedicated to the Sun.

In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa (58.58–59): Having commenced the morning twilight ritual while the stars are still visible, one should practice the Gāyatrī according to the prescribed rule until the appearance of the sun.
[24] Then, having reached his dwelling, the wise man should perform the fire-oblation (homa);
thereafter, he should perform the rites for the deities and observe the auspicious marks of his preceptor.
The forenoon is prescribed for all rites pertaining to the gods;
rites for the gods are to be performed in the forenoon, while those for humans are in the midday.
These rites for the ancestors should be performed with diligence during the afternoon;
however, one should perform all of this during the first part of the day.

“Maṅgala” refers to that which is to be spoken by the Brāhmaṇas and others, as stated by Nārada. The meaning is that all this which has been prescribed regarding duties toward the gods and so forth should be performed during the first parts of the day, specifically in the first division of the forenoon (pūrvāhṇa).
As stated in the Varāha Purāṇa [211.14–15]:
“O twice-born one, whatever man with devotion beholds the sun as it has emerged from its rising...”
Being pure, one should worship with three handfuls of curd and unbroken grains.
Whatever inauspicious [karma] has been accumulated by one who has taken refuge in that state is instantly consumed and reduced to ashes like wood.
“Of one who has taken refuge in being” means of one who has gone for shelter through devotion.
Manu [4.152]: “Friendliness, grooming, bathing, cleaning the teeth, and applying collyrium;”
One should perform the worship of the deities early in the forenoon.

“Maitra” refers to the voiding of excrement, because its presiding deity is Mitra; since the anus is connected to that [deity], it is also described in that way. “Prasādhana” refers to the grooming of the hair, the application of unguents, and so forth.
As stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (3.11.22):
“Then, having sipped water according to the rules, a man should perform the grooming of his hair.”
And the touching of a mirror, collyrium, auspicious dūrvā grass, and so forth.
“Ointment” refers to *sauvīrāñjana* and the like; by the word “and the like,” substances such as curd and so forth are included. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
“If one desires long life, one should behold one’s own self in clarified butter.”
Now, according to Dakṣa:
"In the second part likewise, the practice of the gods is prescribed:
first, the acquisition of the Vedas, then reflection, then non-addiction, and finally recitation."
Giving that [to the teacher] and the fivefold study of the Vedas for his disciples—
this is declared to be the proper time for gathering fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and other such items.
The word "of the taking up" (*upādānasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.

Āpastamba [1.13.19–22; 1.14.1]: "When the establishment of the household has been accomplished, one who desires further learning should dwell for two months each year in the teacher's family with a concentrated mind—so says Śvetaketu. 'For by this method, I acquired further learning than before,' he said. But that is contradicted by the scriptures. When the establishment of the household has been accomplished, the obligatory duties are prescribed: the *agnihotra* sacrifice, guests, and whatever else is similarly enjoined."

[27] “Niveśaḥ” means marriage. “Samāhitaḥ” means with an undistracted mind. “Etena” refers to what was just mentioned, beginning with “two months each. “Yogena” means by way of the connection with the teacher lasting for two months. “Pūrvasmāt kālāt” means from the time prior to the marriage. “Bhūyaḥ” means for a long time. “Śrutam” means the study of Mīmāṃsā. “Akurvi” means I performed. “Vipratiṣiddhaṃ śāstraiḥ” means contrary to the scriptures that establish the lifelong necessity of the Agnihotra and other rites. Āpastamba [2.5.14]:
If one does not shine through that knowledge, one should approach the teacher again and master it.
"Does not shine" means one would not possess radiant knowledge. Yājñavalkya [1.99].
And he should master the meaning of the Vedas and various treatises—
those which quickly increase the intellect and are auspicious, beneficial, and conducive to welfare. (Manu 4.19–20)
[28] He should constantly study the treatises as well as the Vedic scriptures.
For in whatever measure a person masters a treatise,
in that same measure he understands it, and his discernment finds delight in it.

“Those that increase the intellect” refers to logic (*tarka*), hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*), and so forth. “Blessed” means those beneficial for wealth, namely the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*). “Beneficial” refers to medicine (*āyurveda*) and the like. “Rules” (*niyamāḥ*) are works such as glossaries (*nighaṇṭu*) which serve as the basis for determining the meaning of words. “Shines” means it becomes radiant. Yama says:
Those who have set out and those who remain established by following the path of the meaning of the scriptures—
Those great-souled ones who awaken go to the supreme goal.
One does not attain through charity, austerity, sacrifices, or vows of fasting that same state which one may attain through knowledge.

“Gone” means having set out upon the path of the meaning of the scriptures; “established” means having arrived, that is to say, having gone to another world. “They understand” means they practice and remain [in that state].
Dakṣa:
And likewise, in the third part, one should accomplish the welfare of those to be supported.
And the group to be supported consists of:
mother, father, teacher, wife, offspring, the indigent, those who have sought refuge, guests, visitors, and the sacred fire; this is declared to be the group to be supported.
Gautama [9.63–64]:

One should approach the Lord for the sake of *yogakṣema*; not anyone else, except for gods, teachers, and righteous persons. The acquisition of what has not been obtained is *yoga*; the preservation of what has been obtained is *kṣema*. "Anyone else" means one who is not the Lord.
Manu [4.153–154]: On the sacred festival days (parvan), he should visit the deities, righteous and most excellent brahmins, the Lord for the sake of protection, and his gurus.
[30] He should then salute his elders and offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart.

“*Abhigacchet*” means one should go toward [them] for the sake of worship and so forth. In the phrase “*gurūn eva*,” the particle *eva* is to be understood as displaced [in order], and is to be construed immediately after the word “*gacchet*. Chāgaleya and Yama state that for ascetics (*yatīnām*), there should be seeing, touching, and likewise speaking.
One who performs [this] is purified eternally; therefore, one should indeed look upon it constantly.

The builder of a fire-altar, a tawny cow, one who has completed a sacrificial session, a king, a Brāhmaṇa who has eaten, and the great ocean—these purify by the mere sight; therefore, one should behold them constantly.

By the word "should see" (*paśyet*), touching and speaking are also included through *ajahatsvārtha-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication without abandoning the primary meaning). An "Agnicit" is one who has performed the *agnicayana* rite. A "Kapilā" is a cow of tawny color. A "Satrī" is one who has performed the *satra* sacrifice. A "Bhikṣu" is an ascetic. As stated in the *Varāhapurāṇa* (290.64–65):
"Having seen a dwarf Brāhmaṇa and a boar risen from the water..."
And whoever pays homage with devotion is liberated from all sins.
One who performs sacrifices, gives delicious food, conducts sacrificial sessions, lives for a hundred years, is righteous, and pure—
having seen those established in knowledge and perfected through austerity, one is liberated from sin.
“Pure” means purified by sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth; “established in knowledge” means delighting in the inner self (*adhyātma*).
Nārada says: “In this world, there are eight auspicious things: a Brahmin, a cow, and fire... [17.54–55].
Gold, clarified butter, the sun, water, and likewise the king as the eighth.
Whoever should constantly behold these, bow down to them, worship them,
and circumambulate them, their lifespan shall not diminish.

Furthermore, these acts—seeing, bowing to, worshipping, and circumambulating the eight auspicious objects (*maṅgala*) beginning with the Brahmin—are prescribed as a collective duty to be performed specifically during the third part of the day by one who desires long life. However, during the first part of the day, there is only the touching of the auspicious objects and so forth. As stated in the Vāmanapurāṇa:
"Having performed the head-bath and then the daily rites (*āhnika*)."
Having worshipped the ancestors together with the gods with water,
and having performed the fire-oblation and the touching of auspicious objects, it is then recommended to go outside.
Durvā grass, curds, clarified butter, and then a water-pot,
a cow with its calf, a bull, gold, clay,
cow dung, a svastika, and unbroken grains.
Parched grain, honey, and Brahmin maidens.
One should touch white flowers, as well as the Śamī tree, the sacrificial fire, sandalwood, the orb of the sun,
and the Aśvattha tree.
And then, one should perform the duties of one's own caste.
One should certainly not abandon the precepts of one's country, the supreme family dharma, or the dharma of one's own lineage.

Regarding the statement, “Having honored the ancestors with water,” this indicates that the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) must be performed during the morning bath. Here, having restated everything beginning with the head-bath as it occurs according to its proper time, the third part of the day is prescribed for such acts as “then he should perform the duty of his own caste,” and so forth. The “duty of one’s own caste” consists of the acquisition of wealth and other such activities ordained for each respective caste. Furthermore, the meaning is that one should practice only that specific means of acquisition which has been ordained and not censured for a particular person, within a particular caste, in a particular country, and within a particular family. Now, Dakṣa says:
In the fourth part, however, one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing, as well as sesame, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth; and the bath should be performed in natural water.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), cow-dung, *dūrvā* grass, and so forth are included. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one should perform bathing. [This refers to] a natural river and the like. Śātātapa says: "From anthills, from molehills, from clay, from water, and from the banks of rivers and trees..."
And the seven applications of earth remaining after the purification has been performed should not be taken.

“Ākhūtkaraḥ” means a molehill. “From a smear” refers to the plastering of walls and so forth—this is the ellipsis. “From water” means from within the water. “Of the path and the tree”—the ellipsis is that it belongs to these two.
However, clay should be collected from a pure place, free from pebbles, stones, and the like;
clay is traditionally said to be of three kinds: red, pale-yellow, and white.

The phrase "in a clean place" implies that [the practitioner] is standing there. By the word "etcetera," hair, insects, and so forth are included. Because of the rule regarding redness and other qualities, it is stated that black-colored earth is not a constituent part of the ritual bath. "A wise man should not take earth, nor water, nor cow-dung at night; nor should he take cow-urine at twilight."

In the phrase "at night," the terms "clay," "water," and "cow dung" are each connected [to the word "night"]. Furthermore, this clay and so forth should not be taken at night for the purpose of unseen ritual acts (*adṛṣṭakarman*).
Manu [4.129]: "One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor during the dead of night."
[35] Nor with garments, nor constantly, nor in a body of water that is not clearly discerned.

Regarding the statement, “One should not perform a bath after eating,” Medhātithi explains that this is a prohibition against bathing at will for one who has already finished a meal, since there is no possibility of a mandatory (nitya) bath occurring after eating. However, a bath necessitated by contact with a *caṇḍāla* or similar impurity cannot be prohibited, as it would contradict the injunction, “One should not remain impure even for a moment. The term “of one who is afflicted” (*āturasya*) refers to one suffering from disease; for such a person, there is an absolute prohibition against the ritual bath performed with water (*vāruṇasnāna*). “Midnight” (*mahāniśā*) refers to the middle two watches of the night. “Continually” (*ajasram*) means without interruption, due to dullness of faith or other such causes. “In an unknown [water body]” (*avijñāte*) means [a body] whose depth or shallowness is unknown, or which is of questionable origin because its maker is untraceable, and so forth.
Jābāli says: One should never bathe in another person's water, nor after eating, nor at midnight;
nor should one ever put on a single garment while it is still wet.

Regarding the phrase “in another’s,” one should never bathe in wells or similar bodies of water belonging to others. However, if no natural (unartificial) body of water is available, one may bathe there as well, based on the statement: “even in another’s [water], at times. Furthermore, it is forbidden for a person to always wear only a single wet garment. Thus, since there is a rule that a person must always wear two garments, there is no authoritative basis for discarding them even at the time of bathing.
Likewise: “On the thirteenth, the third, and especially the tenth [lunar day]...”
Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas should not perform ritual bathing under any circumstances.

"Immersion in water for bathing is prescribed for all castes"—this general rule of bathing which has been established is here prohibited for Śūdras and others on the thirteenth day and so forth, respectively.
Baudhāyana [2.6.24–25]:
"One should not bathe naked; one should not bathe at night."

Āpastamba [1.32.7–8]: One should avoid immersing the head in water; likewise, one should avoid bathing after sunset. Having entered the water, one should not, out of mere inclination (*rāgataḥ*), perform an immersion including the head. The phrase "and bathing after sunset" is to be construed with "one should avoid. This also refers specifically to bathing undertaken out of mere inclination.
Parāśara [12.22]:
Bathing during the day is praised when purified by the rays of the sun;
bathing at night is not recommended, except when Rāhu [eclipses the sun or moon] is visible.
Just as bathing and giving gifts are prescribed during a solar eclipse by day,
so too are bathing and giving gifts ordained for a lunar eclipse at night.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
Brāhmaṇas who dwell as householders should bathe at both twilights;
however, those devoted to asceticism should bathe at all three twilights.

An "ascetic" (*tapasvin*) refers to one who has retired to the forest (*vānaprastha*) and others. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Not eating and not naked, he should bathe. He should not urinate in water. He should not perform scrubbing [with earth]. He should not strike the water with his foot or hand, for water is indeed all the deities. He should not cross a flowing stream in vain without pouring out [water as an offering]. He should avoid impure water. He should not bathe in very little water. He should not plunge into the waters of the ocean."

“Not eating” means not consuming betel leaves and the like. “Mehanaṃ” means the voiding of urine. “Udgharṣaṇaṃ” means the removal of bodily impurities. The grammatical connection is: “one should not do these in water. “Atikrāmet” means one should transgress or violate. “Vṛthā” means without purpose. “Anavasicya” means without having performed the libation (tarpaṇa). “Ameghyaṃ” means impure. “Pariharet” means one should avoid doing anything there. “One should not bathe in little water,” provided that abundant and pleasant water is available; this is because of such statements as, “when abundant [water] exists” [39]. “Nāvagāhet” means one should not enter within and bathe.
Devala says: One should not speak of a river while among rivers, nor of a mountain while among mountains;
likewise, while staying at sacred fords (tīrthas) or shrines (āyatanas), one should not praise anything else.
Hārīta says:

"One should not bathe at a crossroads or near a gate. A "crossroads" (*catvara*) is a place where offerings are made to Yakṣas and other deities; "near a gate" (*upadvāra*) means in the vicinity of a door.
Furthermore, Hārīta states:
"One should not offer the best portion of bathing materials or cosmetics, except for those intended for the gods, gurus, and Brahmins.

That by which one bathes is called "bathing" (*snāna*), such as *kuśa* grass and the like. "Cosmetic" (*varṇaka*) refers to fragrant substances, because they produce a coloring effect through the application of ointments and the like.

[40] Viṣṇu [64.1–9]: One should not perform a bath at the drinking-troughs of others. Or, in times of distress, one may do so after removing five lumps of earth. One who is suffering from indigestion, nor one who is ill, nor one who is naked, nor one at night—except during an eclipse of Rāhu—nor during the twilight (saṃdhyā) should bathe. One who is to bathe in the morning should bathe after observing the eastern direction seized by the rays of the dawn. "In times of distress" means when bathing in natural water is impossible. "During the twilight" refers to the evening twilight.

Paiṭhīnasi: Now, the rule for bathing. One should avoid reservoirs and wells constructed by others. In such cases, the builder of the reservoir shall share in the merit; one should bathe after having drawn out three mouthfuls of water. Manu [4.209]:
One should never bathe at water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the misdeeds of the reservoir's builder.

“Belonging to another” (*parakīya*) means merely that which was made by another. Whether it be established or unestablished, there is no distinction; this is according to the statements of Paiṭhīnasi and Baudhāyana regarding the phrase “made by another. However, there is no contradiction in the case of what one has caused to be made for oneself. A “watering place” (*nipāna*) is a reservoir of water. Baudhāyana [2.5.1–5]: “The *tapasya* rite is immersion in water. Having satiated the deities, one performs the libation to the ancestors. One should pour out water along the bank with the verse ‘Carrying strength’ (*ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*). Moreover, they quote as follows:”
While the flowing waters have not ceased, the three twice-born castes,
having risen in the morning, should perform the libations for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
If the [dams or wells] have been destroyed, the builder of the dam shall not claim a share therein;
therefore, one should avoid dams and wells constructed by others.
Or, having drawn up three lumps of earth, he should perform the rite in times of distress, but not at all times;
however, when water is obstructed, he should likewise take three lumps of earth from a well and three jars of water.

“Tapasyam” refers to immersion that is beneficial for austerity (*tapas*). Here, *tapas* is intended as the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth, because one has the entitlement to perform them after bathing. “Anutīrtham” means taking the *tīrtha* [of the hand] as the reference point; the meaning is: by means of the *tīrtha* dedicated to the gods, ancestors, and others. The phrase “carrying strength” (*ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*) is included to indicate that the final element of the libation (*tarpaṇa*) is being taken up, signifying that this constitutes a single ritual performance. “Niruddhāsu” means in those whose flow has been obstructed. — Śaṅkha and Likhita.

One should not offer libations to the ancestors at a site constructed with bricks. At a step-well, a pond, or a natural spring, one should offer libations to the gods and ancestors after removing seven, five, or three lumps of earth.
Yājñavalkya [1.159] states:
"One should not bathe in waters belonging to others without having removed five lumps of earth."
One should bathe in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, and in lakes.

According to the statements of Paiṭhīnasi and Baudhāyana, the removal of three lumps of earth and three jars of water by the one performing the bath pertains to the case of embankments and wells. However, the removal of five lumps of earth mentioned by Viṣṇu pertains to artificial bodies of water other than these. As for the removal of seven, five, or three lumps of earth mentioned by Śaṅkha and Likhita, that refers respectively to large reservoirs (*vāpī*), wells (*kūpa*), and ponds (*taḍāga*) for the purpose of *tarpaṇa*. Manu [4.203]:
"In rivers, in natural pools, in ponds, and in lakes..."
One should always perform one's ablutions at pools and springs.

"In divine excavations and tanks" means in lakes renowned for their connection to the gods. "A pit" refers to what will be described later: "Those whose range does not extend beyond eight thousand bows. "A spring" is a mountain waterfall.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.26]:
"One should perform a bath with water drawn from wells, or on the ground;
or one may bathe with drawn water if it is impossible to do so on the ground."

[44] “In wells”: one standing on the ground may bathe with that water drawn up from them. “In the absence [of such]”: the meaning is that bathing is possible by immersing oneself elsewhere as well, such as in a pond (*taḍāga*) or similar body of water.

Viṣṇu [64.16–17]: “One should bathe in springs, natural excavations made by the gods, and lakes. Water situated on the ground is more meritorious than water drawn up; a spring is more meritorious than that; river water is more meritorious than that; and water accepted by the virtuous is more meritorious even than that. In every case, however, water from a household vessel is to be preferred.”
"‘Well-protected’ means protected by someone like Rāma, such as the Mandākinī and other sites at Citrakūṭa and elsewhere.
Śaṅkha says: ‘All sacred fords are always meritorious and destructive of the sins of men.’"
The wise have declared these to be mutually independent.
All springs are meritorious, all mountain peaks are meritorious,
and all rivers are always meritorious, the Ganges being especially so.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and fame— he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
For men who have committed evil deeds, there shall be the pacification of that evil at a sacred ford;
for men whose souls are endowed with faith, the sacred ford bestows the fruits as they have been described.

“Restraint of the hands” is the cessation from accepting gifts from censurable persons and the like. “Restraint of the feet” is the cessation from traveling to forbidden places. “Restraint of the mind” is the cessation from desire, anger, and so forth. “Knowledge” consists of the true scriptures and the Vedas. “Austerity” includes the *cāndrāyaṇa* and other such observances. “Fame” is renown for being righteous and so on. It has been stated that a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is not entirely fruitless even for a man who has committed sins—this is expressed by the word “of men.
Thus says Yājñavalkya the Yogin: “But when abundant and very beautiful water is available...”
A twice-born man should not bathe in a small body of water, nor should he abandon a river to bathe in an artificial one.
Any rivers that do not flow to the sea yield their fruit after three nights; those that flow to the sea, however, yield it after a fortnight; and the lord of rivers yields its fruit after a month.
Bathing in warm water is in vain; Vedic recitation is in vain;
giving a gift to one who is not learned in the Vedas is in vain; and eating in secret is in vain. [46]

"Yielding the fruit of three nights" means they grant that same fruit which is obtained by bathing for three nights in water other than that of a river. In this way, "of a fortnight" and "of a month" are also to be understood. "In vain" means devoid of the fruit of bathing other than that which consists of the purification of the body.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "The water that stands before one, situated near a Śiva-liṅga..."
That should be known as Śivaliṅga; having bathed there, one shall go to heaven.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* (1.7.140–151) states:
"For two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, all rivers are in their menstrual period;
one should not perform ritual bathing in them, except for those that flow into the ocean."
Between the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not perform ritual bathing in them, nor the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors.
Those whose course does not extend even eight thousand bow-lengths,
and which do not flow with the sound of "nadī," are proclaimed by you as mere hollows (garta).
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, as well as at the ritual bath for the deceased,
and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses, the defect of menstrual impurity is not found.
The Vedas and all the meters, the celestial dwellers beginning with Brahmā,
the ancestors seeking water, and likewise the sages beginning with Marīci;
At the commencement and at the conclusion of the Vedic term,
the disembodied beings, being greatly delighted, follow those expounders of the Veda who are desirous of going for the sake of their ritual bath.
Wherever there is a meeting of these [three], all other impurities of existence surely come to destruction; how much more so a single speck of river-dust?
Taking his place in the space between the sages as they were being sprinkled,
he would drink with his own body the droplets of water released from the assembly.
A Brahmin shall obtain the objects of desire such as knowledge and the like, and a woman shall likewise obtain stable [objects] such as sons;
they shall also attain the pleasures of the next world—of this there is no doubt.
That which is given by an impure person, or with impure things such as raw rice or potsherds,
is consumed by the *preta*s and *rakṣas* who have not yet passed ten days [since death].
On the surface of the earth, all waters—even those situated in wells—become equal to the waters of the celestial river during an eclipse of the moon or sun; of this there is no doubt.

[48] “*Yavya*” means a month; “*yavyā māsāḥ sumekaḥ saṃvatsaraḥ*” (the months are *yavya*, the well-measured is the year), according to the *Śatapatha-śruti*. “*Rajasvalāḥ*” means impure. “*Samudragāḥ*” refers to those whose flow toward the ocean is directly perceptible. A “*dhanuḥ*” is a measurement of four cubits (*hasta*). When the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the *ṛṣis* is being performed, one should “*drink*” (*pibet*)—that is, receive with the body—the mass of water droplets associated with the interval between them. “*Aśuci*” means an impure substance. “*By an impure person*” (*aśucinā puruṣeṇa*). “*With uncooked shards of clay, etc.*” (*āmamṛcchakalādinā*) means with unbaked earthen potsherds and the like. “*Those whose ten days have not elapsed*” (*anirgatadaśāhāḥ*): those who have died within ten days from birth are *pretas*. “*The *rakṣasas* consume it*” means that what is given goes to them. This passage beginning with “*And where there is their meeting*” and so forth—which describes the absence of defects in the water in every respect, such as dust and the like—is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the statement beginning with “*impure by an impure person*” and so forth. “*Svardhunī*” is the Gaṅgā.

[49] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should perform the threefold bath—daily (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and for a specific desire (*kāmya*). And libation (*tarpaṇa*) is proclaimed to be its subsidiary limb."
Bathing is said to be of three kinds: daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya). Among these, that which is the daily bath is further divided into three types.
The removal of impurities by means of water accompanied by mantras is prescribed for the side [of the body];
the twilight bath (saṃdhyā-snāna) involves both; thus are the different types of baths proclaimed.
“On the side” means not in the middle of the water; this is the intended meaning. “Sandhyā-bath” refers to the morning bath. “By both” means both in the water and on land. Śaṅkha [8.1–11]:
The daily, the occasional, the optional, that which is an auxiliary to a ritual act, and that which removes impurities.
Likewise, the ritual bath (kriyā-snāna) is the sixth; thus, the sixfold bath is proclaimed.
A man who has not bathed is unfit for the recitation of prayers, the offering of oblations into the fire, and other such rites;
therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath (*nityasnāna*).
Furthermore, one must bathe after touching a *caṇḍāla*, a corpse, pus, and the like, as well as women in their menses who have not yet bathed.
When one who is worthy of bathing bathes, that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.

Whatever rites, such as the Puṣya-bath and others, are enjoined by the rules of the astrologers, those are indeed designated as optional (kāmya); one should not perform them without a specific desire.
He who, desiring to recite prayers or wishing to worship the deities and ancestors with purificatory rites,
performs a bath— that is proclaimed as the bath that is an auxiliary to ritual action (kriyāṅga).
The bath known as *malāpakarṣaṇa* (the removal of impurities) is preceded by anointing with oil;
its purpose is indeed the removal of impurities, and not otherwise.
In lakes, natural pools, sacred fords, and rivers, the ritual bath (kriyā-snāna) is prescribed; in that context, "ritual" (kriyā) is understood as the act itself.
In that regard, one should perform the optional rites exactly as prescribed by the injunctions,
as well as the obligatory, the occasional, those auxiliary to ritual acts, and those for the removal of impurities.
In the absence of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), however, one should perform the rite with warm water or other water;
likewise for one who has bathed, it may be done with water heated by fire or even with the water of others.
The purification of the body should be understood as such, yet one does not obtain the fruit of bathing;
the limbs are cleansed by water, but the fruit arises from bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
[51] Since the act itself is bathing in lakes, natural ponds, sacred fords, and rivers,
it is held that the fruit of merit arises from bathing.

“Preceded by anointing” (*abhyaṅgapūrvakam*) is an elliptical expression indicating a bath for the removal of impurities. Here, the word *tīrtha* refers to bathing places such as ponds, wells, and tanks that function as sacred sites (*tīrtha*). “Preferred” (*matā*) means desired. “Properly” (*yathāvat*) refers to the prescribed procedure as stated for the *puṣya-snāna* and other rites. By the phrase “regular and occasional” (*nityaṃ naimittikam*), it is implied by the sense of the text that the ritual baths performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) and the functional baths (*kriyā-snāna*) should not be performed with hot water or water belonging to another. “Water belonging to another” (*paravāri*) refers to water created by another, as well as natural water acquired by another. “The fruit of the bath” (*snānaphala*) refers to heaven and so forth. — Hārīta.
Five types of ablutions have been proclaimed for Brahmins by the wise:
the fiery, the watery, the divine, the wind-born, and the celestial.
The Agneya bath is said to be with ashes, the Varuna bath with water;
the Brahma bath is performed with the hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and the Vayavya bath is traditionally known as the dust raised by cows.
The divine bath is said here to consist of these [elements]: sunlight and rain;
having bathed with these according to the mantras, one obtains the fruit of sacred fords (tīrthas).

[52] “Āgneyam”: here, the word *agni* refers by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to ashes, which are the product of fire. The suffix *ḍhak* is applied according to the rule: “The suffix *ḍhak* should be stated after the words *agni* and *kali* in all cases. “*Āpo hi ṣṭhā*”: this is an elliptical expression for the four mantras beginning with that phrase. “By these”: namely, by the *āgneya* and the others. “By means of the mantra”: through the recitation of the mantras that serve as the instruments for touching the clay and so forth. Yogi-Yājñavalkya says: “When, indeed, he is unable [to perform the rite] due to the defects of time or lack of capacity...”
Then, having learned from the sages, he performed the purification seen in the mantras.
The *śanna āpas*, the *drupadāḥ*, the *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, and the *aghamarṣaṇa*—
the ritual bath with mantras (*mantrasnāna*) is declared to consist of these four Vedic hymns.
Bathing with mantras dedicated to the water-deities, the ritual sprinkling (mārjana),
and the restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma) performed with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn are equal to the final purificatory bath of a horse sacrifice.
When a state of impurity has arisen, one should indeed perform a bath;
however, with the previously mentioned mantras, otherwise there shall be a ritual sprinkling (mārjana).

“Defect of time” refers to excessive rain and the like; “incapacity” is the cause of physical unfitness, or the inability to perform the complete ritual of the Varuṇa-bath due to the brevity of the time. Regarding the phrase “bathing with mantras addressed to the waters,” the sequence is: cleansing with mantras addressed to the waters, and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Such bathing with mantras is superior to the previously mentioned bathing with mantras. “Impurity” (*aprāyatya*) means lack of cleanliness. Here, “bathing” (*snāna*) refers to immersion. “Otherwise” means in the absence of impurity. Again, Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
Some wise teachers maintain that there are seven [types of purification], such as mantra-bath and so forth, due to the incapacity of the body and its dependence on time, power, and other factors.
The sevenfold bath is proclaimed to consist of the mantra-bath, the earth-bath, the fire-bath, the wind-bath, the celestial-bath, the water-bath, and the mental-bath.
The bath with water is indeed prescribed by the mantra "apo hi ṣṭhā"; the bath with clay is the earthly (pārthiva) one;
the bath with ashes is the fiery (āgneya); and the bath with the dust raised by cows is remembered as the windy (vāyavya).
That bathing which is performed with rain falling from the clouds is called divine;
that which consists of immersion in water is Vāruṇa; and the mental recollection of Viṣṇu is Mānasa.
The bath as prescribed by the sequence of the mantra-bath is indeed recommended;
however, due to time, place, or incapacity, it is traditionally held that all [alternative methods] yield equal results.
Some wise men maintain that mental bathing is the most excellent,
since it was recited by Vyāsa in the praise of the sacred ford of the Self (ātmatīrtha).

Every bath performed according to the sequence of the mantra-bath as prescribed is indeed praised. The reason for this is stated here: "due to time and place. The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. The Vāruṇa bath is the primary one; however, due to defects in time and so forth, other baths such as the Māntra and others yield results equal to it.
As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Whatever merit is found at Kanakhala and whatever at Prayāga, O beautiful one..."
O Goddess, that entire fruit is obtained day after day through the ritual bath with ashes.
Likewise,
O daughter of Naravāhana, the Vināyakas do not overpower a man who is impure, or negligent, or even one touched by a spirit.
“Negligent” means lacking attentiveness. “They assail” means they overcome.
[55] In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [2.9.12–13, 15–16]:
“Having taken up the water of the celestial Gaṅgā, the sun...”
It immediately casts even that which has reached the cloudless sky onto the earth by means of its rays.
The best of the twice-born, whose mire of sin has been shaken off by contact with that [water], does not go to hell; for that is remembered as a divine bath.
When water from the sky falls upon the odd-numbered lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā while the sun is visible, it should be known as the Ganges-water released by the elephants of the quarters.
And whatever water falls from the sky during the twin constellations, released by the sun,
is immediately drawn up and cast down again by the sun's rays.

"In odd [asterisms]" refers to the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and so forth, such as Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras, Punarvasu, and the rest. "In even asterisms" refers to the even ones, such as Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, and the rest.
Likewise [it is said]:
"O twice-born one, both are exceedingly meritorious for men and destroy their sins."
O great sage, the divine water of the celestial Gaṅgā is for your bath.
In the *Vārāha Purāṇa*: "He who performs an ablution in water reaching up to the navel, using a right-spiraling conch shell and water mixed with sesame seeds,"
But for a man with a one-pointed mind in a river flowing eastward,
the sin committed throughout his entire life perishes at that very moment.
“In *Prāksrotasī*,” which flows toward the eastern direction;
having bathed in the stream with its unbroken lotus petals and water containing all kinds of jewels, a man is indeed liberated from all sins.
Whoever, with a joyful mind, should receive with his head the water contained in an udumbara vessel by means of a right-spiraling conch shell;
The sin committed in that birth perishes at that very moment.
[57] "Audumbara" means copper. "With the head" (*śirasā*) is the instrumental case used in the sense of the locative. [This refers to] Jābāli.
For those engaged in ritual acts who are unable to perform a full bath, the bath may be headless;
they know that the cleansing of the body may also be accomplished by wiping it with a wet cloth.
With the word "head" continuing from the previous context, Manu [4.82] states:
"And one should not bathe without that."
By this, it is stated that when the capacity for bathing exists, the prescribed bath must be performed including the head;
as stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (34.35):
"One who has bathed his head may perform rites for the gods or even for the ancestors."
Now follows the procedure for bathing.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha states (9.1–15):
"I shall now describe the ritual bathing (kriyā-snāna) correctly and in due order."
First, purification must be performed with earth and water according to the prescribed rule;
then, having submerged oneself in water and emerged, one should perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) according to the rule.
One should perform the invocation of the Tīrtha; I shall explain that hereafter:
"I take refuge in the god Varuṇa, the powerful lord of the waters."
"O Tīrtha, grant me what is requested for the removal of all sins;
I shall invoke the Tīrtha that destroys every evil."
By my grace, let those who resort to this water of mine obtain my presence;
I myself, the bestower of boons, take refuge in all the Rudras who dwell within the waters.
Bowing down and standing firm, I take refuge in all those who dwell in the waters;
I take refuge in the god Agni, the dweller in the waters, the destroyer of sin.
I likewise take refuge in the waters, which are meritorious and purifying;
and in the Rudras, Agni, the serpents, Varuṇa, and the waters themselves.
"May they quickly pacify my evil and always purify me.
Having spoken thus, one should perform the cleansing in the water.
He should perform the rite with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā" in their proper order,
and likewise with the four ṛg-verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ."
Likewise, one should recite the mantra "śaṃ no devīḥ," and similarly "śaṃ na āpaḥ," as well as "idam āpaḥ pravahata."
Having thus performed the sweeping,
one who is self-restrained should always recollect the *chandas*, the *ṛṣi*, and the deity of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn.
The meter of this [hymn] is Anuṣṭubh, its seer is Aghamarṣaṇa,
and it is proclaimed that the deity of this destroyer of sins is Bhāvavṛtta.
Then, one should immerse oneself in water and recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times;
just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, removes all sins.
Likewise, the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn removes all sins;
having bathed according to this rite, [one should perform it] while wearing the bathing garment within the water.
If he has changed his garment, he should touch water at the edge of a sacred bathing place;
for until water has been offered, he must not wring out his bathing cloth.

Having bathed according to this procedure, one obtains meritorious fruit. The word "bhajatām" (of those who resort [to it]) is construed with the word "varuṇa," which has been modified [from its original form]. The four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarāḥ" and "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" belong to the Taittirīya and Maitrāyaṇīya [recensions]. "Śaṃ na āpaḥ" and "Śaṃ na āpo dhanvanyāḥ" belong to the Kaṭha branch. The phrase "of the sin-destroying" is construed with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn. [Thus says] Yogiyājñavalkya.
Having heard those words of Yājñavalkya at that time,
the sages of refined souls then asked about the determination regarding ritual bathing.
O sinless one, O Lord, please explain in detail the procedure for bathing, as well as those mantras addressed to the deities of the waters which you previously mentioned.
To them, Yājñavalkya, of immeasurable luster and joyful soul, replied:
"Listen, for I shall describe the bath that destroys all sins."
At the time of bathing, one who is self-restrained and pure should fetch earth, sesame seeds, cow dung, darbha grass, and fragrant flowers for the purpose of bathing.
Having gone to a secluded water's edge and placed this [earth] separately upon the ground,
the wise man should divide that earth into three parts, as well as the cow dung.
One should indeed perform the washing of the lower, upper, and middle parts separately with distinct portions;
there must be no mixing of the earth during the washing.
Likewise: having washed his feet with water and earth and having sipped water (ācamana), being pure,
he should worship the water while circumambulating it clockwise, reciting the verse beginning with "uruṃ hi."
He should stir that water with the verse, "Those hundred of yours...
[61]; then, remembering the deity, he should lift up his joined palms with the mantra, "May they be friendly..."
While meditating on those who are hostile as "the ill-disposed," one should sprinkle water.
One should wash the limbs with water and earth in due order;
having washed the head once, one should likewise wash the area above the navel twice.

Having washed the waist, the bladder, the thighs, the shanks, and the feet— three times each— and having washed his hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should pay homage to that water.
With the mantra "yat kiṃ ca," one should pay homage with palms joined in reverence;
in whatever place there may be a sacred site (tīrtha) or a most meritorious river.

One should meditate upon her, having invoked her mentally, and then contemplate whatever else is desired; one should likewise remember sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā within artificial reservoirs and the like.
Purified and facing the east, one should enter that water with the mantra "ud uttamam";
then, with the three verses beginning "yena devāḥ pavitreṇa," one should perform the ritual touching [of the water].
Thereafter, even though he is already pure, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with the Vyahritis;
then, he should touch his limbs with earth while reciting the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ".
Facing the sun, one should immerse oneself with the verse "āpo asmān" (RV 10.9.1).
Then, having rubbed the limbs, one should indeed submerge and emerge again.
Having sipped water, he should also smear himself with cow dung while reciting the *mānastokīya* hymn;
then, he should consecrate himself in due order with the Varuṇa mantras.
With the two *ṛc*s beginning "imaṃ me varuṇa," and also with "tvam naḥ" and "sa tvan naḥ," as well as with "māpaḥ," "ud uttamam," "muñcatu," and "avabhṛtha."
Having consecrated himself by immersing therein and sipping water again,
he should purify himself with darbha grass while reciting auspicious, purificatory mantras addressed to the waters.
With the three verses beginning "For you are waters," with this verse "O waters, rich in oblation," with the two verses beginning "Divine waters," and with the verse "O gods, the waters."
With the verse beginning "drupadād iva," [he recites] "śanno devīr apāṃ rasam" and "apo devīḥ pāvamānyas"; these nine initial verses purify.
With a concentrated mind, he should slowly purify himself with the mantra "citpatir me," as well as the *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā" and other such hymns.
One should recite the *Taratsamandī*, the *Śuddhavatī*, and the *Pavitra* hymns according to one's ability, as well as the *Vāruṇī* verses and the *Sūkta*, according to one's capacity.
Standing in the midst of the water, the brahmin, with a pure disposition and composed in mind, should remember Hari by means of the syllable Om, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Gāyatrī.
One should indeed perform the consecration in due order both at the beginning and at the end;
likewise, the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) is prescribed for one standing in the midst of the waters.
One should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa mantra three times while submerged in water;
or one should practice the Drupadā verse three times, or the three-verse hymn beginning with "āyaṃ gauḥ."
Having repeated the verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" three times, he should mutter it;
then he should likewise recollect other hymns (sūktas) perceived by the Smṛtis.
Then one should recite the Gāyatrī three times together with the Vyahṛtis and the Praṇava;
or one may repeat the Praṇava, or meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu.
For the waters are the abode of Viṣṇu, and he is called the lord of the waters;
these [waters] are indeed his daughters, therefore one should meditate upon him within the waters.
From Nara, indeed, the waters were produced; therefore they are remembered as "Nārāḥ.
Since those waters are his place of rest (ayana), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
For he is indeed the enjoyer of vows, of the Vedas, of self-restraint, and of discipline;
he is the enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity, and the very object of meditation for those who meditate.
Constantly meditating upon Nārāyaṇa during rituals such as ritual bathing and in all acts of expiation, a person is liberated from evil deeds.

"Whatever part of the ritual action performed during sacrifices may fall away due to negligence, that becomes complete through the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the traditional teaching (smṛti)."
One should immerse oneself repeatedly in the waters with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," for this Gāyatrī belongs to Viṣṇu and is indeed for the constant remembrance of Viṣṇu.
A wise person should not strike water with a foot, a hand, or even a cloth; nor should he splash it, nor speak harshly toward it, nor cause it to become turbid.
One should not cause harm to anyone by deed, thought, or word;
however, while performing the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka), one should not perform other [worldly] actions.
If one is unable to perform that supreme procedure for bathing which has been explained in detail, then this [following] procedure is prescribed.
Likewise, bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling and sipping water,
the consecration of the water, and the visualization of the sacred site (tīrtha).
The performance of the ritual bath by means of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn recited three times daily has been thus prescribed by the high-souled ones.
Or he may, according to his desire, employ other mantras dedicated to Varuṇa;
having understood the appropriate time and place, the wise one should perform them accordingly.

“*Etat*” refers to clay and so forth. The phrase “having divided the cow-dung into three parts” is to be supplied as an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*). “The lower part” is that below the navel; “the upper part” is the head; “the middle part” is from above the navel up to the throat. “Non-mixing of the clay” means not combining portions of clay that have been separated. “*Uruṃ hi*... refers to the verse beginning with “*uruṃ hi rājā varuṇa*. “*Ye te śatam*... refers to the verse beginning with “*ye te śataṃ varuṇa*. “*Sumitriyā*... refers to the *yajus* mantra: “*sumitriyā na āpaḥ*. “*Durmitriyā*... refers to the *yajus* mantra: “*durmitriyās tasmai santu*. “*Yat kiṃ ca*... refers to the *ṛc* verse beginning with “*yat kiṃ cedaṃ varuṇa*. “*Elsewhere*” means in water that has been drawn out. “A desired sacred site” (*iṣṭaṃ tīrtham*) refers to Prayāga and the like. “Artificial” refers to lotus ponds and the like. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “in artificial sites and so forth,” natural bathing places such as lakes are included. “*Ud uttamam*... refers to the *ṛc* verse beginning with “*ud uttamaṃ varuṇa pāśam*. Regarding “one should perform facing the east,” the connection is with the word “touching” (*ālambhanam*). “Touching” (*ālambhanam*) means touching the water of a river or other source with the hand. “*Idaṃ viṣṇur*... refers to the *ṛc* verse: “*idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame*. And the touching of clay is, by implication, for the purpose of washing the limbs, using clay other than the clay already divided into three parts, because that divided clay has already been assigned to the washing of the limbs. “*Āpo asmān*... refers to the *ṛc* verse: “*āpo asmān mātaraḥ*. “One should immerse oneself facing the sun” is to be understood as applying to tanks and similar bodies of water. This has been stated in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*.
"A twice-born man should bathe in rivers and flowing streams standing against the current;
in waters such as ponds and the like, he should perform his bath facing the sun. Thus it is said.

With the verse beginning with *“mānastokyā,”* namely *“mā nastoke tanaye māna.”* With the two verses beginning with *“imaṃ me,”* namely *“imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhī havam”* and *“tat tvā yāmi.”* With the verse beginning with *“tvan na,”* namely *“tvan no agne varuṇasya.”* With the verse beginning with *“sa tvan na,”* namely *“sa tvan no agne ‘vamo bhava.”* With the verse beginning with *“māpa,”* namely *“māpo mauṣadhīḥ.”* With the verse beginning with *“ud uttamam,”* namely *“ud uttamaṃ varuṇa pāśam.”* With the verse beginning with *“muñcatu,”* namely *“muñcantu mā śapathād.”* With the Yajus-mantra beginning with *“avabhṛtha,”* namely *“avabhṛthan icumpuṇa.”* With the verse beginning with *“idam āpa,”* namely *“idam āpaḥ pravahata.”* With the verse beginning with *“haviṣmatīr,”* namely *“haviṣmatīr imā āpaḥ.”* With the two verses beginning with *“devīr āpaḥ,”* namely *“devīr āpo apānnapād.”* With the two verses beginning with *“kārṣir asi,”* namely *“kārṣir asi”* and *“samudrasya tvā.”* With the verse beginning with *“apo devā,”* namely *“apo devā madhumatīḥ.”* With the verse beginning with *“drupadād iva,”* namely *“drupadād iva mumucāna.”* With the verse beginning with *“śan no devīr,”* namely *“śan no devīr abhiṣṭaye.”* With the verse beginning with *“apāṃ rasam,”* namely *“apāṃ rasam udvayasam.”* With the verse beginning with *“āpo devīr,”* namely *“āpo devīr upasṛja.”* With the nine verses beginning with *“punantu mā pitaraḥ,”* which are the *Pāvamānī* hymns, namely *“punantu mā pitaraḥ.”* With the two mantras beginning with *“citpatir mā,”* namely *“citpatir mā punātu”* and *“vākpatir mā punātu,”* both of which have the phrase *“acchidreṇa pavitreṇa sūryasya raśmibhiḥ”* as their supplement (*anuṣaṅga*). And the third mantra is *“devo mā savitā punātv acchidreṇa pavitreṇa sūryasya raśmibhiḥ.”* Having purified [himself] with these mantras—meaning having caused him to be purified—the verses beginning with *“hiraṇyavarṇā”* have been mentioned. Other *Pāvamānī* verses are those beginning with *“pāvamānīḥ svastyayanīḥ.”* The *Taratsamā* verses are those beginning with *“taratsamandī dhāvati.”* The *Śuddhavatī* verses are those beginning with *“etonvindras tvāma.”* The *Pavitra* hymns are the *Puruṣasūkta* and others. There are also other Vāruṇa verses. And there is the Vāruṇa *Sūkta* itself. Regarding the phrase *“at the beginning and at the end,”* this means at the beginning and at the end of the purification. *“Sprinkling”* (*abhiṣeka*) is the throwing of water upon the head with the hand; the meaning is that sprinkling (*mārjana*), like the sprinkling, should also be performed while standing in the water, using the *Praṇava*, the *Vyāhṛtis*, and the *Gāyatrī*. With the verse beginning with *“āyaṃ gauḥ,”* namely *“āyaṃ gauḥ pṛśni akramīt.”* With the verse beginning with *“haṃsaḥ śuciṣad,”* namely *“haṃsaḥ śuciṣad vasu.”* Those seen by the Smṛti authorities—seen by Manu and others who follow the Smṛti—are such as the section beginning with *“yuñjate mana.”* *“Viṣṇu the Imperishable”* means the all-pervading causal Person. In all rites for expiation (*prāyaścitta*), which are causes for the destruction of sin, one is released from evil deeds while meditating on Nārāyaṇa. Even if there should be a deficiency in the constituent parts due to negligence, the result remains complete. With the verse beginning with *“tad viṣṇoḥ,”* namely *“tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti.”* Regarding the word *“others,”* while performing the sprinkling, one should not perform actions ending in kicking or causing pain to others; by this, it is shown that even the bath (*snāna*) becomes deficient in its parts. Regarding the phrase *“if he is such,”* if, however, due to constraints of time, place, or physical inability, one is unable to perform the detailed procedure of bathing, then one should perform the preparation of the sacred site (*tīrtha*), the consecration of the water, the sipping of water (*ācamana*), the sprinkling (*mārjana*), the internal recitation (*antarjala-japa*), and the baths, using the *Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta* repeated three times. Even when only the mantras are stated in a different order than the previously established sequence of items such as the preparation of the sacred site, that same sequence should be understood. But if, due to time and place, one is able, then one should employ other Vāruṇa mantras as well.
[70] Baudhāyana:

[2.8.1–12] Now, having washed his hands and taken hold of his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and a lump of clay, he goes to a bathing place (*tīrtha*) and washes his feet three times and himself three times. Now some say: "A cemetery, water, a temple, a cow-pen, and wherever there are Brāhmaṇas—one must not enter within these without having first washed one's feet. Then he approaches the water, saying: "I resort to Varuṇa with golden horns; grant me a bathing place as I have requested."
Whatever I have eaten from the unrighteous, and whatever acceptance of gifts I have received from the wicked;
Whatever evil deed has been committed by me through speech, mind, or action—may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that for me again and again. Thus.

Then, with his hands cupped in the *añjali* gesture, he scoops up water, saying: "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. Then, having touched water, he turns the water clockwise three times, saying: "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart. Having submerged himself in the water and emerged, there is no straining of urine or excrement while remaining in the water, nor the washing of clothes, nor ritual sipping (*upasparśana*). If they have been driven away [from their homes], he worships them with this: "Homage to Agni accompanied by the waters; homage to Indra; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Vāruṇī; homage to the waters. Having climbed out and sipped water, once he has sipped, he should sip again.
Water indeed is all this; water is all beings; water is the vital breaths; water is [all].
May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me.
May Brahmaṇaspati purify [me]; may that which is purified by the Veda purify me.

"Whatever remains of food that is unfit to be eaten, or whatever evil deed I have committed—may the waters purify all of that in me, as well as the acceptance of gifts from the wicked; svāhā! Thus [he says].

Having prepared the strainers (*pavitre*), he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*) and the four verses beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, and purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*). Having purified himself with this entire section (*anuvāka*) beginning with "The purifying one, belonging to the world of light" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*), he enters the water, performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn, and emerges.
