Then, having wrung out his garment, put on clean, unwashed clothes that have been washed and aired, and sipped water (*ācamana*), he sits upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, facing east, and should repeat the *Sāvitrī* mantra a thousand times.

[72] “Having gone to a *tīrtha*”: here, *tīrtha* is intended to mean merely a body of water. “One should wash oneself (*ātmānam*”) means one’s own body. “Three times” is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). “He approaches the waters” with the mantras beginning with “*hiraṇyaśṛṅga*,” and so forth. “He takes up the waters” (*apa upahanti*): here, the root *upahan* is used in the sense of taking or seizing. “In whichever direction” “his enemy (*dveṣya*)” is located, “of this” person who is performing the bath—this is the connection. “He sprinkles (*nirukṣati*)” means he pours out. “Moving about (*prayamaṇam*)” means going here and there or crossing over. “Washing (*palpūlanam*)” means the cleansing away of dirt. This is the usage of the root *plpūla*, belonging to the *curādigaṇa* (meaning ‘to cut’ or ‘to purify’), with the suffix *lyuṭ*. “Rubbing the limbs (*upasaprāsnam*)” here refers to the scrubbing away of bodily filth. All of this “is not found for one who is in the waters”—this is the connection. “If they should be obstructed”: the word “waters” is to be supplied as the remainder. Obstruction here refers precisely to moving about and so forth. If that is done through negligence, then one should perform the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) of the waters with the mantra beginning with “*namo ’gnaye*. “Purifiers (*pavitre*)” means two blades of grass with unbroken tips, measuring a span (*prādeśa*). “Dried (*upavātāni*)” means dried. “Unwithered (*akliṣṭāni*)” means not decayed.
Kātyāyana [Snānasūtra, 1–20].

Now, therefore, follows the daily bath (*nityasnāna*). [One should perform it] at a river or similar body of water. Having brought earth, cow dung, *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and flowers, and having gone to the water's edge, one should bathe in a clean place. Having washed one’s hands and feet, holding *kuśa* grass, with the topknot tied and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) worn, one should sip water (*ācamana*). Having invoked the *yoga* with the verse "Wide indeed" (*uruṃ hi*), one should recite "Those which are a hundred" (*ye te śatam*). Taking water in his joined palms (*añjali*) with the verse "May they be friendly to us" (*sumitriyā naḥ*), he should pour it out toward an enemy with the verse "May those who are unfriendly" (*durmitriyā*). Having washed three times each the waist, the abdomen, the thighs, the shanks, and the feet with earth, as well as the hands, and having sipped water, he should pay homage and touch the water and his limbs with the verses "This Viṣṇu... (*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*) and "Mānastoke. Facing the sun, he should immerse himself. Having bathed with the verse "The waters, may they... (*āpo asmān*), and having emerged with "Up from the waters" (*ud id ābhyaḥ*), he should immerse and emerge again, sip water, and smear himself with cow dung with the verse "Do not harm our offspring" (*mā nas toke*). Then he should sprinkle himself with the four verses beginning with "Hear this my call, O Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*), and with "O waters, release us from the highest bond," and "The purificatory bath" (*avabhṛtha*). At the end, having immersed himself and sipped water, he should purify himself with *darbha* grass using nine verses: the three beginning with "For you are waters... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*), the two beginning with "These divine waters rich in oblation" (*idam āpo haviṣmatīḥ*) and "O divine waters" (*devīr āpaḥ*), and the seven beginning with "O divine waters, like from a post... (*drupadād iva*), "Grant us, O goddesses... (*śaṃ no devīḥ*), "The essence of the waters" (*apāṃ rasam*), "O divine waters, purify me" (*punantu mā devīḥ*), and "The Lord of Thought, may he purify me" (*citpatir mā*). With the syllable *oṃ*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*, he should do so at the beginning and the end. Within the water, he should repeat the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times; or the triplet beginning with "Like from a post" (*drupadād iva*) or "This bull... (*ayaṃ gauḥ*); or the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) together with the *śiras* formula; or simply the syllable *oṃ*; or the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Vasiṣṭha said: Now I shall proclaim in due order the entire procedure for bathing,
by performing which with faith, the best of the twice-born go to heaven.
One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in natural pools dug by the gods, in tanks, in lakes, and also in pits and springs.
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted by a portion of the evil deeds of the reservoir's maker.
In the absence of divine wells, lakes, or rivers,
one should perform the ritual bath in another person's water after having drawn out four handfuls [of earth].
One should perform the bath early in the morning, especially before midday;
being self-restrained, one should take earth and fresh cow dung.
Having set [the water] aside and sipped water (ācamana) in that manner, one should then perform the bath;
having washed both hands and feet, one should perform the binding of the topknot (śikhābandha).
The head should be washed with one application of clay; likewise, the area above the navel with two;
the area below [the navel] should be treated with four; and the feet likewise with six.
[75] Having washed his entire body and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the rule,
he should then perform the cleansing with earth, first reciting the mantra.
“O Vasundharā, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!
You were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.”
O Earth, I take you along with progeny and wealth;
O Earth, you are bestowed by Brahmā and consecrated by Kaśyapa.
"O Earth, destroy for me everything that has been done by me as evil. O Earth, grant me nourishment; in you all things are established.
And again, with cow dung, saying "the foremost, the foremost," he should apply it.
“The foremost of the foremost herbs, moving through the forest, [drinks] the essence.”
"O cow dung, you are the purifier and the cleanser of the body for those wives of the Ṛṣabhas; O cow dung, drive away my diseases, my sorrows, and my sin!
With these two verses beginning with "From joint to joint," one should touch each limb.
“Growing from joint to joint, from node to node.”
Thus, O Durvā grass, spread forth for us with a hundredfold and a thousandfold;
you who spread with a hundred and grow with a thousand.
"O Goddess Brick, we shall worship you with this oblation.
Having thus performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*) with the mantras beginning with "Aśvakrāntā," one should then proceed.

One should invoke the divine waters for the sake of immortality during the offerings of the pigeon with the two verses beginning "Those which are yours, a hundred," and thereafter one should invoke the sacred bathing-places (tīrthas).
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, Gaṅgā, Prabhāsa, and the Puṣkara lakes—
having [visited] these, one should consecrate [the water] with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and the Gāyatrī.
One should also recite "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and "idam āpaḥ pravahata," as well as "drupadād iva," and likewise the verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and the Pāvamānī hymns at the end.
Then, having looked at the sun and submerged with the syllable *oṃ* within the water,
the wise man should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), as well as the *gāyatrī* and the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
Agitated by those aforementioned [impurities], one should then immerse oneself three times like a staff.
As stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* (Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, 20.145–157):
"Purity and the purification of one's inner disposition do not exist without bathing."
Therefore, for the sake of purifying the mind, bathing is prescribed at the outset.
One should perform the ritual bath with water that has either been drawn out or not drawn out;
the wise one, knowing the mantras, should designate the sacred site (tīrtha) using the root mantra.
[77] "Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa"—this is declared to be the root mantra.
Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, having sipped water according to the rule, being self-restrained and pure;
Having fashioned a square measuring four cubits on all sides,
the wise practitioner should invoke Gaṅgā with these mantras.
“Oṃ! You are born from the foot of Viṣṇu, you belong to Viṣṇu, and you are worshipped by Viṣṇu;
protect us from this sin, from birth until the end of death.”
"Three and a half crores of sacred fords,
O Jāhnavī, exist for you in heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space," so said Vāyu.
Your name among the gods is indeed Nandinī, and also Nalinī;
you are Nandā, Pṛthvī, Subhagā, Viśvakāyā, Śivā, and Sitā.
“Vidyādharī, Suprasannā, as well as Lokaprasādinī,
Kṣemā, Jāhnavī, Śāntā, and Śāntipradāyinī—
one should recite these meritorious names at the time of bathing.”
There, the Gaṅgā, flowing through the three paths, would be present.
Having consecrated water seven times with the mantra, one should place it upon the head with the palms joined, repeating it three, four, five, or seven times.
One should likewise perform the bath with earth, having invoked it according to the ritual rule:
“O Vasundharā, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, trodden by Viṣṇu!”
O Earth, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me;
you were lifted up by the boar Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.
“Salutations to you, O ocean of existence for all the worlds, O you of excellent vows!
Having ascended upon my limbs, release me from all evil. — *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* [57.65–70].
A twice-born man should bathe in rivers and flowing streams while standing against the current;
in waters such as those of tanks and lakes, he should perform his bath facing the sun.
Having sprinkled a clean place with water, one should set down kusha grass, clay, and sesame seeds;
then, having diligently purified one's own body externally with clay and water.
Having thoroughly cleansed his bathing cloth, the wise man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
then, entering the water slowly, he should bow to Varuṇa, the lord of waters.
For by thus remembering Hari with his intellect, one sinks as if into water with an arrow;
then, having reached the shore and sipped water according to the mantra, [one should proceed].
One should sprinkle the god Varuṇa with either mantras or the Pāvamānī verses;
having carefully sprinkled oneself with water held on the tips of kuśa grass.
The twice-born man should apply clay to his body with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and then,
recollecting the god Nārāyaṇa, he should enter the water.
[79] Having fully immersed oneself within the water, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn.
"Facing each sun" means having turned toward the sun (*āditya*).

Having removed impurities with earth and water, one should immerse oneself in the water, sip water, and consecrate the bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse beginning with *idam āpaḥ pravahata*. Then, submerged in the water, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times, or the verse *tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*, or the *drupadā* verse, or the *sāvitrī*, or the section beginning with *yuñjate manaḥ*, or the *puruṣasūkta*. The verse beginning with *idam āpaḥ pravahata* is: "O waters, carry away whatever evil is in me. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.

Having bathed with the hymn beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and having performed purification, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in the midst of water. Bṛhaspati [Ācāra, 22.312] states:
"The mantra 'drupadād iva', which is found in the Vājasaneyaka Veda..."
Having repeated it three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sins.
Dakṣa says:

Cleansing should be performed in the midst of water, followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma) wherever one may be; thereafter comes the ritual attendance (upasthāna), and finally the recitation of the Sāvitrī is prescribed.
“From wherever [it may be],” meaning both in water and on land.
Āpastamba [2.22.13]:
“One should slowly approach the water, striking [the waves] while facing the sun; one should touch the water. This is the rule for touching water in all cases.

“Striking” means splashing water with his hand; the implication is that this is for the purpose of driving away aquatic creatures. “In all cases,” meaning whether [the water] is flowing or not flowing. And because this is recorded in the *Āpastamba-smṛti* within the section on forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), such a bath belongs specifically to the forest-dweller. The *Śāṅkhāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* states: “Having bathed every day with his clothes on, he should put on another garment before performing the water-libations.”

The phrase "wearing clothes" (*savastraḥ*) is for the purpose of obtaining a second garment, because for one who already has a single garment, nakedness is precluded by that very fact; such is the explanation in the *Brahmadatta-bhāṣya*. "Without water" (*an-udakaḥ*) means having not removed the water from the limbs other than the head.
Aṅgiras states: "That bath which is performed without *darbha* grass, and that gift which is given without water..."
And whatever has been recited without counting, all of that is useless.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
When a man is impure, he should immerse himself silently;
thereafter, having sipped water and become purified, he should perform the bath according to the prescribed rule.
A man who performs his bath with water that has been defiled by contact [with impurity],
even if it has been drawn out, shall never become pure.

Water that has been drawn up is indeed unfit to be taken, as is water from its first surge; likewise, water that has been stirred up by anyone or has issued from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) is not to be used.
The ritual procedure for them, beginning with the attendance [of the teacher] and including the recitation of mantras,
which ends with the formal offering— that, the exponents of Brahman say, is "bathing."
From conception until the cemetery, according to the evidence of the Vedas,
no rite whatsoever for the twice-born is performed without a mantra.
Likewise: Fish, turtles, and frogs remain submerged in the water day and night;
even though they dwell there, having bathed, they never deserve the fruit [of that act].
Whatever action is performed by men, joined with faith and the prescribed ritual,
and with a perfectly pure disposition, that conduces to infinity.
Whatever is performed devoid of prescribed rules, corrupted by intention, and done without faith—
that is seized by the Asuras from that deluded person of undisciplined self.
For the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, bathing accompanied by mantras is prescribed;
for the Śūdra, it is traditionally ordained to be performed silently, with a salutation.
By performing ritual bathing, one is liberated from the sin of approaching those who should not be approached, from women, from accepting gifts from the wicked, and from sins committed in secret.
If one is unable to perform the acts of *juhoti* and *yajati*,
the wise person should purify himself through bathing, meditation, recitation, and giving.
Whatever bath one performs with a purified inner self,
by that alone one obtains the entire fruit of ritual sacrifices and ceremonial acts.
Having taken up the bow of Yama, firm and strung with the string of self-restraint,
one should diligently fix the arrow of self-control upon the target of heaven.
He who does not possess this supreme weapon, the means for attaining heaven,
shall not achieve that ultimate goal even in thousands of births.

“Impure” means due to contact with a *caṇḍāla* or similar causes necessitating a bath. “In a river” refers here to a river that was previously dry. “Agitated” means rendered extremely turbid by buffaloes or other animals. “Departed from the bathing-place” means having left the sacred site (*tīrtha*), such that it is no longer recognized as that specific *tīrtha*. “The ritual attendance” is performed with the mantra beginning “*uruṃ hi rājā*. “Of them” refers to the waters. “Ending with the announcement” means ending with the whispered announcement using the mantra “*devā gātuvida*. “Conception” (*niṣeka*) refers to the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*). “Devoid of the prescribed rule” means lacking the procedure as stated above. Regarding the phrase “for a Śūdra, accompanied by a salutation,” the meaning is that a Śūdra should perform merely the immersion in water together with a salutation to the water. “That supreme” means that heaven and so forth are the highest goal.
Furthermore, Yogi-Yājñavalkya says:
"This entire supreme rule for bathing has been declared to you,
along with its merits when practiced and its faults when neglected."
Likewise:
having bathed in this manner and put on two clean, unwashed garments,
one should wash the thighs, the feet, and the hands as well.
In the absence of a washed cloth, one may use hemp, linen, or skins;
or a kutapa or a yoga-band, by which one indeed becomes "doubly clad."
As long as one has not offered libations to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors,
one should not wring out the garment with which one has bathed, nor should one do so in the water.
If one wrings out the bathing cloth before the libation (tarpaṇa),
his ancestors depart disappointed, as do the gods together with the great sages.

“Kutapa” refers to a woolen blanket from Nepal (*nepālakambala*). Regarding the phrase “by which he is doubly clothed,” the state of being doubly clothed must be established even by means of the previously mentioned items such as the *kutapa*. “By which he has bathed” means by which garment he has bathed. The connection is: “and not in water, he should wring out the garment.
In the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* (58.72–73):
“A garment that is dyed red, excessively bright, or worn out is not praised.”
A wise person should avoid clothing that is stained with dirt or worn for less than ten days.
Then the wise man should wash his feet with clay and water.
Parāśara [12.12–13]:
The deities follow a Brāhmaṇa who is coming to bathe.
And the highly fortunate ancestors, having become like the wind, sought water.
Having bathed and discarded his other garment, he washed his shanks in the water;
those two, however, were rendered impure by the dripping water from his loincloth.
The ancestors go forth as hungry ghosts when the wringing out of the cloth is performed;
therefore, one should not wring out the cloth without having first offered libations to the ancestors.
If any twice-born person, weak in knowledge, wrings out his garment while in the midst of the water, his bath shall be in vain.
"Kaupīnaś cyotavāriṇā": *kaupīna* refers to the region of the hips; [the phrase means] "with water dripping from that.
After the ritual of bathing, [one should wear] a conch-shell [amulet].
For, by not pouring out water, one should not wring out the bathing cloth.
Having bathed according to this procedure, one enjoys meritorious fruit.
Hārīta: Having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs, nor shake the head, nor exchange the upper garment. Viṣṇu [64.10–15]:

Having bathed, one should not shake one's head; one should not wipe water from one's limbs; one should not touch oil or fat; nor should one wear a garment previously worn without first washing it. Having bathed, one should wear two washed garments along with a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*). One should not engage in conversation with barbarians (*mleccha*), outcastes (*antyaja*), or those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*). "Oil and fat" (*tailavase*) refers to oil and muscle-fat. The word "previously worn" (*pūrvadhṛtam*) implies [worn] on the limbs. A "turban" (*uṣṇīṣa*) is a head-wrap intended for removing water from the hair and beard, to be used only for as long as it takes to remove that water.
And so it is said in the Mahābhārata:
Having bathed in fragrant water infused with perfumes,
and having donned a turban that resembles a royal swan and is fastened loosely.
Indeed, for the purpose of exhausting the water, he encircled the summit.
"Loosely applied" means not firmly bound.
Manu [4.83]: "One who has bathed his head with oil should not touch any part of his body at all."

When the head-bath has been performed, not even a single limb should come into contact with oil. Furthermore, the word *taila* (oil) occurs in the sense of sesame oil through both its etymological derivation (*yoga*) and its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Its application to mustard oil and the like occurs because of the suffix *-tailac* according to the Vārttika rule: "The suffix *-tailac* is applied after a word denoting an oily substance" (Vārttika 3118).
This concludes the procedure for bathing.
Having bathed at midday, one should then perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) according to the previously stated rules.
"For the twice-born who knows the Self, the three twilight devotions must always be performed"—so says the *Yogiyājñavalkya*. And Śaṅkha, having described the midday twilight devotion, states:
"This very same rule is prescribed for the twice-born during the two twilights."
Because it is stated thus.
This was said by Śaṅkha [9.16–20]:
"Having sipped water (ācamya) in the manner previously described, those [mantras] which were mentioned for the cleansing of the sacred sites (tīrtha)."
One should sprinkle water consecrated by those mantras upon the head and likewise upon the ground.
By water sprinkled upon the head, his sin is destroyed;
by water sprinkled upon the ground, the asuras, the enemies of the gods, are slain.
[87] One should recite the *vyāhṛtis* as well as the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*).
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*) according to the Dharma with this mantra.
“You move within all beings, dwelling in their secret cave, facing every direction;
you are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ* call, you are water, light, essence, and immortality.
Having sipped water (*ācamana*), he should thereafter face the sun and [offer] water.
One should deposit it with the mantra beginning, "ud u tyam jātavedasam."
This very same rule is prescribed for the twice-born regarding the two twilights:
one should stand reciting the prayers during the morning twilight, and likewise sit during the evening twilight.
Then one should recite purifying mantras or a single purifying mantra according to one's capacity;
by virtue of their long twilight devotions, the seers attained long life.

“Those previously mentioned,” beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and ending with *idam āpaḥ pravahata*, are indeed those declared by Śaṅkha. “The purifiers” are likewise those declared by Śaṅkha, such as the *aghamarṣaṇa* and others.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
The Section on Bathing within the Chapter on Rituals for Fixed Times.
[88] 3 Now follows the procedure for recitation (japavidhi).
Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:

Having sipped water, seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, and facing the east, one should repeat the Sāvitrī one thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, provided it is at least ten times. Then one worships the sun with the verses: "Out of the darkness we have risen," "Upwards that one," "The bright," "That eye established by the gods," and "He who has risen. Furthermore, they cite: "The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the Sāvitrī—these five are the Brahmayajñas; day after day they purify the Brāhmaṇa from sin."

Regarding the phrase “an immeasurable number of times” (*aparimitakṛtvaḥ*), it should be understood as referring to a count other than the hundreds and so forth already mentioned, yet exceeding ten and falling short of a hundred, because of the expression “ten at most” (*daśavarām*). “*Ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*” refers to the *ṛc* beginning with: “*Ud vayaṃ tamasas pari paśyanto jyotir uttaram*. “*Ud u tyam*” refers to the verse beginning with: “*Ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam*. “*Citram*” refers to the verse beginning with: “*Citraṃ devānām*. “*Ya udagāt*” refers to the verse beginning with: “*Ya udagān mahato ’rṇavāt*. —Yogiyājñavalkya.
Having sipped water once, one should sip again with the appropriate mantra during bathing and eating;
likewise, one should repeat the Drupadā verse three times and also the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
By reciting the Gāyatrī three times, as well as the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and likewise with the silent Oṃ,
water drunk in this manner destroys all evil.
Having sipped water and purified himself, and having sipped water three times slowly,
he should then worship the Sun with water and flowers held above him.
Having thrown [the water] in, one should recite "ud vayam," "ud u tyam," "citram tat cakṣuḥ," and also "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"; these verses are auspicious and purifying.
With arms raised and composed in mind, he should recite this while gazing at the sun;
having performed the ritual attendance upon the Sun-god with the Gāyatrī mantra according to his ability.
With the Anuvāka beginning with "vibhrāṭ," with the Puruṣasūkta,
with the Śivasankalpa, and likewise with the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa.
[90] The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) should indeed be performed according to one's ability with the Divākīrti hymns, the Saura mantras, and other mantras proclaimed by all the gods.
For the perfection of recitation, various purificatory texts, other [mantras], as well as the secret Upaniṣads and the diverse sciences of the supreme self (adhyātmavidyā) should be chanted.
Having performed a circumambulation from left to right, having paid homage,
and having sat down upon *darbha* grass with *darbha* blades in hand, he should face the east with palms joined in reverence.
One should perform the private recitation of the Veda according to one's ability for the sake of the Brahma-sacrifice;
indeed, such a person performs the highest austerity from the hair of the head down to the tips of the nails.
That twice-born man who, even while wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily according to his ability—
beginning from the beginning and proceeding step by step from top to bottom after having bathed.
That which one studies daily according to one's ability is known as *svādhyāya*.

“Consecrated with mantras such as *mantravat* and *drupadāv iva*”: this option of mantras for the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) is established according to the specific results desired. “Having purified (*pāvya*)” means having performed the sprinkling (*mārjana*). The *anuvāka* beginning with “*vibhrāḍ*” is that which starts with “*vibhrāḍ bṛhat pibatu somyaṃ madhu*. The “*Śivasankalpa*” is that which begins with “*yaj jāgrato dūram*. “With the *Divākīrtyas*” refers to those texts, such as the *Śatarudriya*, which are to be recited during the day according to the tradition of the students. “With those proclaimed in all the Vedas” means those recited in all the Vedas. “Purifiers” means sanctifying. “With the secret *Upaniṣad*” refers to the portion of the *Upaniṣads* that directly teaches the Supreme Self. “Spiritual science” (*adhyātmavidyā*) includes other works besides the *Upaniṣads*. “Wearing a garland” (*sragvī*) is an indicative term for one who has returned home after completing his studies (*samāvṛtta*).
In the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* [58.77,
85, 87, 88]: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, with *darbha* grass in hand, facing east and well-composed,
one should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the scriptures, without sloth."
Having bathed day after day, the twice-born who knows the ritual of recitation should mutter the Sāvitrī;
then, having approached with a handful of flowers, he should offer them to the Sun with his arms raised.
He should also mutter that mantra, "ud u tyam," as well as "citraṃ tac cakṣuḥ";
then, having circumambulated and paid homage to the Lord, he should depart.
Vasiṣṭha and Śaṅkha-Likhita:
"Henceforth, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by the recitation and burnt offerings of which people are purified; of this there is no doubt."
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās, the Kūṣmāṇḍyas, the Pāvamānīs, as well as the Durgā and the Sāvitrī.
The *abhīṣaṅgas*, the *padastobhas*, the *sāmans*, as well as the *vyāhṛtis*,
the *bhāruṇḍa* *sāmans*, the *gāyatra*, and likewise the *raivata*.
The Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa, as well as the Devavratas,
the Abliṅga, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and likewise the Madhvṛcas.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Triṣuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta, the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans known as Indraśuddha;
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these songs purify living beings.
He who so desires shall obtain the recollection of his past births.

The mantras beginning with “*devakṛtam*” and “*devakṛtasyainasaḥ*” [are included]. The verse illuminating Durgā beginning with “*durgā*” and “*jātavedasaḥ*” [is included]. The *Sāvitrī* beginning with “*tat savituḥ*” [is included]. The three *Sāmans* known as the *Abhiṣaṅgas*, beginning with “*purojitī vo andhasaḥ*” [are included]. The four *Sāmans* beginning with the eight *Iḍās* are the *Padastobhas*. Regarding the phrase “*sāmāni vyāhṛtīs tathā*,” the meaning is the *Vyāhṛti-sāmans*. The twenty-one *Sāmans* well-known among the Rāṇāyanīyas, beginning with “*yat te kṛṣṇaḥ śakuna ā tutoda pipīlaḥ sarpaḥ*,” are the *Bhāruṇḍas*. The verses beginning with “*āpo hi ṣṭhā*” are the *Abliṅgas*. The verse beginning with “*gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatim*” is the *Bārhaspatya*. The *Vāksūkta* beginning with “*bṛhaspate prathamaṃ vāco agram*” [is included]. The three verses beginning with “*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*” are the *Madhvṛcas*. The eleven sections (*anuvākas*) beginning with “*namas te rudra manyave*” constitute the *Śatarudriya*. The *Atharvaśiras* beginning with “*brahmā devānāṃ prathamaḥ*” [is included]. The three sections well-known among the Taittirīyas, beginning with “*brahma metu mām*,” are the *Trisuparṇas*. The *Mahāvrata* is the *Sāman* beginning with “*somaṃ rājānam*. The *Gosūkta* and *Aśvasūkta* are two *Sāmans* well-known in the verse beginning with “*yad indrāhaṃ yathā tvam*. The two *Indraśuddha Sāmans* are well-known in the verse beginning with “*etonvindraṃ stavāma*. These are additional in the *Atrisṃṛti*. Atri says:
The *Vimala*, the *Śivasaṃkalpa*, the *Vivarṇa*, and then the *Rohita*.
The *Vimala* begins with "The swan dwelling in purity" (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣad*), and so forth. In the *Viṣṇusmṛti*, the *Nārāyaṇīya* is additional; the *Nārāyaṇīya* is an Upaniṣad of the Taittirīyas.
[Then] Manu.
One should constantly recite the Veda at the proper times without weariness;
for they declare that to be the supreme dharma, while any other is called a secondary dharma.
Through constant study of the Vedas, through purity, through austerity,
and through non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Having recollected his former birth, the twice-born practices Brahman;
through the practice of Brahman, he enjoys eternal and infinite bliss.

[95] “Upadharma” is a practice that yields little fruit. “Tapaḥ” refers to ascetic penances such as the *kṛcchra*. “Brahma” is the Veda. “Anantam” means that which is to be enjoyed for a long period of time. Thus says Hārīta.

The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī* constitute the *sāvitra*; by means of this, one is released from sins. By reciting it a hundred times, one becomes purified from mental sins; by reciting it a thousand times, one becomes purified from verbal sins; by reciting it ten thousand times, one’s self becomes purified in every respect. *Mārjana* (the act of cleansing) is the purifier consisting of the mantra "May you not wipe away my life and vitality"; by means of this, one is released from all sins. One should mutter over the water the verses beginning with "O divine waters, we are pure," "Golden-colored, bright are the waters," and "O mothers, [purify] us"—these are the *śuddhavatīs*. Or, one should offer *apāmārga* stalks as an oblation; thus one becomes pure. One should mutter the verse "This prayer... (*imāṃ dhiyam*), or "A hundred [salutations] to you, O King," or "Crossing over [the flood], O victorious one" (*taratsamandīyas taran*); thus one becomes pure. The verse "O Soma, [from those who have harmed our bodies]" (*tvaṃ soma tanūkṛdbhyaḥ*) is the *tanūkṛt* purifier, by which one is released from harm caused by oneself and by others. One should mutter it over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, and fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. The seven verses beginning with "O Agni, you purify lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*) constitute the *śucimat* purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter them over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. By the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with "O Agni, you are the fuel-stick of the fire; protect me from calumny" (*agneḥ samidasi abhiśastyā mā pāhi*), one is released from accusations. The three verses beginning with "From the ocean, a wave... (*samudrād ūrmir*) constitute the *ṛṣabha* purifier, by which one is released from sins committed against the senses. Having transgressed against one's mother and father, one should worship the Sun with the verse "That which is the intermediate space... (*yad antarikṣam*); thus one becomes pure. The five verses beginning with "This [is for you], O Mitra and Varuṇa" (*ayaṃ vāṃ mitrāvaruṇā*), the four beginning with "Homage to you, O King Varuṇa" (*namas te rājan varuṇa*), and the verses "From every station, the highest... (*dhāmno dhāmna ud uttamam*) and "Away with your anger" (*ava te heḍaḥ*) constitute the *nirvaruṇa* purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter them over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. One should mutter the entire section beginning with "O divine waters" (*devīr āpaḥ*) over water; thus one becomes pure. The hymn beginning with "This praise is worthy of you" (*imaṃ stomam arhataḥ*) is the *rocana* purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter it over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. The hymn beginning with "You are the fair-winged Garuḍa" (*suparṇo 'si garutmān*) is the *sauparṇa* purifier; it is taught for use prior to the *viṣṇukrama* steps in cases of poisoning, snakebite, or injury. The three verses beginning with "By what [means], O wonderful one? (*kayā naścitra*) constitute the *vāmadevya* purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter them over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. The hymn beginning with "Bestow radiance upon us" (*rucaṃ no dhehi*) is the *suruca* purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter it over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. The hymn beginning with "Not him by day" (*na tam ahan*) is a purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter it over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. The hymn beginning with "That I implore of you" (*tat tvā yāmi*) is the *vāruṇa* purifier, by which one is released from all sins. One should mutter it over water, or offer clarified butter, sesame seeds, or fuel-sticks as oblations, and worship the Sun; thus one becomes pure. One should mutter the sixteen *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "May the fathers purify me" (*punantu mā pitaraḥ*) over water; thus one becomes pure. One should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍī* verses beginning with "Whatever offense against the gods, O gods" (*yad devā devaheḍanam*); thus one becomes pure. By reciting the *pavitram asi* and the *drupadād iva* mantras, and the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra three times while submerged in water, one is released even from the murder of a Brahmin. In all afflictions or calamities, one should mutter [the appropriate mantras] until completion; thus one is released from misfortune. If one mutters the *sāvitra* mantra "Aditi" and "Tayet," and the *vāruṇa* mantra "Whatever this is" (*yat kiṃ cedaṃ varuṇam*) three times while submerged in water, one is released from all sins. One should worship the Sun with the verse "With the black [steed]" (*ā kṛṣṇena*); thus one becomes a self purified in every way. By muttering the six verses [beginning with "I am the food of the gods"], one does not enter a womb again and becomes a rememberer of former births. Thus, one should worship the quarters in their respective directions with the mantras dedicated to Indra, Yama, Soma, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni, and the Sun; thus one becomes a self purified in every way.

“From mental” (*mānasāt*) means from mental sin. “From verbal” (*vākkṛtāt*) means from verbal sin. “From all” (*sarvataḥ*) means from sins committed by speech, mind, and body. Because of the designation “cleansing” (*mārjana*), the fruit results precisely from this cleansing with the mantra. “*Apāmārga*” refers to *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, since Hārīta specifically prescribes them as the form of the fuel-sticks for the oblation. “Crossing” (*taran*) is by means of a boat and so forth, according to the wording of the mantra: “May we board a well-oared ship. “From that committed by oneself” (*tanukṛtāt*) means from physical [sin]. “From that committed by another” (*anyakṛtāt*)—the ellipsis is to be supplied as “from sin committed by others,” whether mental, verbal, or by sons, disciples, and so on. “The pure” (*śucimat*) refers to that which establishes purity, as stated in the verses beginning with “*pavasva*. “Accusation” (*abhiśaṃsana*) means a curse; Jayasvāmin holds that this [mantra] belongs to the one who utters the curse. “*Nirvaruṇa*” is its name. “From the Viṣṇu-strides” (*viṣṇukramebhyaḥ*) refers to the mantras beginning with “*Viṣṇoḥ kramo ‘si*. “Poison” (*garaḥ*) is venom whose potency is neutralized by spells, herbs, and the like. “Bitten” (*daṣṭaḥ*) means by a dog or similar creature. “The Vāmadevya” is that seen by the seer Vāmadeva. “Affliction” (*ārtiḥ*) is caused by disease and so forth. “The *Samāptika*” is the section of the text beginning with “*agner manve prathamam*.”

Yājñavalkya [1.101]: For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite according to one's ability the Vedas, the Atharvaveda, the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas, as well as spiritual knowledge (adhyātmikī vidyā).

[99] Viṣṇu [64.36–39]: Having bathed, one should recite purificatory texts according to one's ability, especially the Sāvitrī or the Puruṣasūkta; there is nothing superior to these two. Manu and Yama state this in the first chapter [Manu 2.81–84].
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable Oṃ,
together with the three-footed Gāyatrī— this should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing the form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic rites of oblation and sacrifice flow away;
however, the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as the Imperishable, as Brahman, and indeed as Prajāpati.

“This *gāyatrī*”: [he becomes] “one who has become wind,” meaning one whose movement is as swift as the wind, or one who abides in the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*). “Possessing the form of space,” being all-pervasive like the ether, he becomes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). “They perish” means they become subject to destruction. “The Imperishable” (*akṣara*) is the syllable *oṃ*; its fruit is liberation. It is called “the Imperishable” because it does not decay. And the state of being Prajāpati should be understood as belonging to the *oṃkāra*, since it is that which expresses him. “The state of being the Imperishable” is the state of being Brahman. The sages said to Yama: “What indeed is the supreme Brahman? What indeed is the supreme austerity?”
[100] What indeed is superior to fasting, and what excels silence?
Yama said:
"The syllable Om is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī mantra; and truth excels silence."
All ritual acts performed here on earth according to the Vedas are perishable;
however, one should know that the Imperishable (akṣara) is indeed Brahman and Prajāpati.
The single syllable is remembered as the supreme Brahman and the highest purifier;
there is nothing higher than the Gāyatrī, and truth excels silence.
One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī, the goddess who destroys all sins, consisting of a maximum of one thousand, a middle of a hundred, or a minimum of ten repetitions.
The Lord weighed the Gāyatrī and the Vedas on a scale:
on one side were the four Vedas, together with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas) and their word-for-word analyses (padakrama).
And on one side [he recited] the Gāyatrī; it is remembered as being of equal form.
"He" refers to Prajāpati. "Together with the *padakrama*" means accompanied by the *pada* and *krama* methods. Aṅgiras.
Likewise, the Vedas, beginning with the Praṇava, are contained within the Praṇava;
the Praṇava is the entirety of speech. Therefore, one should practice the Praṇava.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the Praṇava, in the seven Vyāhṛtis,
and in the three-footed Gāyatrī, no fear exists anywhere.
[101] Dakṣa is the seer; Savitṛ is its deity; Agni is its mouth; it stands with three feet;
Viśvāmitra is the ṛṣi; the metre is Gāyatrī; that [Gāyatrī] is preeminent.
"Tripāt": it should be understood that the *gāyatrī* stands with three feet. Yama says:
"A twice-born man does not burn away his sin so effectively by the recitation of the Vedas as he does by [the *gāyatrī*]."
Just as one is liberated from all sins by the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra.

Thus have been declared the purifiers of the Veda. Among these, the Sāvitrī is preeminent. There is nothing superior to the Aghamarṣaṇa for recitation while submerged in water; nothing superior to the Vyāhṛtis for an oblation; and nothing superior to the Sāvitrī for silent recitation (japa). Seated upon a mat of Kuśa grass or one with Kuśa grass spread over it, holding Kuśa blades as a purifier in his hand, facing north or toward the sun, and taking up a rosary, he should perform the recitation while meditating on the deity. He should make the rosary from any one of the following: gold, gems, pearls, crystal, lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, or putrajīvaka. Alternatively, he may count using knots of Kuśa grass or by the movements of his fingers. At the beginning, he should remember the deity, the seer (ṛṣi), and the meter (chandas). Then, having first repeated the Vyāhṛtis preceded by the Praṇava, he should repeat the Gāyatrī. Now, Savitṛ is its deity, Viśvāmitra is the seer, and Gāyatrī is the meter. The syllable *oṃ* is called the Praṇava. *Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam*—these are the Great Vyāhṛtis. *Āpo jyotī raso ’mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ* is the Head (Śīrṣa). Regarding this, there are these verses: [102] *Āpo jyotī raso ’mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ* is the Head. Herein there are also these verses: [103] *The Praṇava is the beginning of all mantras; it is the supreme Brahman. Without the Praṇava, the mantra is like a body without a head.* [104] *The Vyāhṛtis are the limbs of the mantra; the Sāvitrī is its heart. Without the limbs and the heart, the mantra is indeed lifeless.* [105] *He who recites the Gāyatrī without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, the Praṇava, and the Head—he eats only sin.* [106] *One should always recite the Gāyatrī with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Head. This is the highest purification; it destroys all sins.* [107] *Just as fire consumes dry wood, so does the Gāyatrī, when recited with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, consume all evil deeds.* [108] *A thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, accompanied by the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, are equal to the study of all the Vedas.* [109] *Whether one has committed a great sin or even the murder of a Brahmin, the Gāyatrī, recited ten thousand times, purifies him in no time.* [110] *The Gāyatrī is the mother of the Vedas; she is the source of all mantras. She who knows her thus is truly learned; others are merely carriers of books.* [111] *The Gāyatrī is the supreme Brahman, the essence of all the Vedas. To her, the wise offer oblations with devotion through the fire of their speech.* [112] *He who recites the Gāyatrī at dawn and at sunset, with a concentrated mind, is freed from all sins and attains union with Brahman.* [113] *The Gāyatrī is the most excellent of meters, the most auspicious of prayers, and the most sacred of all purifiers; there is nothing higher than her.* [114] *She who protects those who recite her is called Gāyatrī. She is the mother of the three worlds and the sustainer of all beings.* [115] *He who abandons the Gāyatrī and takes up another prayer is like one who abandons the Ganges and seeks a puddle in a cow’s footprint.* [116] *The Gāyatrī is the boat that carries across the ocean of worldly existence; she is the ladder that leads upward to the world of Brahman.* [117] *Therefore, one should always recite the Gāyatrī with devotion, for she is the supreme means of liberation and the destroyer of all suffering.* [118] *The Gāyatrī is the root of the universe; she is the seed of all creation. He who knows her thus is a knower of the Veda and is liberated from rebirth.* [119] *The Gāyatrī is the light of lights, the immortal among mortals, the truth of truths; she is the eternal Brahman, beyond all change.* [120] *May the Gāyatrī, who is the source of the three Vedas and the mother of the gods, grant us long life, wisdom, and the highest bliss.* [121] *Thus ends the exposition of the purifiers of the Veda, wherein the Sāvitrī is established as the most distinguished.* [122] *There is nothing superior to the Aghamarṣaṇa for recitation while submerged in water; nothing superior to the Vyāhṛtis for an oblation; and nothing superior to the Sāvitrī for silent recitation.* [123] *Seated upon a mat of Kuśa grass or one with Kuśa grass spread over it, holding Kuśa blades as a purifier in his hand, facing north or toward the sun, and taking up a rosary, he should perform the recitation while meditating on the deity.* [124] *He should make the rosary from any one of the following: gold, gems, pearls, crystal, lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, or putrajīvaka; or he may use knots of Kuśa grass or count by the movements of his fingers.* [125] *At the beginning, he should remember the deity, the seer, and the meter. Then, having first repeated the Vyāhṛtis preceded by the Praṇava, he should repeat the Gāyatrī.* [126] *Now, Savitṛ is its deity, Viśvāmitra is the seer, and Gāyatrī is the meter. The syllable *oṃ* is called the Praṇava.* [127] *Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam—these are the Great Vyāhṛtis.* [128] *Āpo jyotī raso ’mṛtaṃ brahma bhūr bhuvaḥ svar oṃ is the Head. Regarding this, there are also these verses:* [129] *The Praṇava is the beginning of all mantras; it is the supreme Brahman. Without the Praṇava, the mantra is like a body without a head.* [130] *The Vyāhṛtis are the limbs of the mantra; the Sāvitrī is its heart. Without the limbs and the heart, the mantra is indeed lifeless.* [131] *He who recites the Gāyatrī without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, the Praṇava, and the Head—he eats only sin.* [132] *One should always recite the Gāyatrī with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Head. This is the highest purification; it destroys all sins.* [133] *Just as fire consumes dry wood, so does the Gāyatrī, when recited with the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, consume all evil deeds.* [134] *A thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī, accompanied by the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, are equal to the study of all the
For those who always recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, no fear exists anywhere.
When recited one hundred times, that goddess destroys the sins of the day;
when recited one thousand times, she likewise grants liberation from great transgressions.
Recited ten thousand times, she destroys all sins;
when recited one hundred thousand times, that goddess destroys even the great transgressions.

A Brahmin who has stolen gold, a killer of a Brahmin, one who has violated the teacher’s bed, and a drinker of liquor—all these are purified by a hundred thousand recitations; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) every morning with a concentrated mind,
one is liberated at that very moment from the sins committed during the day and night.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin within a month.
Gāyatrī is the mother of the Vedas; Gāyatrī is the destroyer of sin.
There is no purifier higher than Gāyatrī, neither in heaven nor here on earth.
The goddess Hastatrāṇapadā protects those falling into the ocean of hell;
therefore, a pure Brahmin should constantly practice her in his heart.
One who is devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī should be employed in rites for the gods and ancestors;
no sin remains in him, just as a drop of water does not stay upon a lotus leaf.
[103] One shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt regarding this concerning Brahman.
Whether one performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
The whispered recitation is said to be a hundredfold [more effective], and the mental recitation is remembered as a thousandfold.
A wise person should not perform the recitation aloud, especially in the case of the Sāvitrī.
A person devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī attains heaven;
one devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī also finds the means to liberation.
Therefore, having bathed with every effort and with a restrained mind,
one should recite the Gāyatrī with devotion, for it destroys all impurities.

“Vṛṣī” is a small seat. “Indrākṣa” is *āruka* (the marking nut plant). “Hastopayāma” is the bending of the fingers. “At the beginning” means at the commencement of the recitation (*japa*). “Pure in heart” means having a pure mind. “The means to liberation” is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
[These are taught] by Yājñavalkya, Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, and Hārīta in the first two verses:
“The four *pākayajñas*, together with the *vidhiyajñas*, [are the sacrifices].”
All of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
A Brahmin who has attained perfection through recitation alone—of this there is no doubt—may perform other rites or may not; he is called a Brahmin who is a friend to all (maitra).
Neither while walking, nor laughing, nor looking to the side;
neither leaning against anything, nor talking, nor likewise with his head covered.
One should not recite while stepping with one foot upon the other, nor likewise with the hands;
nor with an unconcentrated mind, nor while causing others to hear.
Secret gifts, knowledge free from egoism,
and well-guarded recitations— their fruit is infinite.
For one engaged in whispered recitation, the merit becomes a hundredfold compared to that which is audible;
mental recitation is said to be a thousandfold, for it is indeed equal to meditative concentration.
Since that which is whispered occurs merely by the movement of the lips,
one should place the tongue in a state free from conceptualization while on the path and contemplate that which is indeed mental.
If standing, he should perform the recitation while gazing at the sun with a concentrated mind;
otherwise, he should face the east, proceeding according to the sequence to be described.
Seated thus on a beautiful seat covered with kusha grass whose tips point eastward— a seat that is neither too high nor too low— with darbha grass in hand and well-composed.
A rosary should be made from crystal, indrākṣa, rudrākṣa, or those produced from the putrajīva tree; each subsequent one is indeed superior to the preceding.
An increase of ten million and so forth occurs, especially when using a rosary;
therefore, it is superior, even more so than the other.
In the absence of a rosary, however, one should perform the recitation with the tips of the fingers using knots of *kuśa* grass,
indeed with a one-pointed mind alone.
One should contemplate the mantra with the mind, without moving the tongue or the lips;
one should not shake the head or the neck, nor should one expose the teeth.
Since yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, siddhas, vidyādharas,
and uragas may carry it off by force, one should therefore practice it in secret.
Either at the edge of water, or in a fire-sanctuary, or even in a temple by the water;
or in a cow-pen, at a sacred ford, in a field of the Siddhas, or in one’s own home.
Recitation performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; at a river, it is remembered as having a two-fold merit;
in a cow-pen, it has a ten-fold merit; and in a fire-sanctuary, it has ten times more than that.
In sacred fields of accomplishment, at holy fords, and in the presence of a deity, [the merit] is a hundred billionfold; but in the presence of Viṣṇu, it is infinite.
Vegetables, barley-gruel, alms-food, milk, roots,
fruits, curd, clarified butter, and likewise water— these are indeed recommended in successive order.
For indeed, fasting, eating alms-food, eating at night, or eating food not requested;
as well as lotus stalks, water chestnuts, lotus roots, and sacrificial foods—these are [permitted].
These are said to be the secondary vows (anuvrata) prescribed for the practice of recitation (japa);
one should not speak during the time of recitation, nor during the performance of vows, fire-oblations (homa), and the like.
But if a most excellent twice-born man should arrive while they are thus occupied,
one should salute that Brahmin and then inquire after his well-being and security.
During the time of recitation, as well as during vows, fire-offerings, and other such rites, one should not speak with women, Śūdras, outcasts, donkeys, or women in their menses.
One should remain silent while muttering prayers upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, a Pukkasa, or others of that sort; having touched water, spoken to them, and bathed, one should mutter the prayers once more.
[106] Having sipped water and being purified, one should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to one's enthusiasm and the *pāvamānī* verses according to one's ability.
Having recited or touched fierce, friendly, demonic, Rākṣasa, or malevolent spells,
one should touch water and then perform other [ritual] acts.
Having uttered these [mantras] beginning with "raudra," and without touching water, whatever action the twice-born performs thereafter becomes improper.
If there should be any lapse in the restraint of speech during the recitation of mantras and the like,
one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.

“*Pākayajñas*” are the sacrifices to the gods (*devayajña*) and so forth, excluding the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). “*Vidhiyajñas*” are the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites. “*Mitra*” means a friend; he is the friend of all beings. And the state of being a friend to all beings is attained by performing the *japayajña*, which consists of non-violence and excludes sacrifices that involve violence as a component. “*Caṅkraman*” means moving here and there. “*Apāśritaḥ*” implies leaning against a wall or similar object. “*Karau*” implies stepping upon with the feet. The meaning is that the *japa* performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*) is “a hundredfold more effective” than that which is “*śaṃsya*,” i.e., to be recited aloud. By the word “ten million” (*koṭi*) and so forth, numbers such as “one hundred million” (*arbuda*) and others are included. “*Prasabham*” means forcibly. “*Carus*” are specific preparations of boiled rice (*śālīpāka*). “*Bisa*” means lotus fiber (*mṛṇāla*). “*Haviṣyānnāni*” refers to grains such as barley (*yava*) and *ṣaṣṭika* rice. “*Anuvratāni*” are the subsidiary observances belonging to the vow of the *japayajña*. “*Eteṣu*” refers to these acts such as *japa* and *homa*. “*Avasaktam*” means occupied or engaged. The connection is: “having addressed them. “*Ayathāyatham*” means fruitless.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa [58.78–82]:
"The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is threefold; learn its divisions:
it is traditionally held to be of three kinds—vocal, whispered, and mental."
Among the three types of recitation-sacrifices (*japayajña*), each subsequent one is superior to the preceding:
that which is performed with syllables clearly articulated through high, low, and circumflex accents.
One should pronounce the mantra clearly; that is the vocal sacrifice of recitation (japa).
One should pronounce the mantra softly, moving the lips slightly.
One should know that when one makes a slight sound oneself, it is remembered as *upāṃśu* (whispered) recitation;
whereas that which proceeds through the mind, syllable by syllable and word by word, is mental recitation.

The practice of contemplating the meaning of the words is said to be mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*). Regarding the statement, "One should know the sound oneself," the meaning is that no other person should perceive that sound. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.
The silent recitation (*japa*) and the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) performed with the *Sāvitrī* through mental self-study (*svādhyāya*) have been explained.

"Recitation" (*japa*) here refers to the recitation of other mantras. The meaning is that just as there is a specific procedure and fruit for the mental self-study of the *Gāyatrī*, so too it applies to this recitation and the sacrifice to Brahman.
Regarding the section on the sacrifice to Brahman, Āpastamba states [1.11.18–20]:

The rule for this is as follows: Having not yet eaten his morning meal, having gone to the edge of water, being self-restrained, he should study in a clean place according to the *svādhyāya*, either by means of speech when reciting, or mentally during a time when there is no formal recitation.

Regarding the phrase "when reciting according to the *svādhyāya*": while abandoning that which has already been studied, he should study by means of speech; however, during a time when there is no formal recitation, he should study mentally. Vasiṣṭha [26.14].
Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
so too does the twice-born man who is constantly devoted to silent recitation and always joined with the mantra.
Yama said:
Having restrained the entire collection of sense-faculties as well as both desire and anger,
one who is a celibate student and a reciter of prayers shall attain the world of Brahmā.
Laghuhārīta states:
During recitation, burnt offerings, giving, Vedic study, and the libation to the ancestors,
one should ensure that the hands are not empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
Yogiyājñavalkya says: A wise man should not perform japa and other rites while standing on dry ground with wet clothes;
for the departed spirits (pretas), surrounding him, drink the dripping moisture from his garment.
Except during a vow, one should not perform [ritual acts] wearing wet clothes or a single garment;
nor should one recite [mantras] while wearing clothes that are worn out, dyed blue, or soiled.
"Enveloping" means wrapping around; "soiled" means stained with dirt.
In the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* [58.77,
85, 87–90]: "Seated upon *darbha* grass, with *darbha* grass in hand, facing eastward, and being well-composed,
one should perform breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to the scriptures, without sloth."
Having bathed day after day, the twice-born who knows the ritual of recitation should mutter the Sāvitrī;
then, with arms raised, he should offer a handful of flowers to the Sun.
One should also recite that mantra, "ud u tyam," and likewise "citraṃ tac cakṣuḥ";
then, having circumambulated and paid homage to the Lord, one should depart.
Then, one should satiate with water the hosts of ancestors, sages, gods, and others—
the gods and the classes of gods, as well as the sages and the classes of sages.
Then he should constantly satisfy the ancestors and the hosts of ancestors;
thereafter, having wrung out his bathing garment, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) once again.

Thus ends the section on the rules for recitation (*japavidhi*) within the *Niyatakālakalpa* chapter of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the libation (tarpaṇa).

Regarding this, Viṣṇu [64.24–25] states: "Having bathed, one who is still wearing wet clothes should perform the libation to the gods and ancestors while remaining in the water; if, however, he has changed his clothes, he should do so after stepping out onto the bank of the sacred site. Yājñavalkya [1.100] says:

"Having bathed, one should satisfy and likewise worship the gods and the ancestors. "The gods" refers to Brahmā and others. "One should worship" means with mantras bearing their respective marks, and with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth. "And the ancestors" refers to [worship] by means of the *śrāddha* rite. Śātātapa says:
And a twice-born Snātaka, being pure, should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) every day,
in due order, for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.

“Pure,” even by means of ritual bathing with mantras and the like. By this, the daily libation (*nityatarpaṇa*) is primarily enjoined, because of the mention of “every day. Having introduced the libation: “Therefore, it must always be performed; by not performing it, a Brahmin is joined with great sin; for by performing it, he sustains this entire universe. [111]
And from such statements as the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.23]: Viṣṇu [64.27–35] states:

"Having bathed, one should perform the ritual sipping (*upaspṛśet*) according to rule. One should offer handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) to Puruṣa with each verse of the *Puruṣasūkta*. At the very beginning, one should also offer a handful of water. One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the gods using the *divya* (heavenly) *tīrtha*; for the ancestors, using the *pitrya* (paternal) *tīrtha*. First, one should perform the libation for those of one's own lineage; then for relatives and kinsmen; then for friends. In this manner, one should be a regular bather (*nityasnāyī*)."
"One's own lineage (svavaṃśyāḥ): those born in the lineages of one’s mother and father, such as the paternal ancestors and the maternal grandfathers.
Regarding the interval between the recitation of mantras, Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.18–23]:
‘One should satisfy the gods with water mixed with barley, and the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds.’”
Uttering "Om" at the beginning and saying "I satiate" at the end of each name.

[He should offer oblations to] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Prajāpati, the gods, the meters, the Vedas, the ancient seers (ṛṣis), the teachers, the Gandharvas, and other teachers; to the year with its parts, the divine Apsarases, the Devanugas, the Nāgas, the oceans, the mountains, the rivers, the divine humans, the Yakṣas, the Rakṣases, the Suparṇas, the Piśācas, the earth, the plants, the domestic animals, the forest trees, and the fourfold host of beings—thus while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī). Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he should practice the offering for each individual: Yama, the servant of Yama, Anala who carries the *kavya* offerings, Soma, Aryaman, the Agniṣvāttas, the Somapas, and the Barhiṣads; then his own paternal ancestors, and his maternal grandfathers. He should also include his eldest brother, his father-in-law, his paternal uncle, and his maternal uncle, as well as those belonging to the lineages of his mother and father, and others who deserve water from him, saying: "I satiate them. This is the final *añjali* offering. Now follows a verse:
As one distressed by the autumn heat desires shade,
as one thirsty desires water, as one hungry desires food,
so does a child [desire] its mother, and the mother her child.
A woman [desires] a man, and a man [desires] a woman.
In the same way, all beings, both stationary and moving, seek water from the Brahmin; for all indeed long for water.
Therefore, a Brahmin must always perform his duties; by failing to do so, he incurs great sin, for by performing them, he indeed sustains this entire universe.

“Of the ancestors” (*purāṇān*) is an epithet of the teachers. By the phrase “one should practice for each individual,” it is stated that the offering of three handfuls of water is repeated for the three paternal ancestors and the three maternal grandfathers.
Following the recitation, Yājñavalkya the Yogin says:
“Then one should satiate the gods, the sages, and likewise the hosts of deities.”
One should first gratify Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati.
The gods, the meters, the Vedas, and the seers whose wealth is asceticism;
likewise the teachers, the Gandharvas, and other teachers as well.
[He described] the year with its constituent parts, as well as the goddesses and the apsarases;
likewise the attendants of the gods, the nāgas, the oceans, and the mountains.
Indeed, [he saw] rivers, as well as humans, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
piśācas, suparṇas, bhūtas, and likewise animals.
With his left hand holding the sacrificial grass and his right hand touching the trees, the plants, and the fourfold host of living beings.
Having invoked [the deities] as before with mantras and having spread auspicious *kuśa* grass, one should pour [water], saying "May they be satisfied," using their names preceded by the *praṇava*.
One should properly offer to the gods on blades with their tips pointing eastward, and to the ancestors on those with tips pointing southward;
then, facing south, one should touch the left knee with both hands.
With the appropriate mantras and their respective marks, the wise man should constantly offer libations with faith to all the hosts of ancestors as well as to his maternal grandfathers.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), one should indeed pour out water mixed with sesame seeds;
if, however, the water has already been drawn up, one should mix the sesame seeds into that water.
Otherwise, however, the wise should take up the sesame seeds with the left hand;
one should sprinkle water according to the rule using the *pitṛtīrtha* on the right hand.
One should take [the water] with the right hand alone, near the *pitṛ-tīrtha*;
however, if even sesame seeds are unavailable, it should be accompanied by gold and silver.
In the absence of that [water], one should sprinkle with *darbha* grass or even with the mantra,
[addressing] Kavyavāḍ, Anala, Soma, Yama, and likewise Aryaman.
The Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Soma-drinkers, and likewise the Barhiṣad Pitṛs—
if one has a living father, he should likewise offer to these divine Pitṛs.
Or he may cause [the offering] to be given to those to whom his father would have given it;
these and those who are about to be mentioned [are for] the twice-born man whose ancestors are deceased.
The Vasus, Rudras, and likewise the Ādityas, accompanied by salutations and the *svadhā* offering—
these are the fathers of all, and upon them depend all human beings.
Water should be offered with mantras that increase the satisfaction of the ancestors, naming the teachers and one's own paternal ancestors, beginning with the father.
"May the Aṅgirases rise up," "May they come," "Strength," "To the fathers," "And those who are here," and the three verses beginning with "Honeyed are the winds."

Meditating upon the ancestors while pouring water, he should indeed recite the mantras in their proper order; then, with palms joined in reverence and body bowed, he should say three times, "Be satisfied."
Having recited "namo vaḥ," one who is established in the supreme dharma should then offer libations to the maternal grandfathers and friends for the sake of compassion.
A mother, a maternal aunt, a maternal uncle’s wife,
a paternal aunt, a daughter, a sister, a pupil, an officiating priest, a kinsman, and a relative.
They should be gratified in due order by name with utterances of "svadhā";
one should offer water to those of the same caste, never to one of another caste.
First, one's own ancestors should be gratified, and afterwards one should gratify others;
yet that son who does not gratify them out of a nihilistic disposition indeed [commits a fault].
"His ancestors, seeking water, drink the discharge from his body.

'With the mantras as before' means with the mantras previously stated in the *Śrāddha-prakaraṇa* of the *Yājñavalkya-saṃhitā*, beginning with 'O Viśvedevas, come hither' and 'Uśantas tvā'. 'Kavyavāhana Anala' is a single deity. 'Or to whomsoever' refers to the father’s ancestors and so forth. 'These divine ancestors,' namely Kavyavāhana Anala and the others to be mentioned hereafter, as well as the Vasus and other ancestors—'endowed with salutations and the svadhā-call,' one should satisfy them; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. And in this regard:"
"One should satisfy all the gods and *brahmarṣis* with water and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Since this is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa* (Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa 20.165) regarding the libation for gods, sages, and humans, barley (*yava*) is prescribed there. However, for the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), because the *Yogiyājñavalkya* in the section on bathing prescribes sesame seeds as a constant constituent in the passage "clay, cow dung, [sesame seeds]," and because it mentions "water with sesame seeds" (*tilodaka*) therein, sesame seeds are mandatory.
But even in the absence of sesame seeds, [the libation should be performed] "provided with gold and silver."

[116] Because of this statement, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors certainly takes place even in the absence of sesame seeds. This rite called *tarpaṇa* consists of the offering of water intended for the deities such as the ancestors; it is not merely the act of sprinkling, because of the use of the verb "one should give" (*dadyāt*), and because the satisfaction (*tṛpti*) of the ancestors and others is heard of in various places in that context. And here, regarding the libation for the gods, there is such a formula: "Oṃ, may Brahmā be satisfied; Oṃ, may Viṣṇu be satisfied"—this kind of formula should be performed for each deity respectively. But in the libation for humans, the formula is of this form: "Oṃ, may the Vasus be satisfied; this water is for them, Svadhā! Namaḥ! In the libation for the ancestors, however, the formula beginning with "Oṃ, may my father, of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, be satisfied; this water is for him, Svadhā! Namaḥ!"—this kind of formula should be performed.
In the *Padmapurāṇa* (*Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, 20.151–170):
First, one should satiate Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati;
as well as the gods, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas, apsarases, and asuras.
Cruel serpents, eagles, trees, jambhaka-demons,
birds, vidyādharas, clouds, and likewise those who travel through the sky.
And for those living beings who have no one to support them, and for those who are devoted to sinful ways—
this water is offered by me for their nourishment.
Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder for the gods, one should then wear it around the neck (nivītī) for humans;
one should then satisfy the humans with devotion, as well as the sons of the sages and the sages themselves.
Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍhu, and Pañcaśikha.
May they all always attain satisfaction through the water given by me:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
One should satisfy Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada,
as well as all the gods and Brahman-sages, with water and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Then, having placed the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder and bent the left knee to the ground,
[he should offer to] the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Saumyas, the Haviṣmants, and the Ūṣmapās.
Furthermore, one should devoutly satisfy the Sukālins, the Barhiṣads, and the Ājyapas,
as well as the ancestors, with water mixed with sesame seeds and sandalwood paste.
Then, with darbha grass in hand, he should satisfy those deceased ancestors according to the prescribed rule by name and lineage, as well as the maternal grandfathers and others.
Having satisfied them with devotion according to the prescribed rite, one should utter this mantra:
“Those who were non-relatives or relatives, or those who were relatives in another birth...”

"May they attain incomparable satisfaction, as well as whoever desires from us. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.11.27–36) Having bathed and wearing clean garments, one should perform the libation for the gods, sages, and ancestors.
[118] Indeed, with a well-concentrated mind, one should perform [the rite] using the very same bathing-place as theirs.
One should offer water three times for the purpose of gratifying the gods;
for the sages, according to the rule, and once for Prajāpati.
O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of pleasing the ancestors, one should likewise offer water three times to the grandfathers and the great-grandfathers.

With a concentrated mind, he should offer [the water] to his maternal grandfather, to that grandfather’s father, and to that grandfather’s father, using the *tīrtha* sacred to the ancestors; now hear from me regarding other optional rites as well.
To one's mother, to the knower (pramātṛ), to that alone, likewise to the wife of the guru, to the guru,
to the maternal uncles and others, to a dear friend, and to the king.
O King, having performed the libations for the gods and others, one should also mutter this mantra and offer water according to one's own desire for the benefit of all living beings.
The gods, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas,
rākṣasas, piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūṣmāṇḍas, trees, and birds—
May all these creatures— those that dwell in water, those that live on land, and those that subsist on air—
quickly attain satisfaction through the water given by me.
This water is offered by me for the nourishment of those who abide in all the hells and amidst the various torments.
May those who were not kinsmen, or those who were kinsmen, or those who were kinsmen in another birth—
may they all attain complete satisfaction, as well as whoever desires anything from us.

“Three times for the sake of satisfying the waters”—from this statement, three handfuls (añjali) are to be offered to each of the gods and the sages individually; to Prajāpati, however, there is only one handful in their midst. But for the ancestors and others, ending with the great-grandfather on the mother’s side (vṛddhapramātāmaha), three handfuls are to be offered to each. The mention of the optional nature (kāmyatva) regarding the libation to the mother and others is for the purpose of stating specific rewards; its obligatory nature (nityatā), however, follows from other Smṛtis. Baudhāyana [2.8.15–2.10.4].

Purified by the five *brahmayajñas*, he satisfies the deities with water in the waters, each succeeding one following the previous. "Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Serpents—these eastern gate-deities, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satisfy. And I satisfy the Vasus. The Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—these southern gate-deities, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satisfy. And I satisfy the Rudras. Mitra, Indra, the Great Pitṛs, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—these western gate-deities, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satisfy. And I satisfy the Ādityas. Varuṇa, the Vasus, Aja Ekapād, Ahibudhnya, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, and Yama—these northern gate-deities, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satisfy. I satisfy all the gods. And I satisfy the Sādhyas. I satisfy Brahmā. I satisfy Prajāpati. [I satisfy the Four-faced One. I satisfy Parameṣṭhin. I satisfy Hiraṇyagarbha. I satisfy Svayaṃbhu. I satisfy the attendants of Brahmā. Om Bhūḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Om Bhuvaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Om Suvaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Om Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ, I satisfy Puruṣa. Om Bhūḥ, I satisfy. Om Bhuvaḥ, I satisfy. Om Suvaḥ, I satisfy. Om Mahas, I satisfy. Om Janas, I satisfy. Om Tapas, I satisfy. Om Satyam, I satisfy. Om, I satisfy the god Bhava. Om, I satisfy the god Śarva. Om, I satisfy the god Īśāna. Om, I satisfy the god Paśupati. Om, I satisfy the god Rudra. Om, I satisfy the god Ugra. Om, I satisfy the god Bhīma. Om, I satisfy the god Mahān. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Bhava. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Śarva. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Īśāna. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Paśupati. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Rudra. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Ugra. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Bhīma. Om, I satisfy the wife of the god Mahān. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Bhava. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Śarva. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Īśāna. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Paśupati. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Rudra. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Ugra. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Bhīma. Om, I satisfy the son of the god Mahān. Om, I satisfy the Rudras. And I satisfy the attendants of Rudra. Om, I satisfy Vighna. I satisfy Vināyaka. I satisfy Vīra. I satisfy Śūra. I satisfy Ugra. I satisfy Varada. I satisfy Hastimukha. I satisfy Ekadaṃṣṭra. I satisfy Lambodara. And I satisfy the attendants of Vighna. And I satisfy the female attendants of Vighna. Om, I satisfy Sanatkumāra. I satisfy Skanda. I satisfy Indra. I satisfy Ṣaṣṭhī. I satisfy Ṣaṇmukha. I satisfy Viśākha. I satisfy Subrahmaṇya. I satisfy Mahāsena. And I satisfy the attendants of Skanda. And I satisfy the female attendants of Skanda. Om, I satisfy Keśava. I satisfy Nārāyaṇa. I satisfy Mādhava. I satisfy Govinda. I satisfy Viṣṇu. I satisfy Madhusūdana. I satisfy Trivikrama. I satisfy Vāmana. I satisfy Śrīdhara. I satisfy Hṛṣīkeśa. I satisfy Padmanābha. I satisfy Dāmodara. I satisfy the goddess Śrī. I satisfy the goddess Sarasvatī. I satisfy Puṣṭi. I satisfy Tuṣṭi. I satisfy Garuḍa. And I satisfy the attendants of Viṣṇu. And I satisfy the female attendants of Viṣṇu. Om, I satisfy Yama. I satisfy Yamarāja. I satisfy Dharma. I satisfy Dharmarāja. I satisfy Kāla. I satisfy Nīla. I satisfy Mṛtyu. I satisfy Vaivasvata.
