I satisfy Citragupta. And I satisfy the attendants of Vaivasvata. And I satisfy the female attendants of Vaivasvata. I satisfy the goddess Bhūmi. I satisfy Kaśyapa. I satisfy Akṣara. I satisfy Vidyā. I satisfy Dhanvantari. And I satisfy the attendants of Dhanvantari. And I satisfy the female attendants of Dhanvantari. Then, wearing the *nivīta* (the sacred thread over the right shoulder), he says: "Om, I satisfy the Ṛṣis. I satisfy the Maharṣis. I satisfy the Paramamaharṣis. I satisfy the Brahmarṣis. I satisfy the Devarṣis. I satisfy the Rājarṣis. I satisfy the Śrutarṣis. I satisfy the Taparṣis. I satisfy the Satyarṣis. I satisfy the Saptarṣis. I satisfy the Kāṇḍarṣis. I satisfy the Ṛṣikas. I satisfy the wives of the Ṛṣis. I satisfy the sons of the Ṛṣis. I satisfy Kāṇva Baudhāyana. I satisfy Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras. I satisfy Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin. I satisfy Vyāsa. I satisfy the Praṇava. I satisfy the Vyāhṛtis. I satisfy Sāvitrī. I satisfy Gāyatrī. I satisfy the Metres. I satisfy the Ṛgveda. I satisfy the Yajurveda. I satisfy the Sāmaveda. I satisfy the Atharvaveda. I satisfy the Atharvāṅgirases. I satisfy the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. I satisfy all the Vedas. I satisfy all the divine beings. I satisfy all beings. Then, on the south side, wearing the *prācīnāvīta* (the sacred thread over the left shoulder): "Om, I satisfy the Pitṛs with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Great-Grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Mothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Great-Grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Maternal Grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Mothers' Grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Mothers' Great-Grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Maternal Grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Mothers' Grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Mothers' Great-Grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Wives of the Teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Preceptors with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Wives of the Preceptors with *svadhā* and obeisance. I satisfy the Friends with *svadhā*

“By the five *brahmayajñas*”: consisting of the recitation (*japa*) of the *praṇava*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*. This is because Baudhāyana himself stated previously: “The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*” [2.7.14]. “In successive order” means that each deity, beginning with Brahmā, is addressed according to that very sequence. “At the *tīrtha*” means aiming at the *tīrtha* of the ancestors and others. Because of the expression “of some,” even wearing wet clothes is intended for the libation performed while standing in water. Furthermore, when the libation is performed by a person either standing in water or on dry land, the casting of the libation water must be done into the middle of the water; there is no rule that it must be done on dry land alone by one standing on dry land. For regarding the libation performed on dry land, Baudhāyana states: “Purified by the five *brahmayajñas*, he satisfies the deities in the water with water itself, in successive order” [2.8.15], thereby specifying that water alone is the locus for casting the libation water. Since the five *brahmayajñas*—consisting of the *praṇava*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and the *gāyatrī*—are prescribed as occurring after the putting on of the garment, the mention of “having wrung out the garment” [2.8.12] indicates that, for the followers of Baudhāyana, that act is a limb of the bath (*snāna-aṅga*) preceding the libation; therefore, the rule “in the water” does not refer to a libation performed while standing in water. On the other hand, the statement of Baudhāyana at the end of the libation, “not with wet clothes” [2.10.4] and so forth, confirms that the libation is indeed to be performed on dry land.

Śaṅkha [13.1–15]: The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these four supports for the mind. What four? They are: the support for the mind that is the basis of joy; the support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity; the support for the mind that is the basis of light; and the support for the mind that is the basis of space. These, monks, are the four supports for the mind. Then the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the purpose of these four supports for the mind? The Blessed One said: “Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is for the sake of abandoning the underlying tendency toward aversion. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is for the sake of abandoning the underlying tendency toward sensual desire. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is for the sake of abandoning the underlying tendency toward ignorance. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is for the sake of abandoning the underlying tendency toward the conceit ‘I am. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a monk dwells with a mind supported by the basis of joy, he does not experience aversion. When he dwells with a mind supported by the basis of equanimity, he does not experience sensual desire. When he dwells with a mind supported by the basis of light, he does not experience ignorance. When he dwells with a mind supported by the basis of space, he does not experience the conceit ‘I am. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy leads to the attainment of the first dhyāna. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity leads to the attainment of the second dhyāna. The support for the mind that is the basis of light leads to the attainment of the third dhyāna. The support for the mind that is the basis of space leads to the attainment of the fourth dhyāna. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the path to the abandonment of the hindrance of ill-will. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the path to the abandonment of the hindrance of sensual desire. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the path to the abandonment of the hindrance of torpor-and-drowsiness. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the path to the abandonment of the hindrance of doubt. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the foundation for the development of loving-kindness. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the foundation for the development of compassion. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the foundation for the development of sympathetic joy. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the foundation for the development of equanimity. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the cause for the arising of the perception of light. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the cause for the arising of the perception of the repulsive. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the cause for the arising of the perception of the beautiful. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the cause for the arising of the perception of emptiness. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the entrance into the gate of liberation of emptiness. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the entrance into the gate of liberation of signlessness. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the entrance into the gate of liberation of wishlessness. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the entrance into the gate of liberation of non-arising. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the basis for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the basis for the cultivation of the powers. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the basis for the cultivation of the limbs of awakening. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the basis for the cultivation of the path. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the door to the attainment of supernormal power. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the door to the attainment of the divine ear. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the door to the attainment of the knowledge of others' minds. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the door to the attainment of the recollection of past lives. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the means for crossing over the flood of sensuality. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the means for crossing over the flood of existence. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the means for crossing over the flood of views. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the means for crossing over the flood of ignorance. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the vessel for the accumulation of merit. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the vessel for the accumulation of wisdom. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the vessel for the accumulation of knowledge. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the vessel for the accumulation of liberation. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the cause for the arising of the fruit of stream-entry. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the cause for the arising of the fruit of once-returning. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the cause for the arising of the fruit of non-returning. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the cause for the arising of the fruit of arhatship. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the basis for the purification of conduct. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the basis for the purification of view. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the basis for the purification of mind. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the basis for the purification of knowledge and vision. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the foundation for the practice of the ascetic virtues. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the foundation for the practice of the dhuta qualities. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the foundation for the practice of mindfulness and clear comprehension. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the foundation for the practice of the foundations of mindfulness. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the cause for the arising of the four right efforts. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the cause for the arising of the four bases of psychic power. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the cause for the arising of the five faculties. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the cause for the arising of the five powers. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the door to the attainment of the seven factors of awakening. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the door to the attainment of the noble eightfold path. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the door to the attainment of the three gates of liberation. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the door to the attainment of the four analytical knowledges. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the cause for the arising of the Tathāgata’s ten powers. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the cause for the arising of the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the cause for the arising of the Tathāgata’s eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the cause for the arising of the Tathāgata’s great compassion. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, the support for the mind that is the basis of joy is the basis for the turning of the wheel of Dharma. The support for the mind that is the basis of equanimity is the basis for the teaching of the Dharma. The support for the mind that is the basis of light is the basis for the proclamation of the Dharma. The support for the mind that is the basis of space is the basis for the establishment of the Dharma. “Moreover, Śāriputra, the

Having bathed and performed his silent prayers (*japa*), with knees bent and facing north, he should satisfy the gods with water through the *divya-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods). Now follows the procedure for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). *Oṃ*, I satisfy the Blessed Śeṣa; Kālāgnirudra; Santānavarāha; Ajina; Rukmabhauma; Śailabhauma; Lalāṭabhauma; Raktabhauma; Śvetabhauma; Kṛṣṇabhauma—thus the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*). The Gaṅgā with its seven streams. The Gaṅgā that flows through the three worlds. The Sindhu; the Sarasvatī; the Yamunā. Prathamapuṣkara; Dvitīyapuṣkara; Tṛtīyapuṣkara. The Apsarases named Muds; the Apsarases named Paśunis; the Apsarases named Āyus; the Apsarases named Sudhās; the Apsarases named Pṛṣṭamas; the Apsarases named Ūrjās. Agnisantā; Svāhā; Agnīdh; Yama; Dharma; Śrī; Satya; Tapas; Saṃyajña; Dakṣiṇā; Dīkṣā; Brahmacarya; Vyavasāya. Dharmarāja; Daṇḍa; Piṅgala; Kālapāśa; Āyudha; Svarga; Mṛtyu; Citragupta; the servants of Yama; Śyāva and Śabala; Virūpākṣa; Nairṛti; the Daityas and Dānavas who are preeminent in righteousness; the Vidyādharas; the Yakṣas; the Rākṣasas; the Piśācas; Diseases; Fever; the Lord of Disease; Health; Varuṇa; Gaurī; the Nāgas; Vāsuki; Ananta; the Serpents; the Lords of the Forest; Vāyu; Śirā; Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Udāna, and Vyāna; the Senses; the objects of the senses; the Individual Soul (*jīva*); Soma; the Constellations; the current constellation; the Ancestors (*pitṛ*); the Ābhāsvaras; the Barhiṣads; the Agniṣvāttas; the Kravyādas; those of similar form; the Ājyapas; the Sukālins; Mahādeva; Pārvatī; Senānī; Skanda; Viśākha; the Skandagrahas; the Bālagrahas; the attendants of Skanda; the attendants of Rudra; the Spirits (*bhūta*); the Earth-Rudras; the Intermediate-Rudras; the Knowledge-Rudras; the All-pervading Rudras; the Mothers; the Yogīśvarīs; the Wives of the Gods; the Hosts of the Mothers of the Gods; the Lords of Wealth; Vināyaka; Mita; Saṃmita; Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa; Kūṣmāṇḍa; the Princes; Dharma; Artha; Kāma; Gati. Without silver and gold, without copper and sesame seeds,
and without *darbha* grass and mantras, [the offering] does not reach the ancestors.
Water with sesame seeds offered by means of vessels made of gold, silver,
or udumbara wood becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors.
Whatever is given with snow, or with milk, or even with honey—
that water mixed with sesame seeds likewise attains inexhaustibility for the ancestors.

“*Antarjānuḥ*” means having the hands placed between the knees. And although here it is stated at the end of all [the names], “*Oṃ, I satiate the Blessed Śeṣa*,” and finally, “*I satiate the Unmanifest Puruṣa*,” nevertheless, the phrase “I satiate” (*tarpayāmi*) should be connected to each [name] individually, starting from Kālāgnirudra and so forth, because [each name] functions as the object (*karman*) and thus requires an action, and because the action “I satiate” is present right here. This offering of joined palms (*añjali*) and the offering of flowers with each verse of the *Puruṣasūkta* occurs within the very procedure of the libation (*tarpaṇa*), following the libation with the words “I satiate the Unmanifest Puruṣa. “*Yathāśraddham*” means toward those who are known [to exist] in whom faith arises. “*Yathāprakāśam*” means according to the knowledge of their names. “*Śaṅkunā*” means by means of a peg (*kīlaka*), [used for] the materials under discussion themselves. “*Guravaḥ*” here refers to the teachers (*ācārya*) and others. Gold, silver, copper, and swords are limbs (*aṅga*) either individually or collectively, as far as possible. Milk, honey, camphor, and sandalwood are the qualities and fruits (*guṇaphala*).
Marīci says: One should give with an open hand and must not display a seal (mudrā) there;
the sesame seeds are to be taken in the left hand, having released the right hand.
One should satisfy the gods and the ancestors; when they are satisfied, one may proceed with joy.
But when one departs without having honored them, then one's journey becomes fruitless.
One may go with the mind to Rājate; one may go to Suvarṇa as soon as it leaves the hand; one reaches Tilas in a moment, but Tāmra takes two muhūrtas.
That which is offered on *darbha* grass with seven *muhūrtas* and accompanied by mantras is inexhaustible;
wherever and for whomever it is intended, there it attends to that person.
Just as a son finds his lost mother among many cows,
so indeed that which is given by one with the mind reaches him to whom it was intended.

“Mudrā” refers to a specific joining of the index finger and the thumb. Regarding the phrase “having washed the right hand,” one should make the right hand free of sesame seeds. Regarding the phrase “wherever [and] whomever,” “wherever” refers to the place and so forth; “whomever” refers to the father and so forth; “of whom” refers to the son and so forth. “It reaches him” means it goes to that person. “Offered mentally” means prepared mentally. [This is from] Paiṭhīnasi.

Having sprinkled [the ground] with purificatory substances (*pavitra*), he should pour out water, saying: "To the Vasus, to Brahmā, and to Vaiśravaṇa. With the three mantras beginning with *udīratām*, he should pour out three handfuls of water, pronouncing the names of his paternal relatives: for the teacher (*ācārya*), the mother, the maternal grandfather, and the maternal uncles.
Yama says: "Having first performed the water-rite for the sapinda-relations and the kinsmen..."
Then, one should offer handfuls of water to the groups of friends and kinsmen.
Likewise:
"By offering seven handfuls of water on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
dedicating it to Dharmarāja, one is liberated from all sins."
At a time when the sun has not yet risen, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one who has bathed and offered libations to Yama is liberated from all sins.
Indeed, by bathing in any river whatsoever on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and offering libations to Dharmarāja, one is liberated from all sins.
[134] Manu, Śātātapa, and Yogiyājñavalkya state:
"That best of the twice-born who, having bathed, thus gratifies the ancestors with water,
obtains by that very act the entire fruit of the performance of the ancestral sacrifice."
Śaṅkha says: Having bathed and performed the libation for the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds,
one obtains the merit of the Pitṛyajña and likewise gratifies the ancestors.
Hārīta says: One should not cross a flowing river in vain; for thus it is said:
"Both the gods and the ancestors long for [offerings] at the river."
But when they have not received [anything], they depart as they came, devoid of hope.
In this regard, among the verses of the ancestors, Yama says:
"May he also be born in our lineage who would offer us a handful of water,
especially in rivers abounding with cool waters."
Likewise Viṣṇu [declares]:
"May that being be born in our family who shall offer us a handful of water in rivers abounding with water, especially those that are cool."
Uśanas: One should not perform rites for the gods or the ancestors with one’s head wrapped or while wearing black or saffron-colored garments. [135] Yogiyājñavalkya:
The Śruti declares that the water squeezed from a garment is the portion belonging to those who partake in the remnants of the bath; therefore, one should squeeze it out on dry ground.
Some maintain that the wringing out of the bathing garment should be done beforehand, prior to the libations for the gods and ancestors;
therefore, one should wring it out after that.
Like the preparation of food, one should press it with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (apasavya);
having pressed it, one should thereafter perform the recitation (japa) in great detail.
“Those entitled to the remnants”: for those who died before receiving sacraments, for those who have abandoned their families, and for women of the household—
their allotted share shall be the food-remnants and whatever scattering of food is placed upon the *darbha* grass.
The food remaining on the ground from one who is neither crooked nor deceitful is declared to be the share of the father for his group of servants.

Thus it was stated by Manu. Therefore, having brought these [items] to mind, one should offer the water used for wringing out the garment. "The predecessors" refers to the ancient teachers. "The scattering of food" (*annaprakara*) refers to the offering of scattered food (*vikiro-dāna*) at a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, the "extensive recitation" (*suvistarajapa*) should be understood as the performance of the recitation of the group of purifiers (*pavitravarga*) taught by Yogī Yājñavalkya and others, beginning with the words: "Having sipped water, one should sip again. Likewise:
"Having wrung out the bathing garment, and having sipped water, being self-controlled and pure..."
One should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, free from envy.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship all the gods with mantras pertaining to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Savitṛ, Mitra, and Varuṇa, using those [mantras] that bear their respective characteristics.
Having meditated with a concentrated mind upon the deity preceded by the syllable *praṇava*,
one should offer flowers individually while performing prostrations.
Whatever ritual acts, such as invocation and the like, have not been mentioned by me here,
all of those for the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) should be performed with the *praṇava* alone.
Whoever offers flowers or even water with the Puruṣasūkta,
by him this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, becomes worshipped.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra, as well as the god Viṣṇu and the Sun-god—
therefore, I consider none other to be more worthy of worship than Janārdana.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer incense and other offerings with the Sāvitrī mantra according to one's ability;
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should meditate upon Kṛṣṇa as the stainless one.
Then he should look at the sun with the verse, "The swan dwelling in purity.
He who has bathed and gazes [at the sun] with this [verse] goes to the abode of Brahman.
Then, having worshipped the sun with the mantra beginning "adṛśram asya," he should wipe his face with water using both hands while reciting the mantra "saṃ varcasā."

Having approached with the mantra "svayaṃbhūr" and having circumambulated the sun with the mantra "sūryasya," one should turn back and pay homage to the directions as well as the deities of the directions.
To Brahmā, to Agni, and likewise to the Earth and the medicinal herbs;
to Vāc and to Vācaspati, and to the great Viṣṇu.
Having offered water for salutation and so forth to these deities,
one should pay homage to them in sequence at the conclusion of all ritual acts.
"Salutation to the waters, salutation to the lord of the waters, salutation, salutation to Varuṇa.
Having spoken thus, he should pay homage to the waters and to the gods by name upon the ground.
"O Waters, carry away this [impurity] from every station;
likewise, for the purification of the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should mutter the mantra 'āpyāyasva'."
Having performed the recitation and offering with the mantra "devā gātuvidaḥ," and having washed the area of the sacred water (tīrtha), one should go and perform one's own religious duty.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are to be worshipped with their respective individual *liṅga-mantras*. Savitṛ, however, is worshipped with three, because of the mention of the plural number in the word “*sāvitraiḥ*” (with the Sāvitra mantras), and because that plural number finds its application in exactly three [mantras]. For Mitra-Varuṇa, too, it is with three each, as here also there is the mention of the plural. “With their *liṅgas*” means with those capable of manifesting those deities, Brahmā and the others. By the passage beginning with “having meditated on the *praṇava*,” etc., the mode of worship for those very [deities] is stated. In the worship of Viṣṇu, the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth are performed with the *oṃkāra*, and the offering of flowers or the offering of water is performed with the *Puruṣasūkta*. By the word “*dhūpādi*” (incense, etc.), the lighting of lamps, the food offering (*naivedya*), and musical instruments are indicated. “*Nirañjana*” is the supreme Brahman, free from phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*). “The directions” refers to the east and so forth. “The deities of the directions” refers to Indra and the others. “On the earth” means upon the ground. “Having paid homage to the gods,” the “offering of the recitation” (*japyanivedana*) consists of the form: “May the Supreme Self be pleased by this recitation. “One’s own duty” (*svaṃ dharmaṃ*) is that which is prescribed for one’s own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
Likewise:
"Having sipped water at rivers and the like, even while wearing shoes and without touching [the water],
one who returns with a vessel of water is indeed pure through that effort."
Having sprinkled the ritual substances with that water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), he should then return home and perform whatever daily rites there may be.
One should not perform sprinkling with water drawn up by the right hand that is devoid of a vessel or the like, nor with water squeezed from a cloth.
A vessel made of gold, silver, or copper is proclaimed to be the best;
in their absence, it is prescribed that a vessel which does not leak when held should be used.

"Without touching," the remainder of the phrase being "impure things and so forth. "Sprinkling" refers to substances such as flowers and food offerings kept within the house. Regarding the phrase "which was not held," a coconut vessel or similar item is understood. Śātātapa says:
"Having sipped water outside [the village] by a river or other such place, one remains with water in hand, not touching anything whatsoever."
Even when on the public road, a person here should remain pure through diligent effort.
One should not sprinkle a ritual substance with water held in the left hand without a vessel, nor with water squeezed from a cloth.
One should not fetch water for the purpose of purification with a portion of one’s lower garment;
however, if it has been brought, one should sprinkle it while using the left hand and pouring with the right.

The connection is: "without touching, with effort. "Substance" refers to offerings such as flowers kept at home. Regarding the phrase "with a portion of the lower garment," the meaning is that even in the absence of another water vessel, one should not sprinkle [the offering] with water brought in the lower garment.
Following the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.39–41] states:
"And having performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*), one should then offer a handful of water to the Sun."
Salutations to Vivasvat, O Brahman, the radiant one, the splendor of Viṣṇu.
To the pure Savitṛ, the progenitor of the world and the bestower of action;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of the household deities and the adoration of one's chosen deity.
Through the offerings of water-sprinklings, flowers, incense, and so forth—
in the *Padma Purāṇa*, Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, 20.170–177— it is said:
"Having sipped water (ācamana) according to the rule, one should properly draw a lotus in front."
With unbroken grains of rice accompanied by flowers, sesame seeds, and red sandalwood;
With effort, one should offer the *arghya* and *pādya* while reciting the names of the Sun:
"Salutations to you who are the form of Viṣṇu; salutations to you whose nature is Brahman."
Homage always to you, the thousand-rayed one, to you who possess all splendor;
homage to you whose form is Rudra, homage to you who are affectionate toward your devotees.
O Padmanābha, homage be to you, adorned with earrings and armlets;
homage to you, Lord of all worlds, who awakens even those who are asleep.
[140] You always behold all that is well-done and ill-done;
O God of Truth, homage be to you! Be gracious to me, O Bhāskara.
"Homage be to you, Divākara; homage be to you, Prabhākara.
Having thus paid homage to the Sun and having circumambulated him three times, [he should proceed].
Having touched a twice-born man, a cow, and gold, one should then proceed to the temple of Viṣṇu;
there, having honored the presiding deity, one should also worship the image.

Immediately after the *brahmayajña*, the *Narasiṃhapurāṇa* [58.91–93] states: "Then, having risen, one should offer an *arghya* to the Sun, accompanied by sesame seeds, flowers, and water, with the *ṛc* beginning 'haṃsaḥ śuciṣat' (the swan dwelling in purity), extending up to the crown of the head."
Having paid homage to Jaladeva, he should then return home and worship Viṣṇu there according to the ritual procedure of the Puruṣasūkta.
Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva and the Bali-offering according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, the "Puruṣasūkta-vidhi" is to be understood from another Purāṇa in the section on worship.
Thus [ends the work] by Mahāsāndhivigrahika Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara’s son...
In the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara,
this is the section on libations (*tarpaṇaparva*) within the chapter on fixed times (*niyatakālakāṇḍa*).
[141] 5. The Procedure for the Five Sacrifices, beginning with the Vaiśvadeva.
Now, regarding the skillful one (Dakṣa):
"And likewise, in the fifth portion, a distribution according to what is appropriate for the gods,
the ancestors, human beings, and even insects is prescribed."
"According to what is fitting" means as is appropriate. Vyāsa says:
"One should perform all *pākayajñas* in the nuptial fire."
For even in times of dire distress, one should not neglect the five sacrifices.
They declare that the attainment of heaven and liberation is achieved through the great sacrifices.
The "nuptial fire" is the *āvasathya*. Gautama [5.3–6]:

One who worships the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages; one who is constantly engaged in private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*); one who offers water to the ancestors; and other acts according to one's ability. [142] Worship of humans is the worship of guests. "Worship of sages" is the study and recitation of the Vedas. Although the sacrifice to the sages (*ṛṣiyajña*) and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) were mentioned previously, they are stated again here by the words "constantly engaged in private recitation" and so forth, in order to show that these must necessarily be performed with diligence—even if the performance of the other three sacrifices is incomplete—using even a small amount of water as a substitute for the required materials. This very point is expressed by the phrase "other acts according to one's ability."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"One who eats the remnants [of the offerings] should perform the five great sacrifices every day, even when reduced to mere vegetables and water.
Saṃvarta states that this occurs immediately after marriage.
Then, the twice-born wise man should perform the five great sacrifices day after day;
he should not neglect them, for they are indeed heard of in the Śruti as well.

Then, in that same manner, Devala [says]: Immediately thereafter, one should establish the sacred fires (*agnīn ādadīta*). Having taken up the *agnihotra*, one should perform the purification of the gods, ancestors, sages, guests, visitors, dependents, and oneself, as well as the practice of virtuous conduct. In this regard, one should worship the gods, ancestors, and sages individually with *kavya* (offerings to ancestors), *havya* (offerings to gods), and *svādhyāya* (Vedic study). The commencement of the *agnihotra* with the exclamation "Svāhā" constitutes *havya*; it gratifies the gods. The commencement of the ancestral rites with the exclamation "Svadha" constitutes *kavya*; it pleases the ancestors. The commencement of Vedic study with the syllable "Om" constitutes *svādhyāya*; it satisfies the sages.

[143] “*Abhyāgataḥ*” refers to a guest (*atithi*), as well as any other visitor (*prāghuṇaka*). “*Sucaritraḥ*” means one of good conduct (*sadācāraḥ*). “*Agnihotrapravṛttiḥ*” refers to one whose engagement is in the *agnihotra*; here, the word *agnihotra* refers to any oblation made into fire. Jābāli says:
“Day after day, the worship of the ancestors and the deities must be performed.”
The word "hanta" and the offering made with "hantakāra" are indeed purifying for human beings.
Manu [3.68–69]: "A householder has five slaughterhouses: the hearth, the grinding stone, the broom, the mortar and pestle, and the water-jar; by using these, he causes slaughter."
For the sake of expiating all these [debts] in due order,
the great seers ordained five great sacrifices for householders to be performed every day.
“Sūnā” is a place for slaughtering living beings; “upaskaraḥ” refers to household utensils, vessels, pots, and so forth.
Hārīta says:

Now we shall explain the *sūnās* (slaughter-houses). They are called *sūnās* because they slaughter (*sūdayanti*) living beings, whether mobile or stationary. These are of five kinds. They produce the first [type of *sūnā*] by means of rapid descent, immersion, agitation, tossing about, catching what is not purified, riding, and so forth. They produce the second by means of untimely travel, traveling too openly or too fast, trampling, and so forth. They produce the third by means of striking, seizing, binding, cutting, piercing, grinding, uprooting, and so forth. They produce the fourth by means of trampling, rubbing, crushing, and so forth. They produce the fifth by means of setting on fire, heating, sweating, frying, cooking, and so forth. Thus, these five types of *sūnās* daily create creatures born from the hells. The student (*brahmacārī*) purifies the first three *sūnās* through service to the fire and teacher, and the study of the Vedas. Householders and forest-dwellers purify all five [of the first four] by means of the five *pākayajñas*. Monks purify two *sūnās* by means of pure knowledge and meditation. Those who perform no rites [purify themselves] regarding the *sūnā* of the teeth.

“Sūdayanti” means they deprive [beings] of their lives. “Āturāvataraṇam” means entering the water quickly. “Vikṣobhaṇam” means agitating [the water]. “Vikṣepaṇam” means throwing the water here and there. “Apūtagrahaṇam” means taking up water without first removing worms, insects, and so forth from one's clothes and other belongings. “Ādyām” means the first. “Avelāgamanam” means going out during darkness and such times. “Aviṣpaṣṭaḥ” refers to being on a wrong path and the like. “Drutam” means quickly. “Ākramaṇam” means treading upon with the feet and so forth. “Ākramaṇam” [in this context] refers to the trampling of crops and the like by oxen and so forth. “Ādīpanam” refers to setting fire to wood and the like. “Tāpanam” refers to heating water and the like. “Svedanam” means steaming or swelling of grain and the like. “Bharjanam” refers to roasting barley and the like. “Pacanām” refers to cooking rice and the like. For mendicants (*bhikṣu*), there are two types of slaughterhouses (*sūnā*); the first [is mentioned here] because acts such as cutting down trees are impossible for them. Regarding “aniṣkriyā,” it is said that there is no expiation (*niṣkriyā*) for the sin produced by the “tooth-slaughterhouse” (*dantasūnā*) when one fails to perform the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) just mentioned. “Dantasūnā” is that which occurs when chewing is performed with the teeth.
[145] Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.25–29]: Now, the rule for the five great sacrificial sessions (*sattra*) is being declared,
by performing which a Brahmin would constantly attain the eternal abode.

One should know that the great sacrificial sessions (mahāsattras) of the gods, the ancestors, Brahmā, and humans follow this sequence; these indeed are the great sacrifices (mahāmakhās) in this world.

Teaching is the sacrifice to Brahman; the libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the fathers; the burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods; the bali-offering is the sacrifice to beings; and the honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men.
The Śrāddha rite may be the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), or it may be the offering to the ancestors (pitrya bali);
and that which is declared to be the recitation of the Vedas is called the sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña).
And that [offering] should be performed either before the satiation of the Cārvākas, or after it, or in the morning before the oblation;
or at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite, but not on any other occasion except when there is a specific cause.

The status of *tarpaṇa*, *śrāddha*, *pitṛyajña*, and *balidāna* as *pitṛyajña* is established according to their respective applicability based on the differences in the qualified performers; it is not, however, an equal option (*tulyavikalpa*). Regarding the term *nimittakāt*, since *nimitta* itself means *nimittaka*, the meaning is that one should not perform the *brahmayajña* at any time other than the three times mentioned for the *brahmayajña* in the preceding [verse]. Manu, Yama, Viṣṇu, and Devala state in the third [chapter]: "Teaching is the *brahmayajña*; the *tarpaṇa* is the *pitṛyajña*."
The sacrifice to the gods is the person; the sacrifice to beings is the offering; the sacrifice to men is the honoring of guests.
He who does not neglect these five great sacrifices according to his ability,
even while living constantly in the household, is not tainted by the defects of the slaughterhouse.
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— though he breathes, he does not truly live.
The unoffered sacrifice (ahuta), the offered sacrifice (huta), the well-offered sacrifice (prahuta),
the sacrifice to Brahman (brāhmahuta), and the consumed sacrifice (prāśita)— these are declared to be the five sacrifices.
Recitation is the *huta* sacrifice; the fire-oblation is the *prahuta*; the offering to the spirits is the *bhautika bali*;
worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhma huta*; and the libation for the ancestors is the *prāśita*.

Hārīta says: The *huta*, the *nirvāpa*, the *ahuta*, the *prahuta*, and the *prāśita*—these are the five *pākayajñas*. The *huta* belongs to the gods; the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍanirvāpa*) belongs to the ancestors; the presentation of the *bali* offerings to the guardian of the site and the elemental spirits is the *ahuta*; when one sets aside food and gives it to a Brāhmaṇa, that is the *prahuta*; and what remains he eats—that is the sacrificer’s portion, which they call the *prāśita*. This very thing has been stated in a *ṛc*: "The [food] prepared morning and evening for all creatures..."

"The wise man who bestows the immortal [oblation] eats without debt; but the blind, foolish man who eats what has been prepared without first giving a portion to the gods partakes in evil. Thus it is said.

Therefore, one should offer oblations day after day. In the absence of food, this may be done with anything down to a piece of wood. To the gods, there is the offering of water by pouring; to the ancestors, the offering of water by scattering; to the spirits, the offering of water by pouring; and to humans, vessels of water. Or, one may perform these offerings daily to the deities according to the specific lunar days (*tithi*).

"Nirvāpa" means that in this [act] there is an offering (*nirvāpa*). "This very thing"—that is, this necessity—is established by the *ṛc* beginning with "In the evening and in the morning. And its meaning is as follows: "In the evening and in the morning," having first performed the five-fold *pākayajña* ritual with the cooking [of food], he who eats after having "offered to the progeny"—that is, having given [the portion] for the sake of discharging the debts to the gods and others—eats like nectar, being free from debt to the gods and others. "The wise one" is the man of knowledge. But he who "eats without having offered the prepared portion to the gods" is "unaware"—that is, ignorant—and is "blind," meaning truly sinful. "Nivāpa" is the giving of dry food, fruits, roots, and water-based items to a Brāhmaṇa on behalf of the father. "Every day the deities" should be worshipped; this is the ellipsis. Because of the repetition, these deities are distinct from the Viśvedevas. As Hārīta will say: "Agni and other gods dwell in heaven," and so forth. Or, "on specific lunar days," worship of Brahmā and the other gods should be performed on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) and subsequent days, as stated by Parāśara and others.
Jābāli says: Having bathed, the first [rite] among the great sacrifices is remembered as the libation (tarpaṇa);
then comes the oblation (homa) with the Sāvitrī mantra, and the offering to beings (bhauta) through the ritual of bali.
The *brāhma* sacrifice is performed solely through the recitation of the Vedas; the *nṛyajña* is the honoring of guests.
With materials obtained unasked, one should give a full sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) once they have sipped water.

In the phrase “of great sacrifices,” the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). That which is the “oblation (*homa*) with the *Sāvitrī*” is the “divine sacrifice. And this divine sacrifice consisting of the oblation with the *Sāvitrī* is established in a specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*). The expression “brought without being asked for” is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the means of livelihood prescribed by rule. “With full sacrificial fees (*pūrṇadakṣiṇam*): that worship in which the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is complete is thus described.
Manu [3.80–81]: “The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the elemental beings, and likewise guests...”
One who understands his duty should expect assistance from those householders.
One should honor the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, the gods with burnt offerings according to the rule,
the ancestors with the śrāddha rite, men with gifts of food, and the elemental spirits with the bali offering.

Hārīta says: By that which he offers to the gods, he conquers the world of the gods; by that which he offers to the ancestors, the world of the ancestors; by that which he studies his private Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), the world of the seers (*ṛṣi*); by that which he brings the food-oblation (*baliharaṇa*) to the beings, the world of the beings. Therefore, having made offerings to the gods, ancestors, seers, and beings, he should undertake the consecration (*dīkṣā*) until the milking of the cows. Again, Hārīta says:
For the sake of the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins, as we constantly gather our own wealth according to our own duties, whatever hardship we endure is our austerity.
A Brahmin who gratifies the gods, the ancestors, the sages, all beings, and likewise the Brahmins according to the prescribed rule, becomes fit for union with Brahman.
This glorious path to Brahman was proclaimed of old by the Self-Existent One; a Brahmin who follows it according to the prescribed rule is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
“Sva” means one’s own wealth. “Cinvatām” means for those who are engaged in accumulation. “In their own duties,” such as receiving gifts and so forth.
Manu [3.75–76]: One should be constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas and to rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors.
For it is when joined with divine action that he sustains this world of moving and unmoving beings.
An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Śātātapa states: Whether in the worldly or the Vedic fire, or even in water or on the ground where an oblation has been offered,
the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed for the removal of the five elements.
Those who are devoid of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and abandoned by hospitality—
all those should be known as Śūdras, even if they are twice-born (dvija) and have acquired the Vedas.

"In the worldly" means for the purpose of cooking. "In the Vedic" refers to the *āvasathya* fire. "Offered and abandoned" (*hutotsṛṣṭe*) means that which has been offered by another and then discarded. However, in the reading "taken and abandoned" (*hṛtotsṛṣṭe*), the meaning is "having brought it and wiped it clean. In the absence of the three fires mentioned immediately above, water is used; in the absence of that, the earth. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.34]:
"The Vaiśvadeva and the Bali-offering must be performed every evening and morning."
Even by not eating at all, one would otherwise surely become a sinner.
Likewise,
the fire-oblation (homa) taught by Gautama beginning with "fire" and so forth, or specifically the Śākala rite,
is appropriate even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, along with the bali offerings.

“Beginning with Agni”: this refers to what was stated by Gautama: “Agni, Dhanvantari, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, and Sviṣṭakṛt. And the “Śākala” [offering] consists of the formulas beginning with “Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods,” and so forth. This [offering] takes place in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. It is called the Śākala-homa because it is accomplished by means of wood-shavings, as prescribed by the rule: “One should add six wood-shavings each to the Āhavanīya fire. For one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni)—that is, one who is devoid of both Śrauta and Smārta fires—the rule is: “He should always cook his food in the domestic fire (śālāgni) or even in a common (laukika) fire.”
In whatever vessel one cooks the food, in that very same vessel the oblation is prescribed.
The "household fire" (śālāgni) is the domestic fire (āvasathya). Manu [4.21] states:
"One should always perform the sacrifice to the sages (ṛṣiyajña), the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña), and the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūtayajña)."
One should not neglect the sacrifice to men and the sacrifice to the ancestors as much as one is able.
"According to one's capacity" means that even in the absence of cooked food, [the sacrifice may be performed] with fruits, roots, and so forth.

The restatement of the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*), which were previously established as obligatory daily duties for the householder by the rule "five great sacrifices are prescribed for the householder every day," is for the purpose of making known their status as *snātaka* vows and for the sake of their application in what is to be stated hereafter.
Likewise [4.22–24]: Some people, who are learned in the treatises on sacrifice, constantly offer these great sacrifices into the senses themselves, remaining free from worldly striving.
Some offer the vital breath into speech, and speech into the vital breath at all times,
perceiving the inexhaustible accomplishment of sacrifice within both speech and the vital breath.
Other brahmins always perform these sacrifices with knowledge alone,
perceiving through the eye of knowledge that their ritual action has its root in knowledge.

“Those who know the scriptures of sacrifice” (*yajñaśāstravidaḥ*) are those who know the meaning of the Vedas together with the Upaniṣads. “Without exerting themselves” (*anīhamānāḥ*) means not making efforts for the sake of external sacrificial implements. The grammatical connection is: “they constantly offer oblations” (*satataṃ juhvati*). Since it is impossible for the senses and the sacrifices themselves to be the objects of the oblation, by implication the meaning is that the five functions of the sense organs directed toward form and other objects are the objects of the oblation through the means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*); thus, by means of their restraint, they accomplish the cessation of those five functions. “Some,” being devoted to the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), perform the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in accordance with the function of speech; that is, those devoted to breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) perform speech in accordance with the function of the vital breath. Or rather, they always effect the accomplishment of sacrifice in the utterance of sound and in the activity of the vital breath. Seeing, according to the scriptures, the accomplishment of sacrifice in both speech and the vital breath, they attain “imperishable” (*akṣayām*) [merit] by way of its fruit. And so says the Śruti: [Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.3.2.14]...

As long as a person speaks, he is not able to breathe; at that time, he offers the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into speech. These two infinite, immortal oblations he offers constantly, both while waking and while sleeping.

Thus: "They sacrifice" by means of "knowledge"—either through the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or through the ritual slaughter of the Vaiśvānara and other deities—"by these" [means] by those characterized as described above. "Of these" refers to the sacrifices. "Action rooted in knowledge" means an observance (*anuṣṭhāna*) in which knowledge is primary. "Perceiving" this with the eye of the wisdom of the Upaniṣads, the following is what is meant: when it is impossible for those entitled [to perform rites] to carry out the five external sacrifices using external means, they must nevertheless accomplish the five sacrifices even by means of these [internal ones], such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), in order to remove the fault caused by the omission of the vows of a *snātaka*.
Śaṅkha and Likhita: [152]
Henceforth, the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) is prescribed for all.

It should be performed by offering grains that are not prohibited by the duties of one's specific stage of life (*āśrama*), excluding *kodrava*, *caṇaka*, *māṣa*, *masūra*, *uddālaka*, and *kulattha*. Alternatively, he should give rice to his wife in the morning or cook it himself. Having thoroughly cleansed the house, smeared it with cow-dung, and offered incense, prayers, and being purified and self-controlled, he should perform the necessary rites from the food every evening and morning. He should offer [the first portion] into the fire with the mantra, "Svāhā to Agni Jātavedas," and the second silently. He should worship the sun with the mantra, "Upwards that Jātavedas... (RV 1.50.1).

The phrase “without contradicting the duties of one’s stage of life (*āśramadharma*)” refers to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Therefore, that forest-dweller must perform the sacrifice to the gods and other rites using food prescribed for his own stage of life, such as uncultivated *nīvāra* grain and the like. The phrase “he should give to his wife” implies it is for the purpose of cooking. The phrase “or himself” applies to cases where it is impossible for the wife to perform the cooking. Regarding the words “well-swept,” this refers to the well-sweeping and smearing of the house doors; “incense” is for the sake of the deities and others; and “recitation of purifiers” refers to the chanting of sacred texts. “Purified” means being clean.

“Niyataḥ” means one who possesses restraint. “Annāt” means from food that is fit to be eaten. “Āvaśyakāni” refers to the obligatory rites such as the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) and so forth. “In the fire” (*agnau*), the word “should offer” (*juhuyāt*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. “The second” (*dvitīyām*), the word “oblation” (*āhuti*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
— Āpastamba [2.3.1–17].

Noble persons (*ārya*) who are pure shall prepare the food for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. One should avoid speaking, coughing, or sneezing while facing the food. Having touched one's hair, limbs, or clothing, one should touch water. Alternatively, Śūdras supervised by noble persons may be the preparers of the food; for them, the same rule for sipping water (*ācamana*) applies. Furthermore, they must shave their hair, beards, nails, and body hair every day, and bathe with their clothes on. Or else, they may shave only on the eighth days or on the festival days (*parvan*). Food prepared out of sight should be placed over the fire and sprinkled with water; this is called "the purification for the gods" (*devapavitra*). When the food is ready, standing, he should announce to the master: "It is ready. The response is: "May that well-prepared food, which is the *virāj*, not fail me. Whatever is to be eaten by the householder, its offerings and oblations (*bali*) are connected with heaven and prosperity. When these mantras are employed, there is lying on the ground, celibacy, and avoidance of pungent and salty foods for twelve days. For the final [mantra], there is fasting for one night. For the oblations, the preparation of that place consists of wiping it with the hand, sprinkling it, placing the offering, and finally pouring water around it. One should offer the six primary oblations with the hand into either the domestic (*aupāsana*) or cooking fire, mantra by mantra. There is sprinkling of water both before and after, as previously described.

“Āryas” here refers to virtuous twice-born men (*dvijātis*). “Purified” (*prayatāḥ*) means clean. “In the Vaiśvadeva” means during the Vaiśvadeva rite. “Sneezing” (*kṣavathuḥ*) is hiccups. Regarding “hair,” the rule is that one should touch water upon touching hair, even that which is purified. “Supervised” (*adhiṣṭhitāḥ*) means watched over. “That very same” is the procedure for sipping water (*ācamana*) for the Āryas. “On the eighth days” refers to the lunar dates (*tithis*). “Out of sight” (*parokṣam*) means not supervised by Āryas. “That is a divine purifier” (*devapavitra*): that food is pure even when offered to the gods, how much more so when eaten by oneself. “Householder” (*gṛhamedhin*) refers to the *gṛhastha*. Even when the maintenance of life is sustained by food cooked on fire, the *homa* offerings and *bali* oblations must necessarily be performed with that very food. “At the time of use” (*upayoge*) means at the time of the first application. The vow (*vrata*) consists of sleeping on the ground and so forth, ending with the avoidance of pungent and salty foods. For “the highest,” however, after the twelve nights, there is an additional “one fast” (*upavāsa*) at the time of the first application of the *bali* mantra. The consecration (*saṃskāra*) of that entire place of offering (*balideśa*) is to be done by repetition (*āvṛtti*), not by a single ritual act (*tantra*). “Having scattered” (*nyupya*) means having performed the pouring out (*nirvāpa*). “On both sides” (*ubhayataḥ*) means at the beginning and at the end. “Sprinkling around” (*pariṣecana*) is the encircling of the *balis* with water.

Kātyāyana in the *Candogapariśiṣṭa* (2.153–154) states: "If, at the announcement of the spirits (*bhūtapravācana*), the wife should be absent due to menstruation, illness, or other such reasons, how do the ritualists proceed in that case?"
One should cause a woman of the same caste who prepares the food in the kitchen to announce it;
or one may do so beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*, according to the word of Kātyāyana.

“*Bhūtapravācanam*” (the announcement of the food being ready) means that once the food is prepared, the master or the wife announces, “The food is ready. In this regard, the meaning is that if the wife is not present, one should cause another woman of the same *varṇa* who has performed the cooking to make the announcement. However, if she is unable to say “it is ready,” then she should say something else that conveys consent, such as the syllable *oṃ*; this is the intended sense.
“Of the prepared food for the *vaiśvadeva*, according to rule in the domestic fire...”
A Brāhmaṇa should perform the fire-oblation daily for these deities.
First for Agni and Soma, then for those two together,
then for all the Viśvedevas, and for Dhanvantari as well.
To Kuhū and Anumati, and to Prajāpati,
together with Dyāvāpṛthivī, and finally to Sviṣṭakṛt.
“Of the two together” means with Agni and Soma; “together with Heaven and Earth” means with Heaven and Earth—thus it should be performed. Viṣṇu [67.1–3].

Then, having swept around the fire, sprinkled water around it, spread grass around it, and replenished the fuel, he should take the first portion from all the cooked food and offer it, saying: "To Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, Vāsudeva; to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Indra-Agni, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, Anumati, Dhanvantari, Vastopati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Thus says Gautama [5.11].
The oblations are offered with the formulas: *agnāv agniḥ*, *dhanvantariḥ*, *viśvedevāḥ*, *prajāpatiḥ*, and *sviṣṭakṛt*.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* (1.131):
"Among sacrificial grains, barley is primary; rice is traditionally considered secondary to it."
One should avoid masha, kodrava, gaura, and the like, even if all other grains are unavailable.
“Gaura” is a white mustard seed. [156] Āpastamba [2.15.14–18]:

There is no offering of alkaline substances or salt. Likewise, there is no offering of food mixed with inferior grains. When there is an offering of non-sacrificial food, one should remove hot ashes toward the north and offer it therein; thus it becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire. A woman shall not offer; nor shall one who has not been initiated.

“Alkaline salt” (*kṣāralavaṇam*) means salt from saline soil (*ūṣaralavaṇa*). “Mixed with other food” (*aparānnasaṃsṛṣṭam*) means connected with another kind of food. “Unfit for sacrifice” (*ahaviṣyam*) refers to black gram (*māṣa*) and the like. However, if alkaline salt and such items are indeed to be offered in the oblation (*homya*), then the meaning is: having removed the hot ashes toward the north—that is, toward the northern direction—one should offer them into that fire. Vasiṣṭha [11.3–6].

One should offer the Vaiśvadeva oblation from the food prepared for the evening and morning meals into the domestic fire. One should present the bali offering to the household deities. After giving [portions] to a Śrotriya and immediately thereafter to a student (brahmacārin), one should give to the ancestors. Then one should feed the guests.
"Vaiśvadeva" refers to the food whose deity is the Viśvedevas. Thus says Śātātapa.
The sacrifice to the elements, the ancestral rite (śrāddha), and the constant gratification of guests must be performed in this sequence,
while the study of one's own Vedic recitation (svādhyāya) should always be maintained.
And this sequence of the *bhūtayajña* and so forth is established according to specific Vedic branches. Yājñavalkya [1.103–104]:
"From the food remaining after the oblation has been offered to the gods, one should present the *balih* offering to the spirits (*bhūta*)."
One should cast food upon the ground for dogs, outcastes, and crows.
Then Manu [3.87–93]:

Having thus properly offered the oblation, he should present the bali-offering to Indra, Antaka (Yama), Appati (Varuṇa), and Indu (Soma), together with their followers, while circumambulating in all directions from left to right.
One should offer to the Maruts at the door, and to the pestle and mortar;
one should make an offering to Śrī at the head of the bed, and to Bhadrakālī at the foot.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati in the center of the dwelling;
one should cast the bali-oblation into the air for the Viśvedevas,
as well as for the spirits that roam by day and those that roam by night.
One should offer a bali-oblation on the back part of the house for the sake of all beings;
as for the remainder of the bali, one should carry it all to the south for the ancestors.
One should slowly place [the food] on the ground for dogs, outcasts, dog-cookers, those afflicted with foul diseases, crows, and insects.
[158] Thus, that Brāhmaṇa who constantly worships all beings goes by a straight path to the supreme abode, which is composed of light.
Likewise [3.121]:
"In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer the *bali* without mantras;
for this is called the *vaiśvadeva*, which is prescribed for both morning and evening."

"Thus" means in the manner of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). "At the head" means at the head-end of the householder's bed, or at the head-end of the site of the dwelling (*vāstupuruṣa*). "At the foot" means at the foot-end of the householder's bed itself. "To Brahmā and Vāstoṣpati"—the ritual application for the offering of the *bali* is exactly like this. "On the back of the site" means in the rear of the house, specifically at the place where urination and defecation are performed. "To Sarvānubhūti" means to the deity Sarvānubhūti. "Gently" means so that there is no damage whatsoever to the food. And when the *bali* is offered for the benefit of crows and other such creatures, it should be given in a place where their use is possible. By the word "honors," it is stated that one should not show disrespect even toward dogs and others in the giving of the *bali*. "By a straight path" means by a direct route. "But in the evening," however—this refers to the case where, in the evening, with food already prepared, the wife offers it without mantras in the absence of the sacrificer, his sons, and others. "Should carry" means he should give.
Having prescribed the offering of bali to the elements, beginning with dogs, Yama says:
"One should offer everything according to one's ability, preceded by the prescribed ritual;
thus disciplined, the householder shall go to heaven—of this there is no doubt."
[159] With the word "with the hand" understood, Āpastamba states [ĀpDhS 2.3.18–23; 2.4.1–5]:

Thus, for the offerings gathered in various places, there is a sprinkling of water once at the end. They should be performed with [the food] mixed with broth. To the west of the fire, one performs [the offering] with the seventh and eighth [formulas], ending toward the north. Near the water-vessel, with the ninth. In the middle of the house, with the tenth and eleventh, ending toward the east. In the north-eastern part of the house, with the four following [formulas]. In the place of the bed, with the formula containing the word "desire" (*kāma*). On the threshold, with the formula containing the word "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*). To the north, on the cover, with the following [formulas]. To the south, with the formula containing the word "fathers" (*pitṛ*), wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and with the palm turned downward, he should perform [the offering]. The final one is dedicated to Rudra, as in the case of the other deities. For these two, the sprinkling of water is separate because of the difference in their ritual rules. At night, with the last [formula], the offering is made in the open air. He who performs these rites daily without distraction, according to the instruction, attains heaven and prosperity.

“*Evaṃ balīnām*” (Thus for the offerings): just as in the case of the Vaiśvadeva oblations mentioned in passages such as “*agnaye svāhā*,” there is a “sprinkling around” (*pariṣecanam*) at the beginning and end with mantras such as “*adite anumanyasva*,” so too for the “offerings” (*balīnām*), meaning those that are “assembled” (*samavetānām*) or combined. The word “*sati*” means that when there is space, the offerings should not be made in a place “mixed with soup” (*sūpasaṃsṛṣṭe*), i.e., in a location where they would be intermingled with one another. With the two [mantras] ending in “*svāhā*”: “*dharmāya svāhā*” and “*adharmāya svāhā*,” the completion is toward the north (*udagapavargam*). With the ninth [mantra], “*adbhyaḥ svāhā*,” near the water-vessel (*udadhāna-sannidhau*); “water-vessel” (*udadhānam*) refers to a large storage jar (*maṇika*) and the like. “In the middle of the house” (*madhye gārasya*) means in the center of the dwelling. With the tenth and eleventh [mantras]: “*oṣadhivanaspatibhyaḥ svāhā*” and “*rakṣodevajanebhyaḥ svāhā*,” the completion is toward the east (*prāgapavargam*), meaning arranged facing east. In the “north-eastern region” (*uttara-pūrva-deśe*), that is, in the *aparājita* direction. With the four [mantras] following for the house: “*gṛhebhyaḥ svāhā*,” “*avasānebhyaḥ svāhā*,” “*avasānapatibhyaḥ svāhā*,” and “*sarvabhūtebhyaḥ svāhā*. With the [mantra] containing the word “desire” (*kāma-liṅgena*): “*kāmāya svāhā*. On the “lid” (*apidhānyām*), i.e., the door-panel. The subsequent mantras begin with “*pṛthivyai svāhā*” and end with “*brahmaṇe*. With the [mantra] containing the word “ancestors” (*pitṛ-liṅgena*): “*svadhā pitṛbhyaḥ*. The “Rudra-mantra” is: “*namo rudrāya paśupataye svāhā*. Because of the distinction in the nature of the recipients—as it has been said: “The ancestors desire speech, while the deities desire the inner state”—therefore, for the ancestral offerings, it must be performed with the mantra itself. With the final [mantra], “*ye bhūtāḥ pracaranti*,” one should make the offering only in the air (*vaihāyasam*), and no other.

Gautama [5.18]: To the deities of the directions, according to their respective [locations]; to the Maruts at the doors; having entered, to the deities of the house; to Brahmā in the center; to the Waters by the water-jar; to Ākāśa in the intermediate space; and to the night-walkers in the evening.

"According to their respective [locations]" means that the offering (bali) should be given in whichever direction each deity, such as Indra and the others, belongs. Regarding the phrase "to the deities of the directions," the word "and" (ca) implies [offerings] to their attendants as well. "Having entered" implies "having entered the house. "And in the evening" adds [the requirement] "to the night-walkers."

Then, with the remainder of the food, he should offer the *bali* oblation to the carpenter (*takṣan*) and his assistant (*upatakṣan*). To the east of the fire, on all sides, he should offer to the female spirits (*duli*s) with the following names for each: "Thou art Ambā by name," "Thou art Dulā by name," "Thou art Nitatnī by name," "Thou art Cupuṇīkā by name," "Thou art Amrayantī by name," "Thou art Meghayantī by name," "Thou art Varṣantī by name. Then, moving clockwise around the stakes, he offers to Nandinī, Subhagā, Sumaṅgalī, and Bhadrakālī. To the pillar, to Dhruvā, to Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī, and to the Lords of the Forest (*vanaspati*s). At the door, to Dharma and Adharma, and to Death (*mṛtyu*). At the water-cistern, to Varuṇa. To Viṣṇu at the mortar. To the Maruts at the grinding stone. Above the roof, to King Vaiśravaṇa and to the Spirits (*bhūta*s). To Indra and Indra’s men in the eastern part. To Yama and Yama’s men in the southern part. To Varuṇa and Varuṇa’s men in the western part. To Soma and Soma’s men in the northern part. To Brahmā and Brahmā’s men in the center. Upwards, to Ākāśa. To the spirits that roam by day upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). To the spirits that roam by night, at night. Then, upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, he should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather; and for the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, using their respective names and *gotras*. He should also present ointments, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings for the rice-balls. Having placed a water-pitcher nearby, he should have a prayer for well-being (*svastyayana*) recited. He should scatter food on the ground for dogs, crows, and outcaste dog-cookers (*śvapaca*).
“On both sides” means on the south and north. “In the corners” means in the intermediate directions. “In the upper shelter” means in the upper story. And this is the established rule for the Kaṭhas.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) with the words "Adoration to Brahmā" at the *brahmasthala* (the center of the house); to Soma by the water-jar; to Vāyu in the *vāstu-gṛha* (the air-hole or upper chamber); to Gṛhapati at the door of the house; to Prajāpati in the inner chamber; with "May the divine waters be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*) at the fire-ritual site; to the lords of the quarters and their attendants in the western half; to Soma and the attendants of Soma in the northern half; to Brahmā and the attendants of Brahmā in every direction; to the lunar mansions, the planets, and the deities in the intermediate space; to the Lord of Beasts everywhere; and with "Adoration to the gods" in the north-eastern direction. Having offered the oblation to the ancestors with "Svadhā to the ancestors" at the *brahmasthala*, one should wait for a guest for as long as it takes to milk a cow.
“In the place of Brahmā” means in the middle of the house. “He should wait for” means he should expect.
Regarding the procedure for offering the bali-oblation, Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* (2.44):
“The final disposal is to be performed just like that of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).”
Likewise [2.35–38]:
"An offering is prescribed with the words 'Salutation to such-and-such,' because a salutation is performed for the purpose of presenting the offering."
The utterances *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *namas* belong to the dwellers of heaven;
*svadhā* belongs to the ancestors, and *hantakāra* belongs to human beings.
From this point on, one should always offer the ancestral *bali* with the utterance of *svadhā*.

Regarding that, some perform it with salutations (*namaskāra*), but Gautama says "no. And the *balis* are not to be smaller than the size of a large cat's ear; if they are offered in one place, they must all be complete and not touching one another.

“Like a ball of rice”: just as the ritual treatment of balls of rice involves casting them into the fire and so forth, so too it is for the offerings (*bali*). “And not smaller than the lower limit”: the offerings must not be less than the size of a cat’s ear.
[In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 3.11.42–49:
One should first perform the *agnihotra*, and after that, offer to Brahmā.
One should offer an oblation with devotion, dedicated to Prajāpati.
Then, one should offer to the Gṛhyās, to Kāśyapa, and then in sequence to Anumati;
thereafter, one should pour the remainder of that into the water-jar for Earth, Parjanya, and the Waters.

O tiger among men, one should cast the element for the door and the element for the archway, and in the center, one should offer to Brahmā; now hear from me concerning the deities of the directions of the house.
A wise person should offer the bali consisting of the remnants of the oblation to Indra, Dharmarāja, Varuṇa, and likewise to Indu, in the eastern and other directions.
In the north-eastern direction, the wise man should offer the bali-oblation to Dhanvantari;
thereafter, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
In the northwest, one should offer an oblation to Vāyu; then, to the quarters all around, to the Directions;
and to Brahmā, to the Intermediate Space, and to Manu, one should cast the offering.
O Lord of Men, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) intended for the Viśvedevas, all beings, the ancestors who are the lords of the universe, and Yakṣman.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa [34.94–101]:
Then one should worship the Fire, and oblations should be offered in due order;
one should first offer to Brahmā, and then to Prajāpati.
One should offer the third portion to the household deities, and another to Kāśyapa;
thereafter, one should present an offering to Anumati and likewise give the domestic bali-offering.

Whatever has been previously explained by me regarding the procedure for the performance of daily rites, one should thereafter perform the Vaiśvadeva; now hear from me concerning the bali offerings therein.
Having designated the deities individually according to their respective locations,
one should offer three [libations] at the water-jar for Parjanya, the Waters, and the Earth.
One should offer to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ at the two doorways in sequence;
then to Vāyu, to the intermediate directions, and to the cardinal directions starting from the east, in order.
To Brahmā, to the intermediate space, and to Sūrya in due order;
and likewise to all the gods and to all beings.
Then one should offer to Uṣas and Bhūtapati in the north;
and having said "Svadhā, obeisance," one should also offer to the Pitṛs in the south.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, one should offer water mixed with the remnants of food according to the prescribed rule, saying: "O Yakṣman, this is your ablution-water."
Likewise [as stated in verse 29.21]:
"Then, having taken water for their rinsing of the mouth,
the wise one should pour it out in various places, designating the deities by name."
Then, having taken other food, he should again, with a concentrated mind, offer it at his own will upon a clean spot of ground to all beings without exception. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.11.50–57)
Gods, humans, animals, birds, Siddhas, along with hosts of Yakṣas, Uragas, and Daityas;
Pretas, Piśācas, and all trees.
And those who desire food given by me.
May the ants, insects, moths, and the like,
who are hungry and bound by the fetters of karma,
attain satisfaction through this food offered by me.
May they who have been released from them become happy.
To those who have no mother, no father, no kinsman, and likewise no prepared food or even food itself—
this food offered upon the earth is for their satisfaction.
May they attain satisfaction and may they be joyful.
All beings, as well as this food and I myself— Viṣṇu— are not other than that;
therefore, I am the very essence of the multitude of beings.
I bestow food for their well-being.
This fourteenth class of spirits, and all the hosts of beings who dwell therein—
for their satisfaction, food has indeed been offered by me.
May this [offering] bring them joy.
Having uttered this, a man should offer food endowed with faith for the benefit of beings upon the earth, since the householder is the refuge of all.
Then the man should give [food] on the ground to dogs, *caṇḍālas*, and birds.
Āpastamba [2.4.10–11]:
"The first portion must be given. One should feed the guests first."
“*Agram*” refers to four mouthfuls, as stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*. Baudhāyana [2.5.15] says:
“One should give the first portion (*agram*) to one learned in the Vedas.”

Manu [3.94–98]: Having performed this rite of offerings in this manner, one should first feed the guest; and one should give alms according to the rule to the mendicant and the religious student (brahmacārin).
Whatever merit one obtains by giving a cow to a preceptor according to the prescribed rite,
that same fruit of merit one obtains by giving alms to a mendicant.
One should offer even alms or a vessel of water with respect and according to the prescribed rule to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the Vedas.
The offerings to the gods and ancestors of ignorant men perish when given by donors out of delusion to Brahmins who have become like ashes.
An oblation offered into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins— who are enriched by knowledge and austerity—
delivers one from misfortune and even from great sin.
Viṣṇu [67.26–28]: He should give alms and exert the greatest effort in honoring guests. Yama.
"O monks, for that person who gives alms with due respect,
the Blessed Yama has declared that their merit is equal to the gift of a cow."
Yājñavalkya [1.108]: Alms should be given with due respect to a mendicant and to one who observes his vows.
"One who observes his vows" refers to a student (*brahmacārī*).
Śātātapa says: A single morsel constitutes a *bhikṣā*; four times that is a *puṣkala*. The wise know that four *puṣkala*s constitute a *hantakāra*.

[168] Āpastamba [1.3.26]: For women who refuse [alms], a concentrated student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) takes away their merit of sacrifice, gift, and oblation, as well as their offspring, cattle, Vedic luster, and food. Therefore, one should not refuse a group of students wandering for alms. "For even among these, he may be one of such a kind and observing such a vow," so says the Brāhmaṇa. "Refusing" means rejecting those who have come for the purpose of begging. "Among these" refers to the students (*brahmacāriṣu*). "Observing such a vow" means observing the vow of giving alms.
Yama said: "Alms-food, water, and condiments that have been placed directly into the hand— by eating these one falls into impurity, and by giving them one does not go to heaven."
Vasiṣṭha [11.5]:
Having given the first portion to one learned in the Vedas and immediately thereafter to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), he should offer it to the ancestors.
This occurs under the recurring term "śrāddha"; thus says Śātātapa.
The feeding of worthy Brahmins according to one's capacity is always proclaimed as the constant rule for every concluding rite.
"Abhirūpāṇām" means of the learned. "Apavargaḥ" means the completion of the five great sacrifices.
Manu, Śātātapa, and Śaṅkha state in the first [chapter]:
"One should offer the śrāddha daily with food and water."
Or even by means of water, roots, and fruits, he brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
For the sake of the ancestral rites among the five sacrifices, one should feed even a single Brahmin;
however, for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should not feed any Brahmin at all.
Yogiyājñavalkya says:
One who desires his own welfare should perform the śrāddha rite day by day with food, drink, or even water,
for the sake of satisfying the ancestors.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.30–32] states:
"One should feed even a single Brahmin for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*),
provided there is no other recipient or food available for the rite dedicated to the gods (*adaiva*)."
Furthermore, having set aside some food according to his ability and in accordance with the rules,
a twice-born man should give it day after day to the ancestors and to human beings.
Having said, "This for the ancestors," one should cause the utterance of *svadhā* to be made.
"Non-divine" means devoid of the Viśvedevas.

The daily *śrāddha*: Outside the village, those who are pure prepare [the offerings] in a pure place. Therein are new materials—those by which the food is prepared and those upon which it is eaten—and these he should give to those who have eaten. He should feed those of equal status, and he should not give the remnants to one who does not possess those same qualities. This continues for a year. Among them, he should perform the final [offering] with iron and goat meat. He should also have a covered receptacle (*māna*) constructed; in its northern half, he should feed the Brahmins. They teach that he sees both: the Brahmins eating and the ancestors in the receptacle. From this point forward, [the rites] may be performed or omitted at will.
