Through the *śrāddha*, the ancestors make known their satisfaction.

“*Nityaśrāddham*” means that which is performed daily. The repetition of the word “*śucayaḥ*” (pure) is for the sake of emphasizing that purity is a necessary constituent in every respect. “*Samudetāḥ*” means well-extracted; the meaning is those who are superior by virtue of their birth, learning, and so forth. “*Na cātadguṇāya*” means to one who lacks the aforementioned quality of being well-extracted. Here, “*ucchiṣṭam*” refers to the remainder of the food prepared for the *śrāddha*. Regarding the phrase “*teṣām*,” etc., among those *śrāddhas* performed day after day, that which is the “*uttamam*” (best) *śrāddha* at the end of the year should be performed with food mixed with the meat of a red goat. “*Mānam ca*” means a house, where materials such as beds and seats are measured—that is, placed. “*Praticchannam*” means covered on all sides. And in the “*uttarārdhe*” (northern part) of that house, one should feed the *brāhmaṇas*. And in that house, while the *brāhmaṇas* are eating, one should “*paśyati*” (behold) the ancestors as if they were actually present in the form of ancestors. “*Kṛtākṛtam*” means that when this has been performed once in a year, thereafter the daily *śrāddha* becomes as if both performed and unperformed; the sense is that there is no fault in its non-performance, yet there is merit in its performance. By the word “*śrāddhena*,” it is meant that by this annual *śrāddha* performed in this manner, they make known—that is, declare—their own satisfaction lasting for the duration of their lives.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* (16.5–6):

"I shall now describe the daily [śrāddha], which is devoid of the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana). One should know that it is without the gods (adaiva); the *pārvaṇa* is prescribed for the sacred festival days (*parvan*)."
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.64]: "O King, for the sake of the ancestors, one should also feed at least one other Brāhmaṇa who is a native of that same region,
whose conduct and origins are well-known, and who performs the five great sacrifices."

In the *Padma Purāṇa* (*Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, 15.139–140): "If one endowed with faith feeds a single Brahmin who has mastered the Vedānta, ten million Brahmins have been fed by him; there is no doubt about this."
And in the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.11.66]:
"A wise man should give three portions of alms to wandering mendicants and students;
and if he has the means, he may give as much as he desires without restriction."
In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* (58.98–101): "And one should give alms to a mendicant, a wandering ascetic, or a student,
having taken a portion from the prepared food together with all its condiments."
If a mendicant arrives at the house for alms when the Vaiśvadeva offering has not yet been performed,
one should set aside food intended for the Vaiśvadeva, give him alms, and then dismiss him.
[172] A mendicant immediately removes the fault incurred by performing the Vaiśvadeva rite;
however, the Vaiśvadeva rite does not remove the fault incurred by a mendicant.
In the *Padma Purāṇa* (*Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa*, 15.140–141):
"He who bestows upon ascetics alms sufficient to fill a vessel is liberated from all sins; he shall not fall into an evil state of existence."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Formerly, the Daityas, defeated by the gods and turning their backs in battle, went about with skulls in hand; some likewise observed the vow of nakedness."
Some have shaven heads and red eyes, wearing saffron-colored garments; likewise, there are Sātvatas of wicked conduct, devoid of purity and proper behavior.
Some Dānavas, covered with human bones and hair, acted under a pretext, while others,
remembering that the gods receive a share in sacrifices, remained as Rākṣasas.
A virtuous man should always perform the offering outside the house for the Brahmins, for the images, and for the gods; he should show even greater compassion toward these [beings].
Likewise: "And where even heretics do not beg for alms, nor speak ill of those who have gone outside [the community]."
For those who are patient, firmly established in their own teaching,
and subsisting by alms in the empty forest;
[173] Even if one recites the Vedas, performs the *agnihotra* sacrifices correctly, and observes vows and fasts— what is the use of that if one constantly engages in rivalry with virtuous people?
They commit terrible sins.
Let alone these many prattlings in the midst of heretics and the sick;
those who perform improper actions are even more wicked.
Just as among wicked women, there is one who slays her husband.
Reflecting that this world is agitated by suffering,
and saying, "Homage be to the Dharma," one should offer food while meditating on Viṣṇu as all-pervading.
Having indeed prostrated, [he should do so] for a measure of twelve finger-joints.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* [29.35–37]:
"Alms (bhikṣā) should be the size of a mouthful; four mouthfuls are called an *agra*;
the best of the twice-born say that four times an *agra* is an *hantakāra*."
Whether it be a full meal, a morsel of food, or even a single alms-gift,
one must not eat without first giving according to one's own means.
In the Mahābhārata:
"He who always gives a handful of fodder along with food to another's cow,
without having taken his own meal, goes to the heavenly world."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "O daughters of Surabhi, benefactors of all, pure ones, heaps of merit,
O mothers of the three worlds, may you accept this morsel from me."
One should always give a morsel of food to cows with this mantra.
By scratching the cows, giving them fodder, or providing even a single daily mouthful,
men shall attain great merit equal to the gift of a cow.

In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "He who provides the daily fodder for cows, including grass, water, and other necessities, should know that he obtains the fruit of giving a hundred Kapila cows; of this there is no doubt."
O auspicious one, composed of the five elements, meritorious, pure, and born of the sun;
accept this which is given by me, O daughter of Surabhi; homage be to you!
Following the offering of the bali-oblation, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.58, 59, 63] states:
"Then he should remain in the courtyard of his house for a period of time equal to the milking of a cow,
or longer than that according to his wish, for the purpose of receiving guests."
A householder should honor a guest who has arrived there with a welcome and other courtesies;
he should regard that visitor as Hiraṇyagarbha himself.

Thus ends the section on the Vaiśvadeva and other festivals within the *Niyatakālakalpa-kāṇḍa* (the section on rites for fixed times) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister of peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
[175] 6 Now, the honoring of guests.
In that regard, after the offerings to the ancestors, Vasiṣṭha [states at 11.6]:
"Then one should feed the guests, the superior ones in due order.

"The superior" means those who are distinguished by birth and other such qualities. "In due order" means sequentially. The meaning is that one should feed each person who is superior by birth and so forth first, in succession.
Manu and Viṣṇu state that for a guest who has arrived, one should first offer a seat and water,
and then food according to one's ability, having honored him in accordance with the prescribed rule.
Whatever meritorious fruit is obtained by offering oblations into the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule,
the fruit gained when a Brāhmaṇa is gratified is equal to or even superior to that.
Due to the reversal of mantra-practices, from misfortune, and even from an evil state, that fruit perishes for the doer; this occurs when an act is performed without faith.
Even for one who constantly gathers grains by gleaning and offers oblations into the five fires,
a Brahmin residing unhonored takes away all his merit.
Grass, ground, water, and fourthly, kind speech—
these are never lacking in the house of the virtuous.

“*Saṃprāptāya*” means one who has arrived of his own accord without an invitation. “*Udakam*” refers to water suitable for washing the feet and so forth. “*Vidhipūrvakam*” means according to the manner prescribed for honoring a guest. “*Tatphalam*” is the fruit of the *agnihotra* sacrifice. “*Idam*” refers to the giving of a seat and other such things. “*Śilān*” refers to the remains of harvested grain. “*Uñchataḥ*” means gathering [grain]. By this, it is stated that even a poor person must perform the honoring of guests. “*Sūnṛtā*” is speech that is both pleasant and true. — Śaṅkha and Likhita.

One should wait for as long as it takes to milk a cow. If at that time a guest arrives—one learned in the Vedas, observant of Vedic vows, a mendicant following the rules of asceticism, a lifelong student, or one of similar conduct, or anyone else who comes—he should honor him and then eat. For even a Brahmin of meager means, by not eating, takes away the merit of the host; the offspring of one who eats before honoring guests are cut short.

A *śrotriya* is one who has studied even a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda. A *vedavratī* is a student (*upakurvāṇaka*). One whose duty is that of an ascetic (*yatidharma*) is an ascetic (*yati*). A *naiṣṭhika* is a perpetual celibate (*brahmacārī*). [177] One of "similar livelihood" (*samānavṛtti*) is one whose means of subsistence are equal, such as a householder for a householder. "Of one who eats while [others] wait" (*paryaśnataḥ*) means eating while neglecting a guest. Likewise: "Just as all deer and birds resort to a watering place (*nipāna*)."
In this way, the virtuous in this world seek out a householder who has attained such perfection.

One should not despise a learned Brāhmaṇa; for a Brāhmaṇa is entirely immeasurable like fire. Just as fire—whether consecrated or unconsecrated—is indeed a deity, so too a Brāhmaṇa, whether learned or unlearned, is worthy of honor by all. For where a Brāhmaṇa does not eat, even that which is offered into his mouth is, for him, as if it were not offered into the fire; there, even the gods do not take their own share. Indeed, Brāhmaṇas are beyond the gods; through the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, even the gods conquered heaven.
"Exalted" refers to the fire consecrated by Vedic rites; "surpassing the gods" means superior to the gods. Again, Śaṅkha and Likhita [state]:

To one who is endowed with age, appearance, learning, and austerity, he should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and various kinds of food according to his ability. He should sit with him, engaging in pleasant conversation and answering questions. If the visitor has a vehicle, he should accompany him until he mounts it; if he does not have a vehicle, he should follow him until he receives permission to leave, or at least as far as the boundary of the village, and then bid him farewell. If the visitor wishes to stay there, he should honor him with a bed and other articles of bedding. At nightfall, having taken leave, he should go to sleep; he should wake before [the guest]. When the guest departs, he should follow after him. Having met him, he should turn back in the proper manner. At a sacred altar (*vedi*), a garden, a grove, an assembly hall, a water-station (*prapā*), a pond, a temple, a great tree, a shrine, or a river—whichever of these is available—he should circumambulate the guest from left to right, saying, "May we see you again."
Having said, "In order to see him again," he should circumambulate him at one of the sites, such as the altar (vedī) and so forth. Thus says Hārīta.

When a guest arrives—whether he be an ascetic (*yati*), a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), or a *snātaka* who follows the same mode of life—one should offer him a welcome, water for the hands (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and a seat; one should also bring whatever medicinal herbs are available. As the guest departs, following after him, one performs the steps of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇukrama*). His fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers rejoice. Having been permitted by him, one should return. If the guest stays, one should attend upon him according to the prescribed rule.

“Snātaka” here, by implication, refers to one who has not yet married, since the term “one of similar conduct” (samānavṛtti) already includes the householder. “Herbs” (oṣadhayaḥ) refers to rice and other grains. “Viṣṇu-steps” (viṣṇukramāḥ) are the mantra-accompanied recitations that constitute parts of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice. Again, Hārīta says:

They say that the Brahman of universal form is twofold: the Supreme (para) and the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahma). The Brahman is all the deities. Because they consist of the Brahman, because they originate from the Brahman, and because they have authority over the Brahman, Brāhmaṇas belong to all the deities. Whichever deity a Brāhmaṇa satisfies with food, he pleases that very deity. Indeed, when the Brāhmaṇa is satisfied, the gods and the ancestors are satisfied in turn. For that [offering] does not spill, it does not fall away, and it does not become stale. The Brāhmaṇas are the cause. For fire does not carry the oblation for those who treat Brāhmaṇas with contempt, nor do the gods and ancestors accept it. "For those who treat the Brāhmaṇas—the cause—with contempt, there is neither this world nor the next," so say the teachers. Those wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītinaḥ) belong to the gods; those wearing it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ) belong to the ancestors. Those purified by knowledge (vidyāsnātāḥ) belong to Agni; those purified by vows (vratasnātāḥ) belong to Indra; those purified by both belong to Vaiśvānara. All the deities come to the house of him for whom a Brāhmaṇa knowing this comes. From him who does not rise to greet such a one, the deities of the vital breaths depart; consequently, through his vital breaths, he becomes worse off and reaches a state of exhaustion. When he rises to greet him, the deity of the Brāhmaṇa does not depart from him; therefore, he does not become worse off through his vital breaths, nor does he reach a state of exhaustion. When he says "Welcome," he thereby pleases the deities of the house. When he honors him with a seat and other offerings, he thereby pleases Agni and the sacrifice. When he performs the washing of the feet, he thereby pleases the ancestors. When he honors him with food, he thereby pleases Prajāpati. When he follows him as he departs, he attains all desires—superiority and spiritual splendor (brahmavarcasa)—through that act.

“Viśvarūpa” because it is the source of the world’s activity; “brahmayatvāt” because it consists of the Veda; “brahmasaṃbhavāt” because it originates from the mother Gāyatrī, who is of the nature of Brahman, at the time of initiation (*upanayana*); by the word “brahmaṇi,” there is a reference to the satisfaction of all deities when the Veda exists. Regarding those “who overcome the cause of the Brāhmaṇas”—that is, those who disregard the Brāhmaṇa, who is the cause of the world—[the same applies]. Again, Hārīta says: “Indeed, the gods abide in Brāhmaṇas with their entire being.”
And they say that the twice-born is like fire; therefore, the Brahmin is the presiding deity.
Just as the gods reside in fire, so do they reside in Brahmins.

An *atithi* (guest) approaches like a blazing fire. Having studied one branch (*śākhā*) of each of the Vedas according to the sacred law (*dharma*), one becomes a *śrotriya*. One who approaches a householder engaged in his own duty, motivated by righteousness and for no other purpose, is an *atithi*. Through honoring him, there is peace, heaven, and prosperity. Having approached him face-to-face and greeted him according to age, he should offer him a seat. According to some, the seat should not have many legs if within one's means. He should wash his feet; according to some, two *śūdra* couples should perform this washing. One of them may be present for the sprinkling. According to some, he should offer water in an earthen vessel. One who has not yet returned from his teacher’s house (*asamāvṛtta*) should not offer water; here, the completion of study is the qualification. Having consoled him, he should satisfy him with savory foods, snacks, and water, at least to a minimum. He should provide a dwelling, a bed above, a mattress, a pillow, a coverlet, and ointment. Having summoned him, he should prepare rice or barley for the sake of the meal. He should look at the food that has been set out, thinking, "Is this more? or "Is this not enough? He should simply say, "Bring more. One should not eat the food of an enemy or of one who hates him, nor of one who suspects him of a fault or has been suspected. For it is known that he consumes the sin of that person. This is the sacrifice of the householder dedicated to Prajāpati, which is perpetually extended. The fire for guests is the *āhavanīya*; the fire in the household is the *gārhapatya*; and the fire on which food is cooked is the *anvāhāryapacana*. He who eats before the guest eats the strength, nourishment, progeny, cattle, and the merit of sacrifices and charitable works belonging to the house. Food with milk poured over it is equal to the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice; with clarified butter, it is equal to the *ukthya*; with honey, it is equal to the *atirātra*; with meat, it is equal to the *dvādaśāha*; and with water, there is an increase of progeny and long life. It is known that both dear and unpleasant guests lead one to the heavenly world. When he gives in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, these become the *savana* (pressing) rites. What he attends to is the concluding bath (*udavasanīya*). What he consoles is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and the praise. What he accomplishes are the *viṣṇukrama* steps. What he turns back toward is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Thus says the *Brāhmaṇa*. If a king comes as a guest, he should cause a more exalted honor to be shown to him than to himself. If a guest comes to one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), he should rise to meet him personally and say: "O *vrātya*, where did you stay? "O *vrātya*, [here is] water. "O *vrātya*, satisfy yourself. Before the *agnihotra* oblation is offered, he should mutter softly: "O *vrātya*, may your mind be as you wish"; "O *vrātya*, may your will be as you wish"; "O *vrātya*, may what is dear to you be fulfilled"; "O *vrātya*, may your desire be fulfilled. If a guest arrives when the fires have been taken out but the oblation has not yet been offered, he should rise to meet him personally and say: "O *vrātya*, give me leave, and I shall offer. Only when permitted should he offer; if he offers without permission, the *Brāhmaṇa* declares it a fault. If he entertains guests for one night, he conquers the earthly worlds; for a second night, the intermediate worlds; for a third, the celestial worlds; and for a fourth, the distant worlds; it is known that by an unlimited number of nights, he conquers unlimited worlds. If a guest claiming to be such arrives who has not completed his studies, he should give him a seat, water, and food, saying, "I give this to a *śrotriya*"; thus his gift becomes complete. One should not rise for a guest who has already been provided lodging, nor should one descend from a seat if he was already saluted first. One should eat only the remnants of the guests' meal. One should not consume delicacies in the house without leaving a portion for the guests. One should not cook food for oneself alone.

“Endowed with his own duty (*svadharmayuktaḥ*)” means one who follows the conduct appropriate to his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). “Placing duty foremost (*dharmapuroskāraḥ*)” means being intent on religious duties such as pilgrimages, or being capable of sustaining life by other means, but not being greedy for food. “Having met according to age (*yathāvayas sametya*)” means having gathered together with guests in accordance with their age—whether younger or older—and having welcomed them appropriately with a formal greeting (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) and so forth. “Not many-footed (*abahupādam*)” refers to a two-legged seat and the like. “A Śūdra couple (*śūdramithunau*)” means two Śūdras; between them, one should be occupied with “the sprinkling (*abhiṣecana*)” for the purpose of providing water for washing the feet. “Of him (*tasya*)” refers to the guest; “water (*udakam*)” he should bring for the *arghya* offering. “With an earthen (*mṛnmayena*)” vessel. “He should not cause water to be brought (*nodakam āhārayet*)” is to be connected with the word “earthen. If a student (*brahmacārī*) who has not yet returned home (*asamāvṛttaḥ*) arrives as a guest, then after giving him the *arghya* and other honors, a “recitation-convention (*adhyayanasaṃvṛttiḥ*)” must be performed; something should be studied together with him. “Having consoled (*sāntvayitvā*)” means having offered praise regarding his lineage and other qualities after the recitation. “With juices, foods, and waters, he should honor him to the very end (*avarādhyena*)”; “to the very end (*avarādhyena*)” means by the lowest possible standard. The connection is that even if juices and so forth are unavailable, he should satisfy him even with water. “An upper bed (*upariśayyā*)” is a couch and the like. “A mattress (*upastaraṇam*)” is a woolen rug and so forth. “A pillow (*upadhānam*)” is a bolster and so forth. “A coverlet (*avastaraṇam*)” is a cloth placed over the woolen rug. “An ointment (*abhyañjanam*)” is oil and the like. “Rice or barley (*vrīhīn yavān vā*)” is an illustration for the purpose of providing satisfaction. “Served out (*uddhṛtāni*)” means placed in the eating bowl. “He should say (*brūyāt*)”—the word “to his wife” (*patnīm*) is to be supplied. “Of one examining for a fault (*doṣeṇa mīmāṃsamānasya*)” means of one considering it as a defect. “Of one already examined (*mīmāṃsitasya*)” means of one who is indeed regarded as a defect. “Superior to himself (*ātmanā sreyasīm*)” means more excellent than himself. “The honor (*pūjām*)” [is expressed by] the mantra of inquiry: “O *vrātya*, where did you stay? The mantra for the offering of water is: “O *vrātya*, water. When a guest arrives before the *agnihotra* oblation, these mantras beginning with “O *vrātya*” should be uttered in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). “When the fires have been carried out (*uddhṛteṣu*)” means when they have been moved to the sacrificial ground. “Commanded (*atisṛṣṭaḥ*)” means instructed. “The Brāhmaṇa (*brāhmaṇam*)” is the portion of the Veda containing injunctions. “One who has not attained excellence (*asamudetaḥ*)” means inferior. “Speaking (*bruvāṇaḥ*)” means saying, “I am a guest. The phrase “having formed the thought, ‘I give to a *śrotriya*’” is to be supplied. “By which (*yena*)” house. “Having provided a dwelling (*kṛtāvasathaḥ*)” means having granted lodging. Seeing that householder, the guest should not rise from his seat, nor should he descend from the couch and so forth. “To guests (*atithibhyaḥ*)” who have arrived, he should not eat completely without first setting aside juices such as salt, milk, and the like.

Furthermore, Āpastamba [2.8.14; 2.9.1–4]: Having rejected a guest, if one should remember him after the meal has been consumed, one should stop eating, fast for that day, and on the following day, having satisfied him to his heart's content, one should complete the rite. One should wait for a guest with a vehicle until he departs by vehicle; for others, until he gives leave to depart. If there is no sign of him, one should turn back at the boundary.

"Having rejected a guest" means having failed to provide food and so forth to someone who has arrived according to the duty of hospitality, due to forgetfulness or some other cause. "When the meal is finished" means as long as the meal continues; whether it is only partially done or half-finished, if he should remember [the guest], then "having ceased from that meal"—that is, without taking his evening meal—he should stop. [186] "According to his wish": having satisfied him with whatever is pleasing to him. "Accompanying" means following after. One should follow an arriving guest who possesses a vehicle, such as a horse or the like. For "another," one who lacks a vehicle, one should follow until permission is granted. However, if the guest has no inclination to grant permission, then one should go as far as the boundary of the village and return even without being permitted.

Vasiṣṭha [11.13–15]: They bring water for a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived as a guest. For it is known: "The Vaiśvānara enters the house as a Brāhmaṇa guest; therefore they bring water. Except during the rainy season. And people know that this is a propitiatory rite (*śānti*). Having fed him, one should attend upon him. Then, one should follow him as he departs as far as the boundary of the village, or until he gives leave.

“Because they first bring water for drink and other needs for the sake of giving food to a Brāhmaṇa who has arrived as a guest,”—the reason for this is stated here by the words beginning with “vaiśvānara. And this bringing of water is not to be done at all times; rather, it is “except during the rains” (*anyatra varṣābhyaḥ*), meaning not during the rainy season. For [it is said], “for people know that to be peace” (*tāṃ hi śāntiṃ janā viduḥ*); “that” (*tām*) refers to the “peace” (*śāntim*) characterized by the fetching of water, which is a pacification produced by prayer—that is what “all those people” (*janāḥ*) “know. By this, Bhartṛyajña indicates that this is a well-known tradition.
Gautama [5.32–38]:

One should cause water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), and special kinds of food to be presented to a *śrotriya*; or, at all times, that which is distinguished by ritual refinement (*saṃskāra*). To one who is not learned but of virtuous conduct, food should be given in the middle [of the meal]. But to one of the opposite character, grass, water, and ground. At the very end, a welcome; and there should be no repetition of the honors.

“Various kinds of food” refers to items such as those to be sucked, drunk, or licked. “One should prepare” means one should cook. “Or always”: if one is not capable of providing various kinds of food, then one should always give whatever is cooked in one’s own house, preceded by special honor. “In the middle” means with ordinary hospitality. “To one who is unlearned” means to one who lacks a connection to sacred knowledge (*vidyā*). “To one who is the opposite” means to one devoid of learning. “Non-transgression” means not overstepping this rule. Manu [3.105–107]:
A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening must not be turned away by a householder.
Whether he arrives at the proper time or not, he should not stay in his house without eating.
One should certainly not eat that food oneself which one does not offer to a guest;
honoring a guest brings wealth, fame, long life, and leads to heaven.

One should provide a seat, a dwelling, a bed, attendance while walking behind, and respectful service; toward those who are superior, one should act with excellence, toward those who are inferior, with inferiority, and toward equals, with equality.

“*Apraṇodyaḥ*” means not to be turned away. “*Sūryoḍhaḥ*” means brought by the setting sun. When guests of superior, inferior, or middling status have arrived, the seating and other honors are not equal for all; rather, it is according to the rule: “for the superior, the best. “At the proper time” means at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice. Having stated that one should feed the guest, Viṣṇu (67.31–32) says:
“Just as the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes (*varṇas*), and just as the husband is the lord of women, so is the guest the lord of the householder. By honoring him, one attains heaven.”
Likewise:
"A householder does not attain such worlds through private recitation, the agnihotra sacrifice, formal sacrifice, or asceticism as he does from honoring a guest."
Likewise:
"The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not disrespect a guest who has arrived."
Paiṭhīnasi.

One should give food especially to a guest. The fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers look toward the birth of a son, thinking, "He will feed a *śrotriya*. Fire is satisfied by a welcome; Indra by a seat; the ancestors by water for the feet; and Prajāpati by the offering of food. Or, as has been explained, he who knows that "Brahman is one"—whether a *rājanya* becomes a guest or not is a matter of option; yet he certainly does become one. For him whose house a man learned in this way enters, one should do what is pleasing to him. Regarding the *vrātya*, thinking "that which is dear to you," and having mentally considered both the dear and the non-dear gods, one should serve them accordingly. For such a person, the *vrātya* is called a "proclaimer of the *vrātya*" and becomes the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). The sacrifices beginning with milk have been explained. The year is the guest; all the deities are its limbs. It is known from scripture: "The gods revolve around a common purpose. One should thus secure the entire year. Yet, one should not merely desire prosperity; rather, one should serve those various [guests] according to one's ability—so it is said. One should offer water, vegetables, fruits, and so forth, without hesitation, providing blameless things; thus one goes to the same world as the *ṛṣis*. Grass, ground, water, and kind speech—these in the city of the virtuous never fail. One who conducts himself in this manner attains infinite worlds. A husband and wife should make special effort regarding their bed, ointments, and baths; they go to the heavenly world. On that day, the state of a householder is attained, as well as a distinguished oblation to the fires.

“Especially food” means choice, delicious food. Or rather, the meaning is that he will feed one who “knows Brahman,” as Brahman is “explained” in the Upaniṣads as “the one Brahman. “Optionally” (*vibhāṣā*) means alternatively; and this is not indefinite, for even one who possesses good qualities certainly becomes a guest. “Prosperity” (*bhūtiṃ*) means success; the phrase “for the sake of honoring the guest” is to be supplied. “Distinction” (*viśeṣam*) means excellence. The syntactical connection is: “the couple going to the heavenly world. “On that day” means on the day the guest is honored. “The state of being a householder” (*gṛhitvam*) is for the sake of honoring the guest; the phrase “is supplied. “The offering and oblation become distinguished” means that on that day they become excellent.
Yājñavalkya [1.109]:
One should present a large bull or a large goat to a Śrotriya.
Vasiṣṭha [4.8]: [The same].
Furthermore, it is said: "If a bull or a great goat should be cooked for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who has arrived as a guest, such is the hospitality one should offer him.

Although this implies that the slaughter of a cow should be performed for the sake of satisfying a learned guest (*śrotriya*) who has come to the house, nevertheless, this is not the law (*dharma*) in the Kali age; rather, it applies to other ages.
This has been stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Long-term observance of celibacy, the carrying of a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu),
marriage within the same lineage or within the maternal sapinda relationship, and likewise the killing of a cow.
"In the Kali age, human sacrifice, horse sacrifice, and liquor must be avoided by the twice-born.
Thus [says the text]. Baudhāyana [2.5.11–13]:

"With whatever food one may have for the morning and evening meals, having offered the Vaiśvadeva oblation with that food, one should honor Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have arrived according to one's ability. If one is unable to provide for many, one should give to a single person of merit, or to whoever has arrived first."

“Whatever food one has in the evening and in the morning”: this refers to the food that one eats in the evening and in the morning. “Vaiśvadeva” means an offering (*bali*) intended for the *viśve*, that is, the many deities. “If one should not be able to give to many”: when one is unable to give to many Brahmins and others, then one should give to a single person of good qualities. If they arrive simultaneously, one should give to the one of good qualities; however, if they arrive sequentially, the settled rule is that one gives to the one who arrived first. Āpastamba [2.4.16–21].

To a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied [the Veda], one should give a seat, food, and water; one should not rise to meet him. One should approach him only for the sake of greeting, provided he is worthy of being greeted. The same applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. As for a Śūdra who has arrived as a guest, one should employ him in work. Then, one should give to him [what remains]. Or else, servants brought from the royal household should honor the Śūdra like a guest.

“Worthy of salutation” means because of being older in age and so forth. The connection “and toward a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya” implies that one should not rise [to greet them], as this is appropriate. The syntactical construction is: for that householder (*hṛhiṇa*) to whom a Śūdra arrives as a guest, his servants should treat that Śūdra according to the duties due to a guest. “From the royal family” means from the family of one’s own master. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: A non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa. Hospitality is for a learned (*śrotriya*) and virtuous person. Toward a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, it is like that toward a friend. Toward a Śūdra, it is for the sake of compassion (*anṛśaṃsya*).

The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "hospitality (*ātithya*) must be performed according to the rule. For others, however, the meaning is that "food alone should be given like a friend. "For the sake of benevolence" means for the sake of non-cruelty. Gautama [5.42–45]: There is an inquiry after their welfare, health, and freedom from disease; for a Śūdra, only the last [question]. A non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa unless he is invited to a sacrifice. As for the meal, it belongs to the Kṣatriya after the Brāhmaṇas; others [should be fed] along with the servants for the sake of benevolence.

“Anupraśnaḥ” means speaking in successive order. “Antyam” means health. “Abrāhmaṇaḥ” refers to a Kṣatriya or others. “Saṃvṛtaḥ” means constrained [193] by the lack of wealth and so forth; that is to say, poor. And this qualification applies to the householder. “Anyān” refers to Vaiśyas and Śūdras; the word “should feed” is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus says Śātātapa:
“By birth alone one becomes a highly fortunate person called a Brāhmaṇa.”
He is to be revered by all beings; he is the best of births, the father, and the teacher.
Among them, there is no one else in the three worlds worthy of worship;
they honor one another by virtue of their excellence in asceticism and knowledge.
Brahmins are traditionally regarded as each other’s teachers and each other’s guests;
by assisting one another, they both deliver others and cross over themselves.
For whoever desires to propitiate any particular deity,
he satisfies the brahmins with every possible means and effort.
Certain deities are established within certain material objects;
the Brahmins are all deities, therefore one should always honor them.
Whether with seats, food, and beds, or with water, roots, and fruits—
no guest should dwell in his house without being honored to the best of his ability.

One should not honor, even with a mere word, those who follow heretical paths, those who persist in improper actions, those who act like cats, the deceitful, the rationalists, and those who behave like herons.

“Heretics” (*pākhaṇḍinaḥ*) are those who follow scriptures outside the Veda. “Those engaged in improper acts” (*vikarmasthāḥ*) are those who, though belonging to a stage of life (*āśrama*), fail to perform the duties of their own stage when not in times of distress. [194] A “cat-vowed person” (*baiḍālavratikaḥ*) is one described by Manu with the words, “one who makes a banner of dharma while being ever covetous,” and so forth. A “hypocrite” (*śaṭhaḥ*) is one who, despite being capable of performing religious acts, practices dharma only through pretense. “Sophists” (*haitukāḥ*) are those who employ reasoning contrary to the Veda. “Those who live by usury” (*cakravṛttayaḥ*) are those mentioned in the passage beginning with “one whose gaze is downward,” and so forth. By the phrase “one should not honor them even with mere words,” all forms of honoring are prohibited; however, the mere giving of food is not prohibited.
Śātātapa and Pārāśara state in the first [section]:
"Whether he is dear or even hateful, whether he is a fool or indeed a scholar,
when the Vaiśvadeva rite has arrived, such a guest is a bridge to heaven."
Whether it be alms, or an abundant gift, or even a mere morsel;
in the absence of these, one should always give at least a vessel of water.
A single mouthful constitutes a *bhikṣā*; four times that is a *puṣkala*.
The wise know that four *puṣkala*s constitute an *hantakāra*.

“Beloved” refers to a son-in-law and the like; “hated” refers to an enemy; “foolish” refers to one devoid of study; “wise” refers to one who, having understood things as they truly are through valid means of knowledge, performs actions that yield both visible and invisible fruits; “a bridge to heaven” is a cause for attainment, like a bridge over a river. [195] Dakṣa [3.5–8]:
I shall describe the substances of nectar when a distinguished guest has arrived at the house.
One should offer this fourfold gift: a gracious mind, eye, face, and speech.
Rising to greet him, coming forward to meet him, speaking first with affection,
attending upon him, and following him— these duties should be performed with diligence.
And other minor things, such as earth, water, and grass,
as well as washing the feet, anointing with oil, a dwelling, and a bed.
One should not stay overnight in his house without eating something according to one's ability;
earth and water should be given to a seeker, and these too should always be present in the home.

“Substances easily obtained” (sudhāvastūni) means those things that can be procured without effort. “Attendance” (upāsana) means staying nearby. The connection is: “The ‘slight’ substances are the duties. They are called “slight” because they are accomplished with little effort. The connection is: “[He should have] some bedding. Furthermore, regarding the qualification of an ascetic, Dakṣa [says]: “One who has become emaciated by austerities and recitations, and is unfit for a dwelling due to illness...”
One who is aged, one seized by a planetary spirit, and any other whose sense faculties are impaired.
A mendicant who is healthy and young is not worthy of a dwelling;
for he defiles that place, while one who is old causes it distress.
Even one who is healthy and young perishes through the lack of celibacy;
having perished through the lack of celibacy, he destroys his family and lineage.
If a monk, while residing in a dwelling, indulges in sexual intercourse,
he cuts off even the roots of the owner of that dwelling.
If an ascetic rests for even a moment in someone’s hermitage, what need has he for any other merit? For he is considered to have accomplished his purpose.
Whatever sin has been accumulated by a householder since birth,
an ascetic who has stayed for even a single night wipes it all away.
"One worthy of a guest-house" means one fit to be housed in the home. "The aged" is an indicative term for those who are incapable. "Seized by a planet" means one possessed by a spirit.
Yama says: Not by the Agnihotra sacrifice, nor by giving gifts, nor by fasts or smearing [the body with ashes].
The deities are fully satisfied just as they are by the honoring of guests.
Whatever auspicious thought a guest, when honored, might contemplate in his mind,
the wise say that even a hundred sacrifices are not equal to it.
One should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give pleasant speech;
furthermore, one should rise and offer a seat—this is the fivefold dharma.
He who provides these five— a seat, water for washing the feet, a lamp, food, and shelter— performs a sacrifice complete with all sacrificial fees.
The giver of food is to be known as a giver of life; the giver of a lamp and the giver of clothing are likewise remembered [as such].
Indeed, he who gives shelter is called a giver of everything.
That which is eaten by householders who have completed their studies of the Vedas, or even that which is eaten by an ascetic, is superior; it is not so with others.
Whatever a meditator performs, he bestows half upon the donor;
therefore, giving to a meditator who is a *snātaka* yields great fruit.
A dwelling among yogis is superior to a thousand horse-sacrifices, a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices,
and a thousand Puṇḍarīka sacrifices.
He who gives unblemished food to one who is weary, who has never seen [the destination] before, who is dear, and who is traveling on the road— that is a sacrifice complete with all sacrificial fees.

“Pratiśrayaḥ” means a house for the purpose of dwelling. “Śreyaḥ” means most excellent. “Itaraiḥ” means by others than the aforementioned householder. “Puṇḍarīkaḥ” is a specific type of sacrifice. “Akliṣṭam” means respectfully offered. Bṛhaspati says:
One should give a seat to the one who has arrived, and likewise a bed to the weary.
One should give water to the one afflicted by thirst, food to the hungry;
one should give sight, one should give thought, and one should give pleasant speech.
Manu has declared this to be the common duty for all four social orders:
Agni is pleased by a welcome, and Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, by the offering of a seat.
The ancestors are satisfied by the washing of the feet, and Prajāpati by the food;
as long as the earth remains moistened by the water from the feet of the Brahmins, [so long do they remain gratified].
The ancestors drink water from the hollow of their hands for as long as travelers,
exhausted by the road and emaciated, come to one's house.
By this, the ancestors become possessed of a son and are honored with offerings of grass, ground, and so forth.
"Karṣitāḥ" means afflicted.
Viṣṇu states [in verse 67.46], following the recurring phrase "one should give to the guest":
By giving shelter, as well as bedding and an oil massage for the feet along with a lamp,
one obtains through each of these individual gifts a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.
Yama said:
Those from whose houses a Brahmin guest departs without having eaten have indeed attained the state of a donkey, a camel, or a horse.
If any Brahmin residing in one's house remains unfed,
neither the gods nor the ancestors will partake of his offerings to the gods (havya) or to the ancestors (kavya).
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he departs taking with him whatever merit that person has earned.
In whatever village a guest sleeps without having eaten, even though he has been diligently seeking alms there, the sin of killing a Brahmin is ordained for that place.
Whether one is cooking mere vegetables or subsisting by gleaning ears of grain,
a guest should not be left dejected, whether in one's own country or in a foreign land.
The sacred fires desire a guest; that guest desires heaven;
and heaven, too, desires a donor who performs good deeds correctly.
Parāśara [1.45]:
"If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
that person's ancestors do not eat for fifteen years."

The Agnihotra sacrifice, a marriage to an old maiden, the tethering of cattle at the doorway, and a guest arriving at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite— if these are treated with contempt, they burn the householder.
"Jarat" means afflicted by old age. "Tethering of cattle at the door" refers to the time when fodder, water, and so forth are not being provided. Devala says:
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, Vedic school, sacred study, country, or birth.
When solicited by Brahmins for food, one should certainly give it without hesitation.
When a guest arrives at a house and turns away disappointed and unhonored, he instantly destroys that family.
Yama said:
"Whoever honors a guest who is weary and whom they have never seen before,
it is my conviction that by him a hundred cows along with a bull have been gifted."
One should not inquire about the lineage, conduct, country, name, family,
or learning of a Brahmin who has arrived from afar and is present for the purpose of a meal.
He who gives food after inquiring about one's country, family, and learning does not obtain the fruit of that gift, nor does he go to heaven by having given it.
Parāśara and Śātātapa state:
"One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, Vedic school, sacred study, or even his birth;
rather, one should cultivate a pure disposition toward him when he has arrived of his own accord," so says Vyāsa.
Yama says:
He who reveals his country, lineage, family, or learning for the sake of food is declared,
according to the laws of Vaivasvata, to be a "vomiter-eater" (one who consumes what has been spat out).
Manu [3.108]: But if another guest should arrive when the Vaiśvadeva offering has been completed, one should give him food according to one's ability; one should not perform the Bali offering.

“In the *vaiśvadeva*”: when the cooking for all purposes is finished; “completed” (*nirvṛtte*) means having served its purpose, that is, when it is entirely consumed. “A guest” (*atithiḥ*) is one who possesses the characteristics of a guest. “He should offer the *bali*” is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *pākayajña* sacrifices other than the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*).
Now, Yājñavalkya [says]:
“A traveler should be known as a guest, as well as one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who has mastered them.”
These two are worthy of honor for a householder who desires the world of Brahman.
“*Adhvanīnaḥ*” means one who constantly travels on a journey. “*Śrotriyaḥ*” refers even to one who studies a single *śākhā*.
Thus says Baudhāyana:
“Having studied one *śākhā*, one becomes a *śrotriya*.”
Manu, Viṣṇu, and Śātātapa state in the second [section]:
"A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest."

One should recognize as a guest who has arrived at one's house not only a Brahmin from another village, but also a traveling companion, or even one’s own wife or those for whom the sacred fires are maintained.

The meaning is this: one becomes a guest by staying for a single night, not beyond that; nor does one become a guest for less than a single night even if he is a Kṣatriya or others. An "inhabitant of the same village" (*ekagrāmīṇa*) is one who dwells in the same village. A "familiar associate" (*sāṅgatika*) is one who associates with everyone through various jests, conversations, and so forth. These two, even if they arrive at the time of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, are not guests. "In the house" means in one's permanent place of residence. It is not only in the house that one is a guest; rather, Medhātithi says that one should recognize as a guest anyone who has arrived at another village or in the forest, where his wife, fires, and so forth are located—there too, one should know him to be a guest.
Yama said:
That high-souled person by whom all lunar days, festivals, and celebrations have been abandoned is a guest for all living beings; they know the rest to be mere visitors.
A practitioner or ascetic who stays for a single night is called a guest;
because he dwells there constantly, they know him as a guest.

“Parvans” refers to the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and other such occasions; “festivals” (*utsavāḥ*) refers to weddings and the like; “lunar days” (*tithi*) refers to those distinct from them, such as the first day of the month (*pratipad*) on which lamps are offered. He by whom these have been abandoned for the sake of dharma as causes for obtaining special food is a “guest” (*atithi*). According to the statement of Āpastamba [2.3.5]: “He is a guest who has no other purpose than the pursuit of dharma. Manu, Viṣṇu, and Śātātapa state in the second [chapter]: “A Brāhmaṇa staying for only one night is traditionally known as a guest.”
Since he stays only for a short time, he is therefore called a guest (atithi).
One should recognize as a guest who has arrived at one’s house— not only a Brahmin from another village, but also a traveling companion, or even one’s own wife or the sacred fires.
[203] Gautama [5.41]: A guest is one who does not belong to the same village, who stays for only one night, and who waits for the sun while remaining under a tree.

Regarding the term "one who stays for one night" (*ekarātrika*), it means one whose habit is to dwell for a single night. Maskarin and Bhartṛyajña maintain that the expression "waiting for the sun while remaining under a tree" refers to the evening time.
Parāśara and Śātātapa state in the first [section]:
"One should recognize as a guest (atithi) him who arrives unthought of and uninvited at the proper place and time; one who has arrived previously is not a guest."
One who is afflicted by hunger, thirsty, weary, and has come from a long journey—one should honor such a person with diligence; he is a guest who is a bridge to heaven.

“Place” is that which is near one’s wife and the sacred fire. “Time” begins with the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva rite. Manu and Viṣṇu [state]: “Also others, such as friends and so forth, who have come to the house out of affection.”
One should eat natural food according to one's capacity together with one's wife.

By the word "friends and others" (*sakhyādīn*), relatives and kinsmen are included. "Having honored them" (*prakṛtya*) means having treated them with great respect. "Together with his wife" (*saha bhāryayā*): the householder, accompanied by his wife, should "feed them. The meaning is that the wife as well should perform the serving of food and other such duties. Yājñavalkya (1.108) states:
"And one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen who have arrived at the proper time."
Likewise [1.113]:
"He should sit with learned and beloved kinsmen for the remainder of the day.
"At the proper time" means at the time for eating.

Āpastamba [2.5.4–11]: 4. "One should not eat food that has been brought by another, nor food that has been brought back from a journey, nor food that has been brought from a house where a funeral meal was served. 5. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where a marriage has taken place, nor food that has been brought from a house where a sacrifice has been performed, nor food that has been brought from a house where a birth has occurred. 6. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where a person is suffering from a disease, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a quarrel, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a death. 7. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where a woman who has recently given birth is staying, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a guest, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a student. 8. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where there is a fire-ritual, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a cow-pen, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a shed for storing grain. 9. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where there is a well, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a pond, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a tree. 10. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where there is a temple, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a crossroads, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a burial ground. 11. "Nor should one eat food that has been brought from a house where there is a slaughterhouse, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a distillery, nor food that has been brought from a house where there is a prostitute."

If the teacher should arrive while he has returned home from his studies, he should go out to meet him face-to-face, clasp his feet, and touch water without feeling any disgust. Having placed him in front and attended to him, he should honor him according to the instructions. Whether it be regarding a seat, a bed, food to be chewed, food to be eaten, or clothing, he should occupy a position of inferior status when these things are present. Standing, he should assist the teacher by pouring water for him to sip with his left hand, or do the same for another person of high standing. He should desire to imitate [the teacher’s] standing, sitting, walking, and smiling. When in the teacher’s presence, he should avoid passing wind, urinating, defecating, speaking loudly, laughing, spitting, gnashing teeth, yawning, stretching the limbs, shaking the head, clapping hands, and clearing the throat. He should avoid touching or conversing with the teacher’s wife or children in a manner that implies intimacy. He should avoid contradicting the teacher’s speech with his own, as well as the speech of those who are superior.

[205] “Having grasped his feet”—this is the ellipsis. “He should not touch water with loathing”: while washing the teacher’s feet, he should not perform the ritual rinsing of his own hands out of disgust at the contact. “Having placed him in front,” meaning having performed hospitality such as washing the feet and anointing them; “having presented [him],” meaning having announced that all this—wealth, body, and so forth—is yours. “According to instruction,” that is, according to the scriptures. “When the teacher is present,” he “should offer water for rinsing to the teacher while standing,” not while sitting. “Holding it with the left hand”: having taken the water-vessel held by the right hand, he should also hold it from behind with the left. “Or another who has risen”: the phrase “he should offer water for rinsing” is to be supplied here. And that offering of water for rinsing to one who has risen should be understood as being preceded by the same honors and ceremonies mentioned for the teacher, because such a person is the subject under discussion. “Desiring to imitate”: when the noble one is engaged in activities such as bathing, he himself should likewise follow after him. “When the teacher is present”—this is the ellipsis. “Teeth-cleaning” refers to the cleansing of the teeth. “Spitting” refers to the discharge of nasal mucus. “Clapping” refers to hand-clapping. “Spittle” refers to the discharge of phlegm. By the word “etcetera,” dancing, singing, and instrumental music are included. “Among offspring” means among children. “Touching” means embracing the limbs. “Speech” means conversation; he should avoid these things when they are preceded by excessive intimacy. “Of superiors,” meaning even other excellent persons, “he should avoid opposition”—this is the grammatical connection.

Gautama [5.27–32]: One should carry out the command of one's teacher, father, and friends after having informed them. For the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*), father-in-law (*śvaśura*), paternal uncle (*pitṛvya*), and maternal uncle (*mātula*), there is the offering of *madhuparka* upon their arrival; again, after a year has passed. This applies even before [the completion of] a sacrifice or a wedding. And for a king who is a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), the same applies. For one who is not a learned Vedic scholar, there is merely a seat and water.

“Of the teacher, father, and friends” who have come to the house; “having offered” means having presented prepared food and so forth. “Carrying out their word” means doing whatever they tell one to do. Regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, however, when there is an “arrival” (*upasthāna*)—that is, when they come to the house—a worship with the *madhuparka* must be performed. The grammatical connection is: “upon arrival again after a year, the *madhuparka*. As for the phrase “before a sacrifice or a wedding,” the meaning is that upon the arrival of those [priests] at a sacrifice or a wedding, the *madhuparka* is to be given even before a year has passed. Regarding the term “of a king”: if the king is a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), the *madhuparka* is to be given even before a year has passed. For a king who is not a learned scholar, only a seat and water are to be provided, not the *madhuparka*.

Manu [3.119–120]: One should honor with the madhuparka offering the king, the officiating priest, the snātaka, the guru, and one’s dear father-in-law, maternal uncle, and maternal grandfather, once every year.

Both a king and a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), when present for the performance of a sacrifice, are to be honored with the honey-mixture (madhuparka); it is the established rule that this does not apply when there is no sacrifice.

Yājñavalkya [1.110]: "However, every year, those worthy of the *arghya* offering are the *snātaka*, the teacher, the king, a dear friend, one for whom one has performed a marriage, and likewise the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) at a sacrifice."
Baudhāyana [2.6.35–37]:
One should honor those worthy of honor:
sages, the learned, excellent kings, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests.
These are recorded as the worthy recipients prescribed by the scriptures, according to the divisions of time.
At the commencement of the rite, the ṛṣis, the learned, and the kings have arrived;
the excellent officiating priests, the maternal uncle, and the father-in-law are to be honored with the Saṃvatsara cow.

“Seer” (*ṛṣi*) means one who has perceived the mantras. “Learned” (*vidvān*) means one who knows the meaning of the Vedas. “King” (*nṛpa*) means an anointed Kṣatriya who protects his subjects according to dharma. “Have arrived” implies “at the house. “At the commencement of rites” refers to sacrifices, marriages, and so forth. Āpastamba [2.8.5–9].

One who has studied the Vedas is worthy of the *gomadhuparka* (the cow and honey-mixture). So too is a teacher (*ācārya*), an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a graduate (*snātaka*), or a righteous king. To a teacher, an officiating priest, a father-in-law, or a king who has come to visit after a year has passed, a cow and the *madhuparka* are offered. The *madhuparka* consists of curd mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey; in the absence of these, water may be used. [208] "Vedādhyāya" means one who has studied the Veda. "After a year has passed" (*parisaṃvatsarāt*) means every year. Āpastamba again [states]: [2.9.5–6]

One should make all [beings], down to dogs and *caṇḍālas*, partakers of the *vaiśvadeva* offering. Some say that one should not give to those who are unworthy. "All" refers to those seeking food. "Partakers of the *vaiśvadeva*" means one should make them sharers of the *vaiśvadeva* food. "Down to dogs and *caṇḍālas*"—the prefix *ā* here indicates inclusion. "Unworthy" refers to dog-cookers, heretics, *caṇḍālas*, and so forth. The settled rule is that there is no fault in not giving to the unworthy, but there is merit in giving. —Āpastamba and Baudhāyana.

A distribution of food has been ordained out of consideration for those who are constant dependents (*bhaktika*). One may indeed restrict oneself, one’s wife, or one’s son, but never a slave or a laborer. Likewise, one should ensure that one does not restrict oneself to the extent that one remains capable in one’s duties.
"Dependents" (*bhaktika*) means those worthy of food.
Householders should give according to their ability to those who do not cook for themselves,
and they should share with all beings without causing hardship to their own dependents.
Yama said:
He who, bypassing one who does not cook, provides food to one who cooks,
shall go to the womb of liquor-sellers for more than a hundred years.
Vasiṣṭha and Manu [are mentioned] in the second verse:
"One should honor all beings with food according to one's ability;
the householder alone performs sacrifice, and the householder performs austerity."
Among the four stages of life, however, the householder is distinguished as superior.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their support in the householder.
Just as all living beings live by depending on their mother,
so do all mendicants live by depending on the householder.
“He should honor” means he should worship.
Manu [3.78–79]: Because even those belonging to the three stages of life [are supported] daily by him through knowledge and food...
They are maintained by householders alone; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
It must be maintained with effort by one who desires imperishable heaven and absolute happiness in this world— that which is difficult for those of weak faculties to maintain.

"That" refers to the householder's stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*). "By those with weak senses" means by those whose senses are unrestrained; it is "unmaintainable," meaning impossible to maintain. This is because for those with unrestrained senses, when objects of the senses are obtained at will, the performance of prescribed duties becomes impossible. Therefore, the householder is superior. Bṛhaspati says:
"The origin, the increase, and likewise the protection of the stages of life (*āśrama*)."
He is born perfectly from the householder; therefore, he is remembered as superior to him.
Paiṭhīnasi:

"There are indeed four stages of life (āśrama): the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the mendicant (bhikṣuka). All of these have the householder as their root and depend upon him. Dakṣa [2.57–60]:
Since the householder is daily supported by gods, humans, and animals alike, therefore the one in the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
The householder is said to be the source of the other three stages of life;
by his failing, the other three also fail.
The root is the vital breath (prāṇa), the trunk is the aggregates (skandha), and from the trunk come the branches and the shoots;
when the very root is destroyed, everything perishes.
Therefore, a householder should always be protected with every effort by the king and the other three [orders]; he should always be honored and respected.
[211] Now, Gautama [5.26]:

One should feed first the guest, the child, the sick person, the pregnant woman, the daughter living in the father's house, the elderly, and the dependents. One should feed these "before oneself. "Children" are infants. "Daughters living in the father's house" are married daughters. "Dependents" are servants.

The wise man should honor the guest, as well as his servants, kinsmen, and those who are to be supported. Having given food on the ground for dogs, crows, and others, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas intended for the ancestors.
Yājñavalkya [1.105].
Having fed the children, the daughters living in the household, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, young girls, guests, and servants, the husband and wife should eat what remains.
Devala says:
One should not eat before those who are pregnant, the sick, the elderly, children, the weary, and guests have eaten, nor without first informing them.
Manu and Viṣṇu [3.114]: One should feed these— married women, children, the sick, and likewise pregnant women— to the guests first, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.

“*Agre*” means first. Furthermore, the fact that in the *Smṛtis* of Gautama and others the feeding of guests is established as preceding the feeding of children and the rest is for the purpose of demonstrating the superior honor (*abhyarhitatva*) due to the guest. In the *Manu-smṛti* as well, the mutual sequence between the feeding of guests, children, and so forth is not intended to be emphasized; rather, what is intended is that the husband and wife should eat the remains of that [meal]. The intent of the statement, “But the unwise man who eats before these,” is that one should eat oneself only after these have eaten, since it forms a single syntactical unit with this verse.
Baudhāyana says:
One should feed the guests first; immediately thereafter, those who are pregnant, as well as children, the elderly, the destitute, and especially the sick.
“Dīnāḥ” means those who are suffering.
Yama says: A learned man, devoted to the sacred fire, should constantly worship the ancestors and the deities.
One should first indeed gratify the gurus, guests, and children.
Afterwards, being self-restrained, silent, and pure, he should satisfy himself;
thereafter, he should satisfy women and Śūdras—this is the eternal dharma.

"Gurus" refers to the father and others. Regarding the injunction "one should feed," Vasiṣṭha [11.5–9] states: "One should feed those of one's own *gṛhya* [family]—the girls, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth—and thereafter the other members of the household. One should offer a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, outcasts, and crows. One may give the remains of the meal (*ucchiṣṭa*) or that which is not the remains (*anucchiṣṭa*) to a *śūdra*. The husband and wife should eat what remains. However, if everything has been consumed, the rite must be performed again."

“Women who have recently given birth” (*taruṇaprajātāḥ*) refers to women who have newly delivered. “Household servants” (*gṛhyāḥ*) means those born in the house; that is to say, attendants. This alternative regarding the giving of food that has been tasted or not yet tasted concerns either *śūdras* who are dependent or those who are independent, or *śūdras* who are virtuous or non-virtuous. Regarding “the use of everything”: when all the food has been consumed by the guests, if there is another purpose for it, then for that purpose “cooking again” must be performed. However, the *vaiśvadeva* offering and other such rites are not to be performed again. Manu [3.116–118]:
“And when the Brahmins, as well as one’s own dependents, have indeed finished eating...”
After that, the husband and wife should eat what remains.
Having honored the gods, the sages, human beings, the ancestors, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists solely of what remains from a sacrifice.
The worship of the sages is performed by means of the *brahmayajña*.
Likewise, it is said:
"One should always subsist on *vidhasā* and be a consumer of the *amṛta*."
Vighasa is the remains of what has been eaten by dependents; amṛta, on the other hand, is the remains of a sacrifice.
"Dependent" (bhṛtya) means one who must necessarily be supported.
Baudhāyana [2.13.7] states:
"Of the deities, guests, dependents, as well as of mother, father, and likewise the teacher..."
Remaining silent, one should eat the remains of the meal; in this way, dharma is not lost.
Yama says: One should always be an eater of *amṛta* or, alternatively, an eater of *vighasa*. *Amṛta* is known as the remnant of a sacrifice, while *haviṣya* is considered the proper food.
But he who eats what remains after the servants have been fed, him they call a consumer of vighasa.
Devala says: Having bathed and washed his feet, being pure and adorned with garlands and perfumes,
he who eats what remains after the five great sacrifices has partaken of nectar.

[215] Hārīta says: They call that which remains after the *huta*, *nivāpa*, *āhuta*, *prahuta*, and *prāśita* offerings "immortal nectar" (*amṛta*); by partaking of this, householders and forest-dwellers attain union (*sāyujya*) with Yama.
Yama and Paiṭhīnasi say the same.
One should not cook food for one's own sake, nor should one slaughter animals for one's own sake;
one who cooks for the sake of the gods or for the sake of Brahmins is not defiled.
Yama says: He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
one should avoid cooking in vain that which merely produces gratification for the senses.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
One should not disregard the gods, dependents, guests, ancestors, and oneself; one should eat what remains after these have been provided for.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (29.39–40):
"Householders should be fed according to one's own means when wealth is available;
for that kinsman who suffers while a wealthy kinsman is present [is at fault]."
Whatever has been done by one who is sinking, he partakes of that very sin.
The phrase "equal to oneself" (svasamam) means that one should feed them food equal to what one eats oneself; this is the meaning. [216] In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
O bird, those fools who eat without first performing the Vaiśvadeva rite,
as well as those who do so without a witness, go to the womb of a deer.
Baudhāyana [2.5.17–18]:
One should never eat without having first given [to others]. Moreover, in this regard, they cite two verses concerning food:
"He who eats me without having given to the ancestors and the deities..."
Eating what has been prepared for his servants, guests, and his own kinsmen out of delusion, he eats poison; I devour him,
and I am his death.

He who has offered the agnihotra sacrifice, performed the vaiśvadeva rite, fed his guests, and given to his dependents; who, being contented, pure, and full of faith, eats what remains— such a person eats me.
"In that [state] there would be immortality, and he protects me. Thus [says] Dakṣa [2.61–62]:
"Even a householder engaged in ritual action does not become a true 'house-dweller' (gṛhī) merely by means of his home."
Nor indeed, being deprived of his own karma, does he [live] with his sons and wife.
But those who eat without having bathed, without having offered oblations, and without having given gifts,
become debtors to the gods and others, and go down to hell.
Likewise: "For one person indeed eats food, while another is eaten by the food;
he alone is not truly eaten who eats in the presence of witnesses."
"Then, having made a distribution [of food], the householder should eat what remains.
"Witnesses" refers to guests, servants, and so forth.
(Yama and Śātātapa).
Those lowest of the twice-born who eat without having first offered the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice go to the womb of a crow; that cooking of food is in vain for them.
Āpastamba [2.15.13]:
That food which is not prepared in one's own fire and the first portion (*agra*) of which is not offered, that must not be eaten.
"Of which" refers to the food.
Jābāli said: "One who eats without having bathed consumes impurity; one who recites no prayers consumes pus and blood;
one who offers no oblations consumes worms; and one who gives no gifts consumes poison."
Yājñavalkya [1.121]: Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of Śrāddha rites,
he should not neglect the five great sacrifices by means of the mantra of obeisance.
Parāśara [1.38]: A Brāhmaṇa who is constantly devoted to the six duties, who worships the deities and guests, and who eats only the remnants of the oblation, does not come to ruin.
The six rites, beginning with sacrifice (*yajana*), which will be described hereafter.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*).
In the section on rites performed at fixed times, the worship of the lunar day (atithipūjā).
[219] 7 Now follows the procedure for eating.
In that regard, one should be skillful:
"And likewise, in the fifth part, a distribution according to what is appropriate is prescribed for the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and even insects."
"Then, having made a distribution, the householder should eat what remains.
"Distribution" means giving after having divided [the food].
— Devala.
Having bathed and washed his feet, being pure and adorned with garlands and perfumes,
he who eats what remains after the five great sacrifices is an eater of nectar.
Having washed his feet in a clean, smeared place, being pure and restrained in speech,
he should eat his food facing the east while seated upon a seat.

Having thoroughly washed his hands and feet and sipped water, having taken hold of the food offered in a clean, enclosed place, and having cast away desire, anger, malice, greed, and delusion, he should eat with all his fingers without making a sound. He should not throw the remainder of the morsel into the vessel. Having eaten meat, fish, sesame, or honey mixed together, he should sip water and touch fire.

“Covered” means wrapped with a cloth or the like; the word “having sat down” is to be supplied. “Offered” means brought near. “Having received” means having properly taken [the food] with affection into a vessel placed nearby. “Making no sound” means making no noise such as hissing while eating. “The remainder of the morsel” means the remainder of what was taken to eat. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: “One should enter the place of eating with hands well-washed.”
But he who, out of pride, should sip water while remaining seated in the midst of the row;
That lowest of men takes upon himself all the sins of everyone;
therefore, Bali, having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya) and being properly purified by rinsing his mouth (svācāntaḥ), should enter his home.
On a clean, level, and smooth spot provided with a soft seat,
[one should prepare] a square, a triangle, a circle, or a half-moon shape.
The mandala among the Brahmins and others should be established in due order;
from within the mandala [emerge] Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, Candra, Ārka, and the Vasus.
Because they do not accept food offered by men otherwise,
those of base birth who eat without having prepared a maṇḍala [are reborn as such].
But for them, yakṣas and rākṣasas carry away that strength of their food.
Manu [2.52]: "Eating while facing east promotes longevity; eating while facing south brings fame;
eating while facing west brings prosperity; and indeed, eating while facing north brings truth."

“Beneficial for life” (*āyuṣyam*) means conducive to longevity. “Conducive to fame” (*yaśasyam*) means conducive to renown. Regarding both “prosperity” (*śriyam*) and “truth” (*ṛtam*), the sentence is completed by supplying the word “desiring” (*kāmayamāna*). “Truth” (*ṛtam*) means either reality or sacrifice. Hārīta says: One who desires long life should eat facing east; one seeking fame, facing south; one desiring prosperity, facing west. Not facing north. One should not eat while lying down on a bed, nor while seated on a seat. Not from a vessel of black iron, nor from an earthen vessel, nor from one that is broken or defiled.

"On a bed" means on a couch or similar high bed; "on a seat" means on a stool or similar seat—the phrase "having placed the food vessel" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "In iron" means in a vessel of black metal (iron); "in earthenware" means in a bowl or similar earthen vessel. "Broken" means cracked; "defiled" means rendered impure by the eating of it by outcastes or the like.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa: "And one should not eat here facing south."
And one should not eat facing west. Furthermore, this prohibition against facing south or north applies to those who are free from desire; for one who has desires, [it is said]:
"Facing west, he eats prosperity; facing north, he eats truth."

Thus, because the rule for eating with both faces is prescribed, the prohibition against eating facing south applies specifically to one whose mother is still living. Accordingly, Āpastamba states in the section concerning those desiring prosperity (Puṣṭikāmādhikāra):
"One should eat silently, facing south. However, they teach that eating while facing such a direction is detrimental to longevity for one whose mother is living."

[223] In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.79–80]: O Lord of Men, one should eat wearing more than one garment, with hands and feet not wet, with a pure face and a cheerful mind, and not facing an intermediate direction.

A man should eat facing either the east or the north, and not with his mind distracted; nor should he face an intermediate direction—that is, facing toward the corners such as the southeast (āgneya) and so forth. In the phrase "facing the east or the north," the verb "should eat" (*bhuñjīta*) is to be supplied.
— Yama.
One should eat one's food facing the east, with five limbs moist, restrained in speech, and pure; indeed, one should eat with wet feet, but one should not sleep at night with wet feet.
One who eats with wet feet lives for a hundred years.

"Five things wet" refers to having the hands, feet, and face wet. Having stated "five things wet," the subsequent mention of "wet feet" is intended to emphasize the importance of keeping the feet wet.
(From the Viṣṇupurāṇa).
Having bathed according to rule and performed the libations for the gods, sages, and ancestors,
the self-restrained householder, holding auspicious gems in his hands, should eat.
O King, having had his hair shaved and offered oblations into the fire, he should wear clean garments.

"Excellent jewels" refers to those such as the *gāruḍa* and others. "Having had his hair shaved" means having performed the ritual offering (*nirvāpa*) for the sake of the gods and other deities. [224] Manu says:
Eating in the evening and in the morning is the mealtime ordained by the gods for human beings;
no eating should be done in between, for this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice.

In this context, the words "evening" (sāyam) and "morning" (prātaḥ) refer to night and day respectively. Thus, Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [2.33]: "Twice-daily eating has been prescribed by the sages..."
For the Brahmins dwelling in the world of mortals,
this [should be performed] daily during the day as well as at night, within the final three-quarter watch of the night.

Here too, the word "day" (*ahaḥ*), following the authority of Dakṣa, refers to the fifth division of the day. "Tamasvinī" means night. "Within half a watch and a *yāma*" means within the middle of the first watch and a half.
[As stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"In vessels appropriate to the purpose, together with sons, servants, and one's own kin..."
Having placed the bowl on the ground, one should eat the food in silence.
With the *pavitra* in hand, one shall obtain merit there through the *aghamarṣaṇa*.

"In vessels corresponding to the purpose" means in vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth, according to one's own wealth. "The *aghamarṣaṇa*" refers to the merit produced by the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite.
One should always honor one's food and eat it without disparaging it;
upon seeing it, one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome it in every way.
For food that is always honored bestows strength and vigor;
but when eaten unhonored, it destroys both of these.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Having seen the food, one should first bow down and then speak with palms joined in reverence, saying,
