"May this be ours forever," and one should honor it with devotion.
Janārdana himself has declared that food is Viṣṇu:
"The twice-born who knows the scriptures, while eating, gives me to the life-breath."
One who always meditates upon me for the sake of their life-breath shall always worship me;
holding the vessel with the left hand, it should be placed upon the ground.
Reciting "Tejo 'si," one should bow to the food, for it is nectar;
as stated in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (34.28):
"A wise person should not proclaim any defect in the food except when there is actual spoilage."
[226] Pollution (*upaghāta*) consists of being touched by dogs, crows, and the like.
The elder Śātātapa says:
"The lower garment is worn first; the upper covering comes after."
For food becomes non-naked, as does nectar, when it is accompanied by an upper garment.
That which was previously called "apośana" is the "lower garment," and the subsequent "apośāna" is the "upper covering.
Yājñavalkya [1.106]: By means of the *apośāna* rite, one who eats both above and below [the navel] [is purified].
Food should be made free from fire and indeed immortalized by the twice-born.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "One should take the *apośāna* water, for it contains all sacred fords (*tīrtha*);
with the mantra 'Thou art the under-layer of nectar,' [one takes it] for Viṣṇu, who consists of food."
One should never leap over food with one's hand while it is accompanied by water;
if one who eats leaps over it out of hypocrisy, by that act the food becomes defiled.
And the food of that evil-minded man becomes unfit for consumption;
having first eaten five mouthfuls in some narrow dwelling, [he incurs this fate].
Having lifted up the vessel, one should eat the remainder out of fear of confusion;
while eating during a rite for the ancestors, one should not move the vessel from the ground.
Likewise: "Then, one should offer five oblations accompanied by the *praṇava* (OM) to the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*), into [the fires] resembling the fire of universal dissolution."
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* [3.11.89]:

"One should take five morsels while observing great silence (*mahāmauna*) for the purpose of nourishing the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. By the mention of "great silence," the complete cessation of all sound is intended.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"When the *prāṇa* is satisfied, those whose eyes are the sun and heaven are eternally satisfied;
when the *vyāna* is satisfied, the ears, the skin, and the quarters are likewise satisfied."
When the *apāna* is satisfied, fire, speech, and earth are always satisfied;
when the *samāna* is satisfied, mind, rain, and lightning are satisfied.
When Udāna is satisfied, Vāyu and Ākāśa are always satisfied;
when these are satisfied, the entire world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, becomes satisfied.
Abounding in progeny, he shall be a celibate student; he prospers through cattle and food. A Brahmin who knows the Prāṇāgnihotra becomes a donor and is endowed with prosperity.
Likewise: Having eaten, one should drink water once, once for the purpose of sealing the nectar;
so that the food may not remain naked throughout the three worlds, which are the very life-force of all beings.
A Brahmin who always eats in this manner shall attain preeminence among his kinsmen.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
[He should eat food] endowed with the qualities of divine substances and consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti.
The food of the learned, when sprinkled with water consecrated by the deities, is prepared according to the prescribed rule.

"Accordant with Śruti and Smṛti" means understood through the Śruti and Smṛti. "Endowed with the qualities of divine substances" means fit for sacrifice. "In the manner ordained by the gods' waters" means eating in exactly that manner in which it has been ordained.
— Hārīta.

Now I shall proclaim the rule for the feeding of Brahmins. Having bathed, wearing unwashed garments, with a purified soul, seated facing the east, and having washed his hands, he should recite the *daśahotr* formula and meditate upon the unmanifest Puruṣa, saying: "Go to Indra, svāhā! He should consecrate the food being brought with the mantra: "Oṃ, you are splendor. He should consecrate the food being given with: "May Heaven give you. Having accepted it with: "May Earth receive you," he should recite: "I am Agni, Jātavedas by birth;
clarified butter is my eye, nectar is in my mouth."
The sun, the threefold chariot of passion, the unaging heat;
I am the oblation by name.
I am the first-born of Cosmic Order, the navel of immortality before the gods.
Whoever gives me away, he indeed shall possess the god.
"I eat the food that eats [me].
Thus one should consecrate the food.
"You move within all beings, in the secret cave, facing in every direction."
You are the sacrifice, you are the exclamation Vaṣaṭ, and you are the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Water, light, essence, immortality, Brahman—Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Om!

Having consumed water with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer of immortality," he gratifies all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) with individual oblations, saying, "To the out-breath, *svāhā*," and so forth. He should swallow them all together. Now follows the opinion of Maitrāyaṇi: one who desires long life should consume these ten oblations of breath, saying, "To life, *svāhā*. For thus it is said: "He partakes according to his desire. Having recited, "Thou movest within," he gratifies the Self, saying, "I offer this into the immortal source, into the true light, the Supreme Self, *svāhā*. With the words, "By that, cause the breaths to swell," he touches the region of the heart and mutters. With "Thou art the knot of the breaths," he touches the region of the breaths. With "Thou art the belly of Viṣṇu," he touches the region of the navel. Then, having again touched the region of the heart, he mutters: "O thou who art the best among the gods, O fierce one, moving along the cord, O bull, grant us immortality; O Rudra, let this be offered unto thee, *svāhā*. Having recited the Sāvitrī verse three times, while wearing wet clothes, he should meditate: "May she, who consumes the essence of many, who is the sacrifice of cooking all food, the consumer of the universe, be pleased"—thus he should meditate on the Unmanifest, the Unmanifest Person. If he steps upon urine, excrement, a road, or a cremation ground, he should sip water again after rinsing his mouth. The Brāhmaṇa who eats in this manner becomes most meritorious; he becomes a sanctifier of the company. He satisfies both sides: he satisfies the gods, he satisfies the ancestors, and he satisfies men. He purifies the food of those whose food is otherwise unfit to be eaten. "He attains union with Brahman," for thus it is said.

The *daśahotṛ* mantra begins with “*cittiḥ sruk cittam ājyam*” and so forth. By the end of the mantra, “*indraṃ gaccha svāhā*,” the *daśahotṛ* mantra beginning with “*cittiḥ sruk*” is thus demonstrated; having recited this mantra, one offers the oblation. “The unmanifest *puruṣa*” refers to the cause of the world. By “*prāṇān*,” there is the inclusion of the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna* breaths. The mention of “*āhiti*” (the offering) is for the purpose of taking up food that can be grasped solely by the ring finger and the thumb. Thus, the author of the *Vākya* in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* says: “‘The first oblation is equal’—this is the designation of the nature of the oblation, [referring to] what is taken up in small quantities. And this has been explained by the commentator Vṛddhadraviḍa: “Smallness is indicated, [meaning] as much as is grasped by the ring finger and the thumb. Why? Because it is seen that the oblation is being taken up in such a manner,” says Jayasvāmin. One should “swallow” (*nigiret*) the offered oblation; one should not let it be bitten by the teeth. The other ten oblations, beginning with “*āyuṣe svāhā*,” are optional (*kāmya*). By the phrase “according to desire” (*yathākāmam*), this is stated: there is no fixed rule regarding swallowing in the case of the remaining oblations. Having addressed [the water] with the intention expressed by “*He moves within*,” and so on, ending with the modified formula “*Thou art the covering of immortality*,” one offers the water; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Having recited the *Sāvitrī* three times, one should meditate upon the unmanifest *puruṣa* with the mantra beginning “*Clothed in waters*. Such is the qualification for one who knows the Vaiśvānara-vidyā to eat according to this prescribed procedure. And this matter is indicated at the end [of the section] by the restatement “food” (*annam*), following the words “most meritorious” (*puṇyatamam*) and so forth.

Now we shall explain the *prāṇāhuti* (oblations to the vital breaths) for those of the *śālīna-yāyāvara* class who sacrifice to the Self. At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having sat down facing the east in a place that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung, he should, upon seeing the food being brought out, pay homage with the words, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ," and restrain his speech. Having placed the food down and sprinkled water around it clockwise with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, he should drink water from the front with his left hand while not releasing his grip, saying, "Thou art the under-layer of immortality. Then, with the food, he offers the five *prāṇāhutis*: "Seated in the *prāṇa*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspiciousness, for the sake of non-burning; *svāhā* to the *prāṇa*. Seated in the *apāna*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspiciousness, for the sake of non-burning; *svāhā* to the *apāna*. Seated in the *vyāna*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspiciousness, for the sake of non-burning; *svāhā* to the *vyāna*. Seated in the *udāna*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspiciousness, for the sake of non-burning; *svāhā* to the *udāna*. Seated in the *samāna*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me as auspiciousness, for the sake of non-burning; *svāhā* to the *samāna*. Having thus offered the five *prāṇāhutis* with the food, he should remain silent and consume more, meditating in his mind on Prajāpati. Now they also cite this:

"Sitting down, facing the east, one should eat with speech controlled, not disparaging the food, without spilling it, and with a focused mind; having eaten, one should touch fire and water. One should not bite with the teeth any food, including cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, meat, and so forth. One should not be overly satiated. Having drunk water afterwards with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of immortality," and having sipped water (ācamana), he touches the region of his heart with the mantra: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; enter me, O Rudra, the all-destroyer; through this food, cause me to swell. Having sipped water again, he pours out the remnants from his hands onto his right big toe.
"The Person the size of a thumb, who dwells in the thumb, is the Lord of the entire world; as its Master and the consumer of all, he brings satisfaction. Thus it is said.

With hands raised, one should perform the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*) with these five verses: “Having entered into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through faith, may the immortal oblation enter me as auspiciousness; swell the *prāṇa* with food! Having entered into the downward breath (*apāna*) through faith, may the immortal oblation enter me as auspiciousness; swell the *apāna* with food! Having entered into the pervasive breath (*vyāna*) through faith, may the immortal oblation enter me as auspiciousness; swell the *vyāna* with food! Having entered into the upward breath (*udāna*) through faith, may the immortal oblation enter me as auspiciousness; swell the *udāna* with food! Having entered into the equalizing breath (*samāna*) through faith, may the immortal oblation enter me as auspiciousness; swell the *samāna* with food! And one should unite the self with the syllable “*brahmaṇi ma ātmāmṛtatvāya*” (In Brahman, let my self be for immortality). The sacrificer of the self (*ātmayājī*) excels all sacrificers of ritual acts (*kratuyājin*). Moreover, they cite this:
Just as cotton from the *eṣikā* reed, when cast into a fire, is consumed by flame,
even so are all the sins of one who sacrifices to the Self utterly burnt away.
"They become eaters of nothing but sin; they obtain food in vain. Thus, he should offer oblations every day, evening and morning, or at least in the evening with water.

“Śālīnas” are those whose habit is to dwell in a house (*śālā*). “Yāyāvaras” are specific types of householders whose habit is constant wandering and who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnayaḥ*). An “ātmayājī” is one who worships the fire itself, along with its implements, as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). “Āvaśyakam” refers to that which follows the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*), beginning with bathing. “Saṃsṛṣṭam” means cleansed by means of a broom or similar tools. “Upalipte” means smeared with cow-dung and water. “Uddhṛtam” (taken out)—the word “food” (*anna*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. “Upasthānam” is the act of bowing down while facing that [fire]. “Nyastam” means placed in a vessel. Regarding the phrase “food and water [should be offered] clockwise,” this is its meaning: having taken water, one should perform a clockwise sprinkling of water around the food in all directions. This connects with the expression “five oblations to the vital breaths” (*pañca prāṇāhutīḥ*). Having stated “one should restrain speech,” the further mention of “silently” (*tūṣṇīm*) is for the purpose of preventing the restriction of vocal restraint from applying solely to the five oblations. “Askandayan” means without scattering the food. It is stated that for these *śālīnas* and others, touching the fire at the end of the meal is a mandatory limb of the rite even without eating food mixed with sesame seeds and so forth, as expressed by the words “one should touch the fire. “Kandāni” refers to tubers such as the suraṇa; “mūlāni” refers to roots such as radish. Although cakes and other foods are already included by the mention of “all edible things,” their specific mention is for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the fault [if they are not handled properly]. “One should not bite with the teeth” means that once a portion has been broken off with the teeth, the remainder should not be eaten again. “With five”—the word “with the aforementioned mantras” is to be supplied. With the mantra “May my self be joined to Brahman for the sake of immortality,” one should “join” the self—the individual soul—with the “Imperishable” (*akṣara*), the Supreme Brahman; the meaning is that one should contemplate them as one. “Or with water in the evening”: if an evening meal is impossible, everything including the oblations to the vital breaths must be accomplished with water alone.

Āpastamba [2.1.1–3]: From the taking of the hand onwards, there is a vow for the two householders. There is eating at two times; and there is non-satiety with food. "From the taking of the hand" means after marriage. "Of the two householders" refers to the husband and wife who are established in the householder stage. "At two times" means at the evening and morning times. "Eating" means by means of food. The genitive case is used here in connection with a word having the sense of "sufficiency."
Gautama [9.59]: One should eat in the evening and in the morning food that has been honored, without finding fault with it. Baudhāyana [2.13.10–14]:
Whether he be a householder or a student, if one should practice austerity while fasting,
he would indeed become an outcast by neglecting the *prāṇāgnihotra*.

Except in the case of a penance; regarding that penance, the rule is the same. Furthermore, they cite this example: "He who never eats anything between his morning meal and his evening meal is always one who observes a fast."
"One should mutter the mantras of the *prāṇāgnihotra* when food is withheld,
just as one would mutter the mantras of the three sacrificial fires (*tretāgnihotra*) when the ritual materials are unavailable.
He who conducts himself in this very manner is fit for becoming Brahman.

“Householder” here refers to one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). “Not eating” means performing a fast. “One who has broken his vow of chastity” (*avakīrṇin*) is one who is liable for the penance prescribed for such a transgression. “Except for a penance” means except for a penance involving fasting. The reason for this is stated right here: “In the case of a penance, that very rule applies”; specifically, fasting alone is the rule prescribed for that particular case. By this, the following is meant: where a specific rule for fasting is prescribed with reference to one who maintains the sacred fires, only there does he have the entitlement to perform the act of fasting, and not elsewhere. The same applies to the student (*brahmacārin*). Regarding the phrase “between the morning meal,” etc.: “between” (*antarā*) means in the middle; “meal” (*āśa*) means eating. “Fasting” (*upavāsī*) means one who partakes in the fruit of fasting. This occurs when, although one is fit to eat, the cessation of eating happens precisely because food and other necessities are unavailable. “The three fires” (*tretā*) refers to the *Gārhapatya* and the others. “In the absence of materials” means in the absence of the materials required for the *agnihotra* oblation.
In the section concerning those desiring prosperity, Āpastamba states [2.19.3–12]:

A cup made of *udumbara* wood with a golden center is highly praised; no one else should eat from it. One should not move the food while eating so long as the mouthful has not been swallowed; one should swallow the entire mouthful without dropping it or letting it fall, always including the thumb. One should not make a noise with the mouth, nor should one shake the hand. Having sipped water, one should hold the hands raised until they become wet. Then one should touch fire. During the day, one should not eat anything other than roots and fruits; one should avoid foods intended for the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice and those offered to the gods. One should eat wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and covered by an upper garment.

“*Audumbara*” means made of copper. By the words “nor even by another,” etc., it is stated that even his son must not eat from that vessel. “*Yāvadgrāsam*” means as much as can be swallowed at once. “*Nāpajihīta*” means he should not release the vessel with his left hand; or alternatively, “*apajihīta*” (he may release it). This option regarding holding or not holding the vessel is settled like the rule of taking or not taking the *ṣoḍaśī* cup. According to Kapardi: if the meal was commenced initially with the vessel held, then it must be held; if the meal was commenced initially without holding it, then it must not be held. “*Prodakībhāvaḥ*” means being accompanied by an abundance of water. And this touching of water (*agnyupasparśana*) refers to the context of eating food mixed with sesame, meat, and so forth. “*Divā na bhuñjīta*” (he should not eat during the day)—the word “again” (*punar*) is to be supplied as the remainder. “*Sthālīpākaḥ*” is the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) for the fortnights and other occasions. “*Anuddeśyāni*” means things not intended for the gods, ancestors, and so on. He himself, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*) and having an upper garment (*sottarāchādanaḥ*), i.e., with an upper cloth, “should eat. According to Kapardi’s commentary, one should not use a cord or similar item for the sacred thread at the time of eating, apart from the upper garment.
Vasiṣṭha [12.15–17]: One should eat food facing the east. One should swallow the entire morsel silently with the thumb. And one should not make a sound with the mouth.

By the mention of "food," it is indicated that the rule regarding facing the east and so forth does not apply to betel and similar items. Since silence is already established by the very use of the word "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*), the further prohibition of making a sound with the mouth is intended to exclude sounds such as hissing (*sītkāra*) other than speech.
[240] Manu [4.62]: One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor should one practice excessive satiety;
one should not eat too early, nor too late in the evening, nor having already eaten in the morning, should one eat again in the evening.

“Oil-removed” refers to oil-cakes and the like. “Too early” means when the sun has only just risen. “Too late” means near the time of sunset. “Having eaten in the morning” means being satiated in the morning; one should not eat in the evening. Viṣṇu [68.48]:
“One should not eat a third time, nor ever anything unwholesome.”
Neither too early, nor too late, nor having eaten in the evening, should one eat in the morning.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.11.87]:
"One should eat with the mind focused on that, beginning with sweet flavors;
likewise, salty and sour in the middle, and those that are pungent, bitter, and so forth at the end."
A person should eat liquid food first, solid food in the middle, and liquid food again at the end;
thus, one does not lose strength and health.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: One should eat using all the fingers and never wave the hand [to fan the mouth];
one should take food consisting of milk-rice and should not drink curd afterwards.
One should fill half the stomach with food and one part with water;
one should leave the fourth part empty for the movement of the vital air.
Devala says: A householder should never eat a meal himself without clarified butter;
for they say that ghee is purifying, heart-pleasing, and a destroyer of sin.
Manu [4.55]: "One should not eat at the time of twilight.
Āpastamba [1.17.6–8]: [text omitted as per instructions]

One should not eat on a boat, nor should one eat on a palace or on prepared ground. Regarding "on a boat," the word "seated" is to be supplied. Regarding "on a palace," the meaning is "on top of a palace. Regarding "on prepared ground," it refers to ground made ready by the application of earth. [Thus it is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
But that which one eats with the palm [of the hand], that which is eaten with a hissing sound,
and that which is eaten with fingers spread apart— this is like beef for him.
One should not eat while the previous meal is undigested, nor when one is excessively hungry;
one should not consume food while standing upon an elephant, a horse, a chariot, a camel, or a palace.
Whether situated within a cremation ground or having gone to a temple,
one should not eat while lying down, nor with food held in the hand, nor while seated on a seat.
Neither during the two twilights, nor at midday, nor ever at midnight;
neither with wet clothes, nor with a wet head, nor without the sacred thread.
Nor with his feet outstretched, nor with one foot placed upon the other, nor seated with his knees bound together, nor sitting cross-legged on a couch.
Nor with his head wrapped, nor with a vessel held in his lap,
nor with only one garment, nor in the midst of the wicked, nor wearing sandals or shoes.
Nor [should one eat] from a vessel placed upon leather or one whose sides are wrapped in leather;
nor should one find fault with the impurity arising from the production of food, nor with a defective arrangement of the row.
One should not eat the remnants of a mouthful, nor drink the remnants of what has been drunk;
one should not chew vegetables, roots, fruits, sugarcane, and the like with the teeth.
One should not eat food that has been hoarded, nor food scattered by other food and placed in a vessel;
one should not eat with haste in the midst of many people who are eating.
A Brahmin should not scatter food in vain, nor should he go anywhere while still impure from remnants of food;
he should not touch his own head with a hand that has food particles on it.
One should never discard half-eaten portions of sesame paste, water, milk, curd, honey, ghee, or roasted flour.

“With fingers extended” means with fingers that are not contracted. “And he should not be excessively hungry” means he should not afflict himself with excessive hunger. “Vehicle” refers to a swing and the like. “Paryaṅkikā” means a small chair or stool. “Wicked persons” refers to those who have fallen from their status and so forth. “One whose sides are covered in leather” refers to one who has put on armor and the like. “He should not disparage the impurity of birth or a bad row”: “disparaging birth” is by way of being born in a censured place; “impurity” is filthiness; “one of a bad row” is one whose cooking is censured. “Leftover from drinking” means precisely what remains in a drinking vessel. “By biting with the teeth” means having cut it with the teeth. “With food” means he should not heap together food such as cakes that has been scattered in the bowl. “With a hand that is soiled” means with a hand smeared with leftover food; the meaning is that he should not touch his own head. “Half-eaten” means slightly consumed.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Water, milk-rice, clarified butter, and even the remains of honey—one should discard the remnants of these; they must not be given to anyone."
"Nirasyam" means that which should not be abandoned.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"One should not eat even in a single row together with one's own kinsmen [if they are unworthy]."
For who indeed knows what hidden transgression anyone might possess?
One should break the line with columns of ash, water, doors, or paths.
As stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.11.83, 86]:
"O Lord of Men, [one should not offer] into a vessel placed upon a stool, nor in an improper place."
A man should not eat at an improper time, nor in a place that is too crowded, nor without first giving the first portion.
O Lord of the World, a discerning person should not consume anything in its entirety,
except for scum, water, curd, clarified butter, and roasted flour.

“Āsandī” refers to a seat made of cane and similar materials. “In an improper place” means on a road or similar location. “At an improper time” means at the junctions of day and night (saṃdhyā) and so forth. “Maṇḍa” is defined as follows:
“Barley meal mixed with clarified butter and saturated with cold water—neither too liquid nor too thick—is designated as maṇḍa.”
Thus says Caraka. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should not enter the kitchen for the sake of eating; one should not cook food in vain; nor should one eat food cooked in vain.

Hārīta says: One should not eat while angry, nor with a distracted mind, nor while speaking; one should not eat while scolding children, nor without having first given to those who look on. And he should eat that [food] by which he would not fail to fulfill his obligations to the gods, the ancestors, and men. For thus it is said: "He whose eating is for his own sake, and whose sexual union is for pleasure alone..."
And for him by whom study has been undertaken merely for the sake of a livelihood, his life is fruitless.
Whatever one eats with the head covered, whatever one eats facing north,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes— all that should be known as belonging to the Asuras.

“Prekṣamāṇebhyaḥ” means looking intently and with longing at others besides children. “For the sake of gods, ancestors, and humans” is an elliptical expression for the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). That which is eaten is “food” (*bhojana*), meaning edible grain.
Yama says: “He who eats in the midst of his dependents...”
A single person, whose mind is greedy for flavors, eats sweet food while being gazed upon even with the sidelong glances of the wretched;
clearly, he consumes the Hālāhala poison.
“Rasagṛdhnubuddhiḥ”: one whose intellect is greedy for *rasa*; that is to say, one whose mind desires *rasa*.

One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun, nor during a calamity affecting a king. A person who maintains the *agnihotra* fire should eat only when he considers the *agnihotra* offering to have been performed; likewise, he may eat when he considers the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice to have been performed, and on the new and full moon days (*parvan*) when he considers the ritual to have been completed. One should not eat while suffering from indigestion, nor at midnight, nor at midday, nor during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). One should not eat while wearing wet clothes, nor with only one garment, nor naked, nor while standing in water, nor in a squatting posture (*utkuṭuka*), nor seated on a broken seat, nor lying down, nor from a broken vessel, nor from one's lap, nor directly on the ground, nor from the hand. Furthermore, one should not eat that salt which has not been given to him. One should not eat while scolding a child, nor eat delicacies alone, nor food from which the oil has been extracted. One should not eat parched grain by day, nor anything related to sesame seeds at night, nor curd-mixed barley meal (*dadhi-saktu*), nor the greens of the *kovidāra*, *vaṭa*, *pippala*, or hemp plants. One should not eat without having first given [to others], nor without having offered [to the gods], nor with unwashed feet, nor with unwashed hands and face. One should not take clarified butter (*ghṛta*) while still impure from a previous meal. One should not gaze at the moon, the sun, or the stars, nor touch the crown of one's head, nor recite the *brahman*. One should eat facing the east or the south, after praising the food. One should be cheerful, adorned with a garland, and anointed with unguents. One should not consume everything until nothing remains, except in the case of curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, parched grain flour, meat paste, and boiled rice.
One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor while standing;
many should not look on at one person, nor should many eat together in one place.
[247] In an empty house, a firehouse, or a temple, one should by no means drink water from one's cupped hands, nor should one practice over-satiety.

“During an affliction of cows or Brahmins” means when cows or Brahmins are in distress. “Having gone abroad” means having left the place of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and gone to another village. “Not squatting” means not sitting in the *utkaṭaka* posture. “Broken” means cracked. “Not on the ground”—the word “having placed” is to be supplied. “In the hand”—the word “situated” is to be supplied. “He should give”—the word “to the gods and others” is to be supplied. By the phrase “without having given,” it is stated that one should not eat without having first given to Brahmins and others. By the phrase “that which he would not give,” it is meant that even after giving to those of other castes, one should not eat from anyone else. “One who eats without leaving a remainder” means one who eats everything. Since eating in the unsupported space of the sky is impossible, the prohibition “not in the air” refers to [eating] on a stool or similar object. “On one [thing]”—the word “looking at” is to be supplied.
Likewise:
"One should not eat food that is corrupted by one's mental state, nor from a vessel defiled by such a state;
nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth between the knees."
“Defiled by its nature” means suspected of being impure.
Manu says: One should not eat wearing only a single garment, nor with the door closed.
Nor should one eat food from a broken vessel, nor by placing it directly on the ground.
[248] Likewise: When someone has died in one's own village, or even in a neighboring village,
the wise person should not eat food that is unrighteous, because it causes grief.

Regarding the phrase "nor food in a broken vessel," the word "one should not do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "In one's own village" means among the inhabitants of one's own village. "Near the village" means among the inhabitants of a neighboring village. "Unrighteous" means a means for accomplishing unrighteousness. Bṛhaspati says:
"While eating, one should never touch the food with the left hand."
One should not touch one's feet, head, or bladder with the feet, nor should one touch a vessel with the feet.
Regarding the continuation of the phrase "he should eat," Uśanas states:
"Neither having sipped water [inappropriately], nor reclining on a bed, nor lying on one's back, at any time.
Gautama [9.56–57] states:

One should not eat foods while holding them in one's lap, nor what has been brought by a servant at night. Regarding "at night" and "by a servant"—meaning by a slave or the like—Maskarī states that nothing whatsoever should be eaten. Yājñavalkya [1.131]:
One should not eat while looking at one's wife, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing.
Regarding "while looking at one's wife," it means while the wife is looking on. Manu [4.43]:
One should not eat together with one's wife, nor should one look at her while she is eating. "Aśnatīm" means "while she is eating. Vasiṣṭha [12.29].
"One should not eat together with one's wife, for it is stated in the Vājasaneyaka that the offspring will lack vigor. If one should ever eat together with a Brāhmaṇī, or [eat] her leavings,
the wise do not consider that to be a fault at all."
If a Brāhmaṇa should ever eat the leavings of other women, he should be known as one requiring expiation; he is a man of mixed caste and deluded mind.
The mention of a "Brāhmaṇī" is intended as an illustration for [a wife] of the same caste as the husband. Even with a Brāhmaṇī, eating together is permitted only on a journey.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"One may eat in some places along the road together with a Brāhmaṇī wife."
"Having eaten together with a woman of a different caste, one falls from [one's status] at that very moment.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A Brahmin, having performed this ritual sipping (*upaspṛśya*), [should touch] the big toe of his right foot."
With both hands, one should offer [the water] according to the mantra and perform the ritual washing (avanejana) according to the rule.
Having wiped his arms and knees, he shall obtain the fruit of the gift of a cow;
and having eaten, he should rise, but not with wet hands.
Even after sipping water, one remains pure only so long as the vessel has not been lifted;
even when it has been lifted, one remains impure so long as the ground has not been wiped clean.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.11.90–95]:
Having eaten properly, one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), facing either east or north;
having sipped water once, one should sip again after washing both hands from the base [to the fingertips].
Being healthy and with a tranquil mind, having taken up his seat,
he should then perform the recollection of his chosen deities.
May Agni, impelled by the wind and granted space by the ether, nourish the earthy elements; may he digest them, and may there be happiness for me.
May this food serve for the strength of my earth, water, fire, and air;
may there be unimpeded happiness for me upon its digestion.
May food be nourishing for the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna breaths; may there be unimpeded happiness for me.
May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest without remainder the food eaten by me;
and may there be for me the well-being arising from its digestion.
May he grant it, and may freedom from disease abide within my body.
Just as the Lord Viṣṇu alone is the sovereign of all senses, bodies, and embodied beings,
by that truth may this entire food be [sufficient].
May this transformation of mine lead to the granting of health.
Viṣṇu is the eater, and likewise he is the end and the transformation;
by that truth, may this food which has been eaten be digested.
Having recited this and rubbed his own abdomen with his own hand,
he should perform his duties without weariness and with alertness, ensuring they cause him no exhaustion.
Āpastamba [2.4.24]:

In whatever place it is eaten, one should sweep that place, remove [the remains], sprinkle it, scrape the residue from the vessels, wipe it with water, and pour [the water] out toward the north in a clean spot for Rudra. In this way, the dwelling becomes auspicious. “Sweeping” (*samūhana*) means cleansing with a broom (*vardhanī*) or similar tool. “Removing” (*nirharaṇa*) means taking away the swept-up leavings. “Sprinkling” (*avokṣya*) means pouring [water]; according to customary practice, with cow-dung water. “Vessels” (*amatrāṇi*) here refers to cooking pots. “Toward the north” means from the house. “Dwelling” (*vāstu*) means the house. “Auspicious” (*śiva*) means blessed.
Hārīta says: "Afterwards, the wife should offer the remaining oblation.
Jayasvāmin maintains that this offering to Rudra must be performed with the food remaining in the cooking vessel.
Now, regarding what may and may not be eaten,
Gautama [17.1] states:
A Brāhmaṇa may eat the food of twice-born men who are praiseworthy in their own duties.
“Of the praiseworthy,” meaning those who are subjects of praise due to their steadfastness in their own respective duties; “of the twice-born,” meaning the members of the three higher castes.
Regarding these, Yama [is the authority] for the first [caste], Hārīta and Jamadagni for the second, and Paiṭhīnasi for the third.
One may always eat at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, and at that of a Kṣatriya on the festival days (parvan).
And among those born of their own class, this applies to the Vaiśya, but never to the Śūdra.
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is nectar; that of a Kṣatriya is traditionally held to be milk;
and the food of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras [is likewise to be consumed].

“Having eaten the food of such-and-such a person, a Brahmin indeed goes to that very womb upon death. Regarding the term “on the parvan days,” it refers to the full moon and other such occasions. Regarding the term “in specific rites,” it refers to particular undertakings such as the *gomaṅgala* (the auspicious rite of cows) and so forth. “Of whom” refers to a person such as a Śūdra. Furthermore, the prohibition of a Śūdra’s food concerns the food of an unworthy Śūdra; and even regarding the food of a worthy Śūdra, it applies when the acquisition of [food from] cows and the like is impossible. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
On the festival days of kings, or on the auspicious occasion of cows belonging to Vaiśyas,
one may eat in the house of a virtuous Śūdra for the sake of cattle, land, gems, or gold.

The syntactical connection is: “he should eat. Āpastamba [1.18.9–13]: One who has returned from his teacher’s house (samāvṛtta) should not eat the food of the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya. By nature, the food of a Brāhmaṇa may be eaten; it is forbidden for reasons [of impurity]. Where there is no penance required for the performance of an act, but where penance is required, one may eat after the penance has been performed. Some say that the food of all castes may be eaten if they abide by their own duties, with the exception of Śūdras.

Because of the mention of "one who has returned" (*samāvṛtta*), begging for alms from among all castes is not forbidden for a *brahmacārin*. "By nature" (*prakṛtyā*) means by his own innate disposition; the ellipsis is "remaining intent upon his own duty. "On account of a cause" (*kāraṇāt*) means due to the occurrence of a minor sin (*upapātaka*) or the like. "Non-penance" (*aprāyaścitta*) refers to obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites other than penance; this is already indicated by the word "by nature. "In one who possesses penance" (*prāyaścittavati*) means when there is the presence of sin which is the cause for penance. "For one who has performed the expiation" (*caritanirveṣasya*) means for one who has completed the penance. Furthermore, this permission to eat the food of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are devoted to their duty is restricted to occasions of festivals and auspicious rites, according to the statement of Yama.

[254] Manu [4.223]: A learned twice-born man shall not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra who does not perform ancestral rites (śrāddha). He may accept from such a person only raw grain as a one-night provision in the event of a lack of other means of subsistence.
"Aśrāddhinaḥ" refers to one who does not perform the daily *śrāddha*. "Avṛttau" means in times of distress. "Ekarātrikam" refers to food sufficient for sustaining one day. Hārīta says:
"But he who dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach..."
He indeed incurs the state of an ass, the state of a camel, and the state of a Śūdra.
Vasiṣṭha [6.26, 25, 27]: Any twice-born man who dies with the food of a Śūdra still within his stomach shall become a village pig or be born into that [Śūdra’s] family.
For one whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, even if he constantly studies the Vedas, performs fire-sacrifices, or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher state.
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra—
his sons indeed belong to the one whose food was eaten, and he shall not be worthy of heaven.
Yama says: A Brāhmaṇa who, while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach, casts off his body—
even if he is one who has maintained the sacred fires and performed sacrifices— shall attain the destiny of a Śūdra.
But that Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires yet does not refrain from the food of a Śūdra—five things perish for him: his self, the Veda, and the three sacrificial fires.
Aṅgiras:
That twice-born man who for six months eats the censured food of a Śūdra becomes a Śūdra while alive and, after death, is reborn as a dog.
Paiṭhīnasi states: "A householder should not eat the food of a Śūdra; [otherwise] longevity, strength, and luster depart. [This is also stated] in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Having sprinkled it thoroughly with water, one may accept the food of a Śūdra that has come to one’s house.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"If a twice-born man should cook the food of a Śūdra according to the rule of offering (*upakṣepaṇadharma*)," [he incurs no fault].
That food would become unfit for consumption, as would that brahmin who serves as the domestic priest.
The food of a Brahmin invited by a Shudra is unfit to be eaten; likewise, the food of a Shudra invited by a Brahmin is unfit to be eaten.
[256] Eating the food of a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra,
and receiving any knowledge from a Śūdra— these may cause even one who is blazing with merit to fall.

“*Upakṣapaṇadharma*” refers to the offering of food belonging to a Śūdra owner into a Brāhmaṇa’s house for the purpose of cooking. As for the verse: “Just as water from whatever source becomes pure once it has entered a river, so too food that has entered the houses of Brāhmaṇas from a Śūdra is always pure.”
This is the statement of Aṅgiras; it refers to food obtained from a Śūdra by means of acceptance as a gift and so forth by a Brāhmaṇa.
Yājñavalkya [1.166] states:
"Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, and the sharecropper..."
One may eat the food of a barber and of one who offers himself [as a servant].

Bhartṛyajña maintains that the food is to be eaten only by him whose cattle a cowherd (*gopāla*) tends. A "family friend" (*kulamitra*) is one with whom friendship has descended through family lineage. An "associate ploughman" (*ardhasīrī*) is a cultivator who works together [with another]. A "barber" (*nāpita*) is one who subsists on the craft of shaving; he too is [to be considered] as one's own. "Self-surrender" (*ātmanivedana*) is the seeking of refuge after first declaring one's intent toward the master—regarding one's family, character, and specific services for both seen and unseen purposes.
And thus Manu [4.254]: "Whatever his nature may be, and whatever he intends to do..."
"And one should offer oneself in such a way as one would serve him. Thus says Devala:
"One's own slave, a barber, a cowherd, a potter, and a farmer..."
These five born of Śūdra wombs are also those whose food may be eaten by Brāhmaṇas.

Regarding the term “farmer” (*kṛṣīvalaḥ*), according to the statement of Yājñavalkya, it refers to one who owns half a plough-team. The raw food of these persons may be accepted even when there is no distress; however, in times of distress, even their cooked food may be accepted. Regarding the section on Śūdras, Gautama [17.6–7] states: “Cattle-herders, cultivators of fields, family friends, those who cause work to be done for them, and personal attendants are those whose food may be eaten; so too a merchant who is not an artisan.”

“Kārayitā” (the one who causes to do) refers to a barber; such is the commentary of Maskari. If a Śūdra is a “vaṇik” (trader) and is “aśilpī” (not a craftsman), meaning he is not a carpenter or the like, then his food may be eaten. Regarding the section on Śūdras, Āpastamba [1.18.6–8] states:

“Even in the case of this person who has approached for the sake of dharma, one may eat after giving him gold or a livestock animal. One should not settle there permanently. Having obtained a livelihood, one should desist.”

The meaning is that one may eat even from a Śūdra who has approached according to the law, whether after giving gold or after giving an animal. "One should not settle there permanently" means that even when other means of livelihood are unavailable, one should not take pleasure in eating his food. And one may eat from a Śūdra: cow's milk products, barley meal, oil, oil-cake, cakes, and whatever else is made with milk.
“Made with milk” refers to inspissated milk (*kilaṭā*) and the like. Hārīta says:
“Food baked in an earthen vessel, food cooked in fat, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), curd, and parched grain flour (*saktu*).”
Manu has declared these to be foods that may be eaten by those who do not consume the food of Śūdras.
Parāśara says: The food of a Śūdra remains such only so long as it has not been touched by a twice-born man;
once it is touched by the tip of the hand of a twice-born man, all of it is called sacrificial oblation (havis).
Yama said: Just as water that has flowed out [of a vessel] is undrinkable, yet that same water when it has entered a river is drinkable once again.
Likewise, food and drink that have arrived according to the prescribed rule do not become defiled when they have been passed through the vessels of the twice-born.
“Outflows” (*nirgamanāni*) refers to places where streams of water falling from streets and the like enter.
One should not eat at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), nor likewise at one offered by one who does not perform sacrifices (*agayājī*).
A Brahmin should never eat at a sacrifice offered by a woman or a eunuch.
This is offensive to the virtuous, wherein these people mock the oblation;
this is contrary to the will of the gods, therefore one should avoid it.

One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease; nor that of one who is "unlearned" (*aśrotriya*), meaning one devoid of Vedic study, whether he be a priest (*ṛtvij*) or a patron (*yajamāna*). Regarding the term "tate," the meaning is "extended" or "commenced. A "village-priest" (*grāmayājī*) is one who performs sacrifices for many people. Based on the consideration of the statement, "and he who initiates many," Viśvarūpācārya explains this as one who performs the initiation (*upanayana*) for many; the food of one whose *homa* is performed by such a person must not be eaten. "By a woman" (*striyā hute*) refers to where the morning Vaiśvadeva and other rites have been performed by a woman. "Ugliness" (*aślīka*) means that which causes lack of prosperity. "Adverse" (*pratīpa*) means contrary or hostile.
Likewise:
"Food smelled by a cow, and especially food announced [beforehand],
the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, and that which is despised by the learned;"
And likewise from a thief, a singer, a carpenter, a usurer,
one who has been consecrated for a sacrifice, a miser, and one who is bound in fetters.
[260] The food of one accused of a crime, of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, and of a hypocrite; as well as food that is soured, stale, or the leavings of a Śūdra.
The food of a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats leftovers;
the food of a fierce man, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and food from a house where a death has occurred within ten days.

When gifts are being given at the conclusion of a ritual, that which is offered unequally by two Brahmins who are themselves equal, or equally by those who are unequal, should neither be accepted nor given away.
Meat not honored by a ritual, meat obtained in vain, the food of a woman without a husband,
the food of an enemy, the food of a city official, the food of an outcast, and food that has been sneezed upon.
The food of the slanderer and the liar, the food of one who sells the sacrificial offerings,
the food of a butcher and a tailor, and likewise the food of an ungrateful person.
Of the blacksmith, the Niṣāda, the stage-player,
the goldsmith, the bamboo-worker, and likewise the seller of weapons;
[One should avoid the food] of dog-keepers, of liquor-sellers, of a washerman of clothes,
of a dyer, of a cruel man, and of one in whose house a paramour resides.
Those who tolerate a paramour, those who are entirely conquered by women,
and food that has not been tasted [by others], as well as food offered to the deceased that causes no satisfaction— [these are forbidden].

“*Ghuṣṭānnam*” is food given after having proclaimed, “Let whoever desires food eat! “*Gaṇaḥ*” means a multitude. “*Gaṇikā*” means a prostitute. “*Viduṣā*” refers to one who knows the meaning of the Vedas and is impartial. “*Jugupsitam*” means censured; from that very censure, one infers the presence of invisible (transcendental) defects in it. “*Gāyanaḥ*” is one who lives by singing. “*Kadaryaḥ*” means a miser. “*Baddhasya*” means of one restrained by ropes and the like. “*Nigaḍasya*” means one possessing shackles, by implication of the possessive sense (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*); or rather, it means “of one bound by shackles,” where the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. “*Puṃścalī*” means an unchaste woman. “*Śuktam*” is a substance that has turned sour due to contact with another substance; that which is excessively sour is to be avoided, according to the statement of Vṛddha-Bṛhaspati: “That which is extremely sour is called *śukta*. “*Śūdrocchiṣṭam*” is that which is left over after feeding a Śūdra. “*Krūraḥ*” is one of a crooked nature. “*Ucchiṣṭabhojī*” is one who eats forbidden leavings. “*Ugraḥ*” is one of cruel deeds; the author of the *Mañjarī* says, “*Ugra* is the king. “*Sūtikānnam*” is food prepared for a woman who has recently given birth; that food must not be eaten even by members of her own family. “*Paryācāntam*” is food at which someone sips water while others seated in the same row are being served, thereby showing contempt for them. “*Anirdaśam*” refers to food belonging to a family in a state of impurity due to childbirth. Food given when two Brahmins of equal learning and status are treated unequally is unfit to be eaten; likewise, food given when two of unequal status are treated equally is unfit to be eaten—the meaning is that the giver should not act in such a manner. “*Anarcitam*” is that which is given with contempt to one deserving of honor. “*Vṛthāmāṃsam*” is meat not prepared for the sake of the gods, ancestors, and so forth. “*Avīrā*” is a woman deprived of husband and sons. “*Nagarī*” means the lord of a city. “*Piśunaḥ*” is one intent on speaking ill of others behind their backs. “*Anṛtī*” is one who speaks falsehoods excessively, such as a false witness. “*Kratuvikrayikaḥ*” is one who takes money after saying, “May you receive the fruit of my sacrifice. “*Śailūṣaḥ*” is an actor. “*Tunnavāyaḥ*” is a tailor. “*Kṛtaghnaḥ*” is one who does not acknowledge a favor done for him. “*Karmakāraḥ*” is a blacksmith. “*Niṣādaḥ*” is by caste. “*Raṅgāvatārakaḥ*” is one who lives by the profession of appearing on a stage, distinct from actors, singers, and the like. “*Veṇaḥ*” is one who lives by cutting bamboo. Viśvarūpa identifies this as a *baruḍa*. “*Śvavataḥ*” is one who raises animals for the purpose of hunting. “*Śauṇḍikaḥ*” is a seller of liquor. “*Nṛśaṃsaḥ*” is merciless. “*Strījitānām*” refers to those who are under the control of their wives. “*Sarvaśaḥ*” means in all transactions. “*Anirdaśam*” means food given for the sake of a deceased person within ten days; such food must not be eaten even by one who is not in a state of birth-impurity.
Yājñavalkya [1.162]:
"Of the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the vrātya, the hypocrite, and those who eat the leavings of others;
a *vrātya* is one whose *sāvitrī* has fallen."
Likewise, Yājñavalkya [1.164] states:
"Of the cruel, the king, the dyer, the ungrateful, and those who live by slaughter—
the 'vadhajīvī' is one who lives by the killing of living beings."
Likewise [1.165]:
"The food of slanderers, liars, and those who practice usury, as well as that of bards and actors, and likewise that of sellers of Soma, must not be eaten."
A "cakrika" is one who lives by means of carts;
a charioteer; an actor, a dancer, a carpenter, a leather-worker, or a goldsmith.
A wooden post, a eunuch, and a courtesan are proclaimed to be those whose food should not be eaten.
The musician, the blacksmith, the tailor, the weaver,
the wheelwright, the dyer, the gambler, and likewise the thief.
One who bears a banner, one who lives by pride, a teacher of Śūdras, a priest for them,
a potter, a painter, a usurer, and a seller of leather;

In this context, the potter is one who is not his own [kinsman], according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "Of a Śūdra who is not one's own. As for the fact that Devala stated that a potter is one whose food may be eaten, he should be understood as one who is one's own. Sumantu says: "The food of those accused of crimes, outcasts, the son of a remarried woman, an embryo-killer, an unchaste woman, a weaver, a worker in leather, a barber, a cartwright, a liquor-seller, a goldsmith, a scribe, a eunuch, a prostitute, an astrologer, and a courtesan is not to be eaten. Pigs-breeders, hunters, fishermen, dyers, basket-makers, bamboo-workers, leather-workers, and tanners have food that is not to be eaten and are persons from whom gifts are not to be accepted."

“*Paunarbhavaḥ*” is the son of a woman remarried; “*astra*” is a bow; “*viśastra*” refers to various types of weapons such as swords and the like; “*dhvajī*” is a seller of liquor; “*lekhakaḥ*” is a painter; “*ṣaṇḍhakaḥ*” is a eunuch; “*bandhakī*” is an unchaste woman who goes to meet her paramour; “*saukarikaḥ*” is one who lives by breeding pigs; “*niṣpacaḥ*” is one who does not cook for himself—referring to an ascetic (*yati*) and a student (*brahmacārī*).
Regarding the rule that their food is not to be eaten, Vasiṣṭha [states the following] under the recurring context (14.4–11):

Or [the food] of a Śūdra who has become his own master; of a paramour, or one who considers himself a paramour; of one who burns houses; of one who strikes with a weapon worthy of execution; that which is called out for "Who is eating? (i.e., food offered indiscriminately); the food of a *gaṇa* and the food of a courtesan. Moreover, they cite this:

"The gods do not eat the food of one who keeps dogs, nor of the husband of a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*); they do not eat the food of one conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house a paramour resides."
“By one deserving of death,” meaning by one who is despondent and so forth.

[The food of] those who have abandoned their vows, of unchaste women, of those accused of crimes, of those of unknown origin, of those who live by punishment, of carpenters, of misers, of jailers, of physicians, of hunters, of those who carry arrows, of those who eat the remnants of others’ meals, of those who belong to a guild, and of those who hate [their kin]—these are those from whom one should not eat, prior to Durvāsas. Also excluded are foods where the eating is done in vain, or where there is a breach of propriety due to sipping water or rising [from the seat].

“Abandoned” means ownerless. “Without a known lineage” means one whose family conduct is unknown. “A police officer” (*dāṇḍika*) is one appointed to suppress evildoers. “A jailer” (*bandhanika*) is the superintendent of a prison. “A physician” (*cikitsaka*) is one whose livelihood is medical treatment. “A hunter” (*mṛgayu*) is a fowler; this applies if he is “one who does not shoot arrows,” for “one who does not shoot arrows” refers to a snarer. “Prior to Durvāla”: the meaning is that the food of those previously mentioned in the section on *śrāddha* (funeral rites) as unfit for the company—beginning with thieves and ending with those who have renounced themselves—is not to be eaten, provided they have not performed penance. “Food in vain” (*vṛthānna*) is that which is cooked solely for oneself, without being intended for the gods and others. “Defiled by sipping water” (*ācamanavyapeta*) is where one has performed the ritual sipping of water while still half-eaten. “Defiled by rising” (*utthānavyapeta*) is where one has risen from the meal while still half-eaten.
In the context of the rule "food is unfit to be eaten," Āpastamba states [ĀpDhS 1.18.18–33; 1.19.1]:

And [one must not eat the food] of all those who live by crafts; those who live by weapons; those who are sorcerers (*abhicārin*); physicians; usurers; and one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) but for whom the purchase of the Soma has not yet taken place. Only when the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice is completed, or when the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered, may one eat the food of the consecrated. Or, if it has been designated for the sake of the sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder; for so says the *Brāhmaṇa*: "They should eat from the remainder. [One must also avoid the food of: a eunuch; a messenger for kings; one who does not offer oblations; a spy; one who has gone forth as a renunciant contrary to the rule; one who abandons the sacred fires; one who avoids all [duties]; one who eats all kinds of food; a learned *śrotriya* who neglects his duties; the husband of a *vṛṣalī*; one who is intoxicated; one who is insane; one who is bound; one who is in debt; one who sits in protest (*pratyupaviṣṭa*); and one who causes another to sit in protest—for that duration of time.

“*Ādhi*” means a pledge; the word “they live by” (*ājīvanti*) is to be supplied as a connective. A “moneylender” (*vārdhuṣika*) is one who, having taken grain at a low price, gives it back at a high price.

This has been stated by such passages as: “one who has not purchased the King [Soma]” means one who has not purchased the *soma*; “the completion of the *agnīṣomīya*” means the conclusion of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma; “or when the omentum (*vapā*) has been offered” refers specifically to that of the *agnīṣomīya* animal; “designated” means pointed out; “*praiṣa*” is simply a command; “one who does not perform the *havis*-sacrifice” is one who offers oblations in rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) using human blood and the like; “a wanderer” means a spy; “by an improper method” means without the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; “he rejects” implies “by an improper method”; “all” includes even those who are blameless; “one who is excluded” (*nirākṛti*) is one who, though having studied the Vedas, is devoid of teaching and the *brahmayajña* and other such duties; “a debtor” is a creditor; if he is “seated in protest” (*pratyupaviṣṭa*), meaning he sits fasting before a debtor for the sake of recovering his wealth, then for that duration his food is not to be eaten; and “he who causes another to sit in protest” is the debtor who causes the creditor to sit in protest by refusing to pay.

Furthermore, Āpastamba [1.19.9–10] states: "One may eat from one who is meritorious and desirous [of giving]; one must not eat from one who is meritorious but undesirous [of giving]. "Meritorious" means righteous; "desirous" means one who is soliciting [to give].

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One should avoid the food of those who are terrified, weeping, crying out, shouting, sneezing, or eating while distracted; likewise, one should avoid the food of those who are astonished, insane, or have been cast off, as well as the food of a king and a royal priest.

“Frightened” means terrified. “Wept” means having shed tears. “Cried out” (*ākrandita*) means one who has made continuous sounds due to suffering; it refers to such a person. “Reviled” (*avakruṣṭa*) means despised. “Sneezed” (*kṣuta*) means one who has sneezed. “Eaten up” (*paribhukta*) means one by whom food has been consumed on all sides until only a remnant remains. “Amazed” (*vismita*) means one who has become astonished. “Shaken off” (*avadhūta*) means one who has been excluded by the virtuous. In all these cases, the past participle (*kta*) denotes the inception of the action. Therefore, it should be understood that fear and the other states must be present at the time they serve as the cause. “King” means the lord of a realm. “Purohita” (family priest) refers to anyone who holds that office. One must not eat the food of these persons.
Furthermore, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

One should not eat the food of those who bear enmity, of those who have broken their vow of celibacy, of evildoers, nor food from a funeral feast (śrāddha), from a charioteer (sūta), or from a group (gaṇa), nor that which has been treated with contempt.

“Vidviṣāṇaḥ” means one who is habitually hostile. “Śrāddham” refers to one who eats at a *śrāddha* for the deceased. “Sūtaḥ” is one born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Kṣatriya father. “Paribhūtāni” means things that have been treated with contempt.
Devala says: [One should avoid] the food of the fallen (*patita*), the food of those whose food is unfit to be eaten (*abhojya*), and likewise the food of those excluded from the row (*apāṅkteya*).
One should avoid the food of a Śūdra, contemptible food, and food that has been defiled.

“Those whose food is not to be eaten” (*abhojya*) refers to those well-known from other *smṛtis*, such as unchaste women, those accused of crimes, and so forth. “Defiled” (*dūṣita*) means contaminated by hair, insects, and the like. Vasiṣṭha [4.31–32] states:
“He who has eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or during his birth-impurity (*sūtaka*),” [is likewise affected].
He shall go to a terrible hell and be born among the animal realm.
If a twice-born man eats meat through appointment after ten days have passed since an animal's death,
he becomes a worm at the end of his body and consumes that very excrement.

Regarding the term "paraśave": he who has no period of impurity (*āśauca*) is "para" (another) in relation to him; [the phrase refers to] "during the corpse-impurity" (*śave*) of that other person, that is, within the period of impurity caused by a death.
Yama says:
"But that twice-born man who should release his life-breaths after eating a *śrāddha* meal on the ninth day..."
And he is born among the terrible animal wombs that are unfit for sacrifice.
But that twice-born man who conceives a child after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony held on the ninth day does not attain sacred knowledge; he is born with a diminished lifespan.
“Unfit for sacrifice” (*ayājyāḥ*) means other than those fit for sacrifice, such as goats and the like. Śaṅkha [15.24] says:
“He who eats during the period of impurity of another is born in the womb of a worm.”
He upon whose food one eats and then dies is reborn in that person's lineage.
Āpastamba [1.16.18–20]:

One should not eat in a family where someone has died until ten days have passed; likewise while the woman who has given birth has not yet arisen from her confinement; and when there is a corpse within the house.

Regarding "when there is a corpse within the house" (*antaḥśave*): this refers to food in that house where a corpse lies, even if the members of that household are otherwise not subject to ritual impurity (*aśauca*).

Aṅgiras: From the time of birth until the performance of the purificatory rites, and during the first feeding of solid food for the child, those who are not sapinda relations must not eat; this is especially true at the edge of the cremation ground.
The construction is: "of the child" and "the sacraments from birth onwards. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"He who considers himself a householder without having taken the marriage fire..."
One must not eat his food, for he is remembered as one whose cooking is in vain.
Śātātapa says:
"Where the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the guest do not eat, that should be known as 'vain cooking' (vṛthāpāka); one should never eat from it."
Aṅgiras: One should never eat in the house of women who have no offspring;
whoever should eat there out of delusion shall go to the Pūyanaraka hell.
“Childless” means without offspring.
Yama says: Having studied the four Vedas, specifically along with their limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas)...
Having eaten in the house of a lord of men, one is born in the womb of a worm.
The food of a king takes away one’s splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one’s Vedic luster;
and the food of a Vaiśya as well as the food of a woman who has recently given birth, cuts one off from the higher worlds.
Likewise, the food of one who serves a king, the food of a thief,
and food during the period of birth-impurity or death-impurity— such food causes even one dwelling in heaven to fall.
Hārīta says: The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster;
and the food of a multitude or the food of a courtesan cuts one off even from the worlds.
He who desires to know his own self as pure and to attain the desired worlds should avoid from afar the food of a group and the food of a courtesan.
"To be known" means to be experienced.
"The food of a king takes away one's splendor; the food of a Śūdra, one's Vedic luster."
Longevity comes from a goldsmith's food, and fame from the food of a leather-cutter.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; and the food of those who sell weapons is filth.
But as for those others who have been described in succession as persons whose food should not be eaten,
the wise declare that their food consists of skin, bone, and hair.
A "nirṇejaka" is a washerman;
[the food of] a Yama[-like person], the food of a usurer is excrement, and the food of a slayer of a Brahmin is blood.
For the food of a washerman is impurity, and that of a leather-worker is sin.
Likewise, the food of a drunkard and of a bell-ringer is considered sin;
the wise declare that their skin, bones, and hair constitute their food.

Paiṭhīnasi states: "The food of a *gaṇa* (a group) and the food of a courtesan are [like] excrement. The food of a usurer is [like] feces. The food of an astrologer (*sāṃvatsara*), a bell-ringer (*ghāṇṭika*), and a village traitor (*grāmakūṭa*) is [like] poison. The food of unchaste women (*bandhakī*) is semen. The food of physicians and surgeons is pus. The food of one whose younger brother marries before him (*parivitti*), one who marries before his elder brother (*parivedin*), one whose male organ has been pierced (*viddhaprajanana*), the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, the husband of a woman whose younger sister was married first (*didhiṣūpati*), and the son of a remarried woman (*punarbhūputra*) is blood. And the food of outcasts (*patita*). An 'astrologer' (*sāṃvatsara*) is a practitioner of astrology. A 'village traitor' (*grāmakūṭaka*) is one who habitually practices deceitful dealings in the village. A 'one who marries before his elder brother' (*parivedin*) is a *parivitti*. One whose 'male organ has been pierced' (*viddhaprajanana*) is one whose prepuce has been cut off."
Vasiṣṭha [14.14]: One may eat the food of a person who has faith, even if he is a thief, especially so;
but one must never eat the food of one who officiates at many sacrifices or who initiates many pupils.
“Bahuyājyaḥ” means one who performs sacrifices for many. Manu [4.224–225]:
[One should not accept gifts from] a Śrotriya who is miserly, nor from a liberal usurer.
Having deliberated upon both, O gods, you ordained food to be equal.
Prajāpati said to them: "Do not make the unequal equal!
The gift of a generous man purified by faith is [efficacious], while the other is destroyed by lack of faith."
“Generous” means one who speaks kindly and is disposed toward giving. Baudhāyana [1.10.5] states:
[It is not accepted] from one who is pure but lacks faith, nor from one who has faith but is impure.
Having deliberated upon both, the gods ordained that food is equal for all.
Regarding them, Prajāpati said: "Make the unequal equal;
the offering of one who lacks faith is destroyed, while that which is purified by faith excels."
Yama says:

One should not eat the food even of one's guru if it is treated with contempt, if its nature is unknown, if it is served with anger, if it is accompanied by astonishment, or if it is devoid of respectful hospitality.
That which is discarded, that which is leavings, or that which is defiled by speech,
as well as what is offered or given without faith— that must not be eaten by the twice-born.
He who eats the food of one who is arrogant, foolish, ill-behaved, evil-minded,
or lacking in faith, is likewise a killer of an embryo.
He who eats the food of one for whom no funeral libations have been offered eats the impurity of the earth;
they say that food is the impurity of men, and everything is established upon food.
For a person's misdeed remains attached to their food;
whoever here eats another's food, he eats that person's guilt.
“*Avadhūtam*” means defiled. “*Vāgduṣṭam*” refers to even edible food that is spoken of by a word signifying what is inedible. “*Avalipto*” means arrogant.
In the *Ādityapurāṇa*: “One should regard Viṣṇu as a son-in-law; one should not provoke his anger.”
But one should certainly not eat in the house of a man whose daughter remains childless.

One should always provide food especially for those given as a Brahmadeya gift, as well as for those invited for a divine rite; and in the case of a Gandharva or Rājanya marriage, one may indeed practice going and coming [with the wife].
Having given away a daughter as a *brahmadeyā* (to be given only to a Brahmin), one never enjoys [the fruit of that merit];
but if, being deluded in soul, he should enjoy her [with others], he shall go to the Pūyanaraka hell.
Āpastamba [2.6.19–20]:

One should not eat the food of one who hates him, or of one who is hated by him; nor of one who suspects him of a fault, or of one who has been suspected of a fault. For it is known from scripture: "He indeed consumes that person's evil. — Manu, Yama, and Vasiṣṭha.
The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer to their teacher; and a thief to the king.
The term “kilbiṣam” (sinful/impure) is connected individually with each item beginning with food. “Mārṣṭi” means he joins [it] together.

Vasiṣṭha [states]: “The food of a hunter who wanders with arrows is not to be avoided. For it is known that Agastya engaged in hunting during a thousand-year sacrificial session (*sattra*); his sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) were made from the flesh of excellent wild animals and birds, as there was no other sustenance available at that time.
In this context, the "arrow-wielder" is specifically a twice-born man who, emaciated by his livelihood, subsists on hunting. Śātātapa says:
"Those who eat another's food when the moon has entered the forest (the new moon)..."
The oblation performed by them for a month reaches the donor.
“When the soma has gone to the forest” means on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). Manu [3.104]:
“Those foolish householders who subsist on the food provided by others...”
Therefore, after death, those who give food and drink go to the state of being cattle for their givers.
"Annādya" means food itself. Yama says: "He who, while his own cooking is ready, consumes the cooking of another..."
He goes to the state of a dog, the state of a pig, and the state of a donkey.
For a twice-born householder who is nourished by the food of others,
whatever sacrifice he performs, whatever gift he gives, whatever austerity he practices, and whatever study he undertakes— all that belongs to the one whose food he consumes.
When one approaches his wife after having eaten another's food, those sons belong to the owner of that food;
from food, semen is produced.
Yājñavalkya [1.112]:
One should not take pleasure in food prepared by others, except when invited by those who are beyond reproach.
Hārīta and Jamadagni: [same].
By eating the food of a Brāhmaṇa one incurs poverty; by the food of a Kṣatriya, servitude;
by the food of a Vaiśya, the status of a Śūdra; and by the food of Śūdras, one goes to hell.
Then, following the sages' question— "How can death seek to slay the Brahmins when there are things not to be eaten?"— Manu [5.4–6] states:
"By the lack of practice regarding the Vedas and by the abandonment of proper conduct..."
[276] Through indolence and through defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins.
Garlic, leeks, onions, and mushrooms,
as well as anything produced from impure substances, are unfit to be eaten by the twice-born.
One should carefully avoid red exudations from trees, as well as those produced by incisions,
and the śelu fruit and the colostrum of a cow.

“Laziness” (*ālasyam*) is the lack of enthusiasm for performing what must necessarily be done despite having the capacity [to do so]. “Due to defects in food” (*annadoṣāt*) refers to [defects] such as those of caste (*jāti*) and so forth. And thus it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: “That which is corrupted by caste, corrupted by action, and corrupted by the lapse of time...”
And that which is defiled by association or its source, as well as that which is inherently disgusting.
One should avoid garlic, leeks, onions, mushrooms, eggplant, lotus stalks, bottle gourds, and anything that is corrupted by its species.
One should not eat that which is defiled by action, such as that which has been seen separately by outcasts;
moreover, that which is defiled by time should be known as yesterday's food or that which has been kept for a long duration.

Curd is permitted as food, as are its derivatives, provided they are free from honey; however, it is forbidden if mixed with liquor or garlic, or if combined with the milk of a cow that has recently calved (peyūṣa), and so forth.
For this is indeed corrupted by association; one should treat it like the leavings of a Śūdra.
The "leavings of a Śūdra" should be understood as that which was previously demonstrated regarding a Śūdra.
But when doubt arises in the heart regarding food, it should be known as *sahṛllekha*; however, by its very nature, it is feces.
For it has been demonstrated that food corrupted by taste is so because of a transformation of the flavor;
likewise, milk-rice, milk, and cakes [are forbidden] on that very same day.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "kāladuṣṭam" is as follows: "hyastanam" (yesterday's) refers to everything that has stood overnight (*paryuṣita*) and is unfit for consumption. Regarding "curd" (*dadhi*), it is fit for consumption; and regarding "its derivatives" (*vikārāḥ*), such as those produced from barley, wheat, and so forth—even if they have stood overnight, those which are permitted for consumption must not be eaten if they have been "long-standing" (*cirasaṃsthitāḥ*), meaning their taste and smell have become excessively altered. However, "honey" (*madhu*), even if long-standing, is fit for consumption; thus it is said, "with the exception of honey. "Gṛñjana" is a specific type of bulbous root resembling garlic, well-known in the Northern Region (*Uttarapatha*). "Kavaka" resembles a mushroom and has the shape of a water-lily bud.
And so it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The fat of Madhu, Kaiṭabha, Vṛtra, and the three-headed Asura,
which fell upon the earth while they were being slain by Viṣṇu..."
The *piṇḍopama* is like a small fragment; the *kavaka* resembles a funeral mound (*caitya*);
the *chatrāka* is like an umbrella, both originating from the bodies of demons.

“Produced from impure matter” refers to things such as *taṇḍulīyaka* that are born directly from excrement, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya: “those born from feces. However, those trees which do not grow directly from feces but arise from ground contaminated by impure matter—their flowers and fruits are indeed not defiled.
Thus it was said by Baudhāyana [1.9.4]:
“And those trees grown in impure places that bear flowers and fruit...”
Even for them, the flowers and fruits do not become spoiled.

In this context, by the mention of "trees," there is a prohibition specifically of vegetables and the like of such a nature. Those flowers and fruits that grow directly on trees born of impure substances are already prohibited. "Resin of trees" (*vṛkṣaniryāsa*) refers to the juice exuding from trees that has become solidified. "Cutting" (*vraścana*) means felling. "Likewise those produced by cutting" (*vraścanaprabhavān*): the meaning is that one should likewise avoid even those [resins] that are not red and are produced by cutting. And so says the Taittirīya Śruti: "Now, indeed, whatever is red or whatever exudes from what is cut—that one should avoid; at will, however, [one may eat] that of another. By this, camphor and similar substances are not prohibited. "Śelu" is the *bahuvāraka* (the bitter cucumber). "Pe-yūṣa" is the milk of a cow that has recently calved which, through contact with fire, becomes thickened; if that is derived from a cow, then it is to be avoided.
Yama says: A wise person should always avoid garlic, leeks, mushrooms, *sumukha*, fungi, and onions.
It would be better for one— even if he were a low-born among the twice-born— to slaughter everything himself and eat all the flesh, rather than that he should ever eat *chatrāka* mushrooms.
Those who eat mushrooms, whether they grow from the earth or from trees,
one should know them to be slayers of Brahmins, despised among those who discourse on the Veda.
“Vilaya” is the impurity of ghee. “Viśasya” means having killed. “Apasada” means base or inferior. Hārīta says:
“Mushrooms, the village-pig, onions, and likewise garlic...”
Even a Brahmin who is a knower of all the Vedas would surely fall if he were to eat it.
Devala says: The śleṣmātaka, the vajraphalī, the kaustumbha, the nālamastaka,
and the gṛñjana— these are declared to be among the vegetables that are not to be eaten.
One should entirely avoid onions, garlic, fermented gruel, and resinous exudations; as well as kucunda, white eggplant, and kumbhāṇḍa.
“*Nāla*” refers to the *kalambikā*. “*Śvetavṛntāka*” refers to the white eggplant (*śvetavārtāku*). “*Kumbhāṇḍa*” is a specific type of fruit resembling a pomegranate, commonly known as *kumbhālu*.
Regarding those whose food is restricted by rule, Gautama [17.30–31] states:
sprouts, *kvākula*, garlic, exudations, red [pigments], and cuttings.
