“*Kisalaya*” is a new sprout; “*kyāku*” is the *ahicchatrāka* mushroom.
Regarding the section on forbidden foods, Āpastamba [1.17.25–28] states:
likewise, the *kīlāla* liquor and medicinal herbs; *kalañja*, onions, and *parārīkā*; and whatever else they declare. For the Brāhmaṇa says: “*Kyāku* is unfit for consumption.”

“Kīlāla” is liquor; the “herbs” (oṣadhayaḥ) established for its sake are rice and so forth—the meaning is that [the meat] is a transformation of these. “Kalañja” is a specific type of garlic. “Parārīka” is a specific type of onion. And thus is the verse from the Āyurveda cited by the author of the Smṛtimañjarī: “Rasona, dīrghapatra, picchagandha, mahauṣadha, hiraṇya, palāṇḍu, navatarka, and parārikā.”
Gṛñjana and yavaneṣṭa—these are the ten varieties of onion (*palāṇḍu*).

Regarding the phrase "and whatever else" of this kind, such as the *kovidāra* and so forth, which the learned (*śiṣṭas*) "declare" (meaning they avoid), the implication is that even that is not to be eaten. Thus says Uśanas.
By eating safflower, the nālīkā vegetable, eggplant, or likewise the pautika plant,
even a twice-born man who has mastered the Vedānta becomes fallen.
In this context, "vṛntāka" refers to the white variety; for it is stated in the words of Devala: "the white vṛntāka. Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Vṛntāka, nālikā, pota, kusumbha, and aśmantaka—these among vegetables and fruits are not to be eaten."
"Aśmantaka" is a specific type of tree.
Yājñavalkya [1.171], continuing from the phrase "one should avoid," states:
"The sacrificial oblation intended for the deities, the śigru plant, and likewise red exudations from incisions."
Meat that has not been ritually prepared, and mushrooms growing from dung; these are forbidden.

“*Devatārtham*” refers to offerings such as oblations (*bali*) and so forth. “*Haviḥ*” refers to the sacrificial materials for the *homa*, such as cooked rice (*caru*), sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and the like. “*Śigru*” is the *śobhāñjana* (black mustard). “*Anupākṛtam*” means that which is devoid of the *upākaraṇa*—the ritual touching of an animal with a blade of grass accompanied by mantras at the beginning of an animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) and similar rites.
Likewise [1.173]:
“Fruitlessly prepared *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, *apūpa*, and *śaṣkulī*.”

“Vṛthā” refers to that which is cooked solely for one’s own sake, without being dedicated to a deity or other [worthy recipients], because of the scriptural injunction: “One should not cook food for oneself alone. Since the prohibition of food prepared in vain (*vṛthānnapratiṣedha*) is already established, the specific prohibition of *kṛsara* and the like is intended to prescribe a particular penance (*prāyaścitta*). *Kṛsara* is rice cooked together with sesame and mung beans. *Saṃyāva* is prepared with ghee, milk, and wheat flour; it is commonly known as *utkarikā*. *Śaṣkulī* is fried in oil or ghee, made from the flour of mung beans and other grains, and mixed with sesame. — Hārīta.

One should not cook for one’s own sake *paramānna*, *kṛsara*, *śaṣkulī*, meat, barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), or cakes (*apūpa*). Nor should one eat *vaṭa*, *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *dadhittha*, *nīpa*, or *mātuluṅga*. *Paramānna* is milk-rice (*pāyasa*). *Apūpāḥ* are well known as *pūrikās*. *Nīpa* is the *kadamba*. *Mātuluṅga* is the citron (*bījapūra*). [282] Yama says:
Barley gruel, rice-and-pulse porridge, cakes, milk-rice, fried cakes, meat cooked on a chaff-fire, and even fish that have not been ritually consecrated;
One should avoid all fermented sour substances, as well as the food of the gods and sacrificial oblations; however, one should not avoid everything that is mixed with oil.
“Cooked in the *ṛjīṣa*” means cooked by the heat of the earth. Gautama [9.58] states:
One should not eat things from which the oil has been extracted, such as boiled beans, oil-cakes, and products of churning, once their vital essence (*vīrya*) has been consumed.
“*Āttavīryāṇi*” means those from which the essence has been extracted.
Regarding the phrase “he should eat,” Viṣṇu [states the following at 68.27–31]:

not that from which the oil has been removed; not roasted grains during the day; not anything related to sesame at night; not curd-mixed barley meal; nor the leaf-vegetables of the *kovidāra*, *vaṭa*, *pippala*, or *śāṇa* trees.
Devala says:
A wise man should not consume seeds except in cases of illness;
for by consuming them, he would destroy the infinite fruits that those seeds would otherwise produce.
One should not eat at night with milk, nor should one sleep after having consumed it;
one should not discard milk when it is obtained, for milk is remembered as a sacred substance.
“Seeds” refers to pumpkin seeds.
Yama says: One should not eat from a broken vessel, nor should one eat curd or barley meal at night.
During the day, [one should eat] with wood-apple and grains; at night, with curdled-milk flour.
In the *kovidāra* tree, in a washerman, in a thief, in one who has recently given birth,
and likewise in the *śleṣmātaka* tree, Alakṣmī always makes her abode.
“Sūtaka” refers to the impurity caused by birth or death.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “Rājamāṣas, large mung beans (*sthūlamudga*), as well as vṛṣaka and vāsaka...”
Lentils, dill, safflower, and the abode of Śrī;
"These grains are not to be eaten and must not be given to anyone.
Āpastamba [2.18.1–4]:
"One should avoid molasses, churned butter-milk, oil-cake, honey, and meat."
Black grain, the food of Śūdras, and whatever else is considered unfit to be eaten;
One who desires memory, intelligence, and nourishment should avoid these twelve things: forbidden food, untruth, anger, and that by which one causes another to be angry.

[284] "Black grain" refers to *kaliṅgaka* and the like. "Not to be eaten" (*anāśya*) refers to things such as frogs; those "comparable to them" are considered equal to them. Furthermore, one should personally avoid that action by which anger is provoked in another, even if one is not angry oneself. Viśvāmitra says:
One should not eat what is corrupted by its species, action, or inherent nature, nor what is corrupted by association with the wicked, nor that which causes nausea.

“Corrupted by disposition” (*bhāvaduṣṭa*) means that which is mentally accepted as being similar to forbidden substances, according to the statement of Āpastamba: “equal to what should not be eaten. Vasiṣṭha [14.20–22] states:

“The leavings of one who is not one’s teacher are not to be eaten; likewise one’s own leavings, and that which has been defiled by the leavings of another; and that which has been defiled by clothing, hair, or insects.”
“One’s own leavings” (*svam ucchiṣṭam*) refers to that which has been set aside after one has eaten something oneself. “Garment” (*vasanam*) here means a cloth already worn. Sumantu says:
Food defiled by hair, insects, sneezing, or speech; smelled by dogs; looked upon [by them]; stale; re-cooked; or gazed at by a *caṇḍāla*—is unfit to be eaten, except when touched by gold or water.

“Struck by speech” (*vaco’bhihata*) refers to food toward which speech has been directed. “Gazed upon” (*prekṣita*) means gazed at by dogs alone. “Non-yogurt” (*adadhi*) means anything other than yogurt. “Stale” (*paryuṣita*) means prepared food that has been left overnight. “Re-cooked” (*punaḥsiddha*) means cooked twice. “Gold-water” (*hiraṇyodaka*) is water touched by gold. Manu [4.207–208]: One should never eat the food of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease.
And that which is contaminated by hair or insects, or touched intentionally with the foot.
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses,
pecked at by a bird, or even touched by a dog;
“By a winged creature” means by a bird. “Licked” means tasted.
Yājñavalkya [1.167–168]:
Sour food, stale food, leavings, that which has been touched by a dog, or looked upon by an outcaste...
One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, food announced [beforehand], and food obtained through bartering.
“*Paryāyānnam*” refers to food belonging to one person that is given under the name of another. For example:
“A Śūdra giving the food of a Brāhmaṇa, or a Brāhmaṇa giving the food of a Śūdra—both of them have food unfit to be eaten; having consumed it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. [286]
Yama says: One should know that food touched by a crow or a cock, or that which is fermented sour, or mixed with worms, is unfit for consumption; such is the word of Dharmarāja.

Āpastamba [1.16.21–33; 1.17.1–5]: 21. "The teacher is the highest authority regarding the Veda. 22. "He should not question the teacher's conduct. 23. "Nor should he reflect upon it. 24. "For the teacher knows what is appropriate for his pupil and what is not. 25. "If the teacher gives him something that ought not to be done, or does not give him something that ought to be done, he should not do either of these two things. 26. "But he should inform him of it when they are alone. 27. "In matters concerning dharma, however, he should not be told twice. 28. "He should not sit on a seat higher than his teacher's. 29. "Nor should he sit on the same seat as his teacher, unless it is a bed or a chariot. 30. "He should not walk ahead of his teacher on a road. 31. "If there is a choice between different paths, he should follow the one that is more difficult for the teacher. 32. "He should keep his gaze lowered while walking behind his teacher. 33. "When the teacher is eating, sitting, or lying down, he should not sit nearby. 1.17.1. "He should rise before his teacher and go to sleep after him. 2. "He should always yield the way to his teacher. 3. "He should not sit with his hands on his knees or with his arms akimbo. 4. "He should not speak with his head covered. 5. "And he should not converse with his teacher while standing, if he is seated; while walking, if he is standing; while running, if he is walking; or from a place where he is out of sight, if he is within sight."

Food defiled by one who is impure (*aprayata*) is not pure, yet it is not necessarily unfit for consumption. However, food defiled by an impure *śūdra* is unfit for consumption. So too is food in which there is hair, or other impure matter; food touched by impure things; food containing an insect that frequents impure places; or food containing the limb of a mouse. Also, food touched by a foot, or by a garment (*sic*), or seen by a dog, or by a vessel used for excrement; or food brought by a female slave at night; or where a *śūdra* might touch one while he is eating; or where one eats in the same row as those unworthy to sit with; or where, while people are eating, someone might stand up and offer him leavings or make him rinse his mouth; or where they might serve him food after having reviled him; or food smelled by humans or by other impure things.

“*Aprayatopahatam*” means touched (*upahatam*) by that which is *aprayatena*, i.e., impure (*aśucinā*). “*Aprayatam*” means impure. However, it is not necessarily unfit for consumption; rather, by performing purification through placing it on fire and so forth, it becomes fit for consumption. That which is touched by an *aprayatena*—that is, a Śūdra—is in no way fit for consumption. “*Amidhyam*” refers to saline soil (*ūṣaramṛttikā*), etc. “*Amidhyaiḥ*” refers to *kalañja*, onions (*palāṇḍu*), and the like. “*Avamṛṣṭam*” means touched. “*Kīṭaḥ*” means an insect that frequents impure things; the sentence concludes with the idea that food in which such an insect is found is unfit for consumption. “*Mūṣakalā*” means the excrement of a mouse. “*Aṅgam*” means the tail, feet, or other limbs of a mouse. “*Padā upahatam*” means touched by a foot. “*Sicā*” means touched by a cloth—even if the cloth has been washed—the food is touched by its wind. It is also [unfit] if touched or seen by a dog (*śunā*). “*Apapātreṇa*” means by one who is fallen (*patita*) or otherwise disqualified. “*Upahṛtam*” means brought [as an offering]. The feminine gender in the word “*dāsī*” is not intended to be significant. Regarding the phrase “*upaspṛśet*,” the ellipsis is that even if that food has been half-eaten, it is unfit for consumption. “*Anarhadbhiḥ*” means by those devoid of noble lineage, learning, and conduct; food in the same row (*samānapaṅktau*) as such persons is unfit for consumption. Or, if in a row where worthy persons are eating, someone rises up while others are still half-eaten and gives the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) to a servant or similar person, then the food of the others that was half-eaten is unfit for consumption. By this, the rule regarding “*ācāmet*” (one should sip water) is also explained. “*Kutsayitvā*” means having said such things as, “Come, eat poison! “*Manuṣyair avaghrātam*” means smelled by humans; the ellipsis is “with effort. “*Amidhyaiḥ*” refers to cats, donkeys, and the like.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"In that regard, one should avoid things unfit for drinking and unfit for eating. These include [substances] touched by impure matter, outcasts, Cāṇḍālas, Pulkasas, women in their courses, corpses, or those afflicted with leprosy.
A 'Pulkasa' is a specific class of Mlecchas. A 'Kuṇapa' is a corpse."
Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 71; Śrāddha 86a]:
A twice-born man should not eat food that is forbidden by the scriptures, such as various kinds of meat, or food that is censured, or likewise food that has turned sour in many ways.
Excessively sour *śukta* is thus described and censured by those who discourse on Brahman.
"Vigarhitam" means condemned by the learned. Devala says:
They declare that food which has turned sour or has stood overnight is always unfit for consumption,
except for honey, roasted flour, edible items, clarified butter, and molasses.
One should not consume food that has been licked by a dog, a cat, a crow, a cock, or a mouse; for according to dharma, such food is impure.
Even if food is pure, one should avoid it if it is defiled by flies, worms, or threads, or even by hair, body hair, or fingernails.
“Edibles” (*bhakṣya*) refers to sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*) and the like.
Following the injunction “one should eat,” Hārīta states:

One should not eat what is given by a woman in her menses, nor by an unchaste woman, nor by one who is angry, nor by one wearing soiled garments. One should not eat what is caused to be given through a side door, nor what is cooked twice, nor what is fermented, nor what is stale—except for items cooked with molasses, flour, groats, oils, dairy products, or sesame oil. One should not drink curd as a beverage with oil, nor eat food over which someone has sneezed, nor anything that is loathsome.

“*Malavadvāsā*” means one whose garment is smeared with impurities. “*Aparayā dvārā*” means by a door other than the principal door. Regarding the phrase “*tailādiṣu*,” the word “etc. (*ādi*) includes the inclusion of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), mustard oil (*sarṣapa-sneha*), and so forth. “*Na tailaṃ dadhyanupānam*” means that one should not eat in such a way that oil or curd serves as the after-drink at the end of a meal. Following the recurrence of the term “*abhojyam*” (not to be eaten), Gautama [17.14] states: “[Food] kept overnight is not to be eaten, except for vegetables, hard foods, oils, meat, and honey.”

The meaning is that one should avoid stale vegetables and the like; so state Śaṅkha and Likhita: "One should not eat food from a market stall, nor food cooked twice, nor what has turned sour, nor what is stale—except for preparations of *rāga*, *cukra*, *ṣāḍava*, curd, molasses, wheat, and barley flour."

“*Rāgas*” are syrups (*pralehas*) made from mung beans, pomegranates, meat, and so forth, strained through cloth. “*Ṣāḍavas*” are likewise syrups characterized by sweet, sour, pungent, and other such flavors.

One may eat food that has become stale, food spoiled by its nature, food that was once poured out and cooked again, raw food, or food cooked in a frying pan; however, one may eat it at will if it has been sprinkled with curd or clarified butter.

“Āma” refers to rice and similar grains. By the statement, “One may eat it at will, provided it is sprinkled with curds or ghee,” it is meant that one should eat in this manner only when no other food is available.
(Āpastamba 1.17.14–20).

One should not eat food that has been brought from a market, nor should one consume liquids with the exception of meat, honey, and salt. However, one may use oil and clarified butter after placing them in water. Prepared food that has stood overnight is unfit to be eaten, drunk, or consumed; the same applies to anything that has turned sour. With the following exceptions, all such items are forbidden: molasses, parched grain, rice, *karambha* (curd-mixed meal), roasted barley flour, groats, vegetables, meat, flour preparations, products of milk, medicinal herbs, forest plants, roots, and fruits. Sour gruel is also forbidden unless it has been mixed with other substances.

“Market goods” refers to shoes obtained from a marketplace. “Flavors” refers to molasses and the like. “Having placed in water” means having set them in a water-vessel such as a large jar (*maṇika*). Regarding “that which is not to be chewed, drunk, or eaten”: “chewable” (*khādya*) is that which is hard and crisp; “drinkable” (*peya*) is liquid; “eatable” (*ādya*) is soft and solid food such as boiled rice (*odana*). “And sour gruel” (*śukta*) means that even if it has stood overnight, it is not to be consumed—this is the meaning. “Treacle” (*phāṇita*) is a liquid produced by the cooking of a transformation of sugarcane juice. “Parched rice grains” (*pṛthukataṇḍula*) are grains of rice produced by roasting and crushing grain, commonly known as *cipiṭaka*. “Barley-meal mixed with curd” (*karambha*) is parched barley flour mixed with yogurt. “Bharujas” are roasted grains (*dhānā*). Regarding the phrase “and sour gruel when not combined with other things,” this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with different case endings (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), based on the sense that it is that which has no connection (*yoga*) with another food. And that which was described as sour gruel that is undrinkable and uneatable is that which is unmixed with other substances, according to the statement of Gautama: “But sour gruel alone [is forbidden].”
Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 80–81]:
Curd is fit for consumption, as is anything sour that has originated from curd;
however, a fermented liquor made from bulbs, roots, fruits, or commendable flowers is considered *śukta* (sour gruel).
That which remains unchanged is pure; that which undergoes transformation is unfit for consumption.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "by bulbs, roots, fruits, and flowers" is as follows: if a fermented preparation made from bulbs and the like does not produce delusion or other such transformations, then it is "fit for consumption," meaning it may be eaten. Thus says Yama.
A twice-born man should never eat foods that have turned sour;
however, if he is in a state of distress, they become faultless once they have been washed.
[292] That which is mixed with lentils and beans, as well as that which has become stale,
one should eat after having washed it and sprinkled it with clarified butter.

The meaning is that whatever is "sour" and whatever is "stale," provided it is mixed with lentils or black gram, one should wash it, sprinkle it with clarified butter, and eat it in times of distress.
Whatever food, whether solid or soft, is mixed with oil or fat and is not otherwise censured...
That may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, as well as all remnants of sacrificial oblations (havis).
Even if it has been stored for a long time, all products derived from barley and wheat, as well as preparations of milk, may be consumed by the twice-born even if they have not been treated with oil.
Yājñavalkya [1.169]: Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been kept for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil or fat.
Yama said: Cakes,
parched grain flour, fried grains, small cakes, barley meal,
vegetables, meat, large cakes, soup, and rice-and-sesame porridge.
Barley gruel, milk-rice, and whatever else is mixed with fats—
all of this may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, but one should avoid anything that has turned sour.

[293] Vasiṣṭha [14.37–38]: One should avoid cakes, fried grains, *karambha*, parched barley flour, *vaṭaka* balls, oil, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), vegetables that have turned sour, and other products made from milk and flour. In the Devīpurāṇa:
One should not eat kṛsara, cakes, milk-rice, honey, clarified butter, or meat that has been prepared in vain— that is, without being offered to the ancestors or the gods.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "By means of Caṇḍālas, outcasts, impure things, corpses, as well as lepers,
by those who have killed a Brahmin, women in childbirth, menstruating women, dogs, and those belonging to their families..."
Or, if it is desirable food contaminated by hair or insects, one should eat it after purifying it with earth, ashes, gold, and water;
provided it is thoroughly cleansed, free from impurities, abundant, and indeed warm.
"Kauleyaka" means a dog. Likewise:
"If a server is touched by a Śūdra who has food remnants on his hands..."
But one who has an object in hand should give whatever it may be, yet he must not eat food [if he has no such object].
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Likewise, that which is placed in a broken vessel, wiped away by the breath from the mouth,
cooked by heat but not steamed, licked, or unrefined."
O Prince, preparations made from flour,
vegetables, sugarcane, and milk, as well as preparations of meat, should be avoided if they have been kept for a long time.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "One should not eat what remains after a Śūdra has eaten, even if it is still contained within the vessel. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
If food is served in an iron vessel,
the eater consumes it as if it were excrement, and the giver shall go to hell.
Using a finger as a tooth-stick, consuming visible salt,
and eating clay— these are equal to the consumption of beef.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: One should not consume ghee, oil, salt, water, or milk-rice (pāyasa) given by a single hand, nor that which is offered by a Śūdra.
Alms that have been stolen or given by one who has been struck down should never be accepted anywhere at any time.
Now, regarding milk products, Manu [5.8–9] states:
"The milk of a cow within ten days of calving, the milk of a camel, and likewise that of one-hoofed animals..."
[295] The milk of a sheep, the milk of a cow that has recently calved, and the milk of a cow whose calf has died;
And among all wild animals, except for the buffalo,
as well as the milk of females and all fermented acids, these indeed must be avoided.

“Anidaśāyāḥ” refers to one whose ten days following birth have not yet passed. “Ekasaphāḥ” are single-hoofed animals, such as horses and the like. “Āvikaṃ” is the milk of a ewe. “Sandhinī” is one who is in heat and desires a bull; for Hārīta states: “One should not drink the milk of a *sandhinī*—that is, one longing for a bull—for she is in her season. “Vivatsā” is one deprived of her calf. “Āraṇyā mṛgāḥ” are wild animals, such as the ruru deer, the buffalo, the spotted deer, and so forth. Gautama [17.20–23]:

The milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving, as well as that of a goat or a buffalo, is forbidden during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). Sheep's milk is always unfit for drinking; so too is camel’s milk, the milk of one-hoofed animals, and the milk of those that "drip" (*syandinī*), those that have miscarried (*yamasū*), and those that are in heat (*sandhinī*).
A "dripping" cow is one whose udders flow even without a calf. A "twin-bearer" (*yamasū*) is one that gives birth to twins.
[Baudhāyana 1.12.9–10]
The milk of a cow that has not passed ten days since calving is unfit for drinking; so too the milk of one whose calf is dead or of one whose calf is another’s.
"Another's calf" means one joined with the calf of another.
Āpastamba [1.17.21–24].

[The following milk is] not to be drunk: likewise the milk of an *elakā* (female antelope), camel’s milk, the milk of a doe, the milk of a cow in heat (*sandhinī*), the milk of a cow that has recently given birth (*yamasū*), and the milk of a cow within ten days of calving (*anirdaśā*).

Regarding the rule "one should not drink milk," Hārīta states in continuation [of the previous context]: "Not [the milk] of a cow whose calf is stolen, because of the association with theft; not [the milk] of one whose calf is killed, because she is overcome by grief; not [the milk] of one whose calf has been removed, because of its lack of essence; nor should one eat [the milk] of another [cow] after cutting it off for oneself. Likewise, not [the milk] of one that has recently calved, because of her being in her menses (*sarajas*). Some say [this applies] after seven nights; others, after ten nights; others say that after a month it becomes *peyūṣa* (fresh butter-milk). For thus he says:"

For two months one should let the calf suckle; in the third month, one should milk it from two teats; in the fourth month, one should milk it from three teats, according to the rule and according to its strength.
[297] "Vivatsā" here means one whose calf is far away. "Nirṇiktāyāḥ" means from one whose milk has been completely drained. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The froth from ghee, the scum from ghee, or even the colostrum of a cow..."
Likewise, curd that has been mixed with jaggery, sprinkled with black pepper, or has become stale.
If one has consumed out of negligence buttermilk that is broken, undrinkable, tasteless, and frothy,
one must observe a vow in the forest for a fortnight.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "The Śūdra who drinks [the milk] of a tawny cow (*kapilā*) is cooked in hell;
a Brāhmaṇa should drink only the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*), otherwise he becomes a beast."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Even at the time of departure, one should not consume curd at night,
except by choice when it is for the purpose of offering the *madhuparka*."
Alakṣmī dwells in parched grains by day and in curd-mixed barley-meal by night; she always resides in kovidāra trees and in kapittha fruits.
[298] Now, regarding birds in that regard, Manu says [5.11–16]:
One should avoid all carnivorous birds, as well as those that dwell in villages, those not specifically mentioned, those with uncloven hooves, and the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird.
The kalaviṅka, the plava, the haṃsa, the cakrāhva, the domestic cock,
the sārasa, the rajjudāla, the dātyūha, the parrot, and the maina.
Pecking birds, web-footed birds, the koyaṣṭi, claw-scratching birds, those that dive for fish, meat from a slaughterhouse, and dried meat; these one should avoid.
The crane, the heron, the raven, the wagtail,
fish-eaters, village pigs, and all kinds of fish.

“Carnivorous animals” (*kravyādāḥ*) refers to meat-eaters such as vultures and the like. “Village-dwellers” (*grāmanivāsinaḥ*) refers to pigeons and the like; in both cases, the term “birds” (*śakuni*) is to be connected [to these]. “Not specifically mentioned” (*anirdiṣṭān*) means those not declared as edible in the Veda (*śruti*). For in the Veda, certain single-hoofed animals are mentioned in some places as being edible, such as: “One should sacrifice a *vāḍava* belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, and one should eat its meat. Therefore, those which are stated in the Veda as being edible in some specific sacrifice should not be eaten elsewhere on the basis of that [instance], because those single-hoofed animals are not designated as edible in other contexts. The *kalaviṅka* is the village sparrow (*grāmacaṭaka*). Since its prohibition is already established by virtue of being a village-dweller, the mention of “village” again is for the purpose of prohibiting even the wild variety, as it dwells in both villages and forests. The *plava* is that which obtains its food solely by floating. The *rajjudāla* is a woodpecker. The *dātyūha* is the *kālakaṇṭha*, commonly known as the *ḍāḍaka*. “Pecking birds” (*pratudāḥ*) are those that eat by pecking with their beaks. “Web-footed birds” (*jālapādāḥ*) are the *āṭya* (heron) and others. The *koyaṣṭi* is a particular species of bird. “Scratchers” (*nakhaviṣkirāḥ*) are those that eat by scratching with their claws. “Fish-eaters that dive” (*nimajjato matsyādāḥ*) refers to the *madgu* (diver) and others. “Meat from a slaughterhouse” (*saunaṃ*) is meat produced in a place of slaughter. “Dried meat” (*vallūraṃ*) is dried flesh. The *kākola* is the *droṇakāka* (drona-crow). “Fish-eaters” (*matsyādāḥ*) are crocodiles and the like. “In every way” (*sarvaśaḥ*) means in every manner.
Yājñavalkya [1.172–173]: Carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, pecking birds, the ṭiṭṭibha,
the sārasa crane, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds [are forbidden].
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, baka, and viṣkira birds;
likewise, the kalaviṅka, kākola, kurara, and rajjudālaka.
Web-footed birds, wagtails, and other unknown species of beasts and birds.
Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, dried meat, or fish, one should dwell for three days observing a fast.
The *kurara* is the osprey (*kurala*). The *cāṣa* is the blue jay (*kikīdivi*). The "red-footed" birds are the *kadamba* and others. Devala says:
the crane, the swan, the gallinule, the *bhṛṅgarāja*, and the *kacitraka*.
Owls, ospreys, hawks, vultures, cocks, and crows.
The cakora, the cuckoo, the rajju, the kuṭila, the blue jay, the water-hen, the heron, the sāra-vaṇa, the vulture, the woodpecker, and the monkey.
The osprey, the peacock, the curlew, the ruddy goose, the bee-eater,
the pigeon, and the dove— these groups of birds are recorded as unfit for consumption.
The *bhrṅgarāja* is the *dhūmrāṭa*, commonly known as the *dhanacchū*. The *citraka* is the *citrakapota*. The *kaṅka* is the red-winged one.
Regarding the term "not to be eaten," Vasiṣṭha [14.48] continues [the rule].

Among birds, there are the raptors, the scatterers, and the web-footed; the *kalaviṅka*, the water-fowl, the swan, the *cakravāka*, the *bhāsa*, the crow, the pigeon, the wild cock, the *sāraṅga*, the grey dove, the *krauñca*, the *krakara*, the *bakā*, the *balākā*, the *madgu*, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the *māndhāla*, the night-prowler, the woodpecker, the *cātaka*, the *tailātaka*, the *hārītaka*, the wagtail, the village cock, the parrot, the *sārikā*, the cuckoo, the carnivorous birds, and those that frequent villages.

“Vidhuna” means one that shakes. “Bhāsa” refers to a specific type of vulture frequenting those regions. “Sāraṅga” is a deer. “Krakara” is a chameleon. “Māndhāla” is a cockroach. “Naktañcaras” are owls and other such nocturnal creatures. “Dārvāghāṭa” is a woodpecker. “Hārītaka” is a pigeon-shaped bird with green wings. “Grāmopacāriṇaḥ” are those who always roam only in villages.
Regarding these, Gautama [17.26–27] states that they are “not to be eaten” (abhakṣya) based on their future nature.

The *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the *cakravāka*, and the *haṃsa*; the crow, the *kaṅka*, the vulture, and the hawk; water-birds with red feet and red beaks; and domestic cocks and pigs—these are not to be eaten. This follows from the [preceding] rule. Yama says: "The *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the *cakravāka*, the *haṃsa*, the *bhāsa*, and the *sārasa*; and whatever other birds there are that are peckers (*pratuda*), scratchers (*viṣkira*), web-footed (*jālapāda*), or have red feet, such as the *koyaṣṭika*."
Furthermore, Yama says:
Having eaten mushrooms, village pigs, web-footed birds, and cocks, even a Brahmin who is a knower of all the Vedas would fall [from his status].

In this section on forbidden foods (*abhakṣya*), Āpastamba [1.17.32–36] states: "Of the *viṣkira* birds, the cock; of the *pratuda* birds, the *plava*; carnivorous birds; and the *haṃsa*, *sārasa*, *cakravāka*, and *suparṇa*. [This applies] except for the *kruñca*, *krauñca*, *vārdhrāṇasa*, and *lakṣmaṇa*. Gautama [17.32–33] states: [the same].

The *nicu*, woodpecker, crane, *balākā* heron, *śuka* parrot, water-fowl, *tiṭṭibha* sandpiper, *māndhāla*, and nocturnal prowlers are not to be eaten. Those that peck (*pratuda*), scatterers (*viṣkira*), and web-footed birds (*ajālapāda*) are to be eaten.
Following the word "to be eaten," Baudhāyana [states]:
"Among birds, the *tittiri*, pigeon, *kapiñjala*, *vārdhrāṇasa*, *tṛṇamaya*, and *mayūra*; and among the five types of scatterers (*pañcaviṣkira*), excluding the *vāraṇa*."
Śaṅkha [17.27]: Yama has always declared that the partridge, the peacock, the quail, the francolin, the vārdhrāṇasa crane, and the bustard are edible.
Now, regarding animals there,
Devala says:
Among the species of animals, cows, donkeys, camels, horses, and elephants are not to be eaten.
Lions, tigers, bears, śarabhas, serpents, pythons, and cobras.
Moles, mice, cats, mongooses, village pigs,
dogs, jackals, deer, leopards, baboons, monkeys, and humans.

[304] “*Ṛkṣaḥ*” is a bear; “*śarabhaḥ*” is an eight-legged animal; “*ajagaraḥ*” is a species of serpent; “*ākhuḥ*” is a large *undurū*; “*mūṣikaḥ*” here refers to a small mouse; “*dvīpī*” is a leopard; “*golāṅgūlaḥ*” is a black-faced monkey; “*nā*” is a human; “*markaṭaḥ*” is a monkey. Paiṭhīnasi says: “One should avoid carnivorous beasts and birds; as many as are mentioned as eaters of all kinds of flesh, so many are unfit to be eaten.”

Yama says: Having eaten beef, horse-flesh, donkey or camel meat, as well as that of dogs or jackals, or having consumed birds that scratch for food or those that peck, a twice-born man indeed falls immediately from his caste.
In the context of the recurring phrase "always unfit to be eaten," Gautama [17.26] states:
"Those with teeth in both jaws, the *keśī*, those without hair, the single-hoofed animals, the *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the *cakravāka*, and the swan.
"Those with teeth in both jaws" refers to humans. "The *keśī*" is the yak (*camarī*). "Those without hair" refers to snakes and the like.

Again, Gautama says: [17.29] "Meat from animals that have not fallen [naturally], meat from those that are emaciated, and meat prepared in vain. [305] "From animals that have not fallen" means that as long as the teeth have not fallen out naturally, even if the animal is fit to be eaten, it is unfit to be eaten. "Emaciated" refers to one who is afflicted by disease. "Meat prepared in vain" is that which is not cooked for the sake of the gods, ancestors, or others.

Vasiṣṭha [14.43–47], continuing from the term "not to be eaten," states: "The white ox, the gavaya, and the śarabha; likewise those not specifically mentioned; and cows and bulls whose teeth have fallen out. It is known in the Vājasaneyaka that cows and bulls are edible and pure. However, there is a dispute regarding the rhinoceros and the wild boar."

The *gaura* is a wild animal resembling a horse. The term *medhya* means "fit for sacrifice" (*medha*), referring to those that are constituent parts of a sacrifice. Regarding the statement, "There is dispute concerning the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*) and the non-domestic pig," some sages declare the rhinoceros and the domestic pig to be edible, while others declare them inedible; thus, there is an option (*vikalpa*). And this option is regulated by whether one is engaged or not engaged in a *śrāddha*. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"A twice-born man should not cause the meat of an animal being slaughtered to be taken."
Whether it be meat from the back, the flesh of the womb, or even dried meat;
One should carefully avoid eating cooked meat or the dregs of grain that have been buried underground and covered over with earth.
Manu [5.17]: One should not eat solitary animals or birds that are unknown,
nor any five-toed creatures, even if they are specified among those permitted for consumption.

“Moving alone” (*ekacara*) refers to those such as snakes who generally wander solitary by their very nature. “Unknown” (*ajñāta*) refers to those whose names, natures, tastes, potencies, and post-digestive effects (*rasavīryavipāka*) are not known even by experts. Because they fall within the category of edible things (*bhakṣya*) since they are not subject to general or specific prohibitions, it is said: “even among those designated as edible. Regarding this, Āpastamba states in the section on non-edibles [1.17.37]:
“Among five-toed animals, with the exception of the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the hedgehog, the rhinoceros, the hare, and the *pūtikhaṣa*.”

“*Śvāvit*” is the porcupine (*sedhā*). “*Śalyaka*” is a specific type of animal resembling a porcupine that possesses quills. “*Pūtikhaṣa*” is well-known in the Himavat mountains, according to Kapardin.
Manu [5.18]: “The porcupine, the *śalyaka*, the monitor lizard (*godhā*), the rhinoceros, the tortoise, and likewise the hare...”
Among five-toed animals, they say that those with a single row of teeth, excluding the camel, are edible.
“Ekatodataḥ” means those with teeth on one side. Baudhāyana [1.12.5] states:
“The porcupine, the monitor lizard, the hare, the hedgehog, the tortoise, and the rhinoceros—these five five-toed animals are edible, with the exception of the rhinoceros.”
In the Mahābhārata:
"One should avoid the meat of goats, cows, and peacocks. Hārīta says:

One may eat domestic and wild animals, such as goats, sheep, buffaloes, deer, rhinoceroses, ruru-deer, spotted deer, antelopes, and mahāraṇya-hogs; likewise, rabbits, porcupines, sedhas, monitor lizards, tortoises, vartakas, partridges, peacocks, vārdhrīṇasas, quails, kuraras, and francolins; and one may eat scaled fish that have been obtained through lawful means.

[308] “Ruru” is a deer with many branched antlers. “Pṛṣata” is a deer variegated with spots. “Ṛśya” has soft antlers; it is commonly known as a *rojha*. “Nyaṅku” resembles a Śabara and is devoid of horns. “Sedhā” is covered in quills. Paiṭhīnasi says: There are fourteen domestic and wild animals. The seven domestic animals are: the cow, sheep, goat, horse, mule, donkey, and human. The seven wild animals are: birds, monkeys, buffalo, reptiles, ruru-deer, spotted deer, and [other] forest animals.
Now, there were two humans there among the fish:
he who eats the flesh of another is called a meat-eater of that [creature].
One who eats fish is an eater of all kinds of meat; therefore, one should avoid fish.

Āpastamba [1.17.38–39]: Among fish, the *ita* is inedible. The *sarpaśīrṣa*, the *mṛdura*, the *kravyāda*, and those with deformed mouths, such as those with human heads—the *sarpaśīrṣa* is one whose head is like that of a serpent; the *mṛdura* is the crocodile (*makara*); and the *kravyāda* are those that generally eat flesh, such as the *nakra* (crocodile) and others.

[309] Yama says: The makara, the snake, the reptile, the water-crow (*madgu*), the peacock, the *varmika*, the crocodile, the crab, and the *śiśumāra* are not to be eaten; nor are others with horse-like ears, nor other scaleless fish that have mouths on both sides. Here, "snake" refers to the water-snake (*duṇḍubha*); "reptile" here refers to the leech (*jalaukā*); "water-crow" is the aquatic crow; "peacock" here refers to a water-dwelling bird resembling a peacock; "armored one" (*varmika*) is a fish resembling a small snake; "those with mouths on both sides" means those with faces on both ends.
Furthermore, Yama states:
"One who studies the Veda should avoid all fish that lack scales.
Here, the term "one who studies the Veda" refers to a member of the three higher castes.
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"The *kulīra*, the eggplant (*vārtāka*), the *pṛtana*, the *jalānarta*, the *kṣipraga*, and others are not to be eaten; likewise those with snake-like heads and those with deformed faces."
In the context of the phrase "not to be eaten," Vasiṣṭha [14.41–42] states:
"Among fish, the *veṭa*, *gavaya*, *śiśumāra*, *nakra*, and *kulīra*; as well as those of deformed shape and those with serpent-like heads. Devala says:
The śambūka, the pearl-oyster, the nakha-śukti, the porpoise, the monkey-fish,
and fish of deformed shape— these aquatic creatures are not to be eaten.
“Nakhaśukti” is a long oyster shell; “plavaṅgama” is a frog. Manu [5.16] states:
“The *pāṭhīna* and *rohit* fish are to be eaten first when employed in offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).”
The rājīvas, siṃhatuṇḍas, and saśalkas in their entirety.
“Appointed for the *havya* and *kavya* offerings” means they are assigned for the purpose of the *śrāddha* and other rites. “The first two” refers to those fit to be eaten.
Śaṅkha [17.25]:
“The *rājīva*, the *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and likewise the *saśalka* [fish].”
Furthermore, among fish, the pāṭhīna and rohita are declared to be edible.
In the context of "those that may be eaten," Baudhāyana [1.12.8] states:
"Fish with a thousand teeth, the cilicima, the armored one, the large-headed, the hairy, the karī, the rohita, and the rājīva. Hārīta says:
And he may eat fish that have their scales, provided they are obtained in accordance with the law. Regarding this, Gautama [17.34] continues the phrase "are edible" [from the previous rule]:
"and fish that are not altered."
Yājñavalkya [1.177–178]:
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the iguana, the tortoise, the hedgehog, and the hare may be eaten;
and among fish, those with the shape of a lion's snout and the Rohita may be eaten.
Likewise, the pāṭhīna, rājīva, and saśalka fish may be eaten by the twice-born;
therefore, hear now the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
Now follows the rule for abstaining from the consumption of meat. Regarding this, Manu [5.26–32] states:
"Thus has been declared in its entirety what is edible and what is inedible for the twice-born."
Therefore, I shall now declare the rule regarding the eating and the avoidance of meat.
One may eat meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of Brāhmaṇas,
or when one is enjoined according to the rule, or when there is a danger to life.
Prajāpati ordained all this as food for the vital breath (prāṇa):
everything both moving and stationary is the sustenance of the vital breath.
The immobile are the food of the mobile; those without fangs are the food of those with fangs;
the handless are the food of those with hands; and the timid are the food of the brave.
The eater is not defiled by eating those living beings that are fit to be eaten, even day after day;
for both the eaters and those fit to be eaten were created by the Creator himself.
"Eating meat for the sake of sacrifice—this is remembered as the divine ordinance;
any practice other than this is called the demonic ordinance."
Whether having purchased it himself, produced it himself, or even received it from another,
one does not incur sin by eating meat after having first honored the gods and the ancestors.

The statement, “This has been said regarding the twice-born,” serves to exclude the Śūdra from the previously mentioned rules concerning what is fit and unfit to be eaten, by specifying that these apply to the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, there is no fault for him in eating garlic and the like. However, the eating of crows and other such animals mentioned therein brings about sin because they are condemned by the great community (*mahājana*). Therefore, the injunction for the avoidance of meat to be mentioned later applies equally to all four castes. As for the rule regarding avoidance, it takes the form of a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), like not looking at the sun. “*Prokṣita*” here means consecrated by mantras for the sake of sacrifice, based on the supplementary scriptural passage: “animals unconsecrated by mantras. “And at the desire of Brāhmaṇas”: when certain Brāhmaṇas each individually desire, “Meat should be eaten by you,” then there is no fault for one who eats meat once at their request, according to the saying of Yama: “Once, at the desire of Brāhmaṇas. “At the risk of life”: when a loss of life is likely to occur through disease or lack of food unless meat is eaten, then meat may be eaten; this is the meaning. The explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) for these aforementioned points are those beginning with “Food of the vital breath. “Moving creatures” are deer and the like. “Non-moving creatures” are grass and the like. “Fanged creatures” are tigers and the like. “Non-fanged creatures” are deer and the like. “Handed creatures” are humans and the like. “Handless creatures” are fish and the like. “Brave” refers to those emboldened for battle and the like. “Timid” refers to the cowardly. “For sacrifice” means for the purpose of sacrifice. “Eating” (*jagdhi*) means consumption. “Having produced it oneself” refers specifically to the Kṣatriya.
And likewise in the Mahābhārata:
"Hear from me also that rule which is seen for Kṣatriyas,
by which one does not incur sin while eating meat acquired through valor."
O King, in ancient times Agastya declared that all wild animals are consecrated to all the deities; therefore, for one by whom hunting is practiced, it is considered a form of worship.
There is no such thing as hunting without abandoning one's own self;
only by attaining equanimity can a man slay a living being.
"Therefore, O Bhārata, all royal sages go out on the hunt;
they are not tainted by fault, nor do they consider this a sin.

By the phrase "having purchased it or [obtaining it] oneself," the absence of fault in consuming meat is demonstrated when preceded by the worship of the gods and ancestors. As for the scriptural mention of rewards resulting from the avoidance of meat, that too refers to the avoidance of meat obtained through such means as those described, and not to meat prescribed for ritual purposes (*niyukta*) and the like; for a fault is heard to accrue from consuming it otherwise.
Yajnavalkya and Vishvamitra state: "In a life-threatening emergency, at a Shraddha ceremony, when sprinkled with water for a twice-born guest's desire,
or after having worshipped the gods and ancestors— one who eats meat incurs no fault."
Devala says:
Even while eating meats, one who eats only the remnants is not defiled,
provided it is for medicinal purposes, in cases of incapacity, by command, or for the sake of a sacrifice.

“Eater of remnants” (*śeṣabhojī*) means one who eats what remains after the worship of the gods, ancestors, and others. “For medicinal purposes” (*auṣadhārtham*) means for the sake of medicine. “In case of inability” (*aśaktau*) means when one is overcome by disease. The meaning is that where medical authorities have determined that the removal of illness cannot occur without the consumption of meat, there it may be eaten. “Invitation” (*niyoga*) refers to being invited to a *śrāddha* ceremony. “For the sake of sacrifice” (*yajñakāraṇāt*) means for the purpose of accomplishing a sacrifice. The syntactical connection is: “eating, he is not defiled. Yama says: “One may eat meat that has been set aside, once, out of a desire to please a Brāhmaṇa.”
One appointed to a rite for the gods or a śrāddha ceremony should avoid [these] during the period of observance.

“Once” means one time; this is connected with the phrase “out of a desire for Brahman. “When the restriction”—that is, the vow of abstaining from meat—is observed, this [rule] applies to all cases except for consecrated (prokṣita) meat. It does not apply to consecrated meat, because that would contradict direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Likewise, regarding other permissions to eat meat mentioned in other Smṛtis, one should connect the rule “one should avoid it when under a restriction” by setting aside those instances that fall within the scope of stronger authority. Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 84, 81]:

One who is ill, one appointed by ritual rule, one for whom an oblation has been offered, and likewise one invited by a Brahmin—these four are proclaimed as those for whom meat may be eaten; this is the enumeration.
But he who eats otherwise than this, abandoning the prescribed rule like a Piśāca,
shall suffer death as many times as there are hairs on the animal's body.

"Patient" here refers to one for whom the removal of disease occurs through meat alone. "According to rule" means in the manner prescribed by the scriptures. "Offered" means the remains of what has been offered. "Requested by a Brahmin" means solicited by a Brahmin. "Enumeration" here refers to a specific listing. This is because in another Smṛti, meat-eating is permitted through other modes as well, such as: "One who eats meat after having worshipped the gods and the ancestors incurs no fault."
Hārīta says: Meat not intended for sacrifice must not be eaten; having consumed it, a wise man should perform the Kṛcchra penance.
However, at the request of Brāhmaṇas, he may eat it according to their desire.
Manu and Viṣṇu [state]: A Brahmin, adhering to the eternal rule, should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras; however, he may eat those consecrated with mantras.

Regarding what was previously stated, "One may eat meat that has been consecrated," he specifies its scope with the words, "But those prepared with mantras. "Eternal" (*śāśvata*) means because it is established by the eternal Veda. "Resorting to" (*āsthita*) means having taken recourse to. Yama says:
"One should eat meat prepared with *yajus* mantras according to the prescribed rule."
One should not eat meat in vain; one should avoid meat from the back of an animal.
"Back-meat" refers to meat connected with the back. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"One may eat meat at a Śrāddha ceremony, as well as on account of a guest."
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, for so long does he go to hell.
"In the *śrāddha*," the word "invited" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "On account of a guest" means that whatever has been set aside for the sake of a guest is to be eaten by that guest.
As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "The sacrificial oblation (*havis*) which has been consecrated with mantras, sprinkled, and purified is pure."
And according to the manner prescribed in the Vedas, during the rites for the ancestors.
Manu has declared that meat other than this is useless and unfit for consumption. Likewise:
"Meat that has been consecrated by sprinkling, or offered out of affection for a Brāhmaṇa..."
In this case, it should be known that there is little fault; however, in the opposite case, one is defiled.
Likewise: "In sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods, the oblation is said to be consecrated;
having consumed that according to the rite seen in the Vedas, one does not incur sin in this world."
Manu [5.35]: But that man who, being duly appointed according to the rule, does not eat meat,
goes after death to the state of an animal for twenty-one births.
Yama says: But he who, having been invited to a Śrāddha or a rite for the gods, should discard meat,
shall dwell in hell for as many years as there are hairs on the body of that animal.
Hārīta and Śātātapa state:
"But he who, being appointed to a śrāddha, does not eat meat,
shall dwell in hell for as many years as there are hairs on the body of the animal."
They praise meat acquired by Kṣatriyas through the ritual of hunting,
as well as that killed by lions and tigers, at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony.
They do not indeed commend meat killed by poison or a deceptive trap, nor that killed by a hunter or a beast of prey, nor that which is devoid of mantras, at a śrāddha ceremony.

“By hunting” means by the chase. “According to rule” means with valor free from the consumption of poison and so forth. “Wild animals” here refers to beasts other than lions and the like. Gautama [17.36]:
One may consume meat killed by predators, provided it is not seen to have defects and is commended by word, after sprinkling it with water.

“Beasts of prey” (*vyāla*) refers to lions, tigers, and so forth, as mentioned in another *Smṛti*. “Of unobserved defect” (*adṛṣṭadoṣa*) means of uncertain defect. Regarding “commended by word” (*vākapraśasta*): the meaning here is that when something is doubtful as to whether it is pure or impure, if it is then commended as “excellent” by another person’s speech, one may use it after sprinkling water over it. Āpastamba [1.16.16] states:
“Meat cut with a knife intended for killing is unfit to be eaten.”

That which is "cut" for the purpose of killing—that is, specifically for the sake of slaughtering living beings—is what is meant here; the mention of the sword is merely illustrative. Manu and Viṣṇu state this second [rule]:
"A twice-born man who knows the law shall not eat meat that has not been prepared according to rule, except in times of distress."
For having eaten meat contrary to the prescribed rule, one is helplessly devoured by those very creatures after death.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as grave as that of one who eats meat in vain after death.
"He shall devour me in the next world, whose flesh I eat here"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "flesh" (māṃsa).
There is no doer of greater demerit than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another.
Yama said:
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another shall be born here or there, afflicted by disease.
But having eaten meats out of delusion for the sake of his own nourishment,
a man who has not performed purification for himself is cooked in the wombs of animals.
“Purification of the self” means expiation. Hārīta says:
The birth of a living being results from the impurities of both the mother and the father.
Whoever eats the flesh of another eats that person's sin.
But when one who has eaten meat performs purification with water,
the gods laugh at that impure person who perceives himself as pure.
"Sin" (*kilbiṣam*) here refers to semen and blood. "Its sin" means that flesh; because it is composed of those [semen and blood], it is called sin. Manu [5.51]:
"The one who consents, the one who dissects, the one who kills, the buyer, and the seller..."
The preparer, the server, and the eater are all killers.
Devala said: For one's own sake, out of a desire for delicious food, one should not kill living beings;
for a livelihood based on the flesh of living creatures is miserable, as it involves the nature of a predator.
“Alas! because it is a cause of evil. Yama says: “But he who eats the flesh of living beings who desire to live—”
And as it is with those who have struck down and those who have died, so too is he who strikes them down.
The one who consents, the one who dissects, the one who kills, the buyer, and the seller—all these are indeed slayers; the one who cooks the meat is called the sixth.
The one who consents through instruction, the one who dissects by command,
the one who kills by the act of killing, and likewise the buyer for the sake of wealth.
The seller [is defiled] by the non-payment of the price; the preparer by setting it in motion;
and furthermore, by the wealth, by the enjoyment thereof, and by slaughter or imprisonment.
Killing should be known as threefold, and among these, the consumer is the most excessive;
six types of killers have been enumerated, and the consumer is the seventh.
Of those six, however, the consumer is the one who exceeds the rest:
one quarter of the sin falls upon the buyer, and one quarter reaches the consumer.
The foot serves the killer; therefore, the other three feet meet their destruction.
If there were no eater of that [meat], the killer would likewise not exist.
The eater, the killer, and the buyer—these three are equal, without a doubt.
Flesh is not born from the earth, nor does it grow from trees.
Having committed the terrible act of killing living beings, one should therefore avoid meat;
for that Brāhmaṇa, the most learned in the Vedas, who eats meats—
He is cooked in the supportless hell (*nirālamba-naraka*) because of that karma. Manu [5.50]:
"But he who eats meat, disregarding the rule, like a *piśāca*..."
He becomes unpopular in the world and is indeed afflicted by diseases.
Yama said: Furthermore, he who does not consume even those meats that are fit for eating—
by abstaining from such meats, Dharma himself is directly pleased.
In the eating of all meats indeed there is great fault;
but in not eating them, there would be merit—this is our traditional teaching.
Manu [5.53–54]: He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by subsisting on pure fruits and roots or by eating the food of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
Yājñavalkya [1.181]: Even while dwelling at home, a brahmin becomes a sage by abstaining from meat; he attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "A wise man should not eat meat— which is moist, foul-smelling, transformed, and a source of loathing— even if it is most delicious and beneficial."
And that mortal who, remaining steadfast in his own duty, is devoted to the service of his guru,
shall go to the auspicious world of the gods, frequented by the deities.
On that very day, one who abstains from meat would attain the world;
so too the man of pure mind who avoids meat for an entire month.
He goes to incomparable heaven, enriched with divine enjoyments,
having performed that terrible penance and made firm resolve for a hundred years at Puṣkara.
Having performed [other] austerities, one obtains that fruit which is attained by the renunciation of meat;
indeed, he who might give away the earth with all its moving and unmoving beings during a lunar or solar eclipse [does not equal him].
But that man who performs severe penance at Gayā for a hundred years,
such a person shall attain the highest worlds.
One who always abstains from meat attains these worlds,
as does one who provides instruction to another high-souled person.
"He who avoids meat shall obtain the fruitless result of abstaining from it; as stated in the Mahābhārata:
'He who might perform the horse sacrifice month after month for a hundred years...'"
And he who does not eat meat—these two are equal, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Likewise: "He who might perform most severe austerities for a full hundred years,
and he who would abstain from meat for a single day— whether these two be equal or not equal [is to be considered]."
O lord of men, one should especially avoid all meats during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, for it is dharma that is prescribed therein.
He who avoids even meat during the four months of the rainy season attains four auspicious things: renown, long life, fame, and strength.
Alternatively, by abstaining from all meats for even a single month,
one may transcend all sufferings and live happily, free from disease.
Those who avoid meats for a month or even for a fortnight—
for those who have desisted from violence, the world of Brahmā is ordained.
But for one month during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, he was avoided by all kings—
those who have become the self of all beings and who understand the higher and lower truths.
By Nābhāga, Ambarīṣa, and the high-souled Gaya;
by Āyu, Anaraṇya, Dilīpa, and the sons of Raghu.
By Kārtavīrya and Aniruddha, by Nahuṣa and Yayāti,
by King Viṣvaksena, and likewise by Śatabindu.
And likewise by Yuvanāśva, by Śibi the son of Uśīnara,
by Mucukunda, by Māndhātṛ, or by Hariścandra, O Lord.
Speak the truth, not untruth; truth is the eternal dharma.
Indeed, Harishchandra moves in heaven like the moon by means of his truth.
With Śyenacitra, Rājanya, Somaka, and Vṛka;
with Devatrā, Rantideva, Vasu, and Sañjaya.
By Duṣyanta, Karūṣa, Rāma, Alarka, Nala,
Virūpāśva, Nimi, and the wise Janaka.
Indeed, by Nīla and Pṛthu, by Vīrasena, by Ikṣvāku, Śambhu, Śveta, and Sagara;
By Aja, by Dhundhu, and likewise by Subāhu;
by Haryaśva, O king of kings, by Kṛpa, and by Bharata.
By these and other lords of kings, meat was not eaten in former times;
because they avoided the meat of the autumnal moon-bright season, they attained heaven.
And they dwell in the world of Brahmā, blazing and surrounded by splendor,
being worshipped by Gandharvas accompanied by thousands of women.
Thus, those great-souled ones who practice this supreme, auspicious dharma characterized by non-violence dwell upon the vault of heaven.
Those righteous ones here constantly avoid honey and meat;
and all those who have abstained from liquor since birth are remembered as sages.
Bṛhaspati [Ācār.
85, 82]: "He who, though afflicted by disease or even honored [with an invitation], does not eat meat because he is free from greed, obtains without effort the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices."
Intoxicants, meat, and sexual intercourse are known as the delight of living beings;
by performing those very acts according to the prescribed rule, a human being attains heaven.
Manu [5.56]: "There is no fault in eating meat, nor in liquor, nor in sexual intercourse;
for these are the natural inclinations of living beings, but abstention from them yields great fruit."

“Abstention” (*nivṛtti*) is the resolve to refrain. It is “of great fruit” (*mahāphalā*), meaning it has heaven and so forth as its fruit, because heaven and such are greater fruits than the satisfaction produced by eating.
Now, regarding the injunctions and prohibitions concerning the injury of animals, Manu says [5.22–23]:
Excellent beasts and birds may be slain by Brahmins for the sake of sacrifice;
indeed, in ancient times, Agastya practiced this even for the sake of providing sustenance for his dependents.
For even in ancient sacrifices and in the rites of the Brahmins and Kshatriyas, the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) consisted of the flesh of wild animals and birds.

The phrase “for the sake of sacrifice” (*yajñārtham*) is for the purpose of providing an illustration. “Commended” (*praśastāḥ*) means those well-known as fit for consumption. “Ancient” (*purāṇāḥ*) refers to the sacrifices of the sages (*ṛṣiyajña*), such as the twenty-six-year sacrifice and others. For in that context, the killing of wild animals is heard [in the scripture]: “When the day has concluded, the householder goes out on a hunt. Whatever wild animals he kills there, their flesh becomes the *puroḍāśa* cakes. “When it has concluded” (*saṃsthite*) means when it is finished. “Marrow-like” (*tarasāḥ*) means consisting of meat.
Manu and Viṣṇu [5.39–42, 44]:
"Animals were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world; therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."
Herbs, animals, trees, quadrupeds, and likewise birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain supreme advancements.
"Manu has declared that animals may be slain only in these instances— the offering of madhuparka, the soma sacrifice, and rites for the ancestors or the gods— and nowhere else."
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, when killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animals to the highest state.
One should know that violence which is ordained by the Vedas and is restricted to this world of moving and non-moving beings is indeed non-violence; for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
Vasiṣṭha [4.5, 8]:

"One may indeed kill an animal even for the worship of ancestors, deities, and guests; such is the teaching of Manu. Furthermore, they say that for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who has arrived as a guest, one should cook a large bull or a large goat; in this way, they provide hospitality to him. "Ancestral deities" refers to the Aṣṭakā ritual.
Yama and Paiṭhīnasi:
One should not cook food for one's own sake, nor should one slaughter animals for one's own sake;
one who cooks for the sake of the gods or for the sake of Brahmins incurs no taint.
Manu and Viṣṇu [state] in the third [chapter]:
"Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress."
In times of distress, one may offer a sacrificial animal made of ghee, or likewise one made of flour;
however, under no circumstances should one ever desire to kill an animal in vain.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal, so many times does the killer of animals undergo death here in this world,
and in vain, he suffers it in birth after birth after passing away.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor when dead.

“Dwelling with a guru” refers to a *brahmacārī* (celibate student). “Dwelling in a house” refers to a *gṛhastha* (householder). “Dwelling in the forest” refers to a *vānaprastha* (forest-dweller). “Not prescribed by the Vedas” means not ordained. “In times of distress” (*āpadi*) refers to suffering such as hunger; however, when there is a threat to life, violence must indeed be performed, as it is then ordained. “A ghee-animal” (*ghṛtapasu*) means that for the purpose of an animal sacrifice, one should use clarified butter. “In connection with” (*saṅge*) refers to occasions such as the Sītā-sacrifice which have come into practice through worldly custom where the slaughter of an animal occurs; the meaning is that in such cases, one should make an animal out of ghee or flour. Yājñavalkya [1.180]: He shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the body of the animal.
One of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule is considered equal [to such a sinner].
Manu [5.46–47]: He who does not desire to inflict the suffering of bondage or death upon living beings,
but seeks the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one performs, and wherever one fixes one's delight—
that very thing one obtains without effort, provided one does not harm anything whatsoever.
Hārīta says:
The wise man who desires well-being for others just as he does for himself is glorified in the world of Brahmā, the most excellent of all worlds.
Now, regarding intoxicants,
Yama says:
"Meat is the impurity among foods, and liquor is the impurity among meats."
For liquor is said by the gods to be the stain among all evils in the teachings of Dharma.
Therefore, this [liquor] must not be drunk by the twice-born, nor should it be accepted by them under any circumstances.
"Samalam" means impure. Regarding "in the dharmas," that is, in the treatises on Dharma:
Manu and Hārīta exclude the fourth [caste], while Yama excludes both the first and the fourth.
Surā is indeed the dregs of foods, and evil is called a dreg;
therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink surā.
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī—liquor is to be known as threefold.
Just as one is so are all; they must not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
The food of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas— namely liquor, meat, and fermented spirits—
must not be consumed by a brāhmaṇa who partakes of the sacrificial oblation (havis) for the gods.
Intoxicated by liquor, a Brahmin might fall into impurity, or he might recite Vedic texts,
or he might perform some other improper act, being deluded by intoxication.
He whose Brahman residing in the body is once drenched by intoxicating liquor loses his status as a Brāhmaṇa and becomes a Śūdra.

“Gauḍī” is liquor produced from molasses; “paiṣṭī” is that produced from flour; “mādhvī” is that produced from honey. “Surā” is primarily the *paiṣṭī* (flour-based) variety. Regarding the phrase “just as one,” just as the single *paiṣṭī* type is not to be drunk by any of the three twice-born classes (*dvijāti*), so too “all [types] indeed are not to be drunk by the ‘best of the twice-born’ (*dvijottama*),” namely, the Brāhmaṇas. In Hārīta’s version, however, the reading is “by the twice-born” (*dvijātibhiḥ*). And here the word “twice-born” refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas, because of the supplementary statement: “that must not be eaten by a Brāhmaṇa. For even a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, though well-composed, [may drink it] out of desire.
Let them both drink honey; they shall not incur any fault whatsoever.
Thus, from the words of Yama: "Regarding 'yakṣa-rakṣas'": since this—namely liquor, meat, wine, and spirits—is the food of the yakṣas, rakṣasas, and piśācas, it must not be consumed by a brāhmaṇa.
Yama says: "If a vipra, having drunk liquor, should ever recite the Veda..."
Even with a thousand oblations of clarified butter, he attains nothing at all.
Likewise: "But that sacrificer who repeatedly strives for the status of a Brahmin must not drink liquor, nor should he give it to anyone."
Uśanas says: liquor is not to be drunk, not to be given, and not to be accepted.
"Not to be accepted" means it is not to be taken possession of.
In the context of the recurring phrase "he should avoid," Gautama [2.26] states: "A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid liquor. Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 75] says:
Likewise, in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, liquor is declared to be edible in the Śruti.
Viṣṇu [22.82–84] states:
"Sura should be known as threefold: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from flour (paiṣṭī), and that made from honey (mādhvī)."
Just as one [woman] is, so are all; they must not be touched by those of the twice-born caste.

The honey-wine (mādhūka), the sugarcane-wine (aikṣava), the ṭāṅka, the kaula, the dates-wine (khārjūra), the jackfruit-wine (pānasa), the grape-wine (mṛdvīkārasa), the madhvīka, the maireya, and that produced from the coconut— these are the various types of liquor.
These ten intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya are not defiled by touching them.

“By the twice-born” means by Brāhmaṇas. “Mādhūka” is that which originates from *madhū* flowers. “Aikṣava” is that which originates from sugarcane juice. “Ṭāṅka” refers to the *ṭaṅka*, a specific type of wood-apple (*kapittha*); it is that which originates from it. “Kaula” is that produced from the fruit of the jujube (*kola*). “Khārjūra” is that produced from the date-palm fruit (*kharjūra*). [333] “Pānasa” is that produced from the fruit of the breadfruit tree (*kaṇṭakiphala*). “Mṛdvīkārasa” is that produced from the liquid of grapes (*drākṣā*). Regarding “maireya,” Vācaspati states in the *Śabdārṇava*: “It consists of *dhātupuṣpa* (flower of the mineral/ferment) combined with molasses, grain-water, and so forth. Devala, in the section on what may and may not be eaten, says: “That which is not stale, flavorful, fresh, and well-strained...”
Among substances, this is remembered by those who know the Dharma as the most pure.
Surā, ariṣṭa, maireya, honey-wine (madhu), grape-wine (mādhvīka), and āsava; as well as fermented grain-water (śukta)—the wise know that these must be avoided and are not to be drunk by Brāhmaṇas.

“*Ayātayāma*” means not yet used. “*Rasavat*” means whose flavor has not diminished. “*Pariśruta*” means strained through a cloth; such [liquor] that is *apariśruta* (unstrained) is unfit for consumption. “*Ariṣṭa*” refers to substances having the form of wine and so forth, prepared from *khadira* wood and other materials. “*Āsava*” is a fermented liquor (*saṃdhānaka*). “*Dhānyāmbu śukta*” refers to grain-water that has turned sour.
Now, regarding the duties following a meal, one should be skillful therein [2.68–69].
Having eaten and rested comfortably, one should digest that food;
one should spend the sixth and seventh parts of the day with the study of Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and similar works.
In the eighth [chapter], however, is the worldly course; then follows the external twilight ritual once again.
“Having established oneself in comfort”: here, one should establish oneself in a state of ease conducive to the completion of the rite. Yājñavalkya [1.114]:
Having performed the evening twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), having offered oblations into the fires, and having worshipped them...
Surrounded by his servants, having eaten and not yet being fully satiated, he should then retire to rest.
"Having worshipped"—that is, having propitiated—"those fires," he "should lie down.
"The fire-oblation, the time for eating, and whatever other domestic duties there may be..."
And having performed that, one should thereafter practice a little private recitation of the sacred texts.
One should spend the final two watches of the night, beginning at dusk, devoted to the study of the Vedas;
by sleeping for only two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman.
For one who applies oneself to this very [practice] dissolves into this very [state];
therefore, one who desires happiness should practice with every effort.
A Brahmin who eats the remnants of the oblation and whatever sacrificial offering remains during the two middle watches of the night, and who sleeps [at that time], does not come to ruin.
“In this” refers to the two watches (yāmas) of the night following the onset of dusk. “Practicing” means reciting the Veda. “In this Brahman” implies that the study of the Veda is to be performed.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa [2.12.29–34]:
“That which is called Śuśumāra is where Dhruva stands.”
And hear also, O best of sages, its configuration.
Whatever sin one commits by day, one is freed from it upon seeing him at night;
and as many stars as there are here in the sky, all are supported by this crocodile.
They live for exactly that many years, or even more;
furthermore, Uttānapāda is to be known as his upper jaw.
Sacrifice is to be known as his foundation, and Dharma rests upon his head;
Nārāyaṇa dwells in his heart, and the Aśvins in his two forefeet.
Varuṇa and Aryaman are his two thighs in the west;
the year is his penis, and Mitra is established in his apāna.
In the tail are Agni, Mahendra, Kaśyapa, and then Dhruva;
this quartet of stars belonging to the Śuśumāra never sets.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
For all three social classes, there should be a vigil during the first parts of the night.
Now, regarding the duties of the night, as stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa [3.11.108–110]:
O King, having performed the purification of his feet and other limbs and having eaten in the evening,
the householder should then go to a bed that is not cracked, even if it is made of wood.
One should not occupy a bed that is not spacious, nor one that is broken, uneven, dirty, infested with insects, or lacking a covering.
O King, for a man who is always sleeping, the head is recommended toward the eastern direction or toward the south; however, the opposite [position] brings about disease.

One should not sleep with wet feet; nor with the head toward the north or the west; nor naked; nor along the length of the bed; nor in the open air; nor on a bed made of *pālāśa* wood; nor on one made of five kinds of wood; nor on one made from wood broken by an elephant; nor on one scorched by lightning; nor on a cracked one; nor on one consumed by fire; nor on one sprinkled with water from a jar; nor in cremation grounds, empty dwellings, or temples of the gods; nor in the midst of the fickle; nor in the midst of women; nor above grain, cows, teachers, fire, or the gods. One should not sleep while impure from food remnants; nor during the day; nor during the two twilights; nor on ashes; nor in an unclean place; nor on anything damp; nor on the summit of a mountain.

“Another” means the western one. “Along the beam” (anuvaṃśam) means following the length of the beam; a beam is a long wooden plank at the top of a house. “In the open air” (ākāśe) means in an uncovered place. “Made of five kinds of wood” means constructed from five types of timber. “Fickle” (capalaḥ) here refers to one who is addicted to vices. The word “in a moist place” is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. — Hārīta.

One should not sleep at the junction of day and night; nor on a bed previously used by another; nor on one spread with bamboo mats; nor on one with a stone slab as a pillow; nor with the head pointing sideways, toward the north, or toward the west; nor naked; nor while impure; nor on a seat; nor while still having remnants of food; nor on a broken bed; nor at dawn. One should not speak loudly at night.
Regarding the term "previously used by another" (*anyapūrva*), it refers to that which has been enjoyed before. Regarding "at dawn" (*prage*), it means in the morning.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state, following the rule "one should sleep with the head toward the west": [the above prohibitions apply].

Not on a broken bedstead; nor on one used by another caste without having sprinkled it with water; nor in abodes of spirits, yakṣas, or grahas; nor in the shade of trees in a cremation ground; nor on a festival day or during a sudden celebration.

"Festival" (*parvan*) refers to the junction between the first and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight. "Sudden celebration" (*rabhasotsava*) refers to a joy-inducing celebration such as the birth of a son. [338] Manu [4.57]:
One should not sleep alone in an empty house (Gautama 9.60). One should never go naked at night.
Bhartṛyajña says that the word "should sleep" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Uśanas states:
"One should not sleep with oil smeared on one's head."

Paiṭhīnasi: One should not sit on a broken couch; one should not enter through anything other than the door; likewise, one who has not been initiated should not sleep upon a black antelope skin. Baudhāyana [2.4.24]: [The same].
Neither by one habituated to sleeping during the day, nor by one who eats all kinds of food,
nor by one who has fallen from a high position, can it be possible to go to the sky at will.
Āpastamba [1.32.6]:
"One should always adorn oneself for one's wife at night.

He should approach his wife during her fertile period, always remaining devoted to his own wife; observing that vow, he may approach her out of a desire for pleasure, except on the forbidden lunar days.
The natural menstrual period of women is traditionally said to consist of sixteen nights,
together with four other days that are censured by the virtuous.
Of these, the first four nights, as well as the eleventh and the thirteenth, are censured; the remaining ten nights are recommended.
Sons are born from women on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during her season on an even night.
A male is produced when the male seed is in excess; a female when the female seed is in excess.
When they are equal, a neuter is born, or sometimes both male and female; when they are diminished or scanty, the opposite occurs.
He should avoid women on the other eight censured nights;
for wherever he may dwell within the stages of life, he remains a celibate student.

“*Ṛtuḥ*” (the season) is the state of women fit for conception; the time characterized by that is “*ṛtukālaḥ*” (the period of the season). One whose vow (*vrata*) is to approach [his wife] only during that is “*ṛtukālābhigāmī*” (one who approaches during the period of the season). The suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of a vow (*vrate*). Regarding “*parvavarjam*” (except on sacred days), this applies both during the season and outside of it. “*Tadvrataḥ*” means one whose vow is to engage in sexual intercourse solely out of a desire for pleasure with his wife. And this engagement is for the sake of protecting her when she has desire. By the mention of the natural [state], it is indicated that otherwise may also occur due to disease and so forth.
