The three nights beginning with the eleventh are reckoned here with respect to the commencement of the season, not with respect to the lunar date (*tithi*). “*Ayugmāsu*” means on uneven nights, such as the fifth and so forth. “*Saṃviśet*” means he should approach. “*Same*” means when the semen (*śukra*) of the woman and the man is equal. “*Apumān*” means a eunuch (*napuṃsaka*). According to the statement of Devala: “One should know that a eunuch is born where the two exist simultaneously. “*Puṃstriyau vā*” means that when [the semen] is divided into two parts equally, a pair consisting of a woman and a man is born. “*Kṣīṇe*” means devoid of essence. “*Alpe*” means small in quantity. “*Viparyayaḥ*” here means the non-production of an embryo. “*Nindyāsu*” refers to six nights: the first four, the eleventh, and the thirteenth. “*Aṣṭāsu cānyāsu*” means that even among other nights that are not censurable, he should avoid certain ones. By approaching women only during two nights, he “becomes a celibate (*brahmacārī*) indeed,” meaning he obtains the fruit of celibacy. “*Yatra tatrāśrame*” means even while being a householder.
Yama says: "The menstrual period lasts sixteen days; eight nights are censured.
Among those, however, the first four, as well as the seventh and the eleventh [nights], are forbidden."
On the thirteenth, fifteenth, ninth, and likewise the fifth lunar days—
on these even days sons are born, while on the odd days daughters are born.
Where both exist simultaneously, one should know that there is a neuter;
where the male is diminished, there a female is born.
For where the male is predominant, a male child is born there;
however, if at the time of union the man is deluded by passion, [a female child is born].
If one emits semen in two ways, twins are born there;
due to an imbalance of semen and blood, one is born blackish-brown.

Thus, sons so produced die with their life-span unfulfilled. “Vartete” means they proceed. This is an indicative mark of the deficiency of semen (*śukra*). “Hīyate” means [the woman] is deficient in semen. “Adhikaḥ” also refers to semen alone. “Vaiṣamyam” means a disorder or abnormality. By the term “kṛṣṇapiṅgala,” there is an indication of complexion. “Evam utpāditāḥ” means those produced from a conception resulting from intercourse on an irreproachable night. “Agatāyuṣaḥ” means those whose life-span is not complete. Yājñavalkya [1.79–81]:
The sixteen nights of women constitute the seasons; among these, he should approach his wife on the even nights.
He should remain as one practicing celibacy, avoiding the sacred festival days (parvan) and the first four nights.
Proceeding in this manner, a man should avoid a woman who is emaciated, as well as the asterisms Maghā and Mūla;
when the moon is in a favorable state, he shall once beget a son endowed with auspicious marks.
Or he may act according to his desire, mindful of the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife, for it is traditionally taught that women must be protected.

“Parvans” refers to the full moon, the new moon, the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, and the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*). “*Kṣāmā*” means one who has little strength. If this lack of strength does not arise from the observances (*vrata*) during her menstrual period, then it must be remedied by repetition [of practice], light food, and so forth. “When the moon is well-situated” means when the moon is strong; the mention of the moon is intended to indicate other auspicious planets as well. “Once” means one should go once in a single night, not twice—this is the meaning. “*Lakṣaṇya*” means endowed with auspicious characteristics. Thus says Hārīta.

On the fourth day, when she has bathed during the even nights, he—endowed with the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*—places the *brahmagarbha* within her. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "On the night of the fourth day, a wise man should approach her once she has bathed."

And by this statement, the intended meaning is that the prohibition found in the *Mānava* tradition—"the first four [of those nights]"—and the prohibition in the *Paiṭhīnasi* tradition—"one should not call [her] on the fourth [night]," are for the purpose of avoiding defects such as short lifespan in the offspring. This is because of the *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra* statement: "From the fourth night until the sixteenth, each subsequent one is for the sake of the excellence of progeny. Devala says:
"For a Brāhmaṇī woman, the retention of the menstrual flow as declared in the Vedas should last for twelve days."
For the remaining [faculties], ten, eight, and six are prescribed respectively in order.
Even among these, having first avoided her during the three days of menstruation,
they should approach their wife when she is pure and has bathed for the sake of obtaining a son.

However, this statement regarding Brāhmaṇas and others observing the *ṛtu* for twelve days and so forth intends to refer to the period of approachability (*gamyatva*), not to the actual time of the menstrual cycle (*ṛtukāla*), because it contradicts the statement of Manu: "The natural *ṛtu* of women is recorded as sixteen nights. [The term] "pure" (*śuddhām*) refers to purity in terms of time.
Bṛhaspati [Saṃhitā 30.34–35; 33.33]:
One should engage in intercourse during the fertile period, avoiding the forbidden lunar days (parvan).
If the woman’s *śukra* is in excess, she will give birth to a girl; if the man’s is in excess, a boy will be born.
Therefore, for the sake of increasing semen, one should consume aphrodisiacs and unctuous foods;
one should cause the woman to take light food; in this way, one shall procreate a son.
[343] A man should diligently approach his wife during her fertile period, or he may do so at any time except on forbidden days; for that is indeed what women desire.
Gautama [5.1–2]:
He should approach his wife during her season; or he may do so at all times, except for those occasions that are prohibited.
Devala: [as above].
From a man’s failure to visit sacred fords and from a woman’s concealment of such fords, there shall be a loss of dharma for both; this is especially so when it is done out of malice.
If the sacred sites are simultaneous, however, he should proceed according to the order of marriage;
or, for the sake of protection, he may follow the order of the unmarried women, or even the order of their formal acceptance.

“Tīrtha” means the fertile period (ṛtu). “Saṃgūhana” means concealment. Regarding the phrase “one who has no son”: among other wives who already have sons, even if their fertile periods coincide, he should approach her first. “In the order of taking” means according to the sequence of taking the fertile periods.

During the fertile period (*ṛtu*), when there is union with his wife in accordance with her vow, even during the intervening periods, he should approach his wife alone. And according to the word of the Brāhmaṇas, there should be sexual intercourse. The union should take place while she is still wearing her woman's garment. They should lie together until the union is complete; thereafter, they should separate. There is the touching of water for purification. Or else, having washed off the stains and sipped water (*ācamana*), there should be a sprinkling of the limbs.

“Conjunction” (*saṃnipāta*) means union. “In accordance with the vow” (*anuvratam*) means following the vow consisting of the avoidance of the sacred festival days (*parvan*) and so forth. “In the interval” (*antarāle*) means during the non-season (*anṛtu*). Here, “Brāhmaṇa” refers to a portion of the Veda; for instance, in the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā], it says, “We choose a boon,” and so on. “Separately” (*nānā*) means they should sleep apart. “Touching water” (*udakopasparśanam*) means bathing. This applies during the season (*ṛtu*). During the non-season (*anṛtu*), however, there is “sprinkling” (*prokṣaṇa*). For Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: “But because of the suspicion of pregnancy during the season, bathing alone is prescribed.
During the non-season, however, purification must always be performed as in the case of urine and feces.”
Āpastamba [1.32.2]:
Having engaged in sexual union, he should not sleep with her for the entire night.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
These two, husband and wife, would both be impure when they have gone to bed;
once the woman has risen from the bed, she becomes pure, while the man remains impure.
“Purity” exists even apart from bathing and sprinkling. Gautama [9.26]: “One should not delay regarding purification after having engaged in sexual intercourse.”
Parāśara [4.15]:
"He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him goes to a terrible hell; likewise, he is called a 'slayer of a Brahmin'."
Yama says:
He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is cooked in the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
But he who does not approach his wife when she is in her season and in his presence—
his ancestors lie for that entire month upon that very semen.
Devala says:

He who, being in good health, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses, incurs the sin of killing an embryo (bhrūṇahatyā) once a fetus has been conceived; he destroys that very fetus.
“Susthaḥ” means free from disease and other ailments. Baudhāyana [4.1.19, 21]:
He who does not approach his wife when she is in her season for three years...
He undoubtedly incurs a fault equal to that of killing a Brahmin.

They say that the fault of one who does not approach his wife during her season and of one who approaches her outside her season is equal, as is the fault of one who discharges seed in a place other than the womb.
Even if he is impassioned, he should not approach a woman during her menstrual period;
nor should he sleep with her on the same bed.
For when a man approaches a woman overwhelmed by her menses,
his wisdom, splendor, strength, sight, and even his lifespan diminish.
For one who releases her when she is covered with dust,
wisdom, fortune, fame, vision, and lifespan indeed increase.
[347] Devala says: If one should approach her for sexual intercourse on impure days,
that man’s lifespan, wisdom, and merit will perish.
Therefore, for three nights one should avoid a Caṇḍālī woman who has reached her menses;
and one should constantly observe her by means of [placing] road-dust and ashes [upon her].

“One should observe” means one should guard [the mind]. Regarding the phrase “by resorting to the dust of the road,” the third case ending is used in connection with the word *utsuka* (eager/attached), which is supplied from the context; thus, the meaning is that one should ward off eagerness for those things.
Vasiṣṭha [12.5–7]: One should not lie down with one who is wearing soiled clothes, nor with a woman in her menses, nor with an unsuitable woman.
“Unfit” means one who has not yet reached puberty.
Gautama [9.29–32]: One should not take pleasure with a woman who is unwell, nor with one who is menstruating, nor should one embrace her, nor a maiden.

“*Akalyām*” means one who is diseased. “*Na kanyāṃ śliṣyet*” means he should not take pleasure with her; this is the meaning. [348] Regarding the period following a *śrāddha*, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: “One should avoid a woman who has bathed after her menses for that day and night. One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the menstrual period. One should not go to her for intercourse by day. Eunuchs and those of little virility are born from intercourse by day, as are those of short lifespan. Therefore, one who desires offspring should avoid this. He should not here cut off the lineage of the ancestors. By failing to maintain it through self-restraint, one falls into a state of instability. Therefore, one who desires stability should establish himself through progeny.”

“Tantu” means continuity (*saṃtāna*). “For non-interruption” means for the non-interruption of that continuity. “Yena” means because of which. By the word “no,” there is a negation. Being “without support” (*apratiṣṭhaḥ*), meaning not having attained a foundation due to the non-production of progeny, one “falls. Therefore, one must strive for the sake of production. Viṣṇu [69.1–17].

One should not approach a woman on the eighth or fourteenth days of the lunar fortnight; nor after eating at a *śrāddha* feast; nor after having given a gift at one; nor when invited to a *śrāddha*; nor while observing a vow; nor while initiated for a sacrifice; nor in a temple; nor in cremation grounds, empty houses, or at the roots of trees; nor during the day; nor during the two twilights; nor one who is unclean; nor one who has anointed herself with oil; nor one who has anointed oneself; nor one afflicted by disease; nor one who is afflicted by disease;
nor one with missing limbs, nor one with extra limbs, nor likewise one who is advanced in age.
One who desires to live a long life should not approach a pregnant woman.

“Dīkṣitaḥ” means one who possesses the consecration known as *dīkṣā*, until the *avabhṛtha* (concluding) sacrifice, because at that point the *dīkṣā* is released. “Rogārtām” means afflicted by disease; the disease intended here is either one produced by sexual intercourse with a woman or a man, or one aggravated thereby. “Vayodhikā” here refers to one whose menses have ceased. Manu [4.128]:
[One should avoid sex on] the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth.
A twice-born man who has completed his studies should always remain a celibate student, even during the fertile period of his wife.
Vasiṣṭha [12.21–24]:
He should approach his own wife during her fertile period, avoiding the forbidden days (*parvan*). He should not approach her at an improper place (*atīrtha*);
here, "place" (*tīrtha*) refers to the vulva.
Moreover, they cite this example:
"But he who performs sexual intercourse in the mouth of his wedded wife—
for that month her ancestors subsist upon his semen."
That pleasure which exists without transgression is based on the Dharma.

"Without transgression" means without overstepping the [proper] source. Furthermore, it is known from the *Kāṭaka* scripture: "May our daughters, when they give birth tomorrow, have bodies [united] with their husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra.
Baudhāyana: "But for him who engages in sexual intercourse by entering the mouth of his wedded wife, there is no atonement here in this world; thus spoke Prajāpati."

Paiṭhīnasi says: One should sow [the seed] with an odd number [of nights]; a female is born [then], while with an even number a male comes into being. One should invite [the husband] for sexual intercourse in a secluded place. Not on the first night; not on the second; not on the third; one should not invite him on the fourth.
Now, the rules regarding a woman in her courses (*rajasvalā*).

Regarding this, Hārīta states: "If she has reached her menses (*rajas*), she should sleep on the ground; she should not perform rites for the gods (*devakārya*). She should eat from the ground, from a vessel of black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*), or from an earthenware vessel. "Having reached her menses" means one who has experienced menstruation. "On the ground" means upon the earth. Since her very state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) already establishes the prohibition against performing rites for the gods directly, the explicit statement "she should not perform rites for the gods" is intended to mean that she should not even look at the food, nor look at the substances, flowers, offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth used therein. "Black iron" (*kārṣṇāyasa*)... [text continues]
An iron vessel. Vasiṣṭha [5.6–10].

For three nights a woman in her courses is impure. She should not apply collyrium; she should not anoint herself; she should not bathe in water; she should sleep on the ground; she should not sleep during the day; she should not touch fire; she should not let go of a rope; she should not clean her teeth; she should not eat meat; she should not look at the planets; she should not laugh; she should not perform any [mundane] action; she should not drink from the hollow of her joined palms; she should not drink from a broken vessel, nor from one made of iron. For it is known: After Indra had slain Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son, he was seized by evil and thought of himself thus: "I am bound by great unrighteousness. All beings reviled him, crying out, "O slayer of the embryo! He fled to women, saying, "May you accept a third part of this murder of an embryo for me. They asked, "What will accrue to us? He said, "Choose a boon. They said, "May we obtain offspring in season, and may we unite according to our desire until the time of birth. "So be it," they agreed, and they accepted it. This very Brahman-murder manifests itself month after month. Therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman in her courses, for she stands there having assumed the form of the murder of an embryo. Regarding this, they say: "She must not be given even collyrium or ointment, for that is the food of a woman. Therefore, people do not feel disgust toward her food, thinking, "Lest she should come to me as sacrificial food."
Those who cohabit with a menstruating woman, those who maintain no sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.

“*Grahān*” refers to the planets, beginning with the Sun (*āditya*). “*Kiṃcit*” means even something as small as the plastering of a house and so forth. “*Kharvaḥ*” is the left hand. “*Lohitāyasena*” means by means of a copper vessel. “*Pāpmagṛhītam amanyata*” means he formed the thought, “I am seized by sin. Regarding “*ā vijanitoḥ saṃbhavāma*,” the meaning is: “from birth (*vijanana*) until procreation (*prasava*), we *saṃbhavāma*—that is, we engage in sexual union (*mithunībhavāma*). In the term “*ā vijanitoḥ*,” the suffix *tosun* is used according to the rule beginning with “*bhāvalakṣaṇa*. “*Pratimucya*” means having bound or fastened. “*Añjanam abhyañjanaṃ ca*”: “*Añjana*” here signifies sexual intercourse due to the similarity of its characteristics to an unguent (*snehadravya*); “*Abhyañjana*” here refers to embracing, because that action occurs directed toward the *añjana*. This is in accordance with the statement of Gautama: “*Na caināṃ śliṣyet*. “*Aśnīyāt*” means one should consume or enjoy. Here, “*Bhrūṇahatyā*” refers to the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). Since for her, the very act of *añjana* and *abhyañjana* constitutes food, therefore people do not feel disgust (*bībhatsante*) or censure her for food in the form of rice and other such items. If she were impure merely through *añjana* and *abhyañjana*, then she would be pure during the performance of sacrifice; thus he says, “*Maivaṃ medham upāgāt*. “*Medhaḥ*” means sacrifice. The meaning is: “Being of such a nature, she should not go to the sacrifice. “*Anvāsate*” means she performs attendance or service.
Paiṭhīnasi says:

Now, one should avoid a woman during her menses. Indra struck down Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, with his thunderbolt; the gods called him a "feticide" (*bhrūṇahan*). He ran to the women, saying: "Accept a third part of this feticide of mine; I will grant you a boon. Thereupon, the women took a third part of that [sin] of Brahman-murder. Likewise, the earth and the trees each took a third. Being pleased, he granted them boons: stability for the earth, the regrowth of trees after being cut, and sexual enjoyment for women at all times. Therefore, one should not approach a woman during her menses. When she has bathed after four nights, one may have her perform all ritual acts, even though she was affected by Brahman-murder.
“*Sarvakarmāṇi*” refers to all rites other than those for the gods and the ancestors. Furthermore, Paiṭhīnasi says:

For three nights, she who wears soiled garments shall not bathe; she shall not anoint herself; she shall not cut her nails; she shall not cleanse herself; she shall not touch a rope; she shall not brush her teeth; she shall not wear a garland; she shall not use perfumes; she shall not comb her hair; she shall not drink from a broken vessel; she shall not drink from leaves; she shall not drink from her cupped hands; she shall not drink from a cow-trough; nor shall she drink water like cows. Regarding this, the Taittirīya Śruti states: "He who approaches a woman with soiled garments is born as one accused of a crime; he who approaches her in the forest is born as a thief; he who approaches her while she is facing away is born as one with a dejected face and is impudent; she who bathes gives birth to a child afflicted by water-demons (*apsu-māruka*); she who anoints herself gives birth to one with skin disease; she who scrapes herself gives birth to one who is bald or suffers from skin eruptions; she who applies collyrium gives birth to one who is one-eyed; she who brushes her teeth gives birth to one with blackened teeth; she who cuts her nails gives birth to one with deformed nails; she who spins thread gives birth to a eunuch; she who weaves a rope gives birth to one destined to hang himself; she who drinks from a leaf-cup gives birth to one prone to madness; she who drinks from a broken vessel gives birth to one who is deformed. Therefore, for three nights she should observe a vow, or she may drink from her cupped hands or from a non-broken vessel, for the protection of her offspring."

Thus ends the section on the duties of day and night within the *Niyatakālakāṇḍa* (Section on Fixed Times) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*).
Now, the duties on the festival days (parva).
In this regard, Manu [4.150] states:
"One should always perform the Sāvitra and Śānti oblations on the Parvan days;
one should also constantly worship the ancestors on the Aṣṭakās and the Anvaṣṭakās."

“Sāvitrāḥ” means those having Savitṛ as their deity. And these should be performed with *gāyatrī* [mantras] and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), according to the statement of Śaṅkha: “One desiring peace (*śānti*) should offer oblations with *gāyatrī* and unbroken rice grains while pure. Peace (*śānti*) is the cessation of undesirable worldly effects through the medium of *dharma*. “On the *parvan* days,” i.e., on the fourteenth day and so forth. From the inclusion of the word “regularly” (*nitya*), it is understood that this must necessarily be performed on the *parvan* days.

Viṣṇu [71.86–89]: On the festival days (parvan), he should perform propitiatory fire-offerings (śāntihoma). He should not cut even a blade of grass. He should remain adorned. Thus should he be one who practices right conduct. "He should cut" means he should harm.

Āpastamba [1.31.21–22]: By day the sun protects living beings; by night, the moon. Therefore, on the night of the new moon (amāvāsyā), one should especially desire protection for oneself through purity, celibacy, and conduct appropriate for the time; for on that night the sun and the moon dwell together.

“*Svādhīyaḥ*” means more intensely. “*Guptiḥ*” means protection. “*Prāyatyena*” means by the thorough accomplishment of purification and ritual sipping (*ācamana*), including the avoidance of approaching public roads and other acts that cause a loss of purity. Likewise with “*brahmacaryeṇa*” (celibacy). “*Kālecaryayā*” means by performing those duties at the primary times, such as the morning and so forth.
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
“Sleeping on the ground is prescribed for the full moon and the new moon days.”
Even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, this [rite] is prescribed after the fire.
"One who has not established the sacred fires" (*anāhitāgni*) here refers to one who maintains the *smārta* (domestic) fires.

Baudhāyana [1.21.19–21] states: "On the *parvan* days, he should not study; he should not eat meat; he should not approach a woman. For on the *parvan* days, *rakṣas* and *piśāca* demons become prone to transgression."

[356] Paiṭhīnasi: On the festival days (parvan), one should not use oil, a razor, engage in sexual intercourse, or eat meat. One should not cut green plants on the new moon day (amāvāsyā). "One should engage in" means one should consume.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa [2.12.10]: "He who cuts down plants when the sun is situated among the constellations of the plants, or causes even a single leaf to fall, incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin."
“*Vīrutsaṃsthe*” means situated upon a tree. Yama says:
“An oil massage on the head on the fourteenth day destroys one’s family up to the seventh generation.”
Regarding the eating of meat, the fifteenth day is [prohibited] for the dharma of desire, and likewise the eighth day.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
Using a tooth-stick on the new moon day, sexual intercourse on the fourteenth day,
and taking oil on the eighth day destroys one’s family for seven generations.
On the sixth, eighth, fifteenth, and fourteenth days of both fortnights—
sin is present here in oil, meat, the razor, and the female organ.
Oil applied on the sixth day shortens one's lifespan; likewise, meat on the eighth day [is forbidden];
shaving on the fourteenth day, as well as sexual intercourse on the lunar festival days (parvan), [should be avoided].

Since the general prohibition of all oils and such on all festival days (parvan) and on the sixth lunar day is already established, the specific prohibition of particular items like oil in connection with specific lunar days is intended to indicate a particular degree of fault. Devala says:
"On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, and the eighth [lunar day], the wise man..."
One should completely avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and the razor.

In this context, because words such as "the sixth" (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth—which denote lunar days (*tithi*)—express a specific portion of time delimited by the motion of the moon, the prohibition of meat and other items applies only for the duration of the time of that specific lunar day, such as the sixth, and not for the entire twenty-four-hour period (*ahorātra*) by way of implication (*upalakṣaṇa*). This is because there is no evidence for taking them in an implied sense. For this very reason, since rites for the gods and ancestors are prescribed for the forenoon and afternoon respectively, one must respect the lunar day that pervades those times.
As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* (3.11.118–120):
The fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, and the full moon— these, O King of kings, as well as the sun’s transit into a new zodiac sign, are the sacred festival days (parvan).
O King, a man who indulges in oil, women, and meat on these specific festival days goes to the hell known as Viṇmūtrabhojana (the Eating of Excrement and Urine).
Therefore, on all these festival days, men who practice self-restraint should always be devoted to the study of true scriptures, the worship of the gods, meditation, and silent recitation.
In the Varāha Purāṇa,
among the oaths of the Cāṇḍālas:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon, both fourteenth days of the fortnights..."
I shall go the way of those who do not bathe, if I do not return again.
In the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
"If one touches oil on the seventh lunar day, a beloved wife perishes.
In the *Vāmanapurāṇa*: [The same].
One should perform an oil massage on the Nandā days, a haircut on the Riktā days, eat meat on the Jayā days,
and avoid sexual intercourse on the Pūrṇā days.
One should perform all [rites] during auspicious [periods].
One should not perform an oil massage on Sunday nor a haircut on Saturday; one should avoid meat on Friday and Tuesday, and one should not have sexual intercourse with a woman on Wednesday.
In all remaining cases, one should always perform all [the rites].
Oil and shaving should be avoided during Citrā, Hasta, Śravaṇa, Viśākhā, and the first lunar day (pratipad); likewise,
meat should be avoided during Mūla, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and the Bhādrapadas.
A woman [should be sought] under the asterisms Maghā, Kṛttikā, and the Uttarās.
In the Varāha Purāṇa, concerning the Vaiṣṇava [observances], Varāha said:
"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the fourteenth day of both fortnights..."
One should never indulge in sexual intercourse, especially on the twelfth day, which is dear to me.
He who engages in sexual intercourse on the eighth, the fourteenth, the sixth, as well as the twelfth, the new moon day, or the fourth [lunar day], [incurs a fault].
"He goes to the womb of an animal and does not go to my world.
Manu [4.128]: "The new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth..."
A twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies should always remain a celibate student, even during the fertile period of his wife.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Or, if one is not always capable of abstaining from meat,
a man whose mind is set on heaven should avoid it during the primary solstice."
The fourth, the eighth, the twelfth, the fourteenth,
as well as the fifteenth, and the six *aśītimukha* days should be avoided.
Or likewise, on the transit of the sun or on the two equinoxes of the rainy season,
one who constantly abstains from meat goes to heaven for three days.
Alternatively, a man should abstain from eating meat during the month of Āśvayuja;
by doing so, he obtains the merit of having practiced it for six months.
By renouncing the consumption of meat, a person becomes pure-minded;
that man who avoids meat during the month of Kārttika obtains the merit of abstaining from meat for an entire year.
Now follows the determination of the transits (saṃkrānti).
Regarding this, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"Twelve equal transits are declared."
That too should be understood as sevenfold; listen to how each one is so.
O King, the sevenfold transition (saṃkrānti) is said to be mixed with Rākṣasī: Mandā, Mandākinī, Dhvāṅkṣī, Ghorā, Mahodarī, and [the others].

One should know that when the planets are in fixed signs, the result is slow; likewise, in a mutable sign, it is slow-moving. One should recognize it as cawing (dhvāṅkṣī) through swift signs, and it is proclaimed as terrible (ghorā) through fierce ones.
Mahodarī is to be known by [the presence of] movable signs, while Rākṣasī is [known] by the cruel asterisms;
and when the transition occurs through mixed asterisms, it is designated as Miśritā.
Three, four, five, seven, eight, nine, and twelve ghaṭikās respectively— this indeed is their ultimate merit.
The past and future experiences consist of fifteen channels;
indeed, the presence of the planets occurs there during the transit of the sun.
Worldly convention is characterized by the moon and the sun;
when time decays, everything from Brahmā downwards, including all that is moving and unmoving, falls into ruin.
The Goddess bestows the fruit according to the distinction between merit and demerit;
even that which is performed but once becomes multiplied by millions upon millions of times.
For from righteousness (dharma) one’s lifespan increases, as do sovereignty, sons, happiness, and so forth;
whereas from unrighteousness (adharma) arise disease, grief, and the like, especially during the equinoxes and solstices.
Whatever is chanted or given during the equinoxes becomes inexhaustible;
likewise, so it is at Viṣṇupada and at the beginnings of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods.

“*Kalpanāḥ*” means divisions (*bhedāḥ*). “*Samāḥ*” means equal. They are equal insofar as they consist merely of transits (*saṃkrāntimātra*) and thus produce results that are merely desirable or undesirable; however, the specific distinctions to be mentioned later consist in their particular forms, such as the solstices (*ayanādi*). Although there may occasionally be thirteen months due to an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), nevertheless there are twelve transits and not thirteen—this is indicated by the particle *eva*. “*Dhruvāṇi*” (fixed) refers to the three Uttaras and Rohiṇī. “*Mṛdūni*” (soft) refers to Anurādhā, Citrā, Revatī, and Mṛgaśīrṣa. “*Kṣiprāḥ*” (swift) refers to the light [nakṣatras]: Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya. “*Ugrāḥ*” (fierce) refers to the three Pūrvās, Bharaṇī, and Maghā. “*Carāḥ*” (movable) refers to Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Svātī, and Śatabhiṣā. “*Krūrāḥ*” (cruel) means sharp; they are Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, and Ārdrā. “*Miśrā*” (mixed) refers to Kṛttikā and Viśākhā. “*Krameṇa*” means according to their respective order. “*Pāramārthikaṃ*” means the primary fruit. The meaning is that the merit (*puṇya*) arising from the performance of rites such as the *vasordhārā* at the time of the subtle transit (*sūkṣmasaṃkrānti*) exists even during these *nāḍikās* (periods). “*Tāḥ*” refers to the *ghaṭikās* (units of time). Because they are the cause of merit, they are called “*puṇyam*. “*Bhogaḥ*” means pervasion. The point is that in the proximity of the time of the subtle transit, there is the state of being most meritorious (*puṇyatamatva*). The words beginning with “*sāṃnidhyam*” are a praise of that very time.
Śātātapa says:
Sixteen nāḍīs before and sixteen after [the moment of transition]—
this time during the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti) is proclaimed by the learned to be meritorious.
Thus he states the sanctity of the sixteen nāḍīs on both sides.
Likewise, Jābāli also says:
"The meritorious time for the transit [of the sun] consists of sixteen kalās on both sides."

And from the observation of this statement, it should be understood that the movement through the fifteen *nāḍīs* occurs from both sides as well. "Vikalate" means she falls away from her own nature. "Devī" refers to Durgā; [this is stated] in the *Devīpurāṇa* itself at the commencement of the *saṃkrānti*:

"O All-pervading One, the Goddess is omnipresent, according to the sequence of year, solstice (*ayana*), season (*ṛtu*), month, fortnight (*pakṣa*), day, and so forth, through the division of gross and subtle."
Because of this statement: "In proximity" means at the time of enjoyment. The nature of the *viṣṇupadī* and the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* is described in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* as follows:
"The *ṣaḍaśītis* occur in Sagittarius, Gemini, Virgo, and Pisces;
the *viṣṇupadī* is traditionally taught to occur in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo."
[Furthermore, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Listen as I declare the distinction regarding the solstices:
whatever merit is gained when twenty *kalās* have been traversed, that belongs to the northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*)."
When the sun is seen without its disk at the end of the day during the southern solstice,
and when midnight has not yet fully arrived, the merit of the day has not yet come.
Whether at the completion of midnight, or at sunrise or sunset, or when the sun has reached half its course during the night—
even if the portion of the night is not yet full— therein lies the merit of half a measure.
When both [the periods] are complete, the gift should be given; if there is an excess, it should be given on the following day;
or when the six-aśīti-mukha has passed, or when either of the two equinoxes (viṣuvad) has occurred.
Merit shall accrue during the northern course and even after it has passed;
one should know that merit exists at the beginning as well, provided the lunar day remains unbroken.
When midnight has passed, it should be understood that [the rite] belongs to the following day.

“Twenty *kalās*”: merit lasts for as long as the twentieth *kalā* remains after the moment of the transit (*saṃkrānti*). “In the partless” (*niraṃśe*): meaning devoid of parts; for at the time of transit, the sun is indeed devoid of its parts (*aṃśaka*). According to the astronomers, a “day” consists of thirty *nāḍikās* as refined by solar corrections; “at its end” means merit [is gained]. “Daytime merit is yet to come”: the meaning is that since the merit of the transit occurs during the day, the rites for the transit must be performed during the daytime portion, even before the actual moment of transit. “When midnight is complete”: from the beginning of sunrise until the end of sunset. “Half the measure is meritorious”: “measure” (*māna*) refers to the length of the day; “half of that” refers to the time indicated by the sun. “A portion” (*dalam*) means half. Here too, the phrase “half the measure” is to be supplied. When the transit occurs at “complete midnight,” the “half of the measure” of both the preceding and following days is to be “given,” meaning added [to the merit]. “If there is an excess, on the next day”: here too, the phrase “half the measure is to be given” is to be supplied. “When it has passed” (*vṛtte*) means when it is over. Thus, even among the twelve solar transits occurring at night, if the transit occurs before midnight, the latter half of the preceding day is meritorious. But if it is at complete midnight, the latter half of the preceding day and the first half of the following day are meritorious. However, if it is after midnight, only the first half of the following day is meritorious. As for the passage beginning “when the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* has passed,” etc., this refers specifically to transits during the day by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*). The fact that fifteen or sixteen *nāḍīs* on either side are meritorious also refers only to the *Viṣṇupadī* (the equinox) occurring during the day, by process of elimination. Regarding “at the beginning,” etc.: “at the beginning” means on the very preceding day. “Unbroken” (*abhinnā*): meaning that on the preceding day and at the time of transit, it is one and the same. By this, the statement regarding merit on both sides when the transit occurs at midnight applies to cases where the lunar date (*tithi*) is different. The essential meaning is: “But when midnight has passed,” even if the lunar date is not broken by the preceding day, the first half belongs to the following day alone.
Likewise:
*Mandā* is praised among the Brahmins; *Mandākinī* is also [praised] among kings;
*Dhvāṅkṣī* is to be known [as auspicious] among Vaiśyas; and *Ghorā* bestows good fortune upon Śūdras.
Mahodarī brings victory to thieves and vintners,
as well as to Cāṇḍālas, Pulkasas, and others who perform cruel deeds.
When mixed with all the products of artisans, it increases prosperity;
kings are afflicted during the forenoon, but the best of the twice-born during midday.
Likewise, Vaiśyas [take possession] in the afternoon, Śūdras at sunset,
Piśācas at dusk, and Rākṣasas at midnight.
When midnight has passed, actors and dancers are afflicted;
at the time of dawn during the transit [of the sun], it kills the people belonging to the masters of cattle.
At the time of twilight, however, the transit [of the sun] destroys all those who have gone forth [into the religious life].
This has been proclaimed as the coarse division for one desiring worldly enjoyment.
O best of kings, I shall tell you the number according to the ultimate truth:
it is as long as the eye of a man, sitting comfortably and at ease, blinks.
The thirtieth part of that is proclaimed as a *tatpara*;
a hundredth part of a *tatpara* is designated as a *truṭi*.
The time it takes for the sun to cross [one degree] is one-thousandth part of a *truṭi*;
at that moment, the three worlds, including all moving and stationary beings, become liquefied.
In the case of a *vyatīpāta* [yoga], it would likewise be so, and the merit would be even greater than that;
regarding this, even Brahmā, O best of gods, spoke with uncertainty.
One obtains the distinguished merit of giving, study, recitation, and so forth, through the *vasordhārā* fire-oblations; otherwise, it can never be attained in any way.
Śātātapa says:
At the beginning of the solstices, whatever desirable wealth is in the house should always be given away;
likewise at the commencement of the Ṣaḍaśīti periods, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Sixteen nāḍīs before and sixteen after [the sun's transit] are to be known;
this time of the sun's transit has been proclaimed as meritorious by the learned.
Whatever offerings to gods and ancestors are to be given by performers at the time of the sun's transit,
the Sun-god bestows those constantly, birth after birth.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "When the sun has reached the balance at the day of the equinox,
grains and desired objects should be given to the Brahmins."
During the three transits beginning with Aries, the sun is in its northern course;
at that time, all the gods, including Indra, go to the world of Brahmā.
Therefore, for three months, their images made of stone should be covered with ghee and cloth, and likewise protected at all times.
They should always be accepted with flowers, garments, and with desire;
they should be worshipped every day, as well as the Brahmins, with offerings of food.
Likewise, cows should be satiated with grass, salt, and water;
and the fire should be constantly kindled, for it increases the bodily fire of men.
"Meṣa" here refers to Capricorn (makara). "Born of stone" means fashioned from rock. Likewise:
when the sun is about to enter Meṣa (Aries), [one should offer] the winter garment of ghee.
Having extracted [the deity] from the body, worship should be performed for the gods with great effort.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "Gold, diamond, sapphire, ruby, and pearl—
these five jewels one should place upon the top of the liṅga."
And even in the absence of jewels, having fashioned a piece of gold weighing one karṣa or half a karṣa, one should perform it during that very same northern course of the sun.
And having worshipped him duly in that manner with abundant clarified butter from a cow,
one should wash him, rub him, and offer the "butter-blanket" (ghṛtakambala).
Having further given household utensils to the Brahmins along with the ascetics,
and having fed them and honored them with gifts, he should provide an unrestricted supply of provisions.
Having fasted, one should indeed perform all of this preceded by devotion;
having drunk the five products of the cow mixed with sesame seeds, one should personally complete the rite.
A wise person should perform his bath with sesame seeds and likewise use them for anointing the body;
he should also perform the libation for both the deities and the ancestors with those same seeds.
One should always perform the fire-oblation with those [materials], especially during the northern course of the sun;
one should indeed give them, together with gold, to the gods and to the Brahmins.
If a man, having fixed his mind upon Śambhu, acts in this way even once,
why should he grieve after reaching the northern solstice?

“Kuliśa” means diamond. “Having gratified” (dakṣayitvā) means having honored with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). “One should prepare” (kalpayet)—the word “food” (bhojana) is to be supplied as the object. “One should complete” (pārayet) means one should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa). No specific sequence between the sesame bath and the breaking of the fast is intended here. In the phrase “by both,” the dative case is used in the sense of purpose. [This is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
“When the sun enters its transit (saṃkrama) on the seventh day of the bright fortnight...”
Then indeed the seventh lunar day, beloved of the Sun, becomes Mahājayā.
Bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and the worship of ancestors and gods—
all these are declared by the highly effulgent Tapanas to be multiplied ten millionfold.
But that man who, with devotion, bathes the Sun in this [tirtha] with clarified butter,
shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and thereafter go to the city of the Sun.
The devoted man who bathes the Sun with milk,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the same world as the Sun.
By means of a variegated celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
he shall be like the sun in brilliance and equal to Atri in luster.
Having stayed there for a long time, one becomes King Kiñjaya;
this seventh [day], O Destroyer of Tripura, is called Mahājaya.
By fasting with devotion to this immovable goddess born from the lotus,
a man attains the Supreme Brahman, reaching which he no longer grieves.

Now follows the determination of the [auspicious] time for seizing [the offerings]. Regarding this, Jābāli says: "The meritorious time for the transit (saṃkrānti) consists of sixteen *kalās* on both sides."
And during an eclipse of the moon or sun, for as long as they remain within the range of vision.

Since the solar and lunar eclipses are established as the causal conditions (*nimitta*) for ritual acts, and since only that which is known can serve as a causal condition, it might follow that mere knowledge [of the eclipse] would suffice. However, because of the statements "as far as it is within the range of vision" and "the sight of Rāhu," it is established that only that which is the object of visual perception (*cākṣuṣajñāna*) functions as the causal condition. This is because the term "sight" (*darśana*) has its primary meaning in the context of visual perception. Consequently, one should not perform bathing or other rites when the sun or moon is obscured by clouds and the like. Likewise, on the following day, when the eclipsed body has set, the subsequent sight of its liberation must also be visual. Viṣṇu [68.1, 3]: [Text follows...]
One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or the sun. After they have been released and one has seen them set, one should bathe on the following day. Śātātapa says:
"When there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat for a full day and night."
Having seen the liberation [of the deity], one should eat after performing an ablution according to one's means.
A person goes to the imperishable worlds of the sun and the moon;
with sins washed away and the self purified, he rejoices there like a god.
At the solstices, at the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses,
one who has fasted for a day and night and bathed is liberated from all sins.

“Having fasted for a day and night” means having observed a fast on the preceding day. For the *Bhāulla-smṛti* states: “Eating [only once] during a day and night is for the sake of the fruit. Likewise:
One should not eat before a solar eclipse during the day, nor after a lunar eclipse in the evening;
one should not eat during the time of the eclipse, but should eat after bathing once both have been released.
One should eat when the moon has been released, provided it is not the dead of night;
however, on the following day, having bathed and made an offering, one may eat if both [the sun and the moon] have set while being eclipsed.
“Of the two released” refers to the sun and moon. “The great night” is the four *muhūrtas* following the first half-watch of the night. As stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
“Furthermore, one should not eat at that time when the moon and sun are eclipsed.”
And having performed the ablutions for the two released [images], he should afterwards perform [the rites] in his own house.
Regarding the word "should perform," the term "eating" is understood as being supplied by ellipsis.

During lunar and solar eclipses, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and on the festival days (parvan).

[372] [The beginnings and ends of the Yugas] are described in the Brahmapurāṇa.

out of anger, again cast off the Jāhnavī from his right ear-canal.
When the twenty-eighth Kali Yuga arrived, Viṣṇu worshipped that goddess Gaṅgā, who has the sky as her girdle.
Having become a Buddha, he shall turn the wheel of Dharma for the Śākyas whose dharma has perished;
there he shall be honored with flowers and other offerings for three days.
At all times, the bathing of the Buddha image should be performed with all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, and all jewels, using various auspicious substances as prescribed in the scriptures.
One should perform various meritorious works, such as building shrines and temples,
and one should honor the Śākyas and ascetics with robes, food, and books.
Gifts of flowers, clothing, and food should be given to the poor,
and a festival should be held for three days, filled with actors and dancers.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, black and white sesame seeds were created by the Creator for the satisfaction of all embodied beings.
Therefore, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds and offer sesame seeds into the fire there;
and one should duly present a vessel of sesame seeds to Viṣṇu.
Lamps should be offered to the gods with sesame oil,
and the libation for the ancestors should be performed with water together with sesame seeds.
A meal combined with sesame seeds and honey should be given to the Brahmins,
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should also be bestowed along with sesame seeds mixed with honey.
And one should recite the ancient mantra that has come down through the lineage of succession:
"Oṃ! Sesame seeds have Soma as their deity; they were created by the gods at the Gosava sacrifice."
"May those who bestow heaven and are independent protect me forever.
With this mantra, one should offer vessels of sesame seeds there.
Then, one should recite it to seven or five Brahmins, saying:
"May Dharmarāja be pleased, as well as the other gods."
When this has been done, he shall be liberated from the sins accumulated over hundreds of births.
He should recite the mantra: "May Dharmarāja be pleased. He should also recite for the other gods: "May Vāsudeva be pleased," and so forth. And thus says Viṣṇu [90.10]:
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, by satiating seven Brahmins with sesame seeds mixed with honey and thereby pleasing Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from sins. Thus it is said.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, Revatī is indeed black in color.
One should worship her with black flowers when she has appeared in the world;
for Umā Satī was born in the past on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Therefore, she should be worshipped there by women for the increase of their good fortune,
with various offerings and the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
In former times, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, the white goddess Mahāśanī was born through oblations of milk, garments, and fragrant kunda flowers.
Then, for the destruction of the lords of the Dānavas, one should worship during the bright fortnight;
indeed, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, Viśokā was formerly [worshipped] by Viṣṇu.
She is established with auspicious garlands; therefore, one should worship her there.
In ancient times, when the Vedas first appeared on earth, they were born from the Jyeṣṭhā [constellation].
Then one should diligently honor them there according to one's financial capacity,
having worshipped them along with the ancestors and the gods with offerings of fresh barley-rice.
Then Aṅgulipta, wearing a garland and adorned with new garments,
first fed the pure brahmins who had performed the rites for prosperity.
Free from hatred and passion, one should eat barley facing the east on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha, dedicated to Vināyaka in the cult of Gaṇapati.
There, together with his retinue, he was honored and worshipped with heaps of sweetmeats,
as well as with various foods, garlands, perfumes, and abundant boiled grain.
With very sweet songs and instrumental music, as well as by satisfying the Brahmins,
one should worship that Lord of Obstacles on all the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī days.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the sun named Vivasvān was born under the Pūrvā constellation; therefore, one should always worship him there after fasting.
The statement "one should always sacrifice" is likewise intended to convey that her worship must necessarily be performed.
In a beautiful mandala shaped like a chariot wheel, which grants all desires,
one should offer various kinds of foods to chew and eat, as well as drinks, flowers, incense, and ointments.
On the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, under the conjunction of Svātī, the mighty Vāyu was born;
he is likewise to be worshipped with perfumes, lamps, and the honoring of the twice-born.

With abundant supreme food (*paramānna*), with various groats (*saktu*), and likewise with various kinds of natural substances; with *paramānna* meaning milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and "various" meaning diverse types of raw materials; and with beautiful flowers and manifold blossoms, [he should worship] with faith.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the Blessed Lord Hari always lies upon his serpent-bed in the Ocean of Milk.
Then an image of her, endowed with all auspicious marks, should be fashioned from stone,
clay, or excellent wood, depicted as sleeping upon the couch of Śeṣa.
On plates of copper, brass, or silver, or likewise upon variegated cloth,
[one should depict] Lakṣmī with her feet placed upon her lap or in her hands.
She should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites with various kinds of offerings;
likewise, a fast should be observed and a vigil kept through the night.
When that night has passed, one should likewise perform worship on the twelfth day;
then, on the thirteenth day, one should offer dance, song, and instrumental music.
In a Vaiṣṇava temple, one should give wealth to the performers according to one's ability;
"performers" refers to actors and the like.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should then worship Hari on the full moon day.
Yama says:
Hari reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa in the Ocean of Milk on the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
he abandons sleep on the full moon of Kārtika. One should always worship Him during those two [periods].
He swiftly dispels even a sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin;
what need has that great-souled one for sacrifices characterized by violence?

And by whomsoever Keśava is worshipped both at the time of falling asleep and upon awakening—this [day] of Āṣāḍha is called "Āṣāḍhī," and this [day] of Kārtika is called "Kārtikī. Although the forms "Āṣāḍīyā" and "Kārtikīyā" would have been expected, because a general rule (utsarga) sometimes applies even to a domain where an exception (apavāda) is required, this [form] also falls under that scope. For example, although "śvadaṃṣṭrīya" would have been expected, we have the form "śvādaṃṣṭra" in the sense of "a gem from the dog's fang. And that [worship] is intended for the eleventh day;
specifically, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārtika, one should worship Keśava.
Endowed with faith and devotion, one should awaken [the deity] while it is asleep during the night.
Thus, from the statement in the *Brahma Purāṇa*. In the *Varāha Purāṇa*,
the Blessed One said:
I shall tell you something else: an action for liberation from saṃsāra.
[It involves] the kadamba, the kuṭaja, the dhanaka, and likewise the arjunaka.
One should perform worship with these according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule;
thereafter, having performed the formal installation, the ritual procedure for my mantra is declared.
"Dhanaka" means "kapittha" (wood-apple), according to Vācaspati in the *Śabdārṇava*. "Saṃsthāpana" is the completion of the ritual action just described.
Having uttered "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," one should recite this mantra:
"Even the clouds behold Him who is dark as a cloud."
May the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, accept this earth as it is gradually being drenched;
may he accept this mass of clouds during the rains.
Having understood this yourself, O Lord of Gods, see for yourself; behold, O Lord, the four months of Vaikuṇṭha.
On the twelfth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, he who causes my ritual work to be performed according to this procedure shall obtain auspiciousness that brings all peace.
That man shall not perish during the dissolutions at the end of each age;
as stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa*: "When the month of Āṣāḍha has ended and the auspicious constellation Vaiśvadeva (Jyeṣṭhā) is present..."
There, one should worship those ten Viśvedevas of great power.

"At the end of Āṣāḍha" means on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha. "The Vaiśvadeva asterism" is Uttarāṣāḍhā. "The ten Viśvedevas" are Kratu, Dakṣa, and the others. But when the Lord of Fierce Rays enters Cancer, from that time onward the period shall be known as the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana).
[394] During the rainy season, they should always be worshipped with fruits, flowers, and water;
likewise, one should offer barley-meal mixed with cow's milk to the Brahmins.
Snow, sugar, vegetables, roots, and fruits;
shoes, an umbrella, garlands, and a water-cow, according to the scriptures.
"Himam" here refers to camphor.
On the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
Śaṅkara [struck him] with an arrow that had three joints, three points, and three tips.
"Śalya" means an iron spike.
He cut off the three heads of the sacrifice which had taken the form of a deer;
with those heads, they performed austerities and obtained boons from Śaṅkara.
"These [objects] are to be worshipped by women, and not by men under any circumstances.
Then, having fashioned a linga-shaped object out of clay, he placed it under the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa.
It should be bathed with milk and worshipped according to the prescribed rite, with water-offerings (argha),
flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings (naivedya).
With vegetables, *sauvarcala* salts, and auspicious foods made of flour;
*suvarcalā* is a specific medicinal herb.
And with vessels and musical instruments made of bell-metal, the meal should be served afterwards.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, during the conjunction with Rohiṇī, Kaśyapa was born as the Prajāpati;
he is to be honored there as the one who set the Devas in motion.
Cows, as well as women devoted to their husbands, should be honored with perfumes, garlands, food offerings, and likewise by the satiation of Brahmins.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, Hari, in his Hayagrīva form, first proclaimed the Sāmaveda, which destroys all sins.
The Sindhu river enters the Vitastā at that very place;
therefore, a bath there during the month of Śrāvaṇa bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
Having performed [this], one should worship Viṣṇu, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
furthermore, the Sāman hymns should be heard, and Brahmins should always be honored.
One should play and enjoy oneself right there together with one's kinsmen;
indeed, water-sports with women should be performed for the sake of obtaining a husband.
Then, in the Kali age, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada,
during the twenty-eighth [cycle], that Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, was born.
For the sake of removing the burden and for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas,
Yaśodā and Devakī are likewise to be fully honored there.
With perfumes, garlands, and likewise incenses made from barley and wheat,
along with various foods and drinks containing milk, and also with diverse fruits.
During the night, one should remain awake, filled with dancing and singing;
then, at the time of dawn on the ninth day, the women [should perform the rites].
All of them, clad in red garments and adorned with flower garlands,
carry their respective images, which arise from various forms of wealth.
“Of these”— namely Viṣṇu, Devakī, and Yaśodā—
at a riverbank that is auspicious, delightful, secluded, or by a great lake,
they then perform their ablutions and bathe them there.
Having entered the house again, they eat barley-food,
prepared with products of sugarcane, along with honey, clarified butter, and black pepper.
On the new moon day, when the lunar mansion presided over by the ancestors (Maghā) occurs,
the seven classes of ancestors were born from the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
The wise should perform worship toward them with their whole being;
likewise, the eight-limbed offering (piṇḍa) should be given, and the śrāddha rite should be performed according to one's own means.
In ancient times, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, the blue lord of the nāgas entered the body of Satī; therefore, one should worship him there.
By means of garlands, offerings of clothing, and the propitiation of gods, fire, and gurus;
likewise by means of dance, song, and instrumental music, as well as an abundance of flowers, incense, and food.
One should always worship Sthānanāga according to the prescribed rite;
on the sixth lunar day, Mādhava, the son of Devakī, attained fame.
The Sthānanāga, Kumāra, the cattle, and the Brahmins on earth—
therefore, they should be worshipped there with fruits produced from sugar.
Having given those same items— fully cooked and combined with honey, ghee, and black pepper— in due order to his servants, friends, and wife, he should then eat them himself.
Janārdana, Durgā, Dhanada, Varuṇa,
and Vanaspati— these five [were established] in the Kṛta Yuga on the ninth day.
May they produce wheat here for the satisfaction of embodied beings;
therefore, one should honor them there with foodstuffs derived from wheat.

One should satisfy the Fire with wheat-flour offerings combined with jaggery, clarified butter, and black pepper, along with flowers and incense in due order; and one should worship Hari with wheat-flour offerings.

Having offered the remaining edible foods announced by him to a single Brahmin or to several Brahmins, one who is self-restrained should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) with that very same [remnant].
And in a well-constructed river, in a very meritorious reservoir,
or in a grove abounding with trees, one should eat those [foods] afterwards as well.
Having reached Vijayā-dvādaśī, one should worship Janārdana;
it is the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, occurring on a Wednesday under the Śravaṇa asterism.
The time is praised as being with its increase: the sun is situated in Leo, it is the third decan from Leo, and there is a confluence of the monsoon rains and the river.
A *drekkāṇa* is the third part of a zodiac sign.
A Brāhmaṇa who is full of Vedic knowledge is a worthy recipient (*pātra*) who delights the heart;
likewise are the mantra "Victory to You" (*jitaṃ te*) and wealth acquired through one's own duty (*svadharma*).
These twelve are difficult to obtain even for the gods simultaneously—
those for whom Hṛṣīkeśa, the twelvefold soul, is said to be the deity.
When the sun is situated in Leo and the moon is in Śravaṇa,
the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight accompanied by Mercury does not occur except in the month of Bhādrapada.
That meritorious and auspicious Vijayā-Dvādaśī is extremely difficult to encounter;
for the sake of favoring mortals, it may occur only occasionally and not constantly.
Having obtained that [fast] unexpectedly, those who have gathered all the necessary provisions should first fast on the eleventh day and, being well-composed, [perform the rites] on the twelfth day.
Having performed the ritual bath according to the rules at sacred sites such as Prayāga and at the confluences of rivers, one should worship Hṛṣīkeśa.
Whether on land, in water, in the sky, upon an image, in a jar, or atop a lotus;
whether in fire, in a Brahmin, in a cow, in one's guru, or in one's father or mother.
Then, with extensive rites of invitation, seating, auspicious days, and welcome;
"having invited" means having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*).
And with water for the feet, the respectful offering (*argha*), flowers, incense, lamps, ornaments, and fly-whisks.
With fragrant unguents, with milk or milk-rice (pāyasa),
with various edibles, roots, fruits, vegetables, pure meats, and whatever else is pleasing to the mind;
[399] With honey-mixture (madhuparka), curd, milk, and honey, along with unbroken grains (akṣata), sesame seeds,
and likewise with a measured amount of parched grain (lāja) that is pleasing and produced in the local region;
“Mātrā” refers to coverings such as garments and the like.
[One should worship] with purifying drinks that are pleasing to the heart, with songs, dances, and instrumental music,
and with many hymns from the Purāṇas and well-refined Vedic mantras.
With well-prepared recitations refined by Vedic study,
and with the *Puruṣasūkta*, as well as other Vaiṣṇava hymns,
having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa, one should offer a cow made of water.
“A cow made of water” refers to a water-cow. According to one's capacity, with a mind purified by faith, one should [offer] that [cow] made of gold, silver, copper, tin, or clay to the Brahmins.
A beautiful water-pot (*maṇikā*) filled with water, weighing one *śatamāna*— that is,
measuring one hundred *palas*—
and within that pot, filled with water, [one should place] either gold or silver.
A very beautiful vessel made of copper, brass, or clay,
filled with excellent food, as well as curd, ghee, and jaggery.
One should offer auspicious clothing that has been consecrated with mantras and treated with sugar, milk, honey, sesame seeds, gold, and water.
Having carefully covered that water-cow, together with its vessel,
with a new, high-quality, pure cloth accompanied by a sacred thread (pavitra), [one should proceed].
[400] Having covered everything with a perfectly pure canopy, the knower of the scriptures should protect against the defects caused by celestial wanderers as well as terrestrial obstacles.
With the mantra "jitaṃ te," they remember Hṛṣīkeśa,
being well-composed and relying upon supreme faith in the brāhmaṇas.
In the same manner, he should give sandals and, immediately thereafter, shoes;
likewise silver, a cow, land, gold, or even a gem.
Elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles; houses and beds;
seats as well as vessels, garments, and ornaments.
Having dedicated [the offering] to all the paternal ancestors as well as the maternal ancestors,
and also to those who were the fathers of one's wife, friends, and teachers.
With the names of the lineages and the utterance of *svadhā*, as in the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), he should cause [the guests] to recite:
"May this food be inexhaustible for the ancestors."
Furthermore, the Blessed One Keśava becomes pleased by the gift of food;
the Moon becomes pleased by molasses, milk, ghee, and garments.
Through the gift of water, Varuṇa shall always be well-pleased;
and through the gift of silver, Maheśvara shall be gratified.
By the gift of gold, Agni is constantly propitiated;
and by means of elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and likewise sacrifices, Maghavan is pleased.
Through beds and dwellings Dharma is pleased; through an umbrella the Sun; through sandals Yama is gratified; and through cows, it is proclaimed, the Lord of Beasts (Saurabheya).
By the offering of a pair of sandals, Padmayoni is pleased;
likewise, by ornaments and garlands, Pārvatī, the Mother of the World, is gratified.
Charity, fire-offerings, recitation of mantras, worship, as well as the satiation of Brahmins,
bathing at the confluence of rivers, and likewise giving sacrificial fees to Brahmins.
Everything offered there is said to be a thousandfold and inexhaustible for one who,
endowed with faith, gratifies Hṛṣīkeśa there.
He conquers all worlds and goes to that abode of Viṣṇu;
he shall deliver all his ancestors—ten preceding and ten succeeding generations.
At that time, having reached the Vitastā joined with the Sindhu,
he mixed earth with its very cool, holy water.
One should always, with great effort, embrace at the time of bathing that most fair woman who is endowed with auspicious marks and who bestows the merit of bathing at the confluence.
On the tenth day at the end of the month of Nabhasya, Kaśyapa obtained a boon for an incarnation of the Vitastā in the ancient body of Satī.
Then, on the eleventh day, Rudra instructed his wife Satī;
and by the command of Śaṅkara, she went to the netherworld on the twelfth day.
Then, on the thirteenth day, she was born from Śūlabheda from the netherworld;
on the fourteenth day she disappeared again, and on the full-moon day she arose once more.
Having thus set out, that river then departed by way of the serpent’s path;
and having bathed there during the seven days beginning with the tenth, [the people likewise bathed].
One should always behold, worship, meditate upon, drink,
and bathe [the deity], with perfumes, garlands, food offerings, lamps, and most beautiful incenses.
With various body-pastes, garments, flowers, and ointments,
as well as with red threads, bracelets, and the ornaments of women.
At the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu, she should be worshipped especially with fruits, roots, vegetables, burnt offerings, and the satiation of Brahmins.
A great festival procession should be held, and actors and dancers should be honored;
for Indra was [consecrated] by Viṣṇu in the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight.
Appointed [to this task], the wielder of the thunderbolt strikes down and even fells all crops, rice, fruits, and medicinal herbs.
Out of fear of him, they all cause this entire world to flourish;
therefore, he, together with his wife, should be worshipped there day after day.

Accompanied by his retinue, equipped with weapons, along with his escort and his mounts—the king should especially worship the deity fashioned from a cloth painting, together with his followers and attendants.
"Sānuyātraḥ" means "with his followers.
The deity made from a cloth screen is to be worshipped by the king with particular distinction.
"Made on a cloth or a wall" means painted upon a cloth or a wall.
With edible foods, grains, fruits, roots, garments, and beautiful garlands,
one should honor the Brahmins and likewise those who live by the stage (actors) with that [image] in mind.
On the full moon day in conjunction with the asterism Pūrvabhādrapadā, Pitāmaha [worshipped] Śakra, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Dhanada, and Śaṅkara.
He consecrated the world-protectors for the sake of guarding the three worlds,
and likewise Ananta, the serpent, for the sake of supporting the earth.
The Rakshasa is the "Yatu.
Therefore, one should draw there an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp;
within that pericarp, one should draw the Lotus-born [Brahmā] together with Ananta.

And upon the petals in the east and other directions, one should duly paint Vāsava and the other [guardians], along with their weapons, as well as the planets and the nāgas, each in their proper form and in due order.
Then, having sequentially established the auspicious jars in that very manner,
the deities beginning with Brahmā should thereafter be worshipped with devotion.
[He should worship] properly with water for the guest-offering and for the feet, as well as with incense, garlands, and unguents;
with garments, jewels, fruits, and edible foods; with fire-oblations and the satiation of Brahmins.
With pleasing jaggery and milks produced from all types of crops,
and with dances, songs, and likewise instrumental music, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims.
Then, according to the scriptures, parched grains (dhānā) should be given to the Brahmins and to one's kinsmen;
at night, these parched grains should be consumed by the discerning who remain self-restrained.
Formerly, Varuṇa indeed presided over the third day of the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja;
therefore, he should be worshipped there with extensive offerings according to one's means.
For from Śakra, the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada) obtained the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma;
therefore, on the fourth day, he should be worshipped there by those accompanied by Brahmins.
In ancient times, the goddess Vasudhā was lifted from the netherworld by the Boar;
she should therefore be worshipped there together with the elephants of the quarters.
On the sixth day, certain ancient youths indeed came into being;
with reference to them, well-adorned sons should be honored as the Kumāras.
On the seventh [day], however, Abhimāna conquered the world through his own prowess;
in reference to him, worship should be performed for oneself, as well as among women and children.
When the yoginī Aśokā was formerly perfected on the eighth day of the dark fortnight,
then Yoganidrā, the Vaiṣṇavī, was indeed worshipped there.
Especially by those who have performed their ablutions, wearing well-made garments and smeared with vermilion paste,
preceded by dance and instrumental music.

"With applications of vermilion mud" means with pastes of vermilion powder mixed with water and other liquids. A bed and a seat, provided with coverlets, should be offered to her; "with coverlets" means together with upper cloths.
One should always play with flowers, food, and incense as the primary offerings.
Thereafter, she should eat barley-food mixed with molasses, clarified butter, and black pepper;
then, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, Satī abandoned her body in the water.
Therefore, she who increases all prosperity should be fully honored there with water-offerings,
flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and bracelets.
With saffron, collyrium, and garments useful for women of beautiful hips,
as well as with salt, lac, molasses, and half-ripe fruits;
And with reference to her, women whose husbands are living should be honored—
namely, sisters, mothers, and likewise women devoted to their husbands.
In the bright fortnight, having recognized that the new grain has ripened beautifully,
on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and when a propitious moment occurs;
One should go to the field according to the prescribed rite, preceded by dance and instrumental music;
having kindled a fire there and strewn it with grains according to the scriptures.

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the method prescribed in one’s own *gṛhya-sūtra*— that is, "in accordance with the scriptures"— one should thereafter lead forth the consecrated grain,
accompanied by flowers, garments, fruits, and roots, and joined by elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having thus gratified the gods, the ancestors, and his kinsmen in due order,
he should distribute [the remainder] according to his ability among those who know the stars and those who protect the crops.
Clad in new garments, wearing garlands, well-anointed, and beautifully adorned,
he stands facing the east, joyful, preceded by the chanting of the Vedas.
Delighted by the excellent music and accompanied by auspicious songs and other sounds,
he should eat fresh curd mixed with honey, which has been consecrated by a Brahmin.
Having taken his meal, he celebrates a great festival with songs and instrumental music,
[recollecting] how in ancient times the Kṣīroda ocean was churned from the past.
The goddess Śyāmā was born, endowed with all auspicious marks;
by the command of Nārāyaṇa, she was both delicate and illustrious.
A most beautiful creeper had emerged from Satī’s body;
seeing it there, all the gods and asuras were struck with wonder.
"She is charming and has a beautiful countenance; we shall see her. Having spoken these words, they all indeed beheld her.
They gave it the name by which it is renowned on earth as *drākṣā* (grape);
for this reason, when it is well-ripened, it should indeed be honored with great effort.
Then, with flowers, incense, food, edibles, and the like, as well as by the gratification of Brahmins,
the two children and likewise the two elders should be honored immediately thereafter.
In his small hut, aiming for the goals of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
he lived joyfully with his wife, along with his servants, friends, and sons.
Anointed according to the rules, wearing garlands and a diamond garment,
he himself should offer it to the gurus with devotion and not otherwise.
A festival should also be celebrated, filled with dance and song,
during the auspicious conjunction of the asterism Svāti in the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.
Formerly, the horse named Uccaiḥśravas first brought the sun;
therefore, he should always be worshipped there with faith by men along with horses.
Indeed, the horses should be honored daily until the ninth day,
when rites for peace and prosperity are to be performed for them.
One should tie grains, *bhallātaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*,
and likewise *siddhārthaka* around their necks with a five-colored thread.
Every day, an oblation (homa) should be performed with mantras dedicated to Vāyu, Varuṇa, Sūrya, Śakra, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and likewise Agni.
The horses must be guarded by men with weapons in their hands;
they must never be struck there, nor ever be made to carry loads.
Formerly, during the conjunction of Jyeṣṭhā, eight exceedingly powerful elephants once bore the earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves.
One should worship them there: Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, Vāmana, Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla.
One should worship starting from Śakra and Ṛkṣa up to the ninth [tithi];
therein, on the eighth day, is Bhadrakālī, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
She appeared, most terrible, together with ten million yoginīs;
for this reason, she should be worshipped by human beings on that day.
With worn-out garments, incense, garlands, jewels, and ointments;
likewise with lamps, jewels, edibles, fruits, roots, and grains.
[408] With various kinds of food offerings, vegetables, burnt oblations, and the satiation of Brahmins;
with bilva leaves, śrīphala fruits, sandalwood, and ghee.
With animals, pleasant drinks, and by keeping vigil at night,
weapons should be worshipped in the temple of Durgā by the wise.
Musical instruments, insignia, armor, and weapons—
these must always be worshipped by their respective artisans at night.
On the ninth day, however, all who have performed their ablutions should worship the Brahmins;
having eaten, they should perform a rite for peace during the yoga known as Godhūli.
Whatever has been stated by Śālihotra, whatever opinion is held in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra),
and whatever is proclaimed in the Atharvaveda— that one should perform therein.
One should cut up a cock and a goat within a wooden house constructed for that purpose;
then, at the time of the Śravaṇa asterism or at twilight, one should burn it along with the house.
One should visualize those two as being consumed by fire there while they are departing,
whether toward a peaceful direction, a blazing one, or a scorched one, which yields its respective fruit.
And people with weapons in hand should be observed by the king during the *nīrājana* ceremony.
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, Sumantu said:
On the ninth day, Śrī, joined by all the gods and highly honored by them,
slew the wicked Mahiṣa, who was incapable of being slain by the deities and others.
Having obtained the empowerment, O Giver of Boons, on the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja,
that Caṇḍikā should be worshipped there on the ninth day by the wise.
For it is from that [day] that greatness was attained by the goddess Sarasvatī;
for this reason, this ninth day is always called "Mahatī" (the Great) by the wise.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess Caṇḍikā here on the ninth day,
the hero Brahmā, as well as Viṣṇu and the immortals, attained greatness.
Therefore, this ninth day, which bestows great merit and destroys evil,
should always be observed with diligent effort by all kings.

O King, it should be performed according to the rules by those who subsist on meditation— whether children, the elderly, or those in their youth— especially when conjoined with the Mūla and Uttara stars.
O King, gifts should be given here by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and other means as well, along with fasting, by kings.
O Indra among kings, the Goddess is indeed greatly pleased by gifts of cows, gold, and various garments, when they are offered with one's own flesh and blood.
O King, with the blood of buffaloes, goats,
and sheep, the boon-granting Caṇḍikā becomes satisfied with even a single offering.
