"Sumeka" is a year.
Then, by means of blood, this [earth] was duly gratified for one uraṇa;
likewise, it was gratified with the blood of a goat for ten years.
O hero, Caṇḍikā becomes satisfied with a hundred buffaloes;
she attains satisfaction with a thousand when offered her own body-blood.
Having duly gratified Durgā by piercing her arms and shanks,
she is thus worshipped by various hosts of Mlecchas and all classes of bandits.
[This was said] by the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, Kinnaras, Barbaras, and Śakas.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One should observe a fast and keep a vigil on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*)."
And on the twelfth day, Vāsudeva should always be worshipped.
A festival procession should be held for Viṣṇu on the thirteenth day;
one should observe a fast on the fourteenth day and worship Hari on the full moon day.
In ancient times, the wise proclaimed a desirable oblation to be performed on the full moon of Āśvayuja;
however, when there is great danger, the Fire-god is to be worshipped with oblations at the threshold for the sake of protection.
The Full Moon was well-satisfied with rice grains mixed with barley, unbroken rice, and ghee;
he was also honored with water for the feet, grains, and likewise with fruits.
In the Devadāru forest, Rudra— naked, with an erect phallus, clad only by the directions,
accompanied by his wife, and preceded by Skanda and Nandi— was worshipped.
Aśvapati was always honored by the gods, as was Revanta;
Surabhi, the cow, was likewise honored by the sages and by those possessing cattle.
In this place, the Fire-god, in the form of a goat, was worshipped by the sages;
and among the gods, the Lord of Waters, in the form of a ram, was worshipped.
The mighty elephants and other creatures were created by Vināyaka;
furthermore, the gift of forest lamps was instituted by Viṣṇu.
Kaśyapa caused Nikumbha to come [to him] from the battle;
there, these twelve great festivals must be performed simultaneously.
On the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja, Nikumbha comes forth from the ocean of sand together with his army, after having waged a most terrible battle.
Therefore, in that place, men should diligently clear the paths leading to their own homes and adorn them with mandalas.
The houses should be decorated especially with flowers, water-offerings, fruits, roots, food, and scattered mustard seeds, as well as with various colors.
Men, including children, should be well-bathed and anointed;
discerning persons should not eat there during the day.
Women, fools, the elderly, and children should eat while the gods are being honored;
likewise, the upper walls of the doorway should be worshipped with fruits and flowers.
At the side of the door, the blazing bearer of oblations (Agni) is to be worshipped;
he is to be gratified with rice grains mixed with barley, unbroken rice, and clarified butter.
The full moon should be worshipped with milk and milk-rice (pāyasa),
as well as Rudra together with his consort, Skanda, and Nandi, the lord of the gods.
Surabhi is to be worshipped by those possessing cows; Hutāśana by those possessing goats;
Varuṇa by those possessing sheep; and Vināyaka by those possessing elephants.
Revanta is to be worshipped with horses and extensive offerings according to one's wealth;
thereafter, Nikumbha is to be worshipped with black gram, sesame seeds, and rice.

Having fed the Brahmins with abundant quantities of fragrant foods mixed with ghee known as *kṛsara*— wherein "known as *kṛsara*" refers to the incense called *mahiṣa-guggulu*— one should then eat meatless food oneself.
That night should be passed by those standing beside the fire with songs and dances mingled with the sound of conch shells,
while observing various kinds of games.
Then, at the time of dawn, having anointed themselves and being well-adorned,
they should perform the ritual touching of auspicious objects as well as the worship of the fire.
One should eat together with the Brahmins and sport as one pleases;
when that night has passed, immediately on the second [day].
At dawn, one should play like a *piśāca*, smeared with mud;
and then, everywhere in all houses, one should act shamelessly like Rudra.
For that region was previously obtained from Kaśyapa by the Piśācas, who travel with tranquility, even as the Prajāpati was filled with anger.
Then, having brought forth friendly ointments made from mud,
[he tempted him] with words that kindled the fire of desire and indicated the objects of the male and female genders.
They proclaimed the Paiśāca conduct here and there with their speech,
uttering vulgarities and shouting insults directly in our faces.
On that day, in the forenoon, followers of Nikumbha—
piśācas of lovely appearance— entered those men.
Then, in the afternoon, having bathed, they leave like kinsmen;
yet, due to the fault of pride and self-conceit, [they do not honor] the men who have arrived there.
If one does not worship out of delusion, nor engages in play,
those Piśācas of fierce appearance consume him with rage.
Then, after bathing, the Lord Hari Dāmodara is to be worshipped by men;
having honored the Brahmins, one should eat, being well-anointed and well-adorned.
Then, for six months from that time onward, he was to reside in his own quarters along with his kinsmen, friends, and wives, attended by servants in due order.
Fire should be kept present, as well as *siddhārthaka* seeds and sesame;
for an entire month, a lamp must be offered daily outside the house.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having reached the end of their dalliance, when her husband, the Lord of the Quarters, had departed,
the Goddess rose from her bed and, deeply distressed, performed her purification rites.

Then, as the mountain-dwelling woman touched him who possessed the luster of a rain-cloud, this thought arose in her: "I have neither a son nor a daughter. (This is an address to Vyāsa by the one whose splendor is like a rain-cloud; "dhārādharaprabhā" refers to his cloud-like mass of hair.)
As she was thus reflecting, there was born from the water of her heart a lotus-eyed maiden, formed as if from clay and mud.
Clad in blue garments and veiled in red cloth,
she rose from that mire with her face and hair disheveled.
With her hands joined in reverence, she said to the noble and virtuous Pārvatī:
"Command me what must be done by me, who was born from your body."
Pārvatī, the daughter of the mountain, having embraced that maiden who had arisen from the waters of her heart, smelled the crown of her head and spoke to her.
Since this courtyard has been smeared with the mud-marks of the earth,
therefore there shall be a great festival known as the "Water-Servitude" (udakasevā).
On that day when the festival of Indra arrives in this world,
people will begin a great celebration for you on that very day.
That desire which was Bhairava, belonging to the Goddess and to Bhava,
became Mahābhairava and stood holding the maiden by the hand.
Then the blessed Ambikā, the wife and beloved of the Blessed One, spoke to the man: "Who are you, and why do you seize my daughter?"
Then Bhairava, whose mouth was terrifying with fangs and whose form was fearsome,
stood before Umā and spoke in a low voice, like a cloud charged with lightning.
"That passion which was terrifying for both the Blessed One and Bhava—
born from that very source, I myself shall be he, and she shall become my wife."
[416] Those two, husband and wife, stood there with deformed limbs and clad in shabby garments;
Somabhūṣa looked at them and, filled with suspicion, wondered, "Who are these two?"
Then that couple, having bowed down to the beautiful feet of Maheśa, which are worshipped by gods and asuras, stood there.
Then both of them— Bhava and Bhavapāla— along with Tripurāri, whose matted locks are marked by the moon,
spoke as they lay prostrate at his feet nearby.
Who are you two? What do you say? And what shall I do?
Then Ambikā spoke to Bhava, the Lord of the Mountains, who was radiant with the color of ten million suns, lightning, and fire,
as he turned his face toward her with a smile.
The Blessed Lady, moving with playful grace.
He who was formerly your Bhairava, the source of terror even for the gods— that very desire of mine has indeed been born here on earth as this man.
But it was indeed a woman who was the fuel for my fire of passion.
Then Umā declared him to be the mark of the moon, the one who brings about the moon;
the Lord, wearing the guise of a cowherd, addressed these words to the couple: "You two are husband and wife."
For at the very moment this excellent woman was conceived in your womb,
by my power she became this Bhairava of mine.
"O Goddess, I cannot exist without you, nor can you exist without me;
for this very reason, I have today given you the fire-drill of Lambodara."
And that festival shall be proclaimed by the three Vedas, O beloved of mine;
its first appearance shall occur when the great festival of Kāma has taken place.
Therefore, O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods, the entire world consists of that [nature];
for this reason, O Pārvatī, men and women are mutually attached to one another.
In women, the heart resides in the vulva; in men, the heart resides in the penis. O lady, this entire world is marked by the vulva and the penis.
Men together with the gods, crying out "Bhaga!
Liṅga!", will strike one another down while shouting at each other.
At both the beginning and the end, there will be a Bhairava festival;
likewise, on the day of Śakra’s fall, there will be a festival for Udasevikā.
"At the beginning and at the end"—this refers to the intervals between festivals; for the remainder of the time between festivals, "there will be a festival.
That city, town, or village which this Bhairava enters will all become like one possessed, including its women and elders.
O Daughter of the Mountain, the four castes, though not actually insane,
will become like madmen, intoxicated by the gods and thrilled by the arrival of Bhairava’s scripture.
Just as the deities enter the twice-born when they are appointed for ancestral rites,
even so does Bhairava enter the people during the great festival of Bhairava.
Then, mounted upon donkeys, they were suddenly smeared with mud and adorned with garlands and ornaments made from bitter vines.
With bracelets bound from the fruits thereof, making loud and manifest sounds,
their entire bodies smeared with ashes and their limbs defiled by the mud of excrement and urine.
While cymbals were being struck accompanied by harsh and incoherent words—
"incoherent" meaning unconnected—
the Bhairava, O lady of beautiful hips, was being pointed out together with his wife.
For he will enter the city, generating joy among the people;
O timid one, once Bhairava has entered the city honored by Indra, he will do so.
Then that festival will be both pleasing and terrible to the people. "Pleasing" (rocaka) means an object of delight; that very thing is "terrible" (ghora), meaning intense.
For those who are fearful of a hundred years, and for those who are worn out by old age—
All those men will also celebrate a festival like Vatsaka;
"like Vatsaka" means like Kumāra.
Their limbs will be nourished by various ornaments and adorned with saffron and aloe-wood.
They were wrapped in yellow garments and those of many colors; they wore excellent garlands as ear-ornaments, were ever-adorned with wreaths, and possessed crests upon their heads.
“Sadāmālāḥ” means those wearing garlands. “Cūḍā” refers to an arm ornament; they were adorned with such.
[419] With their hair roughened by the powder of campaka flowers and the like, they slapped their arms, wailed, and made others hear unpleasant words.
In the streets and on the royal highways, they proclaimed here and there how sons of noble family had been rendered bodiless by the noble women.
Showing at every step the resolution of all doubts regarding those matters that are obscure, secret, and established by family custom.
Singing and dancing, and committing acts of impropriety,
they who were formerly possessed of shame have now fallen into a state of shamelessness.
Even when reviling their elders and others who are worthy of respect,
mortals will act according to their own whims through the practice of contempt.
A daughter does not feel shame before her mother, nor does the fire-drill before the wood; a son does not feel shame before his father, nor a grandson before his grandfather.
The nephew is not the maternal uncle's [relative], nor is the maternal uncle the nephew's;
in a mere moment, kinsmen have fallen into a state of shamelessness.
Like fools, they threaten one another with harsh words;
though their bodies are white and soft, they are rough with ash and harsh in speech.
With their limbs smeared with pieces of food, they were beautiful of form and graceful in their movements;
they were mounted upon dogs, oxen, and donkeys.

Some wear the dress of ḍombas, some the dress of cowherds, and others assume the dress of students; some have the appearance of kings, others that of outcasts, while some are young men appearing in the form of the elderly.
Others, O King, in the guise of barbers, were dull-witted;
they used showers of onions and fermented liquor mixed with *śvāsakṛt* [mustard seed].
Some men will offer incense that causes detachment through the sense of smell,
while others will offer the flesh of aquatic creatures to ignorant people.
They will place a foul odor, like something impure, upon their noses;
but others, O Goddess, shall be men adorned in the guise of Vedic priests.
For they rejoice like the immortals while having their poetic works recited;
and he who is not reviled there, and who does not revile another.
The ancestors of that slayer of a Brahmin are terrified,
just as kings are of horses, elephants, and men.
In the same way, a woman who serves her husband brings about his welfare;
neither the gods nor the ancestors partake of his sacrificial offering.
O Pārvatī, I am not pleased with one who maintains neutrality by serving both sides; neither you nor Nandin shall be satisfied with such a person.
And at the cessation [of the sacrifice], a great sorrow caused by the absence of a son will be brought about by you;
thus, through this very act of service, the arrival of Bhairava shall come to pass.
Thereafter, that incomparable abundance of joy which we both possessed no longer shines for us,
just as your palace does not shine because of your grief.
O Girijā, that city will likewise become devoid of its excellence,
with both men and women covered in ashes and mud.
They will render the houses and dwellings lusterless;
O Queen, the city will become like one laid waste by thieves.
Covered with lumps of clay, ashes, feces, and urine, like men surrounded by hungry ghosts (pretas), those men likewise cried out, "This one is dead! He is terrifying!"
"Having laid this man there, covered with grass and wrapped in a garment, let us say these words: 'This Bhairava abandons us.'"
The Brahmins shall carry him away like a deceased, beloved teacher;
having placed him on the bank of a pond or likewise on the bank of a river.
Having bathed and accomplished the rite for Bhairava, they— freed from impurity by the ritual ablution and exhausted by the intensity of the festival— will then return home.
Men will become endowed with wisdom, like those who observe the vows of sages.
Just as these men repeatedly felt ashamed in the Bhairava-āgama, O Pārvatī,
so too did they feel shame once more when confronted by the manifested Bhairava.
They became entirely enveloped by groves of ascetic penance.
But, O beautiful one, that brahmin who recites this Bhairavotsava in an assembly of twice-born men and gods,
at that very moment, together with his sons and grandsons—
One shall attain the auspicious state of Mahāgaṇeśa.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "On the new moon day of the month of Kārttika, having obtained freedom from fear from Keśava, the gods slept happily on the slopes of the Ocean of Milk."
Lakṣmī, released from the fear of the Daityas, slept happily within the interior of a lotus;
meanwhile, Brahmā slept for a thousand cycles of four yugas upon that lotus.
For this reason, people should properly perform the ritual for a comfortable sleep;
one should not eat there during the day, except for children and the sick.
Having worshipped Lakṣmī at the time of dusk according to the prescribed order,
one should likewise set up lamp-trees in the temples of the gods according to one's ability.
[422] At crossroads and cremation grounds, by rivers, mountains, and dwellings;
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, at public squares, and in houses.
The marketplaces for buying and selling should be adorned with garments and flowers;
immediately thereafter, in a place encircled by rows of lamps.
Having first fed the Brahmins and distributed food to those who are hungry,
one should eat while adorned and beautified by new garments.
In ancient times, Śaṅkara engaged in a most enchanting game of dice together with his contented kinsmen, who were affectionate, charming, and skillful.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, O Satyavat,
Śaṅkara was conquered there, and Pārvatī obtained victory.
For this reason, Śaṅkara is sorrowful, while Gaurī always dwells in happiness;
therefore, men should engage in gambling there at dawn.
In that gambling match, for whoever wins, the year shall be auspicious;
but defeat is contrary, as it will lead to the loss of what has been gained.
One should listen to songs, instrumental music, and the like while well-anointed and well-adorned;
one should especially enjoy the meal together with praiseworthy kinsmen.
On that night, a beautiful place for the bed should be prepared,
adorned with perfumes, flowers, garments, jewels, and garlands.
Surrounded by a garland of lamps and likewise perfumed with incense,
that night should be spent together with one's beloveds.
One should honor with new garments the twice-born, kinsmen, and relatives.
In the *Padma Purāṇa*: "In the month of Kārttika, on the new moon day, the lighting of lamps [should be performed]."
One should perform [the rite] for Brahmā in the hall; he shall go to the supreme state.
For as many lamps as one is able to fill with ghee,
for that many thousands of yugas one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), having honored the Brahmins with lamps mixed with jaggery and unwashed garments, one shall indeed go to the abode of Brahmā.
Then, on that first day of the lunar fortnight, he should worship himself with perfumes, flowers, and new garments;
thus he shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
This lunar day is of great merit, characterized by offerings of ghee;
it is eternally dear to Brahmā and is celebrated as Bāleyī.
He who feeds brahmins on this day, and especially himself,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, whose splendor is immeasurable.
O mighty-armed one, in the month of Caitra, the first lunar day is supremely auspicious;
on that day, the best of men who performs a bath after touching a dog-cooker (outcaste) attains great merit.
O King, tiger among the Kurus, no misfortune, nor mental anxieties, nor physical ailments shall befall him; therefore, one should perform this ritual bath.
For that divine lustration ceremony (nīrājana) indeed destroys all diseases;
O King, one should adorn everything there, including cows, buffaloes, and whatever else may be present.
Then, with garments for the monks and other such items, one should lead everyone beneath the archways;
likewise, O scion of the Kuru lineage, one should provide a feast for the Brāhmaṇas.
O descendant of Kuru, O King, these three lunar days were previously proclaimed for the months of Āśvayuja,
Kārttika, and Caitra.
O King, on whichever lunar day occurs in the month of Kārttika, bathing and giving gifts yield a hundredfold merit;
that day on which Bali was offered oblations with clarified butter is auspicious, bestowing blessings and destroying both good and evil fortune.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa,
Trivikrama said to Bali:
"Likewise, there is another meritorious festival that occurs after the great festival of Śakra."
A great festival called the "Hero's Entrance" shall be yours.
There, O tiger among men, joyful, well-nourished, and adorned women will diligently honor you with offerings of flowers and lamps.
During your festivals, there shall be abundance day and night;
and that great Kaumudī festival shall be exactly as it is now in your kingdom.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Having previously deceived the six Dānava embryos, Janārdana created that goddess Yoganidrā for his own protection."
Having worshipped the Goddess Siddhidā, whose deity is Kāla, for one night during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārtika by the command of Keśava, [one attains success].
On the fourth, or the eighth, or the ninth [lunar day], it grants excellent accomplishment;
likewise, on the fourteenth, by women who have properly bathed in due order.
Outside the house, however, wherever there may be a solitary fruit-bearing tree,
one should worship that [tree] with an offering of water, flowers, incense, and food.
A woman who has an only son, restrained in mind, speech, and body,
having taken an excellent morsel provided with the aforementioned requisites, [should offer it].
Then, being well-pleased and desiring to please him, she gives [the offering] to the hawk:
"O Noble One, take this morsel offered to the Blessed Lady."
Having spoken thus, she then goes to her own home with her desires fulfilled;
in the Kṛta Yuga, he is renowned as being like a servant or a hired laborer.
Just as King Uparicara, having placed his own semen in a leaf-cup,
gave it to a hawk to carry to his beloved wife.
In other ages, they may indeed recite the mantra as "anala," yet she leaves that morsel on the ground and goes to her home facing the east.
But as for the invitation that was previously prepared for whichever bird,
it is certain that only that very bird shall take that morsel of food.
First, that woman, being well-composed, eats at home;
afterwards, the master of the house eats, along with his servants, kinsmen, and relatives.
The husband should worship the household goddess according to that very same rite;
neither should he give her a hawk’s mouthful [of food], nor should she take refuge under a tree.
However, one should honor a devoted wife in a secret chamber,
so that when there is no harmony between husband and wife during other even-numbered days, [the rite may still proceed].
At that time, he performs only his own family duty (svakuladharma).
In the Varāha Purāṇa [123.8–11],
Varāha said:
Now, listen to the fruit of merit for one who worships me on that twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
As long as the worlds endure, and as long as you yourself exist, O Mādhavī,
so long shall one born as my devotee not be born as a devotee of another.
Having performed my rites on the twelfth day,
a man devoted to me should recite this mantra for the purpose of awakening me alone.
Oṃ, the mantra is spoken:
You, the sage who are worthy of being saluted by those who are themselves to be saluted, are being worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra.
This twelfth day known as Kaumudī has arrived for you;
wake up, wake up, O Lord of the World!
The clouds have passed, the stainless full moon shines, and the autumn flowers bloom, O Lord of the World;
I give these for the sake of merit.
Awaken and remain vigilant, O Lord of the World!
O illustrious one, those best of men who perform these rites on the twelfth day with devotion to me attain the supreme goal.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, one endowed with faith and devotion should awaken Keśava, who has been asleep, during the night."
With dances, songs, and instrumental music, with the auspicious hymns of the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas,
with the sounds of lutes and drums, and by listening to the Puranas.
And with stories of Vāsudeva, with hymns and other Viṣṇuite praises,
with well-spoken verses, with magical illusions, and indeed with the beauties of the earth.
With flowers, incenses, food offerings, and most beautiful lamps,
with burnt offerings, edibles, cakes, fruits, vegetables, and milk-rice.
With preparations of sugarcane, honey, grapes, and honey-wine,
along with pomegranates, the sprouts of *kuṭheraka*, jasmine, and salt.
Always with two heart-pleasing [ointments], white and red sandalwood,
as well as saffron and lac, and with red threads together with bracelets.
Likewise, with various kinds of flowers and substances acquired through heroic purchase,
when that night had passed and dawn broke on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
First, one should bathe [the image] with ghee, oil, and honey;
then with curd and milk; and thereafter, according to the scriptures, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
An ointment for rubbing the body consists of powdered mung beans, lentils, and āmalaka fruits,
as well as *lodhra*, *kāleyaka*, and *tagara* which restores the natural complexion.
[428] Mustard seeds, priyaṅgu, and the juice of mātuluṅga;
all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, all seeds, and gold.
Auspicious objects according to one's desire, jewels, water with *kuśa* grass,
earth dug up by an elephant's tusk, and earth dug up by a bull's horn.
From the riverbank, from a cow-pen, from an anthill, from what is extracted at a confluence,
from Indra’s abode, from a lake, and likewise from a mountain peak.
With these, one should purify the deity and offer auspicious gorocana;
thereafter, the jars should be presented, well-adorned as previously described.
Adorned with *jātī* sprouts, bearing fruit, and embellished with gold,
they were accompanied by the sound of Vedic recitations on auspicious days and the resonance of lutes and flutes.
With the sweet voices of the sūtas, māgadhas,
and bards, having thus bathed Govinda and having anointed and finely adorned him;
And one should worship the well-attired [deity] with flowers, excellent saffron,
lamps, delightful incenses, and abundant milk-rice.
And by the measured giving of food, with burnt offerings, flowers, and excellent sacrificial fees;
with garments, ornaments, jewels, cows, and charming horses.
The Brāhmaṇas are to be honored, for they are the primordial manifestations of Viṣṇu;
likewise, the Vrātyas of the Sātvata lineage are his heirs and are to be shared with.
Afterwards, the nectar-like remnants of the sacrifice should be eaten together with the Brāhmaṇas;
having shared them out, the dancers should then be entertained on the thirteenth day.
On the fourteenth day one should not eat, or else one should drink milk;
on the full moon day, however, Dāmodara should always be worshipped with devotion.
On that day, one should perform the practice of eating only at night with diligence;
for in ancient times, the Seven Sages, fearing lapses in conduct and delusion, observed it there.
The six Kṛttikās were abandoned, except for the virtuous Arundhatī;
there, the blessed Skanda attained the state of being Kārttikeya.
And by the word of Rudra, Khaḍga arose from the midst of the fire;
there Varuṇa obtained a hundred terrible nooses from Rudra.
And Agni was released there from the great danger arising from Bhṛgu’s curse;
having brought the ocean there, he was honored by Manu as a mortal.
The bulls must bathe there, for it is indeed the time for their release;
there, the gods who desired victory performed the Sāṃgrāmikī sacrifice.
Therefore, the ten ancient festivals should be celebrated here once;
there, at the rising of the moon, the female ascetics and the six Kṛttikās are to be worshipped.
Likewise, Kārttikeya, Khaḍga, Varuṇa,
and Hutāśana should be depicted above the door by fortunate people with spikes at the arrival of night.
With garlands, incense, and likewise perfumes, with various kinds of foods,
with excellent rice-dishes, fruits, and vegetables, one should satisfy the fire and the Brahmins.
With beautiful lamp-trees made from sugarcane products,
with krisara, milk, and likewise with delightful dairy preparations.
Having thus honored the gods well with various unguents and with drinks appropriate for their own kind, a lamp should be offered outside the house.
Then, near the edge of the lamp, a beautiful square pit measuring twenty-four finger-breadths should be made and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
It was filled with cow's milk and protected on all sides;
therein was a beautiful golden fish with eyes made of pearls.
It should be condensed according to the prescribed rite; one should recite "Homage be to Hari" and give that Ocean of Milk to a pleasing Brahmin.
One should give a blue bull together with four young heifers,
along with all kinds of grain and wealth, a delightful place, and all types of fragrant substances.
To a brahmin well-attired, who enables one to cross over a great wilderness—
there is merit equal in number to the hairs that exist upon his body.
The giver of that [gift] dwells in heaven for as many thousands of yugas as there were [units of measure];
then, having worshipped Viṣṇu with red garlands and unguents.
One should consume food consisting primarily of cow's milk products and sleep upon the bare ground during the Ekādaśī and other such days, as well as during those five nights.
And one should bathe day after day even in cool rivers;
Lord Hari is to be worshipped, as are the Brahmins together with the sacrificial fires.
Formerly, at the time of Viṣṇu’s awakening, the gods and asuras sequentially granted the divine gift of fearlessness to all beings for a hundred yugas.
And that supreme word was preserved exactly as it was by the sages;
likewise, the entire period of the sun's northern course, beginning with the awakening of Viṣṇu, was maintained by the gods.
That [kingdom] was protected by his word, but later it was abandoned due to the power of fate,
because of his constant habit of waging war and because of those whose nature is violence toward righteousness.
Devas, dānavas, yakṣas, piśācas,
and rākṣasas avoid the harming of living beings during the five days at the beginning of each month.
Since no food was ordained for them by the Creator other than meat,
from that time forth, each person followed whatever dharma he himself had adopted.
He is constantly protected by that one of celebrated soul, even to this day,
like a sage, like a god, and likewise like a Daitya or a Dānava.
And men should bestow the gift of fearlessness upon all beings on the first day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at its very commencement.
The commencement of the new year was established by the gods in the Kṛta Yuga,
and Kaśyapa created the most beautiful land of Kaśmīra.
Therefore, men should always perform a great festival of merit there with flowers, garlands, songs, instrumental music, and auspicious offerings adorned with wealth.
Through gifts of garments and likewise jewels, always with those aforementioned new ones,
that which is Viṣṇu’s right eye becomes once again possessed of form.
From Kaśyapa and Aditi was born the sun-god named Mitra,
on an auspicious lunar day in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Therefore, that [day] is known in this world as Mitrasaptamī;
on the sixth day, however, a ritual bath should be performed for that Mitra, the Sun.
Just as all prosperity is brought about upon the awakening of Viṣṇu,
so too should a fast be observed there, along with either edible foods or fruits.
One should keep a vigil at night accompanied by song and instrumental music;
having performed the shaving of the head on the seventh lunar day and then bathed, one should worship the Sun.
With various collections of flowers, as well as food offerings made of flour,
and with abundant honey, through fire-offerings, recitations, and meditative absorption.
Afterwards, he should satisfy the Brahmins, as well as the poor and the helpless;
then, on the eighth day, he should likewise provide for the actors and dancers.
And for two days, one should eat food made from flour, drenched in honey;
for that which is Viṣṇu’s left eye is indeed the three worlds.
Candra, the son of Anasūyā, consecrated him with nectar on every full moon day;
therefore, one should always worship him on every full moon day.
[433] Endowed with supreme faith, one should worship with white flowers,
milk, jewels, lamps, offerings, burnt oblations, and the gratification of Brahmins.
On that day, salt should always be given to cows,
because salt was released from the Moon due to Dakṣa’s curse.
The mother, sister, and daughter— these women of noble family—
are to be honored with two pieces of new, high-quality cloth that are dyed red and free of defects.
In that rite, the virtuous twice-born should duly fashion a mere form;
for it is said that through the worship of the full moon, women shall possess a beautiful form.
In the celestial Gaṅgā and on the eighth path of the self,
the lordly elephants, Kumuda and the others, sport, spraying the waters of the Jahnavī with their trunks.
Having seized them, they release them with hissing sounds while facing south;
scorched by the falling rays of Pūṣan and by the proximity of the sun's beams.
For the sake of properly pacifying his own body and quelling the burning sensation,
that water fell from the sky down a great precipice.
Blown by the wind, it attains stability;
and when that merit falls as snow upon the slopes of the Himalayas, it becomes solid.
First, Himavat and Śiśira are to be worshipped there,
as well as Hemanta and the Naga Nīla, who resembles a blue lotus.
The Sthāna-nāga should be worshipped with fruits and leaves from the nameru tree;
*baka* flowers should be offered, and incense made from *guggulu* should be burned.
[434] One should offer to the ancestors a great quantity of snow mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds;
and in whatever region there is no snow, one should say "snow, snow" while offering it.
Likewise, black gram rice mixed with clarified butter should be given to the Brahmins;
thereafter, a festival should be celebrated, filled with song and dance.
In particular, one should eat pleasant and auspicious food;
the goddess Śyāmā should be worshipped with incense, flowers, and unguents.
With foods, edibles, fruits, and roots; well-anointed and well-adorned;
seated upon the snow; and clad in heavy, protective garments.
Together with friends, servants, and kinsmen, one should enjoy food as desired in a distinguished manner, and listen to singing and instrumental music.
The dance of courtesans is to be watched, and likewise women are to be honored;
and fresh liquor is to be drunk by those who drink liquor, each in due order.
Having performed austerities in the world of Brahmā, the ancestors obtained this boon:
that on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, a śrāddha offering of vegetables shall constitute a most excellent meal.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa,
one should worship on the twelfth day the Lord Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
The journey should be undertaken on the thirteenth day; having fasted on the fourteenth, one should worship Viṣṇu on the full moon day with as much elaboration as one’s resources permit.
Formerly, this world was abandoned by Lakṣmī; thereafter, Hari, Purandara, Soma, as well as Pūṣan and Bṛhaspati [abandoned it].
[435] On the full moon day, under the conjunction with the Puṣya asterism, these five, through the power of their asceticism,
once again adorned him with the splendors of good fortune, energy, and beauty.
Therefore, during the Puṣya conjunction, for the sake of increasing good fortune,
men should anoint their own bodies with a paste of white mustard seeds.
Then, having bathed, one should perform the supreme rite for the destruction of misfortune (alakṣmī),
after likewise rubbing the body with water mixed with all medicinal herbs.
Having bathed and taken a new garment for clothing,
one should then behold a hundred auspicious objects adorned with incense, garlands, and grain.
There, Nārāyaṇa, Śakra, Candra, Pūṣan, and Bṛhaspati are to be worshipped individually with flowers, incense, and other offerings, as well as with food oblations.
Having performed an auspicious fire-oblation with praiseworthy Vedic mantras,
the Brahmins were gratified with wealth and adorned with new garments.
Thereafter, nourishing and heart-pleasing rice-pudding with ghee should be eaten;
and during the Puṣya conjunction, the king should always perform his ritual bath.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, a Śrāddha with meat yields great fruit;
since it was requested by the ancestors in the past, one should therefore perform it then.
In ancient times, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, the blessed Lord Yama himself performed most rigorous austerities and caused sesamum seeds to be produced.
King Daśaratha brought them down from the sky;
thereupon, Viṣṇu was installed by the gods as the sovereign lord of the sesame seeds.
Having fasted and bathed on that day, one should worship Hari with sesame seeds;
lamps made of sesame oil should also be offered in the temples of the gods.
One should offer sesame seeds alone, and likewise sesame seeds are to be offered in the fire;
one should give sesame seeds to the Brahmins and likewise eat sesame seeds.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, rays of light issued forth from the body of Viṣṇu by the hundreds and thousands, appearing in the shape of sectarian marks (tilaka).
For one who is asleep upon the serpent-couch and has entered into yogic sleep,
[the breaths] are stirred by the udāna wind throughout all the pores of the skin.

Because they deliver the foremost of yogins once the *vaikārika* [element] has been split apart, those perfected ones (*siddhās*), though subject to destruction within the body, have attained subtlety.
Those of the nature of Tilakas, being established in the essence of nectar,
have become stars [to rescue] from the most terrible and dense ocean of saṃsāra.
The verbal root *tarati* means "to cross" or "to float";
therefore, it is said of them that even when the sun has not yet risen and the stars are still visible, they cross over.
And there King Yama, the sun of dissolution, is to be worshipped;
and from all the joints of his limbs, the rivers of Viṣṇu constantly flow.
At the time of dawn, all those appointed by Viṣṇu always cry out: "Whose sin shall we purify?"
Since this five-starred omen is said to appear there upon the earth,
that night should then be known as the most terrible Tārārātrī.
Having fasted there on the thirteenth day, when the night has come to its end,
at the Vitastā, the Viśokā, or likewise at the Candravatī;
Likewise, on the Harṣapathā, at Trikoṭi, or in due order,
at the Sindhū, at Kanakavāhinī, at other sacred fords (tīrtha), or there [at those places].
Having bathed, one should worship Hari, the Lord of the World, as well as the stars, Yama, the rivers,
the sacred fords, the deities, and likewise the ancestors.
With water-offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, garlands,
and ointments, as well as with various kinds of food offerings and abundant krisara.
The Lord Vahni is to be worshipped with sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with clarified butter;
one should offer handfuls of water accompanied by sesame seeds and joined with the *namaḥ* and *praṇava* mantras.
One should offer seven to Yama, and seven to Dharmarāja;
seven are to be given to Mṛtyu, and likewise seven to Antaka.
Seven others should indeed be given according to the rule to Vaivasvata, seven to Kāla,
and seven to Sarvaprāṇahara.
Immediately thereafter, the Brahmins should be fed kṛsara and other foods;
having performed the śrāddha for the ancestors, he is liberated from all sins.
Then, having distributed [the food] among his relatives,
he himself should eat *kṛsara* on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, accompanied by the hosts of Yoginīs.
Because she first consumed [the seed] and then, having emitted it, created together with the qualities born from her own limbs, she is therefore called Umā Satī.
Therefore, she should be worshipped there with effort by men and especially by women, using *kunda* flowers, lotuses, and unbroken grains of rice.
And with saffron and lac, with red threads and bracelets,
as well as with water-offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and sacrificial oblations.
Women who are not widows should be honored with jaggery, fresh ginger, milk, salt, and refreshing drinks; likewise, Brahmins should be honored with meals.
Furthermore, for the increase of good fortune, one should eat together with one's kinsmen on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha; on that day, the great Sun is named Pūṣan.
The great thousand-rayed one was born to Aditi from Kaśyapa;
therefore, one should worship him there while fasting and with senses subdued.
With water-offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and delightful foods;
with dances, songs, musical instruments, burnt offerings, and the gratification of Brahmins.
Furthermore, on the eighth day, he should be worshipped with edible offerings drenched in ghee and honey;
those same edibles should be given as gifts and consumed by oneself.
On the full moon day, during the conjunction with the Maghā constellation, five crows were born from Indra,
Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and Nairṛti.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha) must be performed for the ancestors with sesame seeds;
likewise, those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and Nirṛti are indeed to be honored.
"O crows of meritorious fame, may they accept this food of mine.
With this mantra, one should give them food soaked in honey to eat.
Having fed the Brahmins, they should then eat together with their kinsmen;
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, the earth is measured.
Urged by Nārada, the sons of Dakṣa, those brahmins desiring to create,
[measured the earth] with great intelligence and subtle calculation, excluding the oceans and mountains.
For this reason, however, a small measure of its greatness is described here;
for the ancestors, the former gods, performed great austerities there.
The Śrāddha rite requested from Janārdana for the sake of human beings was fulfilled with cakes;
then the sages obtained full harvests from the Lotus-born One.
For the sake of increasing the population, on that very day— though she had been born there at all times as the wife of the son of Daśaratha— Jānakī was born.
Having fasted on the shore of the ocean at that time, the Lord of the Raghus [was present];
therefore, an oblation (caru) consisting of all kinds of grain must indeed be prepared there.
There, the Brahmins, kinsmen, and relatives should be honored with cakes;
and Sītā, the daughter of Janaka and wife of Rāma, should also be honored.
Then, on the ninth day, Lakṣmī and the highly learned Brahmins were always honored with pleasing food made of flour mixed with honey.
On the tenth day, friends and kinsmen should be gratified with various kinds of food,
one's own self should be honored, and songs and instrumental music should be listened to.
One should always perform the auspicious rite of touching for three days,
beginning on the twelfth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna when the moon is in the Śravaṇa constellation.
The Blessed Lord Viṣṇu performed the great offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa) and,
in ancient times, performed the Śrāddha ceremony for his grandfathers with sesame seeds.
Therefore, fasting, one should worship Hari there with sesame seeds;
likewise, one should worship the Goddess with sesame seeds and offer oblations of sesame seeds into the fire.
One should offer lamps with sesame oil even in the temples of the gods;
one should give sesame seeds to the Brahmins and offer water mixed with sesame to the ancestors.
One should eat sesame seeds there for the sake of increasing one's own merit;
then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Phālguna, Śaṅkara [is worshipped].
Having deluded Brahmā and Viṣṇu through his illusory power by means of a flaming liṅga,
he instantly filled the world with thousands of liṅgas.
From that time forward, the worship of the Liṅga of Kapardin became established;
therefore, a very beautiful Liṅga made of white clay should be fashioned there.

Having fasted on the thirteenth day, one should perform [the rite] in accordance with the prescribed measurements and worship it with the materials specified in the ritual for the awakening of the deity.
With water-offerings, fragrant garlands, jewels, garments, and ointments;
with various kinds of food offerings, fire oblations, and the satiation of Brahmins.
Having eaten at night, one should then keep a vigil with dance and song;
the Śivadharma scriptures and the manifestations of Śaṅkara should be heard.
Then Śaṅkara, having resorted to the Dharma characterized by non-violence (ahiṃsā),
was to be worshipped with delightful offerings made of flour and with well-adorned animals.
On the new moon day, Rudra, Agni, and likewise the Brahmins are to be honored;
one should also honor oneself along with one's kinsmen with meat-rice and fried cakes.
In ancient times, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, Keśava,
having created the earth together with its mountains, forests, and groves by means of his mind, [established it].
He said to Dakṣa Prajāpati, "Fill my creation.
Having heard those words of his, that sage then [addressed] that earth.
At that very moment, he measured it out according to rule using the great measurement system,
complete with its continents, oceans, winds, lunar mansions, rivers, and rain-showers.
There, the Lord of the Raghus constructed a vast causeway across the ocean, measuring a hundred yojanas in length, using trees, stones, and mud.
And that Blessed One, stationed at the edge of the peak of Trikūṭa,
was amazed upon beholding the vast majesty of that ancient city.
Thinking, "This earth was created by me from my two feet," he seemed as if recollecting the great pride of the slain Kumbhakarna.
Lamps were offered there in great abundance throughout the house, both inside and out;
and the gift of land was constantly made there with garlands and other offerings.
Therefore, listen to how the great and vast rite should be performed:
on the eighth day, those who do not eat food, having bathed well and being well-adorned, [should proceed].
Then Lakṣmī and Sītā should be worshipped with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings;
thereafter, at the time of evening twilight, hundreds of thousands of lamps [should be lit].
Men should offer [these gifts] in every house to all the goddesses,
and then outside the house to the gods and to the ancestors.
And upon them, one should place as many lamps as there are [seats];
then the remaining food should be eaten by one's own kinsmen.
On the second day at midday, the houses as well as the temples should be adorned with beautiful garlands.
Having worshipped Sītā, one should eat amidst the sounds of dance and song;
cooked food should be given there as a constant offering to whoever asks for it.
Nothing else should be sought; whatever is obtained should be accepted without effort. Furthermore, on the tenth day, one should likewise perform the bali-offering for oneself.
One should perform auspicious rites and festivals especially;
wealth should be given to the Brahmins and to the servants in due order.
Grain, food, gold, clothing, and likewise ornaments, as well as cows,
land, jewels, and dwellings, should be given to one who is self-restrained.
One should cause those who have arrived to grasp [the teaching] correctly and must not let their minds become weary therein;
no person who has come should be turned away.
One should drink and give what is prescribed for one's own caste when asked;
likewise, one should provide beds and seats that have been perfumed with scents, flowers, and other offerings.
Women should be honored, adorned, delighted, and well-protected;
having finished their meal, they may dance while sporting at night.
On the full moon day of Phālguna, Aryaman was born to Aditi from Kaśyapa;
and previously, this Moon was born to Anasūyā from Atri.
When the moon has risen, those two should be worshipped there according to the prescribed rites;
then, during the night, a vigil should be observed with songs, dances, and musical instruments.
Furthermore, on the first day of the dark fortnight of Caitra,
great skill in the arts of the jhallas, mallas, and naṭas should always be witnessed.
Indeed, beginning from the first day up until the fifth,
the act of worship should then be performed by women as well as by oneself.
When he asks for food, one should give him a meal consisting mostly of thin pancakes;
however, on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, Kaśmīrā is in her menses.
Therefore, having fashioned that image out of stone, women worship it constantly for three days with oil-massages, garments, and food offerings.
With flower ornaments and incense, they avoid products of the cow;
then, on the eighth day, she is to be bathed by those very women in every house.
By excellent women whose husbands were living,
who were well-bathed and adorned with beautiful garments, garlands, and especially with fragrances.
Immediately thereafter, they should be bathed by the twice-born with waters containing all medicinal herbs,
as well as with perfumes, seeds, gems, fruits, and white mustard.
And having bathed that goddess, one should worship her with perfumes and garlands,
with garments, ornaments, and flowers, as well as with meritorious offerings of cow's milk products.

With triangular cakes made of mung-bean flour, as well as with savory foods prepared from śāli rice, with milk, with delightful milk-rice offerings (pāyasa), with fire-oblations (homa), and with the satiation of brahmins; [444]
One should request the remnants offered by them in every house;
thereafter, one should listen with devotion to music that is enchanting on the lute.
From this time forward, having bathed after her menses, the Earth shall conceive a child—
she who is the queen-consort of the Sun, the ancient goddess worshipped by the gods.
For this reason, the bathing of the queen is renowned there;
[the deities present are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Kaśyapa, and likewise Surabhi.
Indra, the wise Parjanya, Śeṣa, the Moon, the Sun, and Fire;
Baladeva, the plow, the Earth, the two bulls, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Rakṣoghna, Jānakī, Sītā, Yuga, and Gaganam—
these twenty-two are declared to be the auspicious lords of progeny.
On the day of Gomangala, during the great festival at the commencement of agriculture, they should be worshipped individually with water-offerings,
flowers, incense, garlands, and jewels.
By means of circumambulations according to the prescribed rite, with burnt offerings (homa), and with the gratification of Brahmins;
then, with the Śakuni-sūkta and with the abundant sound of musical instruments.
Having bathed himself and being well-adorned, he should plow the ground with a plough;
then, proceeding step by step, he should go toward the auspicious north-eastern direction, the quarter of Indra.
Having performed a circumambulation clockwise, they then face the northeast;
releasing the two bulls, the man endowed with auspicious marks sows the seed.
Satisfied, well-attired, and wearing a garland, one should face the east and prostrate upon the ground before a golden water-vessel accompanied by a golden bowl.
Having sown the seed right there, one should enjoy the fruit together with one's kinsmen;
furthermore, a festival should be celebrated, filled with song and dance.
Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, a certain twice-born man born in the Middle Country wandered over this earth in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
When he had abandoned his domestic life and departed from the house,
the Brāhmaṇī woman became attached to a Śūdra barber in secret.
In time, by the power of destiny, a son was born to her from him;
named Śālikīrti, he grew up endowed with discernment and spoke to his mother.
Having conceived a doubt, he asked about the birth of his father as well as his own;
he was told by her in an indirect manner that these rivers have come from the mountain.
"The rice plants grow in lowlands and thrive in low-lying places.
Having heard those words and having looked at the sun, he became despondent.
Having resolved upon death, he performed very great ascetic penance;
at the time of his departure, he saw a Brahmin standing before him.
The state of being a Brahmin is difficult to attain, yet he did not obtain it;
deluded in his grasp and deprived of reason, he tormented himself.
Therefore, one should perform a fruitless renunciation for the sake of causing pain to others;
having died in a secluded place on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
Then, from a yakṣa and an intoxicated piśācī, he obtained a birth characterized by darkness;
he took recourse in that lowest yakṣa class, the Gūhyakī.
Even today he still experiences that much of the fruit of his tamasic deed;
therefore, he must indeed be worshipped there by women at the very break of dawn.
Whether drawn upon a stone that is roughly circular, or even on clay, [the deity] should be worshipped with water-offerings (arghya),
flowers, incense, and fragrant saffron.
On account of the wool of sheep, fish, and various kinds of food,
the Brahmins must observe a suspension of Vedic study there and exercise restraint over their speech.
Then, at the time of midday, having placed him in a decorated earthen vessel and carried him out through the gate, he was [honored] by women with well-spoken words.
Having thrown it through the opening of a window, he should bring it back into the house;
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, Nikumbha always worships Śaṅkara.
And the powerful, righteous-souled one, accompanied by the Piśācas, performs worship;
on that night, men should always keep a vigil.
Śambhu and Nikumbha are to be worshipped; one should offer an oblation to the Piśācas. Lamps of sesame oil are said to be most auspicious when prepared with a paste.
Abundant fish and meats, as well as auspicious rice mixed with black gram,
various delicacies, excellent cooked rice, and auspicious drinks.
At the roots of trees, in cow-pens, as well as in empty houses,
at crossroads, on carriage-roads, in courtyards, and by rivers;
In holy temples, in the hollows of trees,
in watchtowers and cremation grounds, and always along royal highways.
On that night, children must be protected from *piśāca* demons;
one should not witness the dancing of unchaste women, nor should one indulge in the company of women.
On the new moon day of Caitra,
Vāsudeva obtained from Kāśyapa a boon that there would be abundant food for his dogs.
Born in the lineage of Vaivasvata were two auspicious dogs, Śyāva and Śabala;
for they obtained as a boon the right to dwell at the gate of Yama.
Therefore, having gratified the ancestors and the gods there together with the twice-born,
a plentiful amount of food should subsequently be given to the dogs as desired.
[447] On the first day of every month, a great festival must be performed by all;
likewise, when the solar day is extremely malefic, there should be the touching of auspicious objects.
And on the day of birth, all people, having bathed and holding auspicious items in their hands,
should diligently worship the preceptor, the gods, the sacred fire, and the Brahmins.
Since one's own birth-star, the ancestors, and likewise the god Prajāpati [are honored] every year,
a great festival must indeed be performed.

Thus ends the section on duties pertaining to lunar days (*tithi-kṛtyāni*) within the *Niyatakālakalpa* (the section on fixed times) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to the illustrious Govindacandradeva, the King of Kings.
Now follows the procedure for the offering of lamps in the wilderness and so forth.
Now follows the procedure for offering the *argha* water to Agastya and others,
as stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Nārada said:
O Lord, how indeed should the offering of the guest-water (argha) and other rites be performed for him?
Tell me that procedure for the worship of Agastya.
The Lord said: At the time of dawn, during its rising at night, the wise householder,
wearing white garlands and garments, should perform his bath with white sesame seeds.
One should place a flawless jar, adorned with garlands and cloth,
joined with the five precious gems and accompanied by a vessel of ghee.
It should be provided with various kinds of food and fruits, accompanied by copper vessels,
and likewise contain a golden figure of a man, the size of a thumb, with exceedingly long arms.
Having placed a four-faced jar at its mouth, filled with grains and covered with seven cloths;
Having raised his long-armed, pot-bellied form, he should give to an eminent brahmin a bell-metal vessel joined with unbroken grains and oyster shells, accompanied by the mantra.
With a mind focused on nothing else, he stands facing whichever direction.
If one has the means, a man should bow down and give a white cow with silver hooves and a golden calf,
along with its milk.
[He gave] to the twice-born [a cow] adorned with garments, bells, and ornaments.
Within seven nights of its rising, a person should offer this entire [oblation] to it;
or [it may be offered] for up to seven or ten years.
Furthermore, some even speak thus regarding what is above.
Resembling a kāśa flower, like fire and wind,
son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O pot-born one, homage be to you!
By performing the renunciation of fruit in this manner every year, a person does not come to grief;
having performed the fire-oblation, he should thereafter refrain from taking the fruit.
The man who offers the *argha* according to this rite attains the world of Indra, endowed with beauty and health.
He who offers the sevenfold arghya attains the seven worlds;
and he who performs this throughout his life reaches the Supreme Brahman.
Whoever recites or hears this account of the bestowal of the pair of jewels,
even if they give it but once, they too belong to Viṣṇu.
Having entered the palace, he is worshipped by throngs of people.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The yogi Agastya, the son of Varuṇa, who crushes the foothills of the Vindhya mountains, remains stationed in the sky, having taken recourse to the southern quarter."
Starting from the six western degrees of Virgo and continuing by count up to seventy-two degrees, the Sun occupies these portions within the zodiacal signs.
The blessed Agastya, who feeds on water, rises in the sky from the six western lunar mansions, beginning as before.
For as long as the sun consumes [the nether regions] in succession up to the thirty-sixth,
it becomes exhausted and proceeds to Pātāla, reaching its setting.
Having observed a fast, one should behold the sage Agastya when he has risen;
he is meritorious, the granter of all desires, and the increaser of all good fortune.
And the Blessed One should be honored, endowed with faith and devotion,
with full water-jars, fine eggplants, barley, grains, and ghee.
With pure *jātī* and *utpala* flowers, with auspicious sandalwood,
with cow's ghee, as well as with garments and jewels produced from the ocean.
With sandals, umbrellas, and staffs; with shoes, deerskins, and bark garments; and with abundant supreme food, fruits, and beautiful flowers.
With various kinds of food, edibles, burnt offerings, and the gratification of Brahmins,
he invoked auspicious blessings, directing them toward the desire held in his mind.
[451] “O Blessed One, if I should obtain the desire wished for in my mind,
I shall worship you once again without hindrance through your grace.”
Having spoken thus, he should thereafter worship the astrologers as well as his gurus;
and after having fed the Brahmins, he should then eat himself while maintaining silence.
In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* (67.12): "When the rising of Agastya has occurred, then for seven nights one should offer the *arghya* to Agastya for the sake of increasing great merit."
Having poured water into a conch shell and combined it with white fragrant substances and unbroken grains (akṣata),
one should indeed offer it together with white flowers while reciting this mantra.
The mantra beginning with “kāśapuṣpa” and also “ātāpī bhakṣita” should be recited. Thus,
whoever offers this water-offering (argha) to the great sage Agastya is liberated from all sins and always crosses over the miserable states of existence.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa* [73.1–11],
Pippalāda said:
"Now, therefore, O protector of the earth, listen to the means for pacifying the adverse influence of Venus (*pratiśukra*)."
At the commencement and conclusion of a journey, as well as during the risings of Venus here, [one should perform the rites].
It should shine, either in a golden vessel or again in a bronze one,
joined with white flowers and cloth, and filled with white rice.
Having placed a silver vessel containing white [substances] together with pure pearls,
and yoked to a large white cow, one should present it to a singer of the Sāmaveda.
Homage to you, Lord of all worlds; homage to you, delight of the Bhrigus!
For the sake of accomplishing all my aims, accept this water offering; let there be homage to you.
O Bhārata, he who performs journeys and other rites at the rising of Venus attains all his desires and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the same way, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the worship of Vācaspati:
[one should place] the preceptor of the immortals in a golden vessel, made of gold.

Having bathed with mustard seeds, and with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), sesame, and the [milk] of the palāśa, aśvattha, and bhṛṅga trees, one should represent [the deity] as being endowed with yellow flowers and garments.
One should perform the entire oblation of ghee with yellow unguents;
having prostrated, one should present it to a Brahmin along with a cow.
Homage to you, O Lord of the Aṅgirases, O Lord of Speech, O Bṛhaspati!
Homage, homage to the flood of nectar for those afflicted by malevolent planets!
O son of Kuntī,
by performing worship of Bṛhaspati during the transit of the sun, on journeys, and at times of prosperity, one attains all desires.
Now follows the procedure for the gift of a lamp in the wilderness,
as stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"First, on the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja, being composed in mind..."
And at the beginning of the first watch of the night, being disciplined in mind, speech, and body, [one should practice].
Homage to the ancestors who have passed away; homage to Dharma and Viṣṇu.
Homage to Dharma and Rudra; homage to the Lord of the Wilderness.
One endowed with faith should offer a lamp with this mantra;
for him who does so throughout the entire month of Kārttika, his prosperity increases.
When the sun had reached the crest of the western mountain, not far from his house, he saw a piece of wood from a sacrificial tree, the size of a man, shaped like the sun.
Then, having placed it upon the ground, [he should place it] upon his head.
Having made four strips two cubits long, joined at their centers with a width of five finger-breadths, and shaped like eight-petaled lotuses;
By means of which there would be a following of the eightfold path.
In its pericarp, however, great lights should be offered, as well as eight lamps situated upon the petals;
and one should offer excellent lamps facing north with oil—
And [he should offer] as many as are available, combined with half a portion of clarified butter.
Furthermore, a piece of cloth not stained by the body— whether it be new, deep red, or very white—
and a pleasing cup should be employed with a wick.
But that which is glossy and like the full moon is praised.
Having placed that upon rice flour so that it may neither be destroyed nor shaken,
one should perform everything three times over.
And even for the king of lamps situated in the middle.
One should attach eight bells upon the petals for the sake of beauty and for the attainment of one's heart's desires; they should be adorned with hanging garlands of flowers.
Thereafter, it is endowed with the adornment of a canopy.
Then, having leveled the ground and smeared it with water mixed with cow dung and sandalwood paste,
one should then [draw] the mandala with many colors.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus of appropriate proportions.
Fruits, roots, as well as sugarcane products, parched grain, curd, milk, and likewise food and drink,
along with various kinds of special delicacies.
Accompanied by dance and song, and sweet instrumental music.
Having offered [the oblation] to Dharma, Hara, Dāmodara, and Dharmarāja upon the ground,
and then to the Prajāpatis and the true ancestors;
It is approved for those who remain as hungry ghosts.
Then, from the southwest corner to the southern end,
[one offers] to those beginning with Dharma and ending with the Pretas;
thereafter, having brought cool water, [one proceeds].
Combined with ghee, it is exceedingly pleasing to the heart.
Having filled eight jars with that [water] and placed them starting from the southwest corner,
he should likewise set down the vessel for the fire-oblation and so forth, filled with sesame seeds.
And he should give a covering and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Cows, land, gold, silver, clothing, fruits, roots,
barley, grain, a house, a chariot, a bed, and a vehicle.
And whatever else is pleasing to the heart within the mind.
One should offer [the food] to the most excellent Brahmins stationed in the south-western corner;
furthermore, one should perform the act of gratification for each of them individually here.
From the [category] beginning with *dharma* and ending with *preta*.
One should perform all this in accordance with the prescribed rules, first considering one's own capacity and wealth; then,
having set aside all the lamps.
Then, let the foremost of the brahmins lead them all away.
Having circumambulated [the stupa] for a long time, he then departed; thus, he became one who observes the practice of eating only at night with self-restraint.
Such was his conduct, endowed with such practices.
One should perform this every day at the beginning of the night.
When completed with supreme devotion throughout the entire month on the full moon day of Kārttika,
that which is performed in this manner is superior even to the world of the gods.
May there be happiness for those dwelling in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Then, having bowed, one should perform such [a rite] once during the month of Āśvayuja, or again on the new moon day, or on the day of the ancestors (the Śrāddha),
or on the full moon day of Kārttika.
And for three days, there shall be a great festival of lamps.
Or else, a single excellent lamp should be offered at the arrival of night on the full moon day of Kārttika,
in the homes of the poor or among the cowherds' settlements.
And in cremation grounds, temples, and shrines.
Whether on a riverbank, within a variegated cave, at a solitary liṅga, or at a sacred tree,
he performed one thousand and eight [offerings].
Having placed [the offerings] in a very beautiful vessel, one hundred or [a lesser number].
Then, having measured with *pala*s, or half-*palas*, or even half of those, or with *māṣaka*s,
or with fourteen [units] measuring half a cubit;
Then, having spread out either a cloth or a thread;
The wise one, having examined it there and honored it with hundreds of women's ornaments, should kindle the fire and offer a most pleasing great wick.
And she would be meritorious, illuminating the world.
If one who is dull-witted does not perform this, how can there be any pacification of that darkness?
Now, regarding the service to cows, Viṣṇu says there [in the Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa, 23.57–61]:
Cows are a purifier and an auspicious blessing; the worlds are established upon cows.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all evil.
Cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and yellow pigment (rocanā)—
these six constituents of the cow are supremely auspicious at all times.
The water from a cow’s horn is meritorious and destroys all sins;
likewise, scratching a cow removes every impurity.
By giving a mouthful of grass to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
for the Gaṅgā dwells here in the sacred place of cows, and nourishment is well known to reside in their dust.
Lakṣmī resides in cow-dung and Dharma in prostration;
one should therefore constantly offer salutations to them.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "O twice-born one, that man who bathes in the *prasravaṇa* (spring) of cows under the asterism Rohiṇī quickly burns away all accumulations of sin; of this there is no doubt."
That man who receives upon his head the water uplifted by the tail of [the cow] as she proceeds along the rivers is liberated from all sins.
He who drinks the stream of milk flowing from the udder of a cow,
or receives it upon his head, is liberated from all sins.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Cows are to be praised, cows are to be worshipped, and cows are to be served constantly.
He who performs a circumambulation of cows standing in a cow-pen [attains great merit]."
By him, the world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, was circumambulated;
likewise,
the sacred thread was made by the sages from the hair arising from his tail.
Having obtained that right horn which was broken in battle and fell to the earth,
and having removed its flesh, one should fill it with water according to the prescribed rite.
This bath has always been performed by sages, gods, and perfected beings;
it destroys misfortune, brings fortune, and increases all auspiciousness.
Oṃ! In forests abounding in grass, water, and other provisions, let the cows—along with their bulls and calves—frolic in delight;
let them pour forth milk and sleep in peace.
They are liberated from the fears of cold, heat, and disease.
One whose self is thoroughly purified should constantly recite this mantra with concentrated mind,
whether walking, standing, sleeping, smelling, eating, playing, or breathing.
The twenty-fifth great mantra has been recited by gods and asuras;
it has been heard, rejoiced in, meditated upon, praised, and worshipped in succession.
Then, from the subterranean realm (rasātala), five auspicious cows emerged:
Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhī, Suśīlā, and Sumanā.
Having taken many jewels, including the Kaustubha and others,
they were circumambulated in due order by all the gods and asuras.
Having been consecrated, worshipped, properly beheld, touched, and saluted,
after some time, those divine wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenus) [vanished].
Honored in the abode of Brahmā and being satisfied, they chose this supreme boon:
birth from the patriarch Dakṣa through Marīci and Kaśyapa.
There is a journey to the world of Śiva and no further birth anywhere;
dwelling in the forest, with grass for a bed, water for drink, and food obtained without possessions.
In a house strewn with snares, there is a bond with both firm and soft cords;
there is abundant fodder and the like, yet at night, a brilliant lamp.
Listening to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas accompanied by lute music,
offering a handful of food according to one's ability, and performing service in the proper sequence.
They never experience the distress of being beaten or reviled even in their dreams,
nor do they ever feel any aversion toward urine or excrement.
The cow-pen should always be cleaned with dry alkaline substances and the like;
in summer, it should be situated under trees, while in winter, it should be in a house provided with cool water and mud.
During the rainy season or the cool winter, in a pleasant, warm, and windless place,
the principal forms of Rudra should be installed along with their attendants in a cow-pen.
All mantras should be recited by practitioners for the purification of the self;
moreover, one should not discharge urine, feces, phlegm, or impurities there.
A woman in her menses, one of a different caste, or an unchaste woman must not be allowed entry;
nor should one treat them with contempt while at water or especially in a cow-pen.
One should not leap over heifers, nor play with them in the vicinity of the cow-pen. One must not walk among cows while wearing sandals or shoes.
At times, one should travel by means of elephants, horses, chariots, and carriages; otherwise, one should proceed on foot, keeping to the right and remaining humble.
Cows that are emaciated or afflicted by illness must be protected with faith, like one's own father or mother,
from the dangers of mountain precipices, lions, bears, cold, and heat.
During a terrible great tumult, a gloomy day, or a national upheaval,
one should give grass to the cows and then cool water.
Likewise: Cows must be protected for one year by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are fully composed, for the sake of pacifying all sins.
Hārīta says: One should let the calf suckle for two months; in the third month, one should milk it from two teats;
and in the fourth month, from three teats, according to the rule and according to its strength.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Āśvayuja, Pauṣa, and Caitra—at all times—one should not take the milk of cows; one should give it all to the calves."
One should not drive a bull against a cow, nor should one oppress a cow with a heavy burden;
this applies especially on the first days of the Yugas, at the end of the Yugas, and during the Ṣaḍaśītimukha periods.
When the sun is moving southward or northward, likewise at both equinoxes,
during all solar transits (saṃkrāntis), and during lunar and solar eclipses;
On the fifteenth, the fourteenth, the twelfth, and the eighth days of each month,
the ritual service for the cows should be performed in due order month by month.
Four *pala*s of salt and eight of ghee,
as well as sixteen of another person's milk, should be given.
Having first considered all thirty-two palas of cool water, as well as the [patient's] digestion, strength, and appetite.
However, for the sake of merit, one should give a daily portion of fodder to a cow unexpectedly;
in the morning, salt is given there, and after that, water.
Then there shall be grass for fodder, food free from meat,
a lamp at night with a lute, and divine stories of ancient lore.
When this is done, the fruit shall be equal to that obtained by giving the earth filled with jewels;
indeed, it shall be equal to the merit gained from the gift of cows or from the protection of cows.
Cows must especially be protected by humans with grass, water, and other necessities;
they should always be given [to others], nourished, guarded, honored, and accepted [as gifts].
In the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"O King, cows should always be saluted with this mantra:
'Homage to the cows, the glorious ones, and to the daughters of Surabhi.'"
Salutations to the purifying daughters of Brahmā; salutations again and again!
By the mere recollection of this mantra, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "And those who, according to their ability, indeed give salt to cows— the worlds of those merit-makers go to the world of Brahmā."
He who, observing the cow-vow, being truthful and peaceful, always gives even a small amount of the best food to cows with devotion before eating himself—
such a wise man gains the merit of a thousand cows.
One whose character is rooted in righteousness shall attain it within a year.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"Having touched a cow, having paid homage, and having performed a circumambulation,
the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated by him."
One should not avoid the bones of cows, nor should one shun the smell of death;
for as long as one smells that odor, for that long one is joined with merit.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "He who does not cause smoke [from incense] in a cow-pen where cows in the form of cattle reside,
is devoured by flies in the Makṣikā hell."
But that lowest of men who, having subdued a cow that has lost its calf, drinks [its milk],
shall remain for a long time afflicted by hunger and beaten.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O lord of the earth, he who creates an obstacle for a herd of cows afflicted by thirst at the edge of water, they call him a slayer of a Brahmin."
Having constructed a large shelter for the sake of cows, capable of withstanding cold winds,
one rescues one's lineage up to the seventh generation, O best of the Bharatas.
Regarding oaths, there is the statement of Surabhi:
"May the milking be done with a *balvaja* grass mat as fodder and in a bronze vessel for him who steals my ill-deeds by means of another's calf."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "That Brāhmaṇa who, though not maintaining the sacred fire, possesses a tawny cow (kapilā) in his cow-pen,
goes to that terrible, impenetrable hell consisting of total darkness."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "A cow born in one's house, even if she has faults, must always be personally maintained;
likewise, a twice-born man, even if he is ill-behaved, is worthy of honor, but never a Śūdra, however well-restrained."
In the winter season, one should diligently construct a shelter for cattle that have no protector;
there, grass, water, and fuel should be provided for the sake of merit.
Now follows the ritual of the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga).
In that regard, Viṣṇu says [86.1–20]:

On the full moon day of Kārttika or Āśvayuja, one should first examine a bull. It should be the calf of a cow that has living calves and is full of milk; it must possess all auspicious marks, be either blue or red, with its face, tail, and feet entirely white, and be the leader of the herd. Then, having strewn sacrificial grass around a well-kindled fire in the midst of the cows, having cooked a *caru* offering for Pūṣan, and having offered oblations with the mantra "May Pūṣan follow our cows; may there be delight here," the blacksmith should brand the bull—on one side with a discus and on the other with a trident. One should bathe it with the four verses beginning with "Golden-hued" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*) and the verse "The goddesses have come to us for help" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*). Having brought the bathed and adorned bull together with four bathed and adorned heifers, one should mutter the Rudra hymns, the *Puruṣasūkta*, and the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses. One should recite the verse "Father of calves" (*pitā vatsānām*) into the right ear of the bull, as well as this [following] verse: *imaṃ ca* (And this): "O Bull, you are the father of calves, the lord of cattle, the protector of the herd. Go forth to the world of the Sun, where the cows abide. *Note: The final verse is traditionally understood as follows:* *vṛṣo 'si tvaṃ vṛṣabho vṛṣoddharaḥ | vṛṣā dyaur vṛṣā pṛthivī vṛṣā viśvam idaṃ jagat ||* *Vṛṣo 'si tvaṃ vṛṣabho vṛṣoddharaḥ | vṛṣā dyaur vṛṣā pṛthivī vṛṣā viśvam idaṃ jagat ||* "You are the bull, the best of bulls, the upholder. The sky is a bull, the earth is a bull, and this entire world is a bull."
For the Blessed One, Dharma, is proclaimed as a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion; may he protect me in every way.
I give this youth to you as a husband; sport with him, your beloved,
and do not be deprived of offspring nor of your own bodies.
O King Soma, may we not be subject to our enemy.
One should have a bull yoked with a heifer placed in the northeastern direction;
one should give the officiating priest a pair of garments, as well as gold and bell-metal.
The blacksmith should be given wages according to his heart's desire;
one should provide food with abundant ghee and feed Brahmins there as well.
