In whatever reservoir a bull, having been let loose, drinks, he may there,
being arrogant, scratch the ground with the tips of his horns wherever he pleases.
Abundant food and drink for the ancestors is thereby presented. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Now, the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) should be performed on the full moon day of Caitra, or especially on that of Kārttika."
Furthermore, it should be performed by members of the three twice-born castes under the asterism Revatī.
The bull, however, was a black-spotted Kṛṣṇasāra, fresh and three years old,

Equipped with all necessary implements and containing every kind of grain, this great [cow] should be released according to the prescribed rite, as demonstrated by the Śruti and Smṛti.
In a region sloping toward the northeast, in a pleasant and secluded forest,
no outsider should enter, nor should anyone anywhere drink its milk.
One should offer libations with the cry "svadhā" to the fathers, the mothers, and the kinsmen—
whosoever belong to the father’s side and whosoever are born of the mother’s side.
Those who were born in the families of one's gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen,
those who have fallen into the state of hungry ghosts (pretas), and others who have been deprived of the śrāddha rite;
Through the ritual release of a bull, they all obtain supreme satisfaction;
one should offer water mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken grains while reciting this mantra.
And having briefly offered a sacrificial fee to the ancestors and to the Brahmins,
they were then filled with joy, accompanied by that bull.
The cows play in the forests during the established rites of *vṛṣotsarga*;
when the *vṛṣotsarga* has not yet commenced, the donor [addresses them] with words of indirect speech (*vakrokti*).
He said to the brahmins: "Whatever has been abandoned by anyone in a secluded place, no other person shall take it away; rather, it should be divided in due order."
"There is no other merit on the surface of the earth than the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).
[From the Matsya Purāṇa, 207.2–41:
"First, one should examine a cow that is well-behaved and endowed with auspicious marks."
One that is free from physical defects, not emaciated, with a living calf, and healthy.
With glossy color, glossy hooves, and likewise glossy horns;
captivating in form, gentle, well-proportioned, and not over-exalted.
She who is endowed with right-turning whorls on the right side, and likewise left-turning whorls on the left, and whose hips are broad; [467]
She whose lips are soft, firm, and copper-colored, whose tongue is red and highly honored,
whose mouth is not too long, and likewise whose tongue is clearly visible and red.

O Lord of the Earth, the wise honor these six elevated parts of cows: the chest, the back, the head, the belly, and the two hips.

one whose shoulders and hump are elevated, and who is adorned with a soft tail.
He has great hips, flanks, and shoulders; his eyes are like lapis lazuli gems;
the tips of his horns are the color of coral; and his tail-hair is very long and seasonal.
One with nine, eight, or ten teeth that are sharp-pointed and beautiful should be accepted even in the home; such a Mallikākṣa bestows wealth and grain.
[468] As for color, a coppery-brown (kapila) is praised for a Brāhmaṇa;
white, red, black, fair (gaura), and even pale-red (pāṭala) are likewise commended.
One whose back has the luster of sapphire, who is brindled, marked with five black spots,
who has broad ears, large shoulders, and smooth hair— such a one [is auspicious].
One that has reddish eyes, is tawny, and has red hooves and a red palate;
one with a white belly and a black back—such a bull is recommended for a Brāhmaṇa.
A glossy red complexion is praised for a Kṣatriya;
one with a golden luster for a Vaiśya; and even a black one for a person of the lowest birth.
He whose horn always extends forward, facing his own mouth,
is the accomplisher of all goals for all social classes alike.
A tawny cat with feet like a cat's and tawny eyes is auspicious;
one that is white with feet like a cat's and eyes resembling jewels is also auspicious.
Karaṭa and Piṅgala, as well as Śvetapāda, he whose feet and head were transparent, and Dvipādaśveta; |||
Fortunate is he who resembles a francolin partridge or likewise a partridge,
and whose face shines white as far as the root of the ears.
He should be known as Nandīmukha, who is especially red in color;
and he whose belly and back are white is the Lord of Cows (Gopati).
That bull-faced one, who constantly increases his lineage and is variegated with jasmine flowers, is a blessed leader of men.
By virtue of one's fortune, it becomes variegated with lotuses and even mandalas;
moreover, that which has the color of an *atasī* flower is considered most auspicious.
These are the fortunate ones; likewise, O King, I shall describe to you those who are unfortunate:
those whose palate, lips, and teeth are black, and those whose horns and nails are rough.
Those with indistinct complexions, those who are short, those resembling the color of tiger's ash,
those with the hue of crows or vultures, and likewise those similar to mice;
Those who were dull-witted, one-eyed, lame, or squint-eyed;
those with uneven white feet, as well as those with wandering eyes.
These bulls must not be released, nor should they be kept in the house;
however, I shall further describe the characteristics of those that are to be released and those that are to be kept.
Their horns were shaped like svastikas, their roars resembled the rumbling of a mass of clouds,
they were of immense size, and they moved with the gait of elephants in rut.
They possessed broad chests, deep breaths, and great strength and prowess;
[they had] heads, ears, foreheads, tails, and feet.
The areas at the sides of the eyes should be black, and at their edges, the luster should be like that of the moon;
other parts are praised as white, but for a black horse, these [black areas] are especially recommended.
A bull with a long and thick tail that drags it along the ground,
which is elevated and dark blue at the front, is highly praised.
Those bulls whose row of hair shines with the luster of spears, banners, and flags are blessed;
they bring about the attainment of wealth and victory.
They turn back to the right, having been turned back by him himself;
with their heads and necks held high, they are blessed, for they increase the herd.
If it should be white in color, with red tips on its horns and eyes,
and hooves resembling coral, there is none more fortunate than that.
These should be maintained with effort, or else released if they are bulls;
whether maintained or released, they increase one's wealth and grain.
One should designate that bull as "Nīla" whose feet, face, and tail are white, while its body has the color of lac-dye.

That bull alone should be released; he should not be kept confined in the house. For this reason, this ancient verse circulates in the world: "A cow that has calved once is sufficient for one man; a second is for the sake of prosperity; a third is for the sake of cattle-wealth; and a fourth is for the sake of dharma. Therefore, one should maintain a single cow for the sake of dharma, but one should not keep many cows for the sake of mere worldly enjoyment. One who maintains many cows out of greed incurs sin. Thus, O King, you should maintain only one cow for the sake of dharma, and you should not maintain many. You should release the bull and let him go. He should not be kept confined in the house. For this purpose, this ancient verse circulates in the world.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or marries a wife who is a Gaurī, or sets free a dark-colored bull.
O King, even if he possesses a bull endowed with auspicious marks, born in his own home or purchased,
a high-souled man does not grieve over death when he has relinquished it.
Therefore, I shall now speak concerning the mind set upon liberation.
In the Āditya Purāṇa,
Bhānu said:
"Those who release a bull that is dark blue and very beautiful..."
With its tail drawn back, its entire body covered in hair, possessing horns, and enchanting to the mind.
He who offers worship on the full moon day of Kārttika is liberated from it, of this there is no doubt;
likewise, one should give cows that are three years old and pregnant, as well as a bull.
There, one should mutter the Sāvitrī and likewise the Aghamarṣaṇa;
one should certainly provide the Karṇajāpya for the bull—of this there is no doubt.
One should offer a bell made of iron, along with auspicious horns and bundles of grass,
and one should feed Brahmins before Rudra according to the prescribed rite.
O Sage, for as many pores as there are on the bull, and for as long as the hairs of the cows remain,
for that many thousands of crores of years one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whatever sin a man oppressed by the struggle for livelihood may commit,
all of those go to destruction through the liberation granted by Gopati.
By the sound of the bull, the ancestors together with the grandfathers are seen suspended in the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt.
By casting his tail into the water, the bull causes the water to rise;
through this, the ancestors are gratified for ten thousand years.
As long as the clay remains on the shore, having been uplifted up to the peak,
the ancestors are satisfied by that mountain consisting of various kinds of food and drink.
And when that bull sports in the midst of the cows,
he indeed sports eternally with a thousand throngs of apsarases.
As long as he sports in the waters with his tail raised,
the ancestors remain ever satisfied along with the hosts of Apsarases.
The satisfaction that the ancestors truly derive from gold given according to the prescribed rite by a thousandfold measure is considered equal to that derived from a bull.
One should desire many sons, so that even one of them might go to Gayā,
or perform the horse sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull.
Śaṅkha says: That bull which is red in color, but white at the mouth and tail,
and white in its hooves and horns, is called a *nīla* bull.
Now follows the procedure for listening to the Purāṇas.
In that regard, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states:
Śatānīka said,
"O Blessed One, by what rule should the *Bhārata* be heard by men?"
The life-story of Rāmabhadra, especially as it appears in the Purāṇas.
O best of Brahmins, please describe how the Vaiṣṇava duties, especially the Śiva duties, and also those of the Sauras are to be practiced; let the procedure for hearing them be told.
Sumantu said:
"Indeed, O lord of the people, having heard the Itihāsas and Purāṇas with devotion, I shall now describe to you the rule for listening to the Purāṇas."
O Lord, he who listens in the evening, in the morning, and likewise at night, having become pure, is liberated from all sins, including the killing of a Brahmin.
Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā and Śaṅkara, are pleased with him;
now hear, O lord of the people, the procedure for the reciter here.
Having come from his dwelling, the Śuddhavāsa [deity] goes to that place which is endowed with the ritual convention;
having then performed a circumambulation, he indeed becomes the deity residing therein.
O King, he spoke not too loudly to all of them without exception, like a teacher;
and after the salutation, he made it audible that "May there be auspiciousness" at the end.
O tiger among men, O lord of the earth, [the dharma] is not [attained] from others by any of the castes:
Vaiśyas are before Śūdras, and Kṣatriyas are before Vaiśyas.
O Brahmins, let these Kṣatriyas always listen while standing before you;
then, O King, the reciter, standing in the midst of them all, shall cause [the text] to be recited.
O King, those men who are of mixed castes are to be placed behind the Śūdras;
one should respectfully recognize a Brāhmaṇa as the reciter, and never one born of another caste.
O King, having heard [the Veda] from one born of another caste as a reciter, one shall go to hell;
for thus it is for those castes who listen to it in its proper sequence.
O King, O delighter of the Kurus, there should be a breaking of the fast month after month;
for the sake of his own welfare, O King, let the ruler worship the reciter.
O best of kings, when the month is complete, a gold māṣaka should be given;
O mighty-armed one, two should be given by a Brāhmaṇa, but by a Kṣatriya, two [gold māṣakas] should be given.
O best of kings, three gold māṣakas must likewise be given by a Vaiśya to the reciter, and four by a Śūdra as well. [475]
O King, at the first breaking of the fast, by honoring the reciter according to one's means,
a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O mighty-armed one, from the month of Kārttika onwards, indeed throughout the month of Kārttika,
[one obtains the merit of] the Agniṣṭoma, Gosava, and likewise the Jyotiṣṭoma, O King.
O Lord, O King, [perform] the Sautrāmaṇi, the Vājapeya, the Vaiṣṇava,
as well as the Māheśvara, the Brāhma, and the Puṇḍarīka sacrifices.
O Indra among kings, one obtains the fruit of the Āditya sacrifice, as well as that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha, in succession over twelve months.
Having thus obtained the fruit of the sacrifice, he goes to the highest worlds;
likewise, O King, when the festival is concluded, one should satisfy [the ancestors] according to one's own ability.
One should honor the reciter and the Brahmins with all desired objects—
divine perfumes, garlands, garments, and ornaments.
One should give [these] to the reciter and then honor the Brahmins with gold,
silver, clothing, and cows with bronze milking vessels.
Having given [this] here to a reciter, one shall obtain the fruit of what has been heard;
by whomsoever the reciter is honored, the deities become pleased with him.
Therefore, the wise know that a gift should always be given to him first—
the twice-born reciter who, endowed with faith, partakes in one's śrāddha.
O King, his ancestors remain satisfied for a hundred years;
[the recitation] is clear, wonderful, peaceful, and likewise possesses distinct syllables and words.
O King, one who is always thoroughly understanding the entire meaning of the text, endowed with the proper intonation and possessed of aesthetic flavor and emotion, [attains the highest state].
O King, let him teach the text and its meaning to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas;
O King, he who teaches in this manner is called a Brāhmaṇa Vyāsa.
One who recites otherwise than this should be known as a "Pitṛ-nāmaka" (one named after the ancestors).
Such a reciter, equal to Vyāsa, may dwell wherever he is thus situated.
O King, among all lands and cities, that land is considered the most excellent;
for it is the fruit obtained by men who bow with devotion to the reciter (vācaka).
O joy of the Kurus, that which is attained by a thousand sacrifices is not equal to this:
on one side are all the planets, and on the other side is the sun alone.
Likewise, O King, all the twice-born on one side and that reciter alone on the other constitute the supreme purifier in rites for the gods and the ancestors.
The reciter, the ascetic, and likewise the Brahmin who knows the six Vedāṅgas—
all these, O best of kings, should be known as purifiers of the row.
One should know that the expressive word is threefold, always distinguished by its qualities;
and the disciple, O mighty-armed one, is likewise threefold, distinguished by his qualities.
Understand these two as they are being described by me as I speak:
[reciting] too quickly, or likewise indistinctly, out of tune, and devoid of proper sentiment.
One who lacks the analysis of word-divisions, is likewise devoid of contemplation,
does not understand the meaning of the text, is fickle, and is bereft of enthusiasm;
O Lord of Men, if a reciter who is prone to anger, speaks unpleasantly, and out of ignorance reviles the text should cause such [a rite] to be recited;
And he who does not perceive these difficulties should be known as the lowest of reciters;
[the recitation] should be clearly articulated, wonderful, peaceful, and likewise with distinct syllables and words.
That reciter who recites a text without understanding its meaning— though it be endowed with the proper musical tones and permeated by aesthetic flavor and emotion— is truly ignorant.
That, O King, should be known as rajasic; now hear about the sattvic, O ruler, as one who understands the entire meaning of the text in its fullness.
O King, he who causes this to be recited according to the rules among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, O Monarch, is to be known by the wise as one of a sattvic nature.
[478] O King, he was devoid of faith and devotion, excessively greedy, a slanderer, devoted to rationalist arguments, and likewise possessed of envy.
O mighty-armed King, a man who listens [to this] should give a sacrificial fee— whether constant, occasional, or for a specific desire— to the reciter.
O King, that human disciple should always be known as one characterized by darkness (tāmasa);
O Hero, a wise person should certainly not recite [the scriptures] in his presence.
But he who listens incidentally, devoid of faith and devotion,
and listens merely out of curiosity, should be known by the wise as one of a rajasic nature.
Having renounced all ritual actions, O King, one who is endowed with devotion and faith should constantly worship the reciter with sincere devotion.
O Hero, he who likewise listens while giving [gifts] for obligatory rites, occasional rites, rites for desired ends, or to a preceptor— he is to be known as a Sāttvika by the wise.
O King, just as Vyāsa is to be honored by the Śrāvakas,
so too, O best of kings, the reciter (vācaka) is to be honored first by the wise, according to the word of Vyāsa.
In times of calamity and in times of prosperity, since he is always the guru,
O hero, at the auspicious time of the third lunar day of the month of Vaiśākha, O radiant one.

On the full moon day of Kārttika and likewise on that of Māgha, he should be worshipped first; O Lord, it is traditionally taught that on these festival days he is to be worshipped in accordance with dharma.
Gold, fine gold, wealth, and likewise grain,
as well as cooked food and meat, O joy of the Kurus.
[479] First, the disciples should offer everything with all their devotion to him—
having given flowers, fruits, water, leaves, and even fuel.
Whatever else is essential, that too should be given to him from all sides;
furthermore, O King, all the disciples should likewise perform worship.
O lord of men, O fair-faced one, you should act in such a way that the speaker may always abide in happiness and is not afflicted by the pairs of opposites.
O best of men, in the winter one should give a woolen cloak, and in the rainy season an umbrella;
at the appropriate time, one should indeed give sandals that are soft and covered in wool.
O sinless one, when he is unable to give even a *māṣaka* of gold,
then he should give silver for his own welfare.
In the absence of that, however, one should give gold, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
for even earth should be given by one who makes his learning bear fruit.

Thus has this perpetual [pūjā] been described; it should take place month after month. But on special occasions, O King, such as during eclipses and other festival days, it becomes occasional (naimittikī).
O King, at the conclusion of the festival, one who desires prosperity should give two garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments, O Lord.
Having recognized the conclusion of a festival day, a wise person should worship the reciter;
even by selling oneself, one should desire that the sacred learning be made fruitful.
O dear one, for him who does not give the occasional or regular sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
his learning is always fruitless, even though he hears it.
"O King, O Lord, that sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) which is always fourfold,
O Lord, is prescribed when the festival is completed," thus spoke the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Thus, O King, has this rule for listening to the Purāṇas been declared.

Thus ends [the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsaṃdhivigrahika*) of the illustrious Govindacandradeva, the supreme king of great kings (*mahārājādhirāja*).
The section on rites to be performed at fixed times is completed.
